steps.practice: Match 5 verdicts like WA, TLE, MLE and RE to the most likely bug for each.
steps.detail: Each verdict points somewhere. TLE means complexity or an infinite loop, RE means bounds or division by 0, and WA on test 1 means the sample logic is wrong.
steps.proof: A list pairing each verdict with its 2 most likely causes.
steps.pitfall: Treating every failure as wrong logic.

problems.prompt: RE on test 5. Two likely causes?
problems.answer: Out of bounds access or division by 0.

problems.prompt: TLE on large tests only. Likely cause?
problems.answer: Too high complexity for the largest n.

problems.prompt: MLE with a 10^5 by 10^5 array. Fix?
problems.answer: Use an adjacency list or a smaller structure.

steps.title: Debug Under a Clock
steps.mastery: Set a time box for debugging and switch problems when it runs out.
steps.practice: During a mock contest, give each bug 15 minutes, then move on and come back later.
steps.detail: Debugging without a limit can eat a whole contest. A time box forces you to bank other points, and a fresh look later often finds the bug fast.
steps.proof: A contest log showing each debugging session and its time.
steps.pitfall: Staring at the same code for 60 minutes without a new test.

problems.prompt: You have 40 minutes left and 1 buggy problem plus 1 untouched easy one. What first?
After 15 minutes on a bug with no progress, what should you try?
problems.answer: Write a brute force and stress test, or move on.

problems.prompt: Why does a 10 minute break help find a bug?
problems.answer: You reread the code fresh instead of seeing what you meant.

steps.title: Graph Representation
steps.mastery: Store a graph as an adjacency list.
steps.practice: Build an adjacency list for 6 nodes and 7 undirected edges, and print the neighbors of node 3.
steps.detail: An adjacency list stores each node with its neighbors, using O(n + m) memory. A matrix needs n^2, which fails for n = 10^5.
steps.proof: Each edge appears in both lists, 14 entries in all.
steps.pitfall: Adding each undirected edge in only one direction.

problems.prompt: Memory for an adjacency matrix with n = 10^5?
Undirected edges (1, 2), (2, 3). Neighbors of 2?
A graph has 10^5 nodes and 2 x 10^5 edges. Which storage?

steps.title: Count Components With DFS
steps.mastery: Find connected components with depth first search.
steps.practice: Count the connected components of a graph with 8 nodes and edges (1, 2), (2, 3), (4, 5), (6, 7).
steps.detail: Start a DFS from each unvisited node and mark everything it reaches. The number of DFS starts is the number of components.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting isolated nodes with no edges.

problems.prompt: 5 nodes, no edges. Components?
Edges (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1) on 3 nodes. Components?
Why might recursive DFS crash on a path of 10^5 nodes?
problems.answer: Recursion depth can overflow the stack.

steps.title: Shortest Paths With BFS
steps.mastery: Find shortest path lengths in an unweighted graph with a queue.
steps.practice: Find the shortest distance from cell (0, 0) to (4, 4) in a 5 by 5 grid with walls using BFS.
steps.detail: BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches a node is along a shortest path. Grids are graphs where each cell links to up to 4 neighbors.
steps.proof: The BFS distance matches a hand count of the shortest route.
steps.pitfall: Using DFS for shortest paths, which finds a path but not the shortest.

problems.prompt: Open 3 by 3 grid. Shortest steps from corner to opposite corner?
Why does BFS give shortest paths when every edge has weight 1?
problems.answer: It visits nodes in increasing distance.

problems.prompt: Complexity of BFS on n nodes and m edges?

steps.title: Flood Fill a Grid
steps.mastery: Mark connected regions of a grid with DFS or BFS.
steps.practice: Count the islands of # cells in a 6 by 8 grid using flood fill with 4 neighbors.
steps.detail: Flood fill is DFS on a grid. Each new unvisited # cell starts an island, and the fill marks the whole island. Check bounds before reading a neighbor.
steps.proof: The island count matches a careful hand count.
steps.pitfall: Reading grid cells outside the bounds.

problems.prompt: Grid rows "#.#" and "#.#". Islands with 4 neighbors?
Same grid with 8 neighbors?
A diagonal line of 5 # cells in a 5 by 5 grid: how many islands using 4 neighbors, and using 8?

steps.title: Detect Cycles
steps.mastery: Find a cycle in a graph with DFS colors.
steps.practice: Detect a cycle in the directed graph 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1, 3 to 4 using white, gray and black marks.
steps.detail: In a directed graph, reaching a gray node, one still on the current path, means a cycle. In an undirected graph, reaching a visited node other than the parent means a cycle.
steps.proof: The cycle 1, 2, 3 is found when 3 reaches gray node 1.
steps.pitfall: Treating any visited node as a cycle in a directed graph.

problems.prompt: Undirected edges (1, 2), (2, 3). Is there a cycle?
In the directed graph 1 to 2, 1 to 3, 2 to 3, does DFS ever reach a gray node?
problems.answer: No, so it has no cycle.

problems.prompt: Undirected tree with 10 nodes. How many edges?

steps.title: Dijkstra With a Heap
steps.mastery: Find shortest paths from 1 source when all weights are nonnegative.
steps.practice: Run Dijkstra by hand from node 1 on a 5 node graph with 7 weighted edges, recording each pop from the heap.
steps.detail: Pop the closest unfinished node and relax its edges. A min heap makes each pop O(log n), for O((n + m) log n) total. Skip stale heap entries whose distance is outdated.
steps.proof: Distances to all 5 nodes, with the pop order written down.
steps.pitfall: Processing a stale heap entry that has a larger distance than the stored one.

problems.prompt: Complexity of Dijkstra with a heap on n nodes and m edges?
Edges 1 to 2 weight 4, 1 to 3 weight 1, 3 to 2 weight 2. Distance to 2?
Why must weights be at least 0 for Dijkstra?
problems.answer: A negative edge could lower a distance after its node was finished.

steps.title: Negative Weights
steps.mastery: Use Bellman-Ford when edges can be negative and detect negative cycles.
steps.practice: Run Bellman-Ford on a 4 node graph with 1 negative edge, doing 3 rounds of relaxing every edge.
steps.detail: Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge n - 1 times in O(nm). If a round n still improves a distance, there is a negative cycle reachable from the source.
steps.proof: Correct distances after 3 rounds and no change in round 4.
steps.pitfall: Using Dijkstra on a graph with negative edges.

problems.prompt: How many rounds does Bellman-Ford need for 6 nodes?
A 6th round still lowers a distance in a 6 node graph. What does it show?
Complexity of Bellman-Ford with 10^3 nodes and 10^4 edges?

steps.title: All Pairs With Floyd
steps.mastery: Compute all pairs shortest paths for small graphs.
steps.practice: Run Floyd-Warshall on a 4 node graph and print the full 4 by 4 distance matrix.
steps.detail: For each middle node k, try every pair i, j through k. Three nested loops give O(n^3), fine for n up to about 400.
steps.proof: A 4 by 4 matrix matching hand checks.
steps.pitfall: Putting the k loop inside instead of outside.

problems.prompt: Complexity of Floyd-Warshall for n = 400?
Of the 3 nested loops, which must be outermost?
problems.answer: The k loop over middle nodes.

problems.prompt: Is Floyd-Warshall fine for n = 2000?

steps.title: 0-1 BFS
steps.mastery: Use a deque for graphs whose weights are only 0 or 1.
steps.practice: Find the fewest walls to break from corner to corner of a 5 by 5 grid, where open cells cost 0 and walls cost 1.
steps.detail: Push 0 weight moves to the front of a deque and 1 weight moves to the back. It runs in O(n + m), faster than Dijkstra for this special case.
steps.proof: The fewest walls broken, matching a Dijkstra check.
steps.pitfall: Using a plain queue, which gives wrong answers with 0 weight edges.

problems.prompt: In 0-1 BFS, where does a 0 weight move go?
problems.answer: To the front of the deque.

problems.prompt: Complexity of 0-1 BFS on a 1000 by 1000 grid?
A move of weight 1 from distance 3. New distance?

steps.title: Build the Hidden Graph
steps.mastery: Turn a problem with states into a graph and run a shortest path on it.
steps.practice: Model a USACO problem where each node is a (cell, key held) pair and run Dijkstra over 2 x 10^5 states.
steps.detail: Many Gold problems hide the graph. A state with extra information, like keys or time mod k, becomes a node, and transitions become edges.
steps.proof: A state graph with the node count computed and the answer found.
steps.pitfall: Running shortest paths on cells alone when the state needs more.

problems.prompt: A grid of 100 by 100 cells and 4 key states. Nodes in the state graph?
Time matters mod 3 on a 1000 node graph. How many states?
Why make the state (cell, key) instead of the cell alone in a 100 by 100 grid?
problems.answer: The same cell can be reached with or without the key, giving 2 different futures.

steps.title: Name the State
steps.mastery: Write what dp[i] means in 1 precise sentence before coding.
steps.practice: Write the state, transition and base case for counting ways to climb 30 stairs taking 1, 2 or 3 steps.
steps.detail: dp[i] is the number of ways to reach stair i. It comes from dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2] + dp[i - 3], with dp[0] = 1. A vague state is where most dynamic programming bugs start.
steps.proof: dp[i] = ways to reach stair i, with dp[0] = 1 and dp[30] = 53,798,080.
steps.pitfall: Coding a table before saying in words what each cell means.

problems.prompt: With steps of 1 or 2, what is dp[4] if dp[0] = 1?
With steps of 1, 2 or 3, find dp[5] from dp[0] = 1.
Climbing 6 stairs with steps of 2 or 3 only. How many ways?

steps.title: Knapsack Table
steps.mastery: Fill a 0/1 knapsack table of best value for each capacity.
steps.practice: Solve 0/1 knapsack with capacity 10 and items (5, 10), (4, 40), (6, 30), (3, 50) using a 1D table looped backward.
steps.detail: dp[c] is the best value with capacity c. Looping c from high to low keeps each item used at most once. Looping forward would allow reuse, which is the unbounded version.
steps.proof: The best value is 90, from items (4, 40) and (3, 50).
steps.pitfall: Looping capacity forward and using an item twice.

problems.prompt: Capacity 5, items (2, 3), (3, 4). Best value?
Why loop capacity downward in 0/1 knapsack?
problems.answer: So each of the 4 items is counted at most once.

problems.prompt: A bag holds weight 7. Which of (3, 4), (4, 5), (2, 3) do you pack for the most value?

steps.title: Grid Path DP
steps.mastery: Count or optimize paths in a grid one cell at a time.
steps.practice: Count paths from the top left to the bottom right of a 4 by 4 grid with 2 blocked cells, moving right or down.
steps.detail: Each cell gets the sum of the cell above and the cell to the left, and blocked cells get 0. Filling row by row keeps every dependency ready.
steps.proof: The count matches a careful fill of all 16 cells.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to zero the blocked cells.

problems.prompt: Paths in an open 3 by 3 grid, right and down moves only?
A 2 by 3 grid with no blocks. Paths from corner to corner?
Max sum path from top left to bottom right in [[1, 3], [2, 5]]?

steps.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
steps.mastery: Find the longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n).
steps.practice: Find the LIS length of 3, 10, 2, 1, 20, 4, 6, 7 with the tails array and binary search.
steps.detail: tails[k] holds the smallest possible end of an increasing run of length k + 1. Each number replaces the first tail at least as big, so the array length is the answer.
steps.proof: Length 4, for example 2, 4, 6, 7.
steps.pitfall: Using the O(n^2) version when n is 10^5.

problems.prompt: LIS length of 1, 2, 3?
LIS length of 5, 4, 3, 2?

steps.title: Bitmask DP
steps.mastery: Use a bitmask as the state to handle subsets of up to about 20 items.
steps.practice: Solve a 12 city travelling salesman problem with dp[mask][last] storing the best cost.
steps.detail: With 12 cities there are 4096 masks and 12 ends, about 50,000 states, each tried with 12 next cities. Bitmask DP works when n is around 20 or less.
steps.proof: An O(2^n n^2) solution that finds the best tour.
steps.pitfall: Trying bitmask DP with n = 40, which has 10^12 masks.

problems.prompt: How many masks for 12 items?
States in dp[mask][last] for n = 15?
Is 2^n x n^2 fine for n = 20?
problems.answer: About 4 x 10^8. Borderline, often fine in C++.

steps.title: Union and Find
steps.mastery: Merge groups and check membership with a parent array.
steps.practice: Code union-find for 10 nodes and process unions (1, 2), (3, 4), (2, 4), then check if 1 and 3 are connected.
steps.detail: Each node points to a parent, and the root names the group. Find follows parents to the root, and union links one root under the other.
steps.proof: 1 and 3 are connected after the 3 unions.
steps.pitfall: Linking the nodes themselves instead of their roots.

problems.prompt: Parent array [0, 0, 1, 2]. Root of node 3?
After union(1, 2) and union(3, 4), how many groups among 1 to 4?
After also union(2, 3)?

steps.title: Path Compression
steps.mastery: Speed up find by pointing every node on the path straight at the root.
steps.practice: Add path compression to find, then trace the parent array after find(5) on a chain 5 to 4 to 3 to 2 to 1.
steps.detail: Path compression flattens the tree as you search. With union by size or rank, each operation is almost constant time, even for 10^6 operations.
steps.proof: After find(5), nodes 5, 4, 3 and 2 all point to 1.
steps.pitfall: Writing find so deep recursion overflows on long chains.

problems.prompt: Chain 4 to 3 to 2 to 1. Parents after find(4) with compression?
What does union by size do when merging trees of size 3 and 7?
problems.answer: Attaches the size 3 tree under the root of the size 7 tree.

problems.prompt: Rough cost of 10^6 operations with both tricks?

steps.title: Count Groups
steps.mastery: Track the number of components as unions happen.
steps.practice: Start with 8 separate nodes and print the group count after each of 5 unions, including 1 redundant union.
steps.detail: Each union of 2 different roots lowers the count by 1. A union inside one group changes nothing, and detecting it is how DSU finds cycles.
steps.proof: Counts 7, 6, 5, 5, 4 with the 4th union redundant.
steps.pitfall: Lowering the count even when both nodes were already joined.

problems.prompt: 6 nodes and 2 successful unions. Groups?
A union joins 2 nodes already in 1 group. What does that reveal in a graph?
n nodes, how many successful unions make 1 group?

steps.title: Kruskal With DSU
steps.mastery: Build a minimum spanning tree by adding the cheapest edges that join groups.
steps.practice: Find the minimum spanning tree of 5 nodes and 7 weighted edges using Kruskal with union-find.
steps.detail: Sort edges by weight and add each edge whose ends are in different groups. DSU makes that check fast, so Kruskal runs in O(m log m).
steps.proof: The MST weight matches a check by hand.
steps.pitfall: Adding an edge whose ends are already connected, which makes a cycle.

problems.prompt: How many edges in a spanning tree of 5 nodes?
Complexity of Kruskal on m edges?
problems.answer: O(m log m) for the sort.

steps.title: Offline Connectivity
steps.mastery: Answer connectivity queries by sorting them with the edges.
steps.practice: Answer 5 queries asking if 2 nodes connect using only edges of weight at most k, by sorting edges and queries by weight.
steps.detail: Process queries in order of k and add edges as their weight comes up. DSU answers each query in near constant time. This trick shows up in USACO Silver and Gold.
steps.proof: All 5 queries answered in 1 sweep.
steps.pitfall: Rebuilding the DSU from scratch for every query.

problems.prompt: Edges sorted by weight 1, 3, 5. Query k = 4. Which edges are added?
Why sort the 5 queries by k?
problems.answer: So edges are only ever added, never removed.

problems.prompt: q = 10^5 queries rebuilt from scratch with m = 10^5 edges. Total work?

steps.title: Max Flow Basics
steps.mastery: Find the maximum flow from source to sink with augmenting paths.
steps.practice: Find the max flow in a 6 node network with 9 capacitated edges by hand, using 3 augmenting paths.
steps.detail: Push flow along any path with spare capacity, and allow pushing back along used edges through residual edges. Stop when no path remains.
steps.proof: The max flow found, with the 3 paths written down.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring reverse residual edges and getting stuck below the max.

problems.prompt: Single edge from s to t with capacity 7. Max flow?
2 parallel paths s to a to t with capacities 3 and 5, and s to b to t with 4 and 2. Max flow?
Why add a reverse edge with capacity 0 for each edge?
problems.answer: So later paths can undo flow sent earlier.

steps.title: Min Cut
steps.mastery: Find the smallest set of edges that separates source from sink.
steps.practice: Find the min cut of the 6 node network from the max flow by listing edges from reached to unreached nodes.
steps.detail: Max flow equals min cut. After the last search, the nodes reachable from the source form one side, and the saturated edges leaving it are the cut.
steps.proof: The cut capacity equals the max flow.
steps.pitfall: Listing edges going backward across the cut.

problems.prompt: Max flow is 12. Min cut capacity?
Cut s to t with edges 3, 4 and 7 crossing forward. Its capacity?
A network has min cut 5. Can the max flow be 6?

steps.title: Bipartite Matching
steps.mastery: Match 2 groups so each item is used at most once.
steps.practice: Match 5 workers to 5 jobs they can do using augmenting paths, then report the matching size.
steps.detail: Add a source to all workers and all jobs to a sink, each edge with capacity 1. The max flow is the max matching.
steps.proof: A matching of the largest size, with pairs listed.
steps.pitfall: Assigning greedily and stopping when a worker has no free job.

problems.prompt: If 3 workers can only do job 1, how many get matched?
Workers A: jobs 1, 2. B: job 1. Max matching?
Complexity of simple augmenting paths for 500 workers and 10^4 edges?

steps.title: Spot the Reduction
steps.mastery: Recognize problems that turn into flow or matching.
steps.practice: Model 3 assignment problems from Codeforces as a flow network, drawing source, sink and capacities.
steps.detail: Assigning, covering or separating things often reduces to flow. The work is in the drawing: what is a node, what is an edge and what limits each one.
steps.proof: 3 networks drawn and checked against their solutions.
steps.pitfall: Trying greedy on a problem that is really matching.

problems.prompt: Seats and students with preferences. Which model?
Fewest roads to remove to disconnect 2 cities. Which model?
problems.answer: Min cut with capacity 1 per road.

problems.prompt: Each task needs 2 of 5 machines and each machine has capacity 3. Which model?
problems.answer: Flow with task capacities 2 and machine capacities 3.

steps.title: Faster Flow
steps.mastery: Use Dinic when simple augmenting paths are too slow.
steps.practice: Code Dinic with BFS levels and DFS blocking flow, then test it on a network of 1000 nodes and 10^4 edges.
steps.detail: Dinic finds shortest augmenting paths in phases, which is much faster in practice. On unit networks like matching it runs in O(E sqrt(V)).
steps.proof: Dinic matches a slower algorithm on random tests and runs far faster.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to reset the per node edge pointer each phase.

problems.prompt: Dinic matching on 10^4 edges and 10^3 nodes. Rough cost?
What does the BFS in Dinic compute?
problems.answer: Levels, the distance of each node from the source.

problems.prompt: Why keep an edge pointer per node in the DFS?
problems.answer: To skip edges already found useless in this phase.

steps.title: Combine Techniques
steps.mastery: Solve problems that need 2 or more advanced techniques together.
steps.practice: Solve a USACO Gold problem that combines sorting with DSU, writing the plan in 3 lines before coding.
steps.detail: Gold problems stack ideas. A short written plan, like sort edges, add with DSU, answer queries offline, keeps the pieces in order.
steps.proof: An accepted solution with its 3 line plan.
steps.pitfall: Coding the first idea before seeing that a second is needed.

problems.prompt: Edges added by weight plus connectivity queries. Which 2 tools?
Shortest paths where state includes time mod 2. Which 2 ideas?
Counting paths in a DAG of 10^5 nodes. Which 2 ideas?

steps.title: Topological Order
steps.mastery: Order a DAG graph so every edge points forward, then run DP along it.
steps.practice: Find a topological order of 6 tasks with 7 prerequisites using Kahn algorithm and in degrees.
steps.detail: Remove nodes with in degree 0 one at a time. If nodes remain, there is a cycle. DP on a DAG follows this order so every dependency is done first.
steps.proof: A valid order of all 6 tasks.
steps.pitfall: Running DP in input order on a graph that is not sorted.

problems.prompt: Edges 1 to 2, 1 to 3, 3 to 2. A topological order?
After Kahn finishes, 2 nodes are never removed. What does that mean?
Longest path in the DAG 1 to 2 to 4 and 1 to 3 to 4 with weights 1, 5, 2, 2?

steps.title: Gold Contest Pacing
steps.mastery: Spend 4 hours on 3 Gold problems with partial credit in mind.
steps.practice: Sit a full USACO Gold contest and submit a slower subtask solution on any problem you cannot finish.
steps.detail: Gold partial credit often comes from an O(n^2) solution passing small tests. Securing those points first makes the full solve a bonus.
steps.proof: A contest log with each submission and its test results.
steps.pitfall: Holding back submissions until the perfect solution is ready.

problems.prompt: An O(n^2) solution passes 5 of 15 tests. Points out of 333?
Promotion to Platinum needs about what score?
problems.answer: A cutoff set by USACO each contest, often around 700 to 800.

problems.prompt: 4 hours and 3 problems. Planning time per problem after reading?

steps.title: Study Editorials Deeply
steps.mastery: Learn the key idea behind each Gold problem you missed.
steps.practice: Write 1 paragraph per missed USACO Gold problem on what idea the editorial used and how you could have found it.
steps.detail: The goal is to see the idea next time, not just to know the answer. Asking how you could have found it trains the recognition Gold needs.
steps.proof: A paragraph for each of 3 missed problems.
steps.pitfall: Copying editorial code without understanding why it works.

problems.prompt: The trick was binary search on the answer. What clue in the statement hinted at it?
problems.answer: Asking for the smallest value that makes something possible.

problems.prompt: The editorial used DSU in reverse. When is reversing time useful?
problems.answer: When the problem deletes edges, since DSU only adds.

problems.prompt: A Gold contest has 3 problems and you missed 2. How many should you review?

steps.title: Practice Gold Topics
steps.mastery: Rotate through the core Gold topics each week.
steps.practice: Plan 4 weeks covering DP, shortest paths, DSU and segment trees, with 3 USACO Gold problems per topic.
steps.detail: Rotating topics keeps every tool sharp. The USACO Guide groups Gold problems by topic, which makes picking practice simple.
steps.proof: A 4 week plan with 12 problems chosen.
steps.pitfall: Only practicing the topic you already like.

problems.prompt: 4 topics with 3 problems each. Total problems?
Name 4 core Gold topics.
problems.answer: DP, shortest paths, DSU and segment trees.

problems.prompt: You keep missing DP problems. How should the plan change?
problems.answer: Add 2 extra DP problems per week.

steps.title: Take the Best Now
steps.mastery: Make the locally best choice and argue it stays optimal.
steps.practice: Give change for 87 cents with the fewest US coins by always taking the largest coin that fits.
steps.detail: Greedy works for US coins because each coin value fits well with the ones below it. It fails for coins like 1, 3 and 4, so the argument matters more than the code.
steps.proof: 3 quarters, 1 dime, 2 pennies: 6 coins.
steps.pitfall: Trusting greedy on coin systems where it fails.

problems.prompt: Fewest US coins for 30 cents?
Coins 1, 3, 4. Greedy for 6?
Fewest coins for 63 cents in US coins?

steps.title: Exchange Argument
steps.mastery: Prove a greedy order is best by swapping 2 neighbors.
steps.practice: Prove that sorting jobs by shortest time first minimizes total waiting time for times 3, 1, 2.
steps.detail: If a longer job comes just before a shorter one, swapping them lowers the total. So the best order has no such pair, which means sorted order. This is the exchange argument.
steps.proof: Order 1, 2, 3 gives total waiting time 0 + 1 + 3 = 4.
steps.pitfall: Claiming the greedy is optimal because it passes the samples.

problems.prompt: Jobs 5 and 2. Which first to minimize total completion time?
Total completion time for jobs in order 1, 2, 3?
How much worse is running 3, 2, 1 than 1, 2, 3 in total completion time?

steps.title: Interval Greedy
steps.mastery: Choose intervals by earliest end to fit the most.
steps.practice: Pick the most non overlapping meetings from [1, 4], [3, 5], [0, 6], [5, 7], [8, 9] by earliest end.
steps.detail: The interval that ends first leaves the most room for the rest. Sorting by end and taking each compatible interval is optimal by an exchange argument.
steps.pitfall: Picking the shortest interval first, which can block 2 others.

problems.prompt: Meetings [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]. Most that fit if touching ends are allowed?
Meetings [1, 5], [2, 3], [4, 6]. Most non overlapping?
Fewest points to stab [1, 3], [2, 5], [6, 8]?

steps.title: Greedy With a Heap
steps.mastery: Use a priority queue to always grab the current best item.
steps.practice: Combine 6 ropes of lengths 4, 3, 2, 6, 5, 1 with the least total cost, always joining the 2 shortest.
steps.detail: A min heap gives the 2 shortest in O(log n). This is Huffman style merging, and the greedy is optimal because short ropes should be counted most often.
steps.pitfall: Joining ropes in input order instead of shortest first.

problems.prompt: Ropes 1, 2, 3. Least total cost?
Joining 4 ropes of length 2, what is the cheapest total cost?
Complexity with a heap for 10^5 ropes?

steps.title: Spot When Greedy Fails
steps.mastery: Find counterexamples that show a greedy is wrong.
steps.practice: Find a counterexample for greedy 0/1 knapsack by best value per weight with capacity 10.
steps.detail: Testing a greedy against brute force on small random cases finds counterexamples quickly. When one appears, the problem likely needs dynamic programming.
steps.proof: Items (6, 30), (5, 20), (5, 20): greedy takes 30, best is 40.
steps.pitfall: Submitting an unproven greedy and learning it is wrong on test 15.

problems.prompt: Coins 1, 5, 6, 9. Does greedy give the fewest for 11?
How do you test a greedy on inputs of size 8 quickly?
problems.answer: Compare with brute force on many small random inputs.

problems.prompt: Fractional knapsack with 3 items: is greedy by value per weight correct?
problems.answer: Yes, because items can be split.

steps.title: Fast Input in C++
steps.mastery: Read large inputs quickly by turning off stream syncing.
steps.practice: Add ios::sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr) to a C++ template, then time reading 10^6 integers with and without it.
steps.detail: By default C++ streams stay in sync with C stdio, which makes cin slow. Turning that off can make reading a million numbers 5 to 10 times faster, which matters when the time limit is 1 or 2 seconds.
steps.proof: Two timings, with the fast version clearly quicker.
steps.pitfall: Mixing scanf and cin after turning off sync, which scrambles the input.

problems.prompt: Which line unties cin from cout in C++?
Why should you not mix scanf with cin after sync_with_stdio(false)?
problems.answer: The 2 buffers are separate, so input can be read out of order.

problems.prompt: Reading 2 x 10^5 lines with slow cin takes 0.8 s on a 1 s limit. What is the risk?
problems.answer: Time limit exceeded once the algorithm adds its own time.

steps.title: Fast Input in Python
steps.mastery: Read all input at once in Python instead of calling input() per line.
steps.practice: Rewrite a Python solution to use sys.stdin.buffer.read().split(), then time it on 2 x 10^5 numbers.
steps.detail: Calling input() for every line is slow in Python. Reading the whole input in one call and splitting it into tokens is often the difference between passing and timing out on USACO and Codeforces.
steps.proof: A token based reader that handles 2 x 10^5 numbers well under 1 second.
steps.pitfall: Calling input() inside a loop of 10^5 iterations.

problems.prompt: What does sys.stdin.buffer.read().split() return?
problems.answer: A list of byte strings, one per token.

problems.prompt: Convert the token list data to integers in 1 line.
Your Python reads n = 10^6 lines with input() and times out. Name 2 fixes.
problems.answer: Read all input at once and build output with join instead of print per line.

steps.title: Print Without Flushing
steps.mastery: Build output in a buffer and print it once.
steps.practice: Change a solution that prints 10^5 lines with endl so it uses \n, then measure the speedup.
steps.detail: endl flushes the output every time, which is slow. Using \n and letting the buffer flush at the end, or joining lines in Python, removes most of the output cost.
steps.proof: Output with \n that runs noticeably faster.
steps.pitfall: Using endl in a loop with 10^5 lines.

problems.prompt: In C++, what is the difference between endl and \n?
In Python, how do you print a list ans of 10^5 numbers on separate lines fast?
An interactive problem needs flushing. Should you still avoid flushes?
problems.answer: No. Interactive problems need a flush after each query.

steps.title: A Reusable Template
steps.mastery: Keep one tested template with fast I/O and common helpers.
steps.practice: Write a C++ or Python template with fast I/O, a 64 bit integer type and a test case loop for T cases.
steps.detail: Contests waste minutes when you rewrite boilerplate. A template you have tested many times removes setup errors and lets you start on the problem in seconds.
steps.proof: A template that reads T test cases and prints answers fast.
steps.pitfall: Copying a template from someone else without testing it yourself.

problems.prompt: Which C++ type holds values up to 9 x 10^18?
Your template reads T test cases. What loop do you write in C++?
problems.answer: int T; cin >> T; while (T--) solve();

problems.prompt: Why reset global arrays between 2 test cases?
problems.answer: Values from the last case would leak into the next one.

steps.title: Read Tricky Formats
steps.mastery: Parse inputs with blank lines, strings and grids correctly.
steps.practice: Parse a USACO input with an N by M grid of characters and 3 queries per line into the right arrays.
steps.detail: Many wrong answers come from reading input wrong. Grids are read row by row as strings, and reading tokens instead of lines handles stray blank lines.
steps.proof: Grid and queries parsed and printed back correctly.
steps.pitfall: Reading a grid row with cin >> char and skipping spaces you needed.

problems.prompt: How do you read a line with spaces in C++?
A grid has 5 rows of 8 characters. How do you store it?
problems.answer: An array of 5 strings, each of length 8.

problems.prompt: After cin >> n, why might getline return an empty string?
problems.answer: The newline after n is still in the buffer.

steps.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
steps.mastery: Find all primes up to n quickly by crossing out multiples.
steps.practice: Sieve the primes up to 100 and count them, then time a sieve up to 10^7.
steps.detail: Cross out multiples of each prime starting from its square. The sieve runs in O(n log log n), fast enough for 10^7.
steps.proof: 25 primes up to 100.
steps.pitfall: Starting each crossing at 2p instead of p^2, which wastes time.

problems.prompt: How many primes are below 30?
Smallest multiple of 7 that the sieve crosses for 7?
Memory for a sieve to 10^7 with 1 byte per number?

steps.title: Fast Exponentiation
steps.mastery: Compute a^b mod m in O(log b) by repeated squaring.
steps.practice: Compute 3^13 mod 1000 by binary exponentiation, writing each square and multiply step.
steps.detail: 13 is 1101 in binary, so 3^13 = 3^8 x 3^4 x 3^1. Squaring gives each power of 2 in turn, using about 2 log b multiplications.
steps.proof: 3^13 = 1,594,323, so the result is 323.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying b times, which is too slow when b is 10^18.

problems.prompt: Multiplications to compute a^(10^18) by squaring?

steps.title: Modular Inverse
steps.mastery: Divide under a prime modulus by multiplying by the inverse.
steps.practice: Compute the inverse of 3 mod 10^9 + 7 with Fermat as 3^(10^9 + 5), then check 3 times it is 1.
steps.detail: For a prime p, a^(p - 2) is the inverse of a. This lets you divide in formulas like n choose k under a modulus.
steps.proof: The inverse is 333333336.
steps.pitfall: Dividing normally inside a modular formula.

problems.prompt: Inverse of 2 mod 7?
Inverse of 3 mod 11?
Why does Fermat inversion need a prime modulus?
problems.answer: a^(p - 1) = 1 mod p holds for prime p and a not divisible by p.

steps.title: Binomials Under a Mod
steps.mastery: Compute C(n, k) mod p with factorial and inverse factorial tables.
steps.practice: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to 10^6 mod 10^9 + 7, then answer C(10, 3) and C(10^6, 500).
steps.detail: C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n - k)!). With precomputed tables each query is 2 multiplications, after O(n) setup.
steps.proof: C(10, 3) = 120 and C(10^6, 500) computed instantly.
steps.pitfall: Recomputing factorials for every query.

problems.prompt: Compute C(5, 2).
Setup cost for tables up to 10^6?

steps.title: GCD and LCM
steps.mastery: Use Euclid for gcd and gcd for lcm without overflow.
steps.practice: Compute gcd(462, 1071) by Euclid and lcm(12, 18) as 12 / gcd x 18.
steps.detail: Euclid replaces (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b is 0. Dividing before multiplying in the lcm keeps the numbers small enough for 64 bits.
steps.proof: gcd 21 and lcm 36.
steps.pitfall: Computing a x b / gcd and overflowing on large inputs.

problems.prompt: gcd(F(20), F(15)) for Fibonacci numbers?

steps.title: Advanced Data Structures
steps.mastery: Use segment trees with lazy tags, merge sort trees and sparse tables fluently.
steps.practice: Solve 2 USACO Platinum problems that need a segment tree with lazy propagation.
steps.detail: Platinum assumes Gold structures are automatic. Practice until you can write a lazy segment tree in 10 minutes without looking.
steps.proof: 2 problems accepted with a lazy segment tree written from memory.
steps.pitfall: Copying a structure without being able to change its combine step.

problems.prompt: Sparse table query time for range minimum on 10^5 values?
problems.answer: O(1) after O(n log n) setup.

problems.prompt: Can a sparse table handle 10^5 point updates?
Time to build a sparse table for 10^5 elements?

steps.title: Divide and Conquer
steps.mastery: Split a problem in halves and combine answers, including on trees.
steps.practice: Solve a Platinum problem with centroid decomposition on a tree of 10^5 nodes.
steps.detail: Centroid decomposition splits a tree so each path is counted at 1 centroid, giving O(n log n) or O(n log^2 n). It is a standard Platinum tool.
steps.proof: An accepted solution using centroid decomposition.
steps.pitfall: Picking a non centroid root and getting O(n^2) depth.

problems.prompt: Max depth of centroid decomposition for 10^5 nodes?
Removing the centroid of a 100 node tree leaves parts of size at most what?
Merge sort counts inversions in what time for 10^5 numbers?
problems.answer: O(n log n), about 1.7 x 10^6 steps.

steps.title: DP Optimizations
steps.mastery: Speed up DP with convex hull trick or divide and conquer optimization.
steps.practice: Speed up an O(n^2) DP with transitions dp[j] + b[j] x a[i] to O(n log n) using the convex hull trick.
steps.detail: When each transition is a line evaluated at a point, keeping the lower hull of lines answers the min fast. Recognizing the line form is the key step.
steps.proof: The optimized DP matches the O(n^2) version on random tests.
steps.pitfall: Applying the trick without checking the slopes are monotonic or using a Li Chao tree.

problems.prompt: Transition min over j of m[j] x + c[j]. Which trick?
Speedup from O(n^2) to O(n log n) for n = 2 x 10^5?
Slopes arrive in random order. Which structure?

steps.title: Platinum Contest Plan
steps.mastery: Plan a 4 hour Platinum contest for steady partial points.
steps.practice: Take a full USACO Platinum contest, writing subtask solutions first and full solutions only after.
steps.detail: Full Platinum solves can take hours. Subtasks with smaller limits often give 30 to 50 percent of the points, and they build toward the full idea.
steps.proof: A contest log with subtask points banked on each problem.
steps.pitfall: Spending all 4 hours on 1 full solution that never passes.

problems.prompt: A subtask with n at most 5000 out of 10^5. Which complexity is fine for it?
3 problems and 4 hours. Time to read all 3 first?
You banked 40% on each problem. Total out of 1000?

steps.title: Learn From Top Solutions
steps.mastery: Study the shortest accepted solutions to learn new tricks.
steps.practice: Read 3 top contestant solutions to a Platinum problem and note 2 techniques you did not know.
steps.detail: Strong programmers write compact, clever code. Reading it shows new idioms and structures, which are the main growth path at the top division.
steps.proof: 2 new techniques noted with a short example each.
steps.pitfall: Reading code without retyping and testing it yourself.

problems.prompt: Where can you read past USACO solutions?
problems.answer: The USACO website and the USACO Guide.

problems.prompt: You learned a new trick. How do you lock it in?
problems.answer: Solve 2 more problems that use it.

problems.prompt: Why retype a 50 line solution instead of copying it?
problems.answer: Typing it makes you notice each line and catch what you do not understand.

steps.title: Build a Prefix Array
steps.mastery: Store a running total at each index of an array.
steps.practice: Build prefix sums for 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6 and answer the range sum from index 2 to 5.
steps.detail: p[i] holds the sum of the first i numbers. The sum from l to r is p[r + 1] - p[l] with 0 indexing. Building it is O(n), and each query is O(1).
steps.proof: Prefix 0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25, 31, and the sum of indices 2 to 5 is 23 - 4 = 19.
steps.pitfall: Off by one errors from mixing 0 and 1 indexing.

problems.prompt: Prefix sums of 2, 5, 1?
With p = 0, 2, 7, 8, find the sum of indices 1 to 2.
How long do 10^5 range queries take with prefix sums?

steps.title: Count With Prefix Sums
steps.mastery: Count subarrays with a target sum using prefix sums and a hash map.
steps.practice: Count subarrays of 1, 2, 3, -2, 2 with sum 3 by counting earlier prefix sums equal to p - 3.
steps.detail: A subarray sum is a difference of 2 prefix sums. Storing how often each prefix value appeared lets you count matching pairs in 1 pass.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to count the empty prefix 0 before the first element.

problems.prompt: Count subarrays of 1, 1, 1 with sum 2.
Count subarrays of 3, 0, 3 with sum 3.
Count subarrays of 2, -2, 2, -2 with sum 0.

steps.title: Prefix Sums in 2D
steps.mastery: Get the total of any rectangle of cells in constant time.
steps.practice: Build a 2D prefix array for a 4 by 4 grid and find a 2 by 3 rectangle sum with inclusion exclusion.
steps.detail: P[i][j] is the sum of the top left i by j block. A rectangle sum adds and subtracts 4 corners. This is a USACO Silver staple.
steps.proof: The rectangle sum matches a direct count.
steps.pitfall: Subtracting the overlap corner twice instead of adding it back once.

problems.prompt: Formula for the rectangle sum with corners (r1, c1) and (r2, c2)?
Grid [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. Total sum?
How many queries per second can a 1000 by 1000 2D prefix array answer?

steps.title: Difference Arrays
steps.mastery: Apply many range updates at once with a difference array.
steps.practice: Add 5 to indices 2 to 6 and 3 to indices 4 to 9 of a 10 element array using a difference array.
steps.detail: Add v at d[l] and subtract v at d[r + 1], then take prefix sums at the end. Each update is O(1), so 10^5 updates are fast.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the subtract at r + 1, which spreads the update to the end.

problems.prompt: Add 2 to indices 1 to 3 of 5 zeros. Result?
Difference array d = 1, 0, 2, -1. Final array?
How long do q range adds then 1 final pass take?

steps.title: Prefix Sums of Counts
steps.mastery: Count how many items fall in a range of values with prefix counts.
steps.practice: Count how many of 10^5 cows have ids in each of 10^5 query ranges, using prefix counts over ids up to 10^6.
steps.detail: Store how many items have each value, then take prefix sums of those counts. A query for values from a to b is one subtraction.
steps.proof: Each query answered as c[b] - c[a - 1].
steps.pitfall: Using this when values go up to 10^18 without compressing them first.

problems.prompt: Values 2, 2, 5. Count in range 1 to 3?
Values up to 10^9. What do you do first?
problems.answer: Coordinate compress or sort and binary search.

problems.prompt: Sorted values 1, 4, 4, 7. Count in range 3 to 6 using binary search.

steps.title: Build a Segment Tree
steps.mastery: Store sums of ranges in a binary tree for fast queries and updates.
steps.practice: Build a sum segment tree over 2, 1, 5, 3, 4, 2, 6, 1 and draw every node value.
steps.detail: Each node stores the sum of its range, and its children split the range in half. Building takes O(n), and the tree uses about 4n space.
steps.proof: Root 24, with every node equal to the sum of its 2 children.
steps.pitfall: Allocating only 2n nodes for a recursive tree.

problems.prompt: Root value for leaves 1, 2, 3, 4?
Array size to allocate for a recursive tree on 10^5 leaves?
Height of a segment tree on 10^6 leaves?

steps.title: Point Update, Range Query
steps.mastery: Change 1 value and query a range sum in O(log n).
steps.practice: Set index 4 to 10 in the tree over 2, 1, 5, 3, 4, 2, 6, 1, then query the sum of indices 2 to 6.
steps.detail: An update changes 1 leaf and every ancestor. A query combines O(log n) nodes that exactly cover the range.
steps.proof: After the update the sum of indices 2 to 6 is 5 + 3 + 10 + 2 + 6 = 26.
steps.pitfall: Updating the leaf and forgetting the ancestors.

problems.prompt: How many nodes change on 1 point update with 2^10 leaves?
Range query cost with 10^5 leaves?
Array 1, 2, 3, 4. Set index 1 to 7, then sum indices 0 to 2.

steps.title: Range Minimum Queries
steps.mastery: Change the combine function to answer minimum or maximum.
steps.practice: Turn the sum tree into a min tree and answer minimum queries on 5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3 for 4 ranges.
steps.detail: Only the combine step and the empty value change: min with infinity instead of sum with 0. The same tree handles any associative operation.
steps.proof: 4 range minimums matching a direct scan.
steps.pitfall: Using 0 as the empty value in a min tree.

problems.prompt: Empty value for a max segment tree over values up to 10^9?
Min of indices 1 to 4 in 5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3?
Can a segment tree answer gcd(a[2], ..., a[9])?

steps.title: Lazy Propagation
steps.mastery: Apply an update to a whole range lazily in O(log n).
steps.practice: Add 3 to indices 1 to 5 of an 8 element array with lazy tags, then query the sum of indices 0 to 3.
steps.detail: A lazy tag stores an update for a whole node without visiting its children. Tags are pushed down only when a later operation needs the children.
steps.proof: The query matches applying the update by hand.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to push tags down before reading children.

problems.prompt: Range add of 2 on a node covering 4 elements. Change in its sum?
When must a lazy tag on a node be pushed to its 2 children?
problems.answer: Before any operation that visits those 2 children.

problems.prompt: Complexity of 10^5 range adds and queries with lazy tags?

steps.title: Fenwick Tree
steps.mastery: Use a binary indexed tree for prefix sums with updates in fewer lines.
steps.practice: Code a Fenwick tree with i += i & -i for updates and answer 3 prefix sum queries on 10 elements.
steps.detail: A Fenwick tree stores partial sums at indices chosen by the lowest set bit. It handles point updates and prefix sums in O(log n) with about 10 lines.
steps.proof: 3 prefix sums matching a direct sum.
steps.pitfall: Using 0 based indices, which makes i & -i loop forever at 0.

problems.prompt: What is 12 & -12?
Indices visited by a prefix query from 13?
Can a plain Fenwick tree answer range minimum with updates?
problems.answer: Not easily. Use a segment tree.

steps.title: Spot the Disguise
steps.mastery: Recognize which standard technique a Silver problem hides.
steps.practice: Read 6 past USACO Silver problems and label each as graph, sort, prefix sum or binary search before solving.
steps.detail: Silver problems are standard techniques in a story. Naming the technique first narrows the work to a pattern you have practiced.
steps.proof: 6 problems labeled with a technique, then checked against the editorials.
steps.pitfall: Starting to code before deciding which technique fits.

problems.prompt: Many range sum queries on a fixed array. Technique?
Largest minimum distance when placing cows. Technique?
Can a cow reach the barn through open cells? Technique?

steps.title: Coordinate Compression
steps.mastery: Map large values to small indices so arrays fit.
steps.practice: Compress the values 1000000000, 5, 77, 5 to ranks 0 to 2 using sort and unique.
steps.detail: Values up to 10^9 cannot index an array, but only their order matters for many problems. Sorting the distinct values and binary searching gives each a small index.
steps.proof: 5 becomes 0, 77 becomes 1 and 1000000000 becomes 2.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to remove duplicates before assigning ranks.

problems.prompt: Compress 30, 10, 20.
How many distinct ranks for 7, 7, 7, 2?
Complexity to compress 10^5 values?

steps.title: Two Techniques Together
steps.mastery: Combine 2 basic methods like sorting and prefix sums in one solution.
steps.practice: Solve a USACO Silver problem that needs sorting by position and then prefix sums of weights.
steps.detail: Many Silver problems use 2 tools in a row. Sorting sets up the order, and prefix sums or binary search answer the queries on that order.
steps.proof: An accepted solution using both techniques.
steps.pitfall: Forcing a single technique when the problem needs 2.

problems.prompt: Sort cows by position, then answer range weight queries. Second tool?
Sort intervals, then find how many contain each point. Tools?
problems.answer: Sorting plus a sweep or difference array.

problems.prompt: Binary search a value, then check it with BFS. Combined complexity?

steps.title: Silver Contest Pacing
steps.mastery: Spread 4 hours over 3 Silver problems and secure partial points.
steps.practice: Take a full USACO Silver contest in 4 hours and write a brute force for any problem you cannot fully solve.
steps.detail: A correct brute force often passes the small test cases and earns partial points. It also gives you a checker for your faster solution.
steps.proof: A full contest with a brute force submitted for each unsolved problem.
steps.pitfall: Leaving a problem blank when a slow solution would pass some tests.

problems.prompt: Silver contest: 3 problems in 4 hours. Average time each?
A brute force passes 4 of 10 tests. Points out of 333?
Why keep the brute force after your fast solution passes 10 of 10 tests?
problems.answer: To stress test the fast solution.

steps.title: Upsolve Every Contest
steps.mastery: Finish every unsolved problem after a contest using the editorial.
steps.practice: Upsolve 3 problems you missed in USACO Silver contests and write 1 line on the key idea of each.
steps.detail: Most growth happens after the contest. Writing the idea you were missing builds a list of tricks you will recognize next time.
steps.proof: 3 upsolved problems with the key idea noted.
steps.pitfall: Reading the editorial without coding the solution yourself.

problems.prompt: What is upsolving a USACO problem?
problems.answer: Solving it after the contest ends.

problems.prompt: The key idea was binary search on the answer. Where do you note it?
problems.answer: In a list of patterns to review.

problems.prompt: Should you upsolve within 3 days of a contest or wait a month?
problems.answer: Within 3 days, while it is fresh.

steps.title: Sort Then Scan
steps.mastery: Sort an array so one pass answers the question.
steps.practice: Find the minimum gap between any 2 of 10^5 numbers by sorting and checking neighbors.
steps.detail: After sorting, the closest pair is always adjacent. That turns O(n^2) pairs into O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the scan.
steps.proof: Sort, then the answer is the minimum of a[i + 1] - a[i].
steps.pitfall: Checking all pairs when the sorted neighbors are enough.

problems.prompt: Sorted: 1, 4, 9, 10, 15. Minimum gap?
Complexity of sort then scan for n = 10^5?
Count the distinct values in 7, 3, 7, 1, 3 by sorting.

steps.title: Two Pointers on Pairs
steps.mastery: Find a pair with a target sum in a sorted array with 2 moving pointers.
steps.practice: Find 2 numbers summing to 100 in a sorted list of 10^5 numbers using left and right pointers.
steps.detail: If the sum is too small, move the left pointer up. If too big, move the right down. Each pointer moves at most n times, so the scan is O(n).
steps.proof: A pair found in 1 pass, or a clear report that none exists.
steps.pitfall: Moving both pointers at once and skipping the answer.

problems.prompt: Sorted 1, 3, 5, 8, 12 and target 13. Which pair?
Sum at the pointers is too big. Which pointer moves?
Count pairs with sum at most 10 in 1, 2, 4, 6, 9.

steps.title: Sliding Window
steps.mastery: Keep a window of elements that grows and shrinks as you scan.
steps.practice: Find the longest subarray of 10^5 positive numbers with sum at most 1000 using a sliding window.
steps.detail: Extend the right end, and while the sum is too big, move the left end. With positive numbers, the window never needs to move backward, so the total work is O(n).
steps.proof: The longest window length with sum at most 1000.
steps.pitfall: Using a sliding window when numbers can be negative, which breaks the logic.

problems.prompt: Longest subarray of 2, 1, 3, 1, 1 with sum at most 4?
Why must all 10^5 numbers be positive for this window?
problems.answer: So that moving the left end always lowers the sum.

problems.prompt: In 1, 4, 2, 7, 3, what is the fewest consecutive numbers that add to 9 or more?

steps.title: Sort by a Custom Key
steps.mastery: Sort records by the field the problem cares about.
steps.practice: Sort 10^5 intervals by end time and pick the most that do not overlap.
steps.detail: Interval scheduling is solved by sorting on end time and taking each interval that starts after the last chosen end. Choosing the right key is the whole trick.
steps.proof: The maximum number of non overlapping intervals.
steps.pitfall: Sorting by start time, which picks long early intervals.

problems.prompt: Intervals [1, 3], [2, 5], [4, 6]. Most non overlapping?
Sort pairs (3, b), (1, c), (2, a) by the first value.
Given [1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5], [6, 7], why does picking by earliest start do badly?
problems.answer: It takes [1, 10] first and gets only 1 interval, while picking by earliest end gets 3.

steps.title: Merge Sorted Lists
steps.mastery: Combine 2 sorted arrays in 1 pass.
steps.practice: Merge 2 sorted arrays of 10^5 numbers into 1 sorted array with 2 pointers.
steps.detail: Take the smaller front element each time. This is the core of merge sort and of many problems that count pairs across 2 sorted lists.
steps.proof: A merged sorted array of 2 x 10^5 numbers.
steps.pitfall: Concatenating and sorting again, which wastes the sorted order.

problems.prompt: Merge 1, 4, 7 and 2, 3, 9.
Complexity of merging sorted lists of sizes 10^5 and 10^3?
Count pairs (a, b) with a from 1, 5, 8 and b from 2, 6 where a < b.

steps.title: String Hashing
steps.mastery: Compare substrings in O(1) with polynomial hashes.
steps.practice: Hash every prefix of "abcabc" with base 31 mod 10^9 + 7 and compare the substrings at 0 and 3 of length 3.
steps.detail: A prefix hash lets any substring hash come from 2 prefix values. Equal hashes almost always mean equal strings, and using 2 moduli makes collisions rare.
steps.proof: Both length 3 substrings have the same hash.
steps.pitfall: Using a single small modulus and getting collisions on adversarial tests.

problems.prompt: How many distinct substrings of length 2 in "aaaa"?
Why use 2 moduli for hashing?
problems.answer: To lower the collision chance on 10^5 comparisons.

problems.prompt: Hash of "ab" with a = 1, b = 2, base 10?

steps.title: Z Function
steps.mastery: Compute for each position the longest match with the string start.
steps.practice: Compute the Z array of "aabxaab" by hand.
steps.detail: z[i] is the length of the longest prefix that starts at i. The Z algorithm reuses an interval to run in O(n), and pattern search uses it on pattern + # + text.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the separator between pattern and text.

problems.prompt: Z array of "aaa"?
How do you find "ab" in "xabab" with Z?
problems.answer: Run Z on "ab#xabab". Each 2 marks a match, at text positions 1 and 3.

problems.prompt: Z array of "abab"?

steps.title: KMP Prefix Function
steps.mastery: Build the prefix function to search a pattern in linear time.
steps.practice: Compute the prefix function of "ababaca" and use it to find "aba" in "abababa".
steps.detail: pi[i] is the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix ending at i. On a mismatch, jump back with pi instead of restarting.
steps.proof: pi = 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, and "aba" appears at 0, 2 and 4.
steps.pitfall: Restarting the match from scratch on every mismatch.

problems.prompt: Prefix function of "aaaa"?
Prefix function of "abcd"?
Shortest period of "abcabcabc" from pi?

steps.title: Palindromes
steps.mastery: Spot every string that reads the same both ways, using its middle point.
steps.practice: Find the longest palindromic substring of "forgeeksskeegfor" by expanding around all 31 centers.
steps.detail: Each palindrome has a center, either a letter or a gap. Expanding around 2n - 1 centers is O(n^2), fine for n = 5000. Manacher does it in O(n).
steps.proof: "geeksskeeg", length 10.
steps.pitfall: Only checking odd length centers and missing even palindromes.

problems.prompt: Longest palindrome in "babad"?
How many centers in a string of length 6?
Count palindromic substrings of "aaa".

steps.title: Pick the String Tool
steps.mastery: Choose hashing, Z, KMP or a trie based on the problem.
steps.practice: Solve 3 Codeforces string problems and write which tool fits each and why.
steps.detail: Hashing is the most flexible, KMP and Z are exact and linear, and a trie fits many words sharing prefixes. Naming the tool first saves time.
steps.proof: 3 problems solved with a tool chosen and justified for each.
steps.pitfall: Reaching for suffix arrays when hashing is enough.

problems.prompt: Count occurrences of 1 pattern in a text of 10^6. Tool?
Check if 2 substrings are equal, 10^5 times. Tool?
Store 10^5 words and query by prefix. Tool?

steps.title: Subtree Sizes
steps.mastery: Compute the size of every subtree with 1 DFS.
steps.practice: Compute subtree sizes for a tree of 7 nodes rooted at 1 by adding child sizes after the recursive calls.
steps.detail: A subtree size is 1 plus the sizes of its children. Computing it after visiting the children is the basic shape of every tree DP.
steps.proof: Sizes for all 7 nodes, with the root at 7.
steps.pitfall: Visiting the parent again as if it were a child.

problems.prompt: Root with 3 leaf children. Root subtree size?
A path 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 rooted at 1. Size of node 2?
In any tree with 10 nodes, sum of all subtree sizes when it is a path rooted at an end?

steps.title: Tree DP Choices
steps.mastery: Choose to take or skip each node with a 2 state DP on a tree.
steps.practice: Find the maximum independent set weight in a tree of 6 nodes using dp[v][0] and dp[v][1].
steps.detail: dp[v][1] takes v and skips its children, while dp[v][0] skips v and takes the best of each child. This pattern solves many selection problems on trees.
steps.proof: The best total weight, matching a brute force over all 64 subsets.
steps.pitfall: Letting a node and its child both be taken.

problems.prompt: Path 1 - 2 - 3 with weights 5, 1, 5. Best independent set?
Star with center weight 10 and 4 leaves of weight 3. Best?
Path of 4 nodes all weight 1. Best?

steps.title: Rerooting
steps.mastery: Compute an answer for every root with 2 DFS passes instead of n.
steps.practice: Compute the sum of distances from every node in a tree of 6 nodes using 1 pass down and 1 pass up.
steps.detail: Moving the root from v to child c changes the total by n - 2 x size[c]. One pass computes sizes and the root answer, and a second pushes answers to every child.
steps.proof: All 6 sums of distances, matching BFS from each node.
steps.pitfall: Running a full BFS from every node when n is 10^5.

problems.prompt: Path 1 - 2 - 3. Sum of distances from node 2?
Same path, from node 1?
Moving the root to a child c with subtree size 4 in a tree of 10 nodes. Change in total distance?

steps.title: Lowest Common Ancestor
steps.mastery: Answer which ancestor 2 nodes share deepest, in logarithmic time per query.
steps.practice: Build binary lifting tables up[k][v] for a tree of 8 nodes and find the LCA of nodes 6 and 7.
steps.detail: up[k][v] is the 2^k ancestor of v. Lift the deeper node to the same depth, then lift both while their ancestors differ. Each query takes O(log n).
steps.proof: The LCA found matches a hand check.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to bring both nodes to the same depth first.

problems.prompt: How many levels of tables for n = 10^5?
Distance between u and v using depths and LCA w?
Complexity of 10^5 LCA queries with binary lifting?

steps.title: Euler Tour
steps.mastery: Flatten a tree into an array so subtrees become ranges.
steps.practice: Record entry and exit times for a tree of 7 nodes and answer a subtree sum as a range sum.
steps.detail: A DFS gives each node a time tin when entered. A subtree is exactly the range from tin[v] to tout[v], so range data structures work on trees.
steps.proof: Subtree sums match direct sums on the tree.
steps.pitfall: Using exit times that overlap the next subtree.

problems.prompt: A subtree of size 4 covers how many entries in the Euler tour array?
Node v has tin 3 and subtree size 5. Its range?
After flattening a tree of 10^5 nodes, which structure answers subtree sums with updates?

steps.title: Find Your Talking Pace
steps.mastery: Find the easy pace where you can speak in full sentences while moving.
steps.practice: Run, ride or swim for 20 minutes at a pace where you can say a 10 word sentence without gasping.
steps.detail: Base work happens at a conversational pace. If you can talk in full sentences, you're there. If you can only get out 3 or 4 words, you're going too hard. For most people this feels slower than they expect, sometimes almost embarrassingly slow.
steps.proof: 20 minutes at a pace where a 10 word sentence comes out easily.
steps.pitfall: Running every easy day at a pace where you can only grunt a few words.

problems.prompt: You can only say 4 words before gasping. Is that easy pace?
Your easy pace is 2 minutes per mile slower than your race pace. Is that a problem?
problems.answer: No. It's normal for base work.

problems.prompt: Write a 10 word test sentence you could say while running.
problems.answer: "I am running slowly so that I can keep talking."

steps.title: Build to 30 Minutes
steps.mastery: Extend easy sessions until you can move steadily for half an hour.
steps.practice: Add 5 minutes to 1 easy session each week until you reach 30 minutes nonstop at talking pace.
steps.detail: Time builds the aerobic base. Walk breaks are fine at first. Add 5 minutes a week and no more. If a week feels hard, repeat it before adding. Thirty minutes of easy work is a solid foundation for everything else.
steps.proof: A log showing steady 5 minute increases up to 30 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Jumping from 10 minutes to 40 in a week and ending up sore for days.

problems.prompt: This week you did 15 minutes. What's next week's target?
Week 3 felt hard and your legs ache. What do you do?
Are walk breaks OK while building to 30 minutes?

steps.title: Go Easy 3 Times a Week
steps.mastery: Make easy sessions the bulk of your week.
steps.practice: Schedule 3 easy sessions on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday this week, with rest or other training between.
steps.detail: Most endurance gains come from lots of easy work. It builds the heart, blood vessels and the muscles' ability to use oxygen. Three easy sessions a week is a strong base. Spread them out with rest days between.
steps.proof: 3 easy sessions of 30 minutes done this week.
steps.pitfall: Making every session a hard one because easy feels like it's doing nothing.

problems.prompt: Do 3 easy sessions a week give a strong base, or do you need 7?
Should all 3 sessions be back to back on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday?
problems.answer: Better to spread them out with rest days.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing easy work builds.
problems.answer: A stronger heart, or muscles that use oxygen better.

steps.title: Check Heart Rate
steps.mastery: Use heart rate to confirm easy days are actually easy.
steps.practice: Wear a heart rate monitor on 2 easy sessions and note your average heart rate.
steps.detail: A rough easy zone is about 60 to 70 percent of your max heart rate. A common estimate for max is 220 minus age. If your average is well above 70 percent on easy days, slow down.
steps.proof: 2 easy sessions with average heart rate noted.
steps.pitfall: Trusting feel alone when your heart rate says you're working hard.

problems.prompt: You're 30. What's a rough max heart rate?
What's 70 percent of 190?
Your easy run averaged 165. What do you do next time?

steps.title: Stack Weeks
steps.mastery: String weeks of easy work together for steady gains.
steps.practice: Complete 6 weeks of 3 easy sessions a week and note your pace at the same heart rate in week 1 and week 6.
steps.detail: Base fitness builds slowly. Week by week, you'll often go faster at the same effort. That's the base growing.
steps.proof: 6 weeks logged with pace compared at the same heart rate.
steps.pitfall: Quitting base work after 2 weeks because it feels slow.

problems.prompt: Week 1: 11 minutes per mile at 135 bpm. Week 6: 10:15 at 135 bpm. What does it show?
Should you compare pace after 6 weeks or after 6 days?
Why compare pace at the same 135 bpm heart rate?

steps.title: Match Breath to Steps
steps.mastery: Settle into a steady breathing rhythm tied to your steps or strokes.
steps.practice: On an easy run, breathe in for 3 steps and out for 3 steps for 5 minutes.
steps.detail: A steady rhythm keeps breathing calm and helps you notice effort. Easy running often fits 3 steps in and 3 out, or 2 and 2 as it gets harder. Swimmers do the same with strokes, like breathing every 3 strokes. Find the pattern that feels smooth.
steps.proof: 5 minutes of breathing in a 3 and 3 rhythm.
steps.pitfall: Holding your breath on hills, which spikes effort.

problems.prompt: Easy run: 3 steps in and 3 out. As you speed up, what might the pattern become?
A swimmer breathes every 3 strokes. How many breaths in 30 strokes?
Your breathing goes ragged at minute 4 of a 3 and 3 rhythm. What does it tell you?
problems.answer: The pace is harder than easy.

steps.title: Breathe From the Belly
steps.mastery: Breathe low into the belly and sides to take in more air with less effort.
steps.practice: Before 2 runs, lie down for 2 minutes and breathe so your belly rises, then keep that feeling for the first 5 minutes of the run.
steps.detail: Chest breathing is shallow and tiring. Belly breathing uses the diaphragm and moves more air. Practice lying down first, then carry it into easy running. Under hard efforts, it's normal to breathe faster.
steps.proof: 2 runs started with belly breathing practice.
steps.pitfall: Breathing high in the chest with tight shoulders.

problems.prompt: Your shoulders lift on every breath at minute 3. What does it suggest?
problems.answer: You're breathing high in the chest.

problems.prompt: Is the lying-down practice about 2 minutes or 20?
In a hard 400 meter repeat, is fast breathing a problem?
problems.answer: No. It's normal under hard effort.

steps.title: Use the Talk Test
steps.mastery: Use how easily you can talk as a quick gauge of effort.
steps.practice: During 3 sessions, say a sentence out loud every 10 minutes and rate how hard it was from 1 to 5.
steps.detail: Breath tells you effort before any watch does. Easy: full sentences. Moderate: short phrases. Hard: 1 or 2 words. Use this on every session to keep easy days easy.
steps.proof: 3 sessions with talk test ratings every 10 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring your breathing and only trusting a watch.

problems.prompt: You can only say 2 words. What effort level is that?
You speak in short phrases. What effort is that?
Your watch battery dies at mile 2. Why is the talk test still useful?
problems.answer: Breath shows effort before any device.

steps.title: Breathe Out Longer to Recover
steps.mastery: Use long exhales to recover faster between hard efforts.
steps.practice: After each of 4 hard intervals, breathe out for twice as long as you breathe in for 60 seconds.
steps.detail: Long exhales calm the body and speed recovery. After a hard rep, slow the breath down: in for 2, out for 4. You'll feel ready sooner.
steps.proof: 4 recoveries with long exhales.
steps.pitfall: Panting fast and shallow after every effort.

problems.prompt: In for 2, out for how long?
Why breathe out for 4 counts after a hard rep instead of panting?
problems.answer: It calms the body and speeds recovery.

problems.prompt: Should you use the long-exhale pattern for about 60 seconds or 10 minutes?

steps.title: Breathe Through Side Stitches
steps.mastery: Ease a side stitch by changing breathing and pace.
steps.practice: When the next stitch hits, slow down, breathe out hard as the opposite foot lands, and press on the spot for 30 seconds.
steps.detail: Stitches often hit new runners. Slow down, breathe deeply and exhale forcefully. Pressing on the spot can help. Avoid big meals 2 hours before running.
steps.proof: A stitch eased using this method.
steps.pitfall: Sprinting through a stitch.

problems.prompt: Should you press on the stitch for about 30 seconds or 5 minutes?
You run at 6 pm. When should a big meal end?
A stitch hits at mile 3. Should you speed up?

steps.title: Pick a Backup Sport
steps.mastery: Choose a low-impact sport you can switch to when your main one isn't possible.
steps.practice: Pick 1 backup activity, like cycling, swimming, rowing or pool running, and do 1 easy 30 minute session of it this week.
steps.detail: A backup sport keeps your engine running when a joint needs rest. Pick one that's easy to access and doesn't hurt the same area. Learn it while healthy, so it isn't brand new during an injury. Cycling and pool running are popular with runners.
steps.proof: 1 backup activity chosen and 1 easy session done.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until you're injured to learn a new sport.

problems.prompt: Your shins are sore from running. Name 2 backup options that are easy on them.
Why learn the backup while you're healthy?
problems.answer: So it isn't brand new during an injury.

problems.prompt: Your gym has bikes and rowers, but the pool is 40 minutes away. Which backup makes more sense?

steps.title: Match Effort and Time
steps.mastery: Swap sessions by matching effort and time instead of distance.
steps.practice: Replace 1 easy 40 minute run with a 40 to 50 minute easy ride at the same heart rate or talk test effort.
steps.detail: Distances don't translate between sports. Time and effort do. Match minutes, or add a bit for low-impact options like cycling. Keep heart rate in the same zone you'd use running.
steps.proof: 1 run swapped for a session matched by time and effort.
steps.pitfall: Riding 10 miles to "replace" a 10 mile run.

problems.prompt: Your plan has a 45 minute easy run. What's a fair bike swap?
problems.answer: About 45 to 60 minutes of easy riding.

problems.prompt: Should a 6 mile run be replaced with a 6 mile ride?
Your easy run heart rate is 135. What should the ride be near?

steps.title: Run in the Pool
steps.mastery: Use deep-water running to copy the running motion with no impact.
steps.practice: Pool run for 30 minutes with a flotation belt, using the same arm and leg motion as running, including 6 hard 1 minute efforts.
steps.detail: Pool running keeps the running motion and fitness with zero landing. Wear a flotation belt and run upright, feet not touching the bottom. Heart rate runs about 10 beats lower than on land for the same effort, so use feel too.
steps.proof: 1 pool session of 30 minutes with 6 hard efforts.
steps.pitfall: Leaning forward and paddling instead of running.

problems.prompt: Your land easy heart rate is 140. About what might it be in the pool for the same effort?
In 8 feet of water, should your feet touch the bottom?
problems.answer: No. Use a flotation belt in deep water.

problems.prompt: Name 1 form mistake in pool running.

steps.title: Keep the Hard Sessions
steps.mastery: Protect fitness during an injury by moving hard sessions to the backup sport.
steps.practice: Move your 1 weekly interval session to the bike or pool for 3 weeks of injury, matching rep times, recovery and effort.
steps.detail: Fitness fades fastest when all hard work stops. Easy cross-training alone holds some of it, but intervals hold much more. Copy your usual session in the backup sport with the same rep lengths and recoveries, using effort or heart rate as the guide.
steps.proof: 3 weeks of intervals done in the backup sport and logged.
steps.pitfall: Doing only gentle cross-training for a month and losing your top end.

problems.prompt: Your usual session is 6 x 3 minutes hard with 2 minutes easy. What's the bike version?
problems.answer: 6 x 3 minutes hard with 2 minutes easy on the bike.

problems.prompt: Why keep 1 hard session a week while injured?
problems.answer: Fitness fades fastest without hard work.

problems.prompt: Pool running makes your heart rate about 10 beats lower. How do you judge hard reps there?
problems.answer: By feel and breathing as well as heart rate.

steps.title: Return to Running Gradually
steps.mastery: Ease back into your main sport so the injured area can catch up with your fitness.
steps.practice: Plan 4 weeks back: week 1 with 3 runs of 20 minutes, then about 10 percent more each week, keeping 1 or 2 cross-training sessions.
steps.detail: After cross-training, your heart and lungs are fitter than your bones and tendons. That's the danger. Build running back slowly, and use cross-training to fill the gap. Any return of pain means hold or step back a week.
steps.proof: A 4 week return plan written and the first week done.
steps.pitfall: Jumping back to full mileage because your breathing feels great.

problems.prompt: Week 1 back has 3 runs of 20 minutes. What's the week's total?
In week 2 the old pain returns at 3 out of 10. What do you do?
problems.answer: Hold or drop back to week 1.

problems.prompt: After 3 weeks on the bike, why can 30 miles of running feel easy on your lungs but still be risky?
problems.answer: Bones and tendons lag behind your fitness.

steps.title: Keep It Going When Healthy
steps.mastery: Use regular cross-training in healthy weeks to add fitness with less impact.
steps.practice: Add 1 cross-training session a week for 8 weeks, at easy or moderate effort.
steps.detail: A weekly session on the bike or in the pool adds aerobic work without more pounding. It also keeps your backup sport familiar, so switching during an injury is easy. Treat it as an easy day unless your plan says otherwise.
steps.proof: 8 weeks with 1 cross-training session each.
steps.pitfall: Only touching the bike when injured, so it always feels foreign.

problems.prompt: You run 4 days a week. Where might 1 cross-training session fit?
problems.answer: On an easy day, replacing or adding to it.

problems.prompt: Name 2 benefits of cross-training in healthy weeks.
problems.answer: More aerobic work with less impact, and a familiar backup sport.

problems.prompt: Should the 1 weekly session usually be hard or easy?

steps.title: Eat Before Long Sessions
steps.mastery: Top up carbs before long or hard sessions so you start with fuel in the tank.
steps.practice: Eat a carb-based meal 2 to 3 hours before your next 3 long sessions, like oatmeal with a banana, and note how you feel.
steps.detail: Muscles run on stored carbs during hard and long efforts. A meal 2 to 3 hours before gives time to digest. Keep it familiar, low in fat and fiber, with some carbs. If you train early, a small snack 30 to 60 minutes before, like toast or a banana, works too.
steps.proof: 3 long sessions with a pre-session meal logged and notes on energy.
steps.pitfall: Eating a big greasy breakfast 30 minutes before a hard run.

problems.prompt: Your long run starts at 9 am. When should the main meal be?
You train at 6 am and can't eat a full meal. Name 1 option.
problems.answer: A banana or toast 30 to 60 minutes before.

problems.prompt: Why keep the meal 2 hours before a run low in fat and fiber?
problems.answer: They digest slowly and can upset the stomach.

steps.title: Fuel During Long Efforts
steps.mastery: Take in carbs during sessions longer than about 75 minutes.
steps.practice: On 3 sessions over 75 minutes, take 30 to 60 grams of carbs per hour, starting 30 minutes in.
steps.detail: After 75 to 90 minutes, stored carbs start to run low. Gels, chews, sports drinks or bananas all work. A typical gel has about 20 to 25 grams. Start early and take small amounts often, since waiting until you feel empty is too late.
steps.proof: 3 long sessions with carbs per hour logged.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until you hit the wall to eat anything.

problems.prompt: A gel has 25 grams of carbs. How many gels per hour for 50 grams?
Your session is 2 hours. Roughly how many grams of carbs should you take?
When should the first fuel go in, at minute 30 or minute 100?

steps.title: Train Your Gut
steps.mastery: Practice race fueling in training so your stomach can handle it.
steps.practice: For 6 weeks, use your planned race fuel on every long session and rate stomach comfort from 1 to 10.
steps.detail: The gut adapts to fueling with practice. Use the same gels or drinks you'll race with. Start at the low end and build up. Race day is the worst day to try something new.
steps.proof: 6 weeks of race fuel practice with comfort ratings.
steps.pitfall: Trying a new gel for the first time on race day.

problems.prompt: Your stomach rates 4 out of 10 on 60 grams an hour. What do you do?
problems.answer: Drop to 40 grams and build up slowly.

problems.prompt: A booth hands you a new gel 1 hour before the race. Should you use it?
Over 6 weeks, comfort goes from 5 to 8. What does it show?

steps.title: Find Your Sweat Rate
steps.mastery: Learn how much fluid you lose so you can drink enough without overdoing it.
steps.practice: Weigh yourself without clothes before and after 2 hour-long sessions, add any fluid you drank, and work out loss per hour.
steps.detail: Losing more than about 2 percent of body weight can hurt performance. Drinking far more than you sweat is risky too, since it can dilute blood sodium. A simple weigh-in shows your sweat rate. One pound lost is about 16 ounces of fluid. Hot days push the number up.
steps.proof: 2 sessions with sweat loss per hour worked out.
steps.pitfall: Forcing down water at every stop to be safe, whatever you actually sweat.

problems.prompt: You weigh 150 before and 148 after an hour, and drank nothing. About how much fluid did you lose?
You're 150 pounds. What's 2 percent of body weight?
You sweat 16 ounces an hour but drink 50. Why is that a risk?

steps.title: Refuel After Hard Days
steps.mastery: Eat carbs and protein soon after hard or long sessions so the next one goes well.
steps.practice: Eat a snack or meal with carbs and about 20 to 30 grams of protein within 60 minutes after 3 hard sessions.
steps.detail: After hard work, muscles take up carbs quickly and need protein to repair. A meal within an hour helps, especially with 2 sessions in a day or a hard session tomorrow. Chocolate milk, a turkey sandwich or yogurt with fruit all work.
steps.proof: 3 hard sessions followed by recovery food within 60 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Skipping food after a long run and feeling flat for 2 days.

problems.prompt: Name 2 easy recovery snacks.
problems.answer: Chocolate milk and a turkey sandwich, for example.

problems.prompt: Is a typical recovery target about 20 to 30 grams of protein, or 100?
You have a hard session tomorrow at 7 am. Why does tonight's recovery meal matter?
problems.answer: It refills fuel and starts repair for tomorrow.

steps.title: Write the Race Fuel Plan
steps.mastery: Put race-day eating and drinking on paper so nothing is left to chance.
steps.practice: Write a fuel plan for your next race listing what you'll take, at what times or miles, and how much.
steps.detail: On race day, nerves and adrenaline make it easy to forget fuel. A written plan helps. Use only products you've practiced with. Note where aid stations are and whether you'll carry your own. Tape the plan to a bottle or write it on your wrist.
steps.proof: A written race fuel plan tested in at least 1 long session.
steps.pitfall: Winging it with whatever the aid stations hand out.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 parts of a fuel plan.
Your race has aid stations every 3 miles. How does that change the plan?
problems.answer: Time fuel near the stations or carry your own.

problems.prompt: Name 2 places to keep the plan during a 13 mile race.
problems.answer: Taped to a bottle or written on your wrist.

steps.title: Count Your Cadence
steps.mastery: Find your running or cycling cadence and nudge it toward an efficient range.
steps.practice: Count your steps for 30 seconds during an easy run, double it, and write your steps per minute.
steps.detail: Cadence is steps per minute. Many new runners take long, slow strides that land with the heel far ahead of the body. A slightly higher cadence, often around 160 to 180, means shorter steps and less braking. Don't chase a number, just nudge it up 5 percent.
steps.proof: Your cadence written down from a 30 second count.
steps.pitfall: Forcing a cadence of 180 overnight and feeling awkward and tight.

problems.prompt: You count 80 steps in 30 seconds. What's your cadence?
Your cadence is 150. What's a 5 percent increase?
Why might going from 155 to 165 steps per minute help?
problems.answer: Shorter steps mean less braking and impact.

steps.title: Land Under You
