steps.mastery: Land with the foot under the body instead of out in front.
steps.practice: Film 10 seconds of your running from the side and check where your foot lands compared to your hips.
steps.detail: Landing far in front of the body acts like a brake. Aim to land with the foot closer to under the hips. You don't need to force a forefoot strike. Shorter, quicker steps usually fix it.
steps.proof: A side video with landing position noted.
steps.pitfall: Forcing tiptoe running to "fix" a heel strike.

problems.prompt: Your foot lands 12 inches in front of your hips. What helps?
To land under your hips, do you need to run on your toes 100 percent of the time?
Why is landing 12 inches in front of your hips a problem?

steps.title: Stand Tall
steps.mastery: Run or ride with relaxed, upright posture.
steps.practice: During 1 easy session, check posture 5 times: tall spine, relaxed shoulders, slight forward lean from the ankles.
steps.detail: Good posture saves energy. Run tall with a slight lean that comes from the ankles while the waist stays straight. Keep shoulders down and hands loose. Check in a few times per session.
steps.proof: 5 posture checks in 1 session.
steps.pitfall: Hunching at the waist when tired.

problems.prompt: Your lean is 10 degrees from the waist. Where should it come from?
Name 2 posture cues.
In a 30 minute run, should you check posture once or about 5 times?

steps.title: Relax Your Upper Body
steps.mastery: Keep the arms and hands loose so energy goes to moving forward.
steps.practice: Run 5 strides of 20 seconds focusing only on loose hands and arms swinging front to back.
steps.detail: Tense hands and shoulders waste energy. Imagine holding a potato chip without breaking it. Arms swing forward and back, not across the body.
steps.proof: 5 strides with relaxed arms.
steps.pitfall: Clenching fists and swinging arms across the body.

problems.prompt: Name 1 image that relaxes the hands during 5 strides.
problems.answer: Holding a chip without breaking it.

problems.prompt: On video your arms cross your chest every step. Is that OK?
Should each stride last about 20 seconds or 5 minutes?

steps.title: Practice Drills
steps.mastery: Use short drills to make good form automatic.
steps.practice: Add 3 drills, like high knees, butt kicks and skips, for 2 sets of 20 yards before 2 runs a week.
steps.detail: Drills groove good movement. Do them after warming up, before the main run. Keep them crisp and short.
steps.proof: 2 weeks of drills before runs.
steps.pitfall: Doing drills sloppily when tired.

problems.prompt: Name 3 running drills.
problems.answer: High knees, butt kicks and skips.

problems.prompt: You have a 10 minute warm-up and a 30 minute run. When do the drills go?
problems.answer: After warming up, before the main run.

problems.prompt: Should each drill cover about 20 yards or 1 mile?

steps.title: Slow Down in the Heat
steps.mastery: Adjust pace for hot weather so effort stays where it should be.
steps.practice: On your next 3 runs above 75 F, run by effort or heart rate and note how much slower your pace was than on a cool day.
steps.detail: Heat makes the body send blood to the skin to cool off, so less goes to the muscles. The same pace costs more. Many runners slow by roughly 1 to 3 percent for every 10 F above about 60 F, more in high humidity. Run by effort and let pace fall where it falls.
steps.proof: 3 hot runs logged with effort, heart rate and pace.
steps.pitfall: Forcing your cool-weather pace on a 90 F day and overheating.

problems.prompt: Your easy pace is 10:00 per mile at 55 F. It's 85 F. Is 10:30 reasonable?
problems.answer: Yes. Slowing by 3 to 6 percent in that heat is normal.

problems.prompt: Why does the same pace feel harder at 85 F?
problems.answer: More blood goes to the skin to cool you, so less goes to the muscles.

problems.prompt: Humidity is 90 percent. Should you slow down more or less than on a dry hot day?
problems.answer: More, since sweat can't cool you as well.

steps.title: Plan Fluids and Salt
steps.mastery: Drink and replace salt to match hot-weather sweat loss.
steps.practice: On 2 hot sessions over 60 minutes, carry fluid with electrolytes and weigh yourself before and after.
steps.detail: Hot days can double sweat loss. Plain water alone may not be enough on long hot sessions, since sweat carries sodium. Sports drinks or electrolyte tabs help. Weigh in and out to see how close you got. Aim to lose less than 2 percent of body weight.
steps.proof: 2 hot sessions with fluid, electrolytes and weight change logged.
steps.pitfall: Drinking only plain water through a 3 hour hot effort.

problems.prompt: You weigh 160 and lose 4 pounds in a hot 90 minute run. What percent is that?
Name 2 ways to replace salt on a long hot run.
What's the target for weight lost in a session?
problems.answer: Less than 2 percent of body weight.

steps.title: Get Used to Heat
steps.mastery: Adapt to heat over 10 to 14 days so hot races feel easier.
steps.practice: Run easy in warm conditions for 30 to 60 minutes on 10 of the 14 days before a hot race.
steps.detail: Heat adaptation is real and fairly quick. Over 10 to 14 days, you sweat sooner, blood volume rises and heart rate drops at the same pace. Keep sessions easy. Some athletes use a warm bath after training, but start carefully.
steps.proof: 10 warm easy sessions in 14 days with heart rate noted.
steps.pitfall: Doing hard intervals in the heat on day 1 of adapting.

problems.prompt: Does heat adaptation take about 10 to 14 days, or 2?
Your heart rate at the same easy pace drops from 150 to 140 over 12 days in heat. What does it show?
On day 3 of adapting, should the 45 minute session be hard or easy?

steps.title: Dress for the Cold
steps.mastery: Layer up for cold so you stay warm without overheating.
steps.practice: For 2 runs below 40 F, wear 3 layers: a wicking base, an insulating middle and a wind shell, plus gloves and a hat.
steps.detail: Dress as if it's 15 to 20 F warmer than it is, since you'll heat up. A wicking base keeps sweat off the skin. A light middle layer adds warmth. A shell blocks wind. Hands and ears lose heat fast.
steps.proof: 2 cold runs done with 3 layers, noting comfort.
steps.pitfall: Wearing cotton that gets soaked and freezes.

problems.prompt: It's 30 F. Dress as if it's what temperature?
Why avoid a cotton T-shirt as the base layer at 30 F?
problems.answer: It holds sweat and gets cold.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 layers.
problems.answer: Wicking base, insulating middle and wind shell.

steps.title: Adjust for Altitude
steps.mastery: Expect slower paces at altitude and give the body a week or more to adjust.
steps.practice: If you train above 5,000 feet, slow easy pace by about 5 to 10 percent for the first 7 days and log morning heart rate.
steps.detail: Thinner air carries less oxygen, so paces slow and heart rate climbs at the same effort. The first few days are the hardest. Drink more, sleep well and keep sessions easy at first. Morning heart rate settling back toward normal is a good sign you're adjusting.
steps.proof: 7 days at altitude with pace and morning heart rate logged.
steps.pitfall: Racing a hard workout on day 1 after flying in to the mountains.

problems.prompt: Your sea level easy pace is 9:00 per mile. What's a fair pace at 7,000 feet?
Morning heart rate is 62 on day 1 and 55 on day 7. What does it suggest?
Name 2 habits to increase in your first 3 days at altitude.

steps.title: Plan the Week Around Weather
steps.mastery: Move key sessions to the days the weather allows good quality.
steps.practice: Check the 7 day forecast each Sunday and place your hard session on the coolest or calmest day.
steps.detail: A hard session in 95 F heat or a 30 mph headwind loses much of its value. Moving it 1 or 2 days often fixes that. Easy days are more flexible, so they can take the worst weather. Indoor options like a treadmill help too.
steps.proof: 4 weeks planned around the forecast.
steps.pitfall: Doing intervals on the hottest afternoon of the week because the plan says Tuesday.

problems.prompt: Tuesday is 95 F and Thursday is 70 F. When do intervals go?
A storm is forecast for Saturday, your long run day. Name 2 options.
problems.answer: Move it to Sunday or Friday, or use a treadmill.

problems.prompt: Of your 5 sessions, which can take the worst weather: easy or hard?

steps.title: Run Short Hill Sprints
steps.mastery: Build power with short, near-max uphill efforts and full recovery.
steps.practice: Find a steep hill and run 6 sprints of 10 seconds uphill, walking back down to recover fully between each.
steps.detail: Short hill sprints build leg power with less impact than flat sprints, because the slope shortens your stride and slows the landing. Go hard but stay relaxed. Walk all the way down and wait until breathing settles. Quality matters more than tiredness here.
steps.proof: 6 hill sprints of 10 seconds with full walk-back recovery.
steps.pitfall: Jogging back down quickly and turning power work into a gasping workout.

problems.prompt: Why are 10 second hill sprints easier on the legs than flat sprints?
problems.answer: The slope shortens your stride and softens the landing.

problems.prompt: After sprint 4, you're still breathing hard at the bottom. What do you do?
problems.answer: Wait until breathing settles before the next one.

problems.prompt: How long is each sprint: 10 seconds or 2 minutes?

steps.title: Run Longer Hill Repeats
steps.mastery: Use 1 to 3 minute uphill efforts to build strength and aerobic power together.
steps.practice: Run 5 hill repeats of 90 seconds at a hard effort on a steady grade, jogging down as recovery.
steps.detail: Longer hill reps work like intervals with built-in strength work. Pick a steady, moderate grade. Keep an even effort, not an even pace, since the hill slows you. Lean slightly from the ankles and drive the arms.
steps.proof: 5 repeats of 90 seconds at an even hard effort.
steps.pitfall: Bounding up the first 30 seconds and crawling the rest.

problems.prompt: On 5 hill repeats, should you hold even pace or even effort?
How do you recover between 90 second repeats?
Name 2 form cues for uphill running.
problems.answer: Lean from the ankles and drive the arms.

steps.title: Practice Downhill
steps.mastery: Learn controlled downhill running, where impact and skill both peak.
steps.practice: Run 4 gentle downhill strides of 30 seconds, with quick light steps and a slight forward lean.
steps.detail: Downhill is where the damage happens, since muscles brake as they lengthen. Start on gentle slopes. Take quick, short steps. Lean slightly with the hill rather than back against it. Sore quads the next day are normal at first.
steps.proof: 4 downhill strides done with quick, light steps.
steps.pitfall: Leaning back and slamming the heels on every step.

problems.prompt: Why do 4 downhill strides leave quads sorer than 4 uphill ones?
On a 3 percent downhill, should you lean back or slightly forward?
Should your first 4 downhill strides be on a steep or gentle slope?

steps.title: Roll Through Hilly Easy Runs
steps.mastery: Get stronger legs from rolling routes while the effort stays easy.
steps.practice: Run 2 easy runs a week on a hilly route for 4 weeks, slowing or walking on climbs so you can still talk.
steps.detail: Rolling terrain builds leg strength without a formal session. The catch is effort: climbs push your heart rate up fast. Slow down on the way up, walk the steep parts if needed and let gravity help on the way down. The talk test still applies.
steps.proof: 4 weeks with 2 hilly easy runs a week at talking effort.
steps.pitfall: Charging every hill on an easy day and turning it into a hard session.

problems.prompt: Your heart rate jumps from 135 to 165 on a climb during an easy run. What do you do?
problems.answer: Slow down or walk until you can talk again.

problems.prompt: Is walking a steep 200 meter section of an easy run OK?
You did 2 hilly easy runs and 1 hill session this week. Is that 3 hard days?
problems.answer: No. The easy runs stay easy if you control effort.

steps.title: Find Hills on Flat Ground
steps.mastery: Get hill training when there are no hills nearby.
steps.practice: Run 6 reps of 2 minutes on a treadmill at 6 percent incline, or climb stairs for 6 sets of 1 minute.
steps.detail: Living somewhere flat doesn't rule out hill work. A treadmill at 4 to 8 percent incline, a stairwell, a stadium or a parking garage ramp all work. Match the effort to an outdoor hill rep and walk or jog easy between reps.
steps.proof: 1 session of incline or stair reps done.
steps.pitfall: Skipping hill work all season because there are no hills.

problems.prompt: Name 3 hill substitutes in a flat city.
problems.answer: A treadmill incline, stairs and a parking garage ramp.

problems.prompt: Does a 1 percent treadmill incline work for hill reps, or more like 4 to 8?
You do 6 stair climbs of 1 minute. How do you recover between them?
problems.answer: Walk or jog easily back down.

steps.title: Put Hills Before Speed
steps.mastery: Use a hill phase to build strength before faster flat work.
steps.practice: Plan a 4 week block with 1 hill session a week, followed by a block of flat intervals.
steps.detail: Hills build strength in the calves, hips and feet with less pounding. That strength makes flat speed work safer later. Many plans start a season with hills, then shift to flat intervals as the race gets close.
steps.proof: A 4 week hill block planned before flat intervals.
steps.pitfall: Jumping into fast track intervals in week 1 with no strength base.

problems.prompt: Why do 4 weeks of hills before track intervals?
problems.answer: Hills build strength that makes speed work safer.

problems.prompt: Your race is 12 weeks away. Where might the hill block go?
Name 2 areas hills strengthen.

steps.title: Learn the Common Four
steps.mastery: Know the usual overuse injuries in endurance sports and where each one hurts.
steps.practice: Write where 4 common injuries hurt: shin splints, runner's knee, Achilles pain and plantar fasciitis.
steps.detail: Most endurance injuries come from overuse rather than accidents. Shin splints ache along the inner shin bone. Runner's knee aches around or behind the kneecap. Achilles pain sits in the cord above the heel. Plantar fasciitis hurts under the heel, worst with the first steps in the morning.
steps.proof: 4 injuries written with where each one hurts.
steps.pitfall: Calling every ache "just soreness" without noticing where it is.

problems.prompt: Pain under your heel is worst for the first 5 steps after waking. Which injury fits?
You feel a dull ache along the inner edge of both shins after runs. Which injury fits?
The cord 2 inches above your heel is sore and stiff. Which injury fits?

steps.title: Spot the Early Warning
steps.mastery: Catch an injury in the quiet week before it becomes serious.
steps.practice: After each session for 4 weeks, rate any ache from 0 to 10 and note where it is.
steps.detail: Almost every overuse injury whispers for a week before it shouts. A niggle that's a 2 out of 10 and fades during warm-up is a warning. One that gets worse during a run, or is still there the next morning, needs action now. A simple log makes the pattern obvious.
steps.proof: 4 weeks of ache ratings with locations.
steps.pitfall: Running through a niggle that's been climbing for 10 days.

problems.prompt: Your shin ache goes 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 over 5 runs. What does it tell you?
An ache is 2 out of 10 and fades after 10 minutes of running. Is that a warning sign?
problems.answer: Yes, a mild one. Watch it closely.

problems.prompt: Pain gets worse during a run and makes you limp. What do you do?

steps.title: Use a Simple Pain Rule
steps.mastery: Decide ahead what level of pain means you keep going, modify or stop.
steps.practice: Write a 3 tier rule, like 0 to 2 keep going, 3 to 4 cut volume and intensity, 5 or more stop and rest.
steps.detail: Deciding in the moment goes badly, because you want to finish. A rule made ahead keeps you honest. Mild pain that doesn't change your stride can be OK. Pain that grows or changes how you move means stop. Sharp, sudden pain always means stop.
steps.proof: A written 3 tier pain rule kept with your training log.
steps.pitfall: Using "push through it" as your only rule.

problems.prompt: Your knee is 4 out of 10 at mile 2. Using the 3 tier rule, what do you do?
problems.answer: Cut the run short and make it easier.

problems.prompt: Sudden sharp pain in your calf at mile 1. What do you do?
Pain is 1 out of 10 and your stride feels normal. Can you keep going?

steps.title: Find the Cause
steps.mastery: Trace an injury back to the training change that likely caused it.
steps.practice: For your last ache, look at the 3 weeks before it started and list any jumps in volume, speed, hills or new shoes.
steps.detail: Injuries usually follow a change: more miles, faster sessions, more hills, new shoes or less sleep. Finding the cause stops it coming back. Fix the cause as well as treating the pain.
steps.proof: A list of changes in the 3 weeks before your last ache.
steps.pitfall: Treating the pain but repeating the same mistake.

problems.prompt: Your shins started aching 2 weeks after you went from 15 to 25 miles a week. Likely cause?
Your knee hurt after starting hill repeats 3 times a week. What change might help?
problems.answer: Cut hill sessions to 1 a week.

problems.prompt: Name 3 common changes that come before injuries.
problems.answer: More miles, faster sessions and new shoes.

steps.title: Keep Fit While You Heal
steps.mastery: Maintain fitness without loading the injured area.
steps.practice: Swap 3 runs for pain-free cross-training, like cycling or pool running, at the same effort and time.
steps.detail: Most injuries let you train in some other way. Cycling, swimming or pool running keep your fitness while the injury heals. Match the time and effort of the runs you skip. Keep anything that hurts out of the plan.
steps.proof: 3 cross-training sessions done while healing.
steps.pitfall: Stopping all training and losing fitness.

problems.prompt: Your shin hurts on runs but not on the bike. What can you do instead of a 40 minute easy run?
Name 2 low-impact options for runners.
Pool running hurts your injury too. What do you do?
problems.answer: Try another option or rest that area fully.

steps.title: Know When to See Someone
steps.mastery: Recognize when an injury needs a professional.
steps.practice: Write 4 signs that mean you'll see a doctor or physical therapist, like pain at rest or swelling lasting 3 days.
steps.detail: Some pain needs a professional: pain at rest or at night, swelling, a limp, pain that keeps getting worse, or a pinpoint spot on a bone. Bone stress injuries can turn into fractures if you keep going. Early help is faster help.
steps.proof: 4 written warning signs.
steps.pitfall: Waiting 6 weeks with a limp hoping it goes away.

problems.prompt: Your shin has 1 pinpoint sore spot on the bone that hurts to press. What do you do?
problems.answer: See a doctor. It could be a bone stress injury.

problems.prompt: Swelling around your ankle hasn't gone down after 3 days. What do you do?
Name 2 signs that mean see a professional.
problems.answer: Pain at rest and a limp, for example.

steps.title: Learn the Interval Shape
steps.mastery: Understand an interval session as repeated hard efforts split by planned recovery.
steps.practice: Write out 1 starter session: 10 minute warm-up, 6 reps of 2 minutes hard with 2 minutes easy, and 10 minute cool-down.
steps.detail: Intervals let you spend more total time at a hard effort than one continuous push would. Each rep is hard but controlled. The recovery is easy movement, so keep jogging or spinning. Warm-up and cool-down are part of the session and shouldn't be skipped.
steps.proof: A written session with warm-up, 6 reps, recoveries and cool-down.
steps.pitfall: Skipping the warm-up and starting rep 1 cold.

problems.prompt: 6 reps of 2 minutes hard. How many minutes of hard work is that?
During the 2 minute recovery, should you stand still?
problems.answer: No. Keep moving easily, like a jog or easy spin.

problems.prompt: Add up the whole session: 10 warm-up, 6 x (2 hard + 2 easy), 10 cool-down.

steps.title: Pace Rep 1 Like Rep 6
steps.mastery: Run every rep at an even effort so the last one matches the first.
steps.practice: Run 6 reps of 2 minutes and note the distance or pace of each, aiming for rep 6 within 5 percent of rep 1.
steps.detail: The classic mistake is a heroic first rep and a crawling last one. Pick an effort you could repeat 6 times. If rep 6 is much slower, start easier next time. Even reps train more than one great rep and five bad ones.
steps.proof: 6 reps logged, with rep 6 within 5 percent of rep 1.
steps.pitfall: Sprinting rep 1 and falling apart by rep 4.

problems.prompt: Rep 1 covered 500 meters and rep 6 covered 420. What went wrong?
Rep 1 is 500 meters. What's 5 percent less?
You finish rep 6 feeling you could do 2 more at the same pace. Is that OK?

steps.title: Cap It at 2 a Week
steps.mastery: Keep hard sessions to a dose you can recover from.
steps.practice: Plan 2 weeks with 1 or 2 interval sessions each, with at least 2 easy days between them.
steps.detail: One or two interval sessions a week is the usual dose. More than that piles up fatigue and starts to eat into easy days. Leave at least 2 easy days between hard ones so you show up fresh.
steps.proof: 2 weeks planned with 1 or 2 interval sessions and 2 easy days between.
steps.pitfall: Doing intervals 4 days a week because they feel productive.

problems.prompt: You did intervals Tuesday. When's the earliest next hard day?
Is 4 interval sessions a week a good dose for most people?
problems.answer: No. 1 or 2 is the usual dose.

problems.prompt: Why leave 2 easy days between hard sessions?

steps.title: Match Rep Length to the Goal
steps.mastery: Pick rep lengths that train what your event needs.
steps.practice: Write 3 interval sessions: short reps of 30 to 60 seconds, medium reps of 2 to 4 minutes, and long reps of 6 to 10 minutes.
steps.detail: Short reps train speed and turnover. Medium reps around 3 minutes push your top aerobic power. Long reps near threshold build the ability to hold hard effort. Mix them across a training block.
steps.proof: 3 interval sessions written, 1 for each rep length.
steps.pitfall: Doing the same 400 meter repeats every week for a year.

problems.prompt: Write a session with medium reps of 2 to 4 minutes.
problems.answer: 5 reps of 3 minutes with 2 minutes easy.

problems.prompt: Of the 3 rep lengths, which trains turnover and speed?
You're training for a half marathon. Which rep length matters most later in the plan?
problems.answer: Long reps near threshold, about 6 to 10 minutes.

steps.title: Take Recovery Seriously
steps.mastery: Use the recovery between reps so each rep starts ready.
steps.practice: In your next session of 5 reps, keep recovery at an easy jog or spin and start each rep only when breathing has calmed.
steps.detail: Recovery is part of the work. Too short and later reps fall apart. Too long and the session gets easy. Most sessions use recovery about equal to or a bit shorter than the rep. Keep moving gently.
steps.proof: 1 session with recoveries timed and breathing noted.
steps.pitfall: Standing bent over and gasping between reps.

problems.prompt: Reps are 3 minutes. What's a typical recovery?
Your breathing hasn't settled after 90 seconds of a 2 minute recovery. What do you do?
problems.answer: Keep the full 2 minutes, or extend it a little.

problems.prompt: For a 2 minute recovery, should you walk, jog or stand still?
problems.answer: An easy jog or spin is best.

steps.title: Log and Progress
steps.mastery: Track sessions so you can see fitness improve.
steps.practice: Log rep times or distances for 6 weeks and add 1 rep or 30 seconds per rep every 2 weeks.
steps.detail: Progress shows as more reps, longer reps or faster reps at the same effort. Change one at a time. Logging shows the trend.
steps.proof: 6 weeks of interval logs with steady progress.
steps.pitfall: Changing reps, length and pace all at once.

problems.prompt: Weeks 1 and 2: 6 x 2 minutes. What's a fair weeks 3 and 4?
Name 3 ways intervals can progress.
problems.answer: More reps, longer reps or faster reps.

problems.prompt: Why change only 1 thing at a time?

steps.title: Set Your Long Session
steps.mastery: Pick one session each week that runs longer than the rest.
steps.practice: Choose 1 day a week for your long session and set it at 1.5 times your usual easy session length.
steps.detail: The long session teaches the body to burn fat for fuel and teaches you what fatigue feels like late in an effort. Pick a day with time and no rush, like Saturday morning. Start at about 1.5 times your normal easy session.
steps.proof: A long session day chosen with a starting length written down.
steps.pitfall: Making every session long, which leaves no time to recover.

problems.prompt: Your usual easy run is 30 minutes. What's a fair first long run?
Name 1 good day for a long session if you work weekdays.
Should all 4 of your weekly sessions be long?

steps.title: Grow It Slowly
steps.mastery: Lengthen the long session in small steps so the body keeps up.
steps.practice: Add 10 minutes to your long session every 2 weeks for 8 weeks, logging how you feel after.
steps.detail: Growing the long session too fast is a common route to injury. Ten minutes every 2 weeks is safe for most people. Hold steady on any week that leaves you very sore. Keep it at easy pace the whole way.
steps.proof: An 8 week log with the long session growing by 10 minutes every 2 weeks.
steps.pitfall: Adding 30 minutes in 1 week because you felt good.

problems.prompt: Weeks 1 and 2 are 45 minutes. What are weeks 3 and 4?
After 65 minutes your knee aches for 2 days. What do you do?
problems.answer: Hold at 65 or drop back, and don't add more yet.

problems.prompt: Should the 65 minute long session be at easy pace or race pace?

steps.title: Fuel the Long One
steps.mastery: Practice eating and drinking during long sessions.
steps.practice: On long sessions over 75 minutes, take 30 to 60 grams of carbs per hour and sip water every 15 minutes.
steps.detail: After about 75 to 90 minutes, carbs start to matter. Gels, sports drinks or bananas all work. Start fueling early, around 30 minutes in. Practice in training so your gut gets used to it.
steps.proof: 3 long sessions with carbs and water logged.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until you feel empty to eat anything.

problems.prompt: Your long run is 90 minutes. How many grams of carbs might you take?
In a 90 minute session, should fueling start at minute 30 or minute 80?
Should you sip water about every 15 minutes or once an hour?

steps.title: Learn Late Fatigue
steps.mastery: Notice how your body and mind change in the last part of a long session.
steps.practice: Write 3 notes after each of 3 long sessions on how the last 20 minutes felt.
steps.detail: The last part of a long effort teaches you what fatigue feels like. Form might slip. Thoughts might turn negative. Noticing these helps on race day.
steps.proof: 3 sessions with notes on the last 20 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring how you feel late in the session.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing that might change late in a long run.
problems.answer: Form slips or thoughts turn negative.

problems.prompt: Why note how the last 20 minutes feel?
problems.answer: It prepares you for race day.

problems.prompt: Is 1 long session enough to learn late fatigue, or about 3?

steps.title: Recover After
steps.mastery: Recover well after long sessions so the next week goes well.
steps.practice: After 3 long sessions, eat a meal with carbs and protein within 60 minutes and make the next day easy or off.
steps.detail: Long sessions take more out of you. Eat within an hour. Sleep well. Keep the next day easy.
steps.proof: 3 long sessions followed by food within 60 minutes and an easy day.
steps.pitfall: Doing a hard session the day after a long one.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things the recovery meal needs.
You did a 2 hour long run Sunday. What should Monday look like?
Should the recovery meal come within 60 minutes or 6 hours?

steps.title: Work Out Your Goal Pace
steps.mastery: Turn a goal time into a pace per mile or kilometer you can actually hold.
steps.practice: Divide your goal time by the race distance to get your goal pace, and write it on a card for 1 upcoming race.
steps.detail: A goal time means little in the moment. A pace per mile or per kilometer is something you can check. Base the goal on a recent race or a hard training session, and be honest. A goal that's too fast ruins the whole race.
steps.proof: A goal pace written down for 1 race, based on recent results.
steps.pitfall: Picking a goal pace from a friend's result instead of your own training.

problems.prompt: Your goal for a 10K is 50 minutes. What's your pace per kilometer?
Your goal for a 5 mile race is 45 minutes. What's your pace per mile?
Your recent 5K was 27 minutes. Is a 22 minute 5K goal next month realistic?

steps.title: Start Slower Than You Want
steps.mastery: Hold back in the first part of a race, when adrenaline makes fast feel easy.
steps.practice: In your next race or time trial, run the first 25 percent at 5 seconds per mile slower than goal pace.
steps.detail: Going out too fast is the most common pacing mistake. In the first miles, adrenaline makes fast feel easy. Every second banked early usually costs 2 or more later. Starting slightly slow lets you finish strong.
steps.proof: A race with the first quarter at or just under goal pace, with splits logged.
steps.pitfall: Running the first mile 30 seconds faster than goal because you felt great.

problems.prompt: Your goal pace is 9:00 per mile. What should the first mile of a 10K be?
You ran mile 1 in 8:20 on a 9:00 goal. What usually happens later?
problems.answer: You slow down a lot near the end.

problems.prompt: Why does mile 1 of a race feel so easy?

steps.title: Aim for Even or Negative Splits
steps.mastery: Spread effort so you finish strong, with the back half matching or beating the front half.
steps.practice: Run a 30 minute tempo where the second 15 minutes are as fast or faster than the first 15.
steps.detail: Even or slightly negative splits are how most best times happen. It takes discipline early and courage late. Practice it in training first, so it feels normal on race day.
steps.proof: A 30 minute tempo with second half splits as fast or faster.
steps.pitfall: Starting hard and holding on for dear life.

problems.prompt: First half 15:10, second half 14:55. What kind of split is that?
First half 14:30, second half 16:00. What went wrong?
Why practice negative splits in a 30 minute tempo before race day?
problems.answer: So they feel normal on race day.

steps.title: Pace by Effort on Hills
steps.mastery: Hold even effort on hilly courses instead of even pace.
steps.practice: On a hilly 5 mile run, keep effort steady and let your pace slow uphill and quicken downhill, then compare splits.
steps.detail: Holding goal pace up a hill burns too much energy. Hold effort instead. You'll lose a little time uphill and get most of it back on the way down. Your watch will show uneven splits, and that's fine.
steps.proof: A hilly 5 mile run with splits and effort notes.
steps.pitfall: Charging up a hill to stay on pace and fading for the next 2 miles.

problems.prompt: Your goal pace is 9:00 and a mile has a big climb. Is a 9:30 split OK?
On a 5 mile hilly course, should you hold even pace or even effort?
Downhill mile in 8:40 on a 9:00 goal. Is that OK?

steps.title: Check Splits Without Panic
steps.mastery: Use split times to stay on plan without reacting to every second.
steps.practice: Set your watch to show average lap pace and check it once per mile during your next 2 races or tempo runs.
steps.detail: Checking your watch every 30 seconds causes jerky pacing. Look once per mile or kilometer. If you're more than 10 seconds off, adjust gently over the next half mile. Small swings are normal, especially near turns and aid stations.
steps.proof: 2 runs with splits checked once per mile.
steps.pitfall: Speeding up hard after a slow split at an aid station.

problems.prompt: Your mile 3 split is 9:12 on a 9:00 goal. What do you do?
problems.answer: Pick it up a little over the next half mile.

problems.prompt: In a 10K, should you check your watch about every kilometer or every 30 seconds?
problems.answer: About once per mile or kilometer.

problems.prompt: You're 3 seconds off goal pace. Do you need to change anything?

steps.title: Plan the Last Quarter
steps.mastery: Save energy so the final quarter of a race is your strongest.
steps.practice: Write a 3 part race plan for your next race: the first 25 percent, the middle 50 percent and the last 25 percent, with pace and focus for each.
steps.detail: Good racing saves the push for the last quarter. Start controlled, hold steady in the middle, then go. Writing it down makes it easier to follow under pressure.
steps.proof: A 3 part race plan written.
steps.pitfall: Racing without a plan and fading at the end.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 parts of the race plan.
problems.answer: First 25 percent, middle 50 percent and last 25 percent.

problems.prompt: Of the 3 parts, when should you push hardest?
In a 10K, roughly when does the last quarter start?

steps.title: Set the Goal and the Date
steps.mastery: Anchor a training plan to one event and a date.
steps.practice: Pick 1 goal event at least 12 weeks away and write the date and goal time or finish target.
steps.detail: A plan needs a finish line. Pick 1 main event. Twelve to 20 weeks gives time to build. Write a realistic goal, like finishing comfortably or a time based on a recent race. Smaller races along the way can be practice.
steps.proof: 1 goal event with a date at least 12 weeks out and a written target.
steps.pitfall: Training for 3 big races in 6 weeks with no clear main goal.

problems.prompt: Today is March 1. Is a half marathon on April 10 enough time for a 12 week plan?
Your recent 10K was 55 minutes. Is a 1:45 half marathon a realistic first goal?
problems.answer: Probably too fast. Something near 2:00 is more realistic.

problems.prompt: Name 1 use for a smaller race 6 weeks before the main one.

steps.title: Count Back the Phases
steps.mastery: Split the weeks before race day into base, build and taper.
steps.practice: For a 16 week plan, mark weeks 1 to 7 as base, 8 to 14 as build and 15 to 16 as taper.
steps.detail: Base builds volume with mostly easy work. Build adds harder, race-specific sessions. Taper cuts volume so you arrive fresh. Counting back from race day keeps each phase in the right place.
steps.proof: A 16 week calendar with 3 phases marked.
steps.pitfall: Starting hard intervals in week 1 and burning out by week 8.

problems.prompt: In a 12 week plan, roughly how many weeks might be taper?
Of the 3 phases, which has the most race-specific hard sessions?
Why count back from race day instead of forward from week 1?
problems.answer: So the taper lands right before the race.

steps.title: Keep 80 Percent Easy
steps.mastery: Hold most of your training time at easy effort.
steps.practice: Plan 1 typical week and check that about 80 percent of the minutes are easy and 20 percent moderate or hard.
steps.detail: Most successful endurance plans are roughly 80 percent easy and 20 percent hard. Easy work builds the base, and hard work raises the ceiling. Too much in the middle leaves you tired and slow.
steps.proof: A planned week with about 80 percent easy minutes.
steps.pitfall: Making every session moderately hard.

problems.prompt: Your week is 300 minutes. About how many should be easy?
Your plan has 150 easy and 150 hard minutes. What's wrong?
Why avoid making 3 of your easy days moderate?
problems.answer: It leaves you tired without building as much.

steps.title: Build in Easy Weeks
steps.mastery: Add a lighter week every few weeks so fatigue clears.
steps.practice: Mark every 4th week in your plan as a recovery week at about 70 percent of the week before.
steps.detail: Training breaks you down a little, and fitness is built while you recover. Three build weeks pile up fatigue, and a lighter 4th week lets you absorb it. Keep the routine and 1 short quality session, but cut total time by about 30 percent.
steps.proof: A plan with recovery weeks every 4th week.
steps.pitfall: Building for 16 weeks straight with no lighter week.

problems.prompt: Week 3 is 300 minutes. What's a 70 percent recovery week?
In a 16 week plan with every 4th week light, which weeks are recovery weeks?
You train hard for 3 weeks. When does most of the fitness actually get built?

steps.title: Anchor Each Week on Key Sessions
steps.mastery: Build each week around a few key sessions and fit the rest in around them.
steps.practice: For each build week, write 2 or 3 key sessions first, like the long run and 1 interval session, then fill other days with easy work or rest.
steps.detail: Key sessions are the ones that drive progress: the long session and 1 or 2 hard ones. Place them first with easy days between. Everything else exists to help you show up fresh for them. If the week gets squeezed, protect the key sessions and drop easy ones.
steps.proof: Every build week with 2 or 3 key sessions placed first.
steps.pitfall: Treating every day as a key session and arriving tired at the ones that matter.

problems.prompt: Your week has a Tuesday interval session and a Saturday long run. Where do easy days go?
problems.answer: Between them, like Wednesday, Thursday and Friday.

problems.prompt: A busy week leaves only 3 sessions. Which do you keep?
Name 2 common key sessions.
problems.answer: The long run and an interval session.

steps.title: Set Rules for Missed Days
steps.mastery: Decide ahead how to handle missed training so one bad week doesn't wreck the plan.
steps.practice: Write 3 rules for missed training, like "Miss 1 easy day: skip it," "Miss a key session: move it if 48 hours fit" and "Miss 5 or more days: repeat the week."
steps.detail: Plans break for illness, work and travel. Cramming missed sessions into the next days stacks fatigue and raises injury risk. Simple rules made ahead keep you from bad choices in the moment. After illness, ease back with a few easy days first.
steps.proof: 3 written rules for missed training.
steps.pitfall: Doubling up on Saturday to make up for a missed Thursday.

problems.prompt: You miss 1 easy day on Wednesday. What do you do?
You're sick for 6 days in week 9. What does your rule say?
problems.answer: Ease back in and repeat the week.

problems.prompt: You missed Tuesday's intervals. Thursday is 48 hours later and free. Can you move them there?
problems.answer: Yes, if Saturday's long run still gets a rest gap.

steps.title: Write the Race Plan
steps.mastery: Put pacing, fueling and timing for race day on paper before the day arrives.
steps.practice: Write a 1 page race plan with 4 parts: wake time and breakfast, warm-up, pacing by section, and fuel by time or mile.
steps.detail: Race day is full of noise and adrenaline. A plan made calmly beats decisions made in the moment. Keep it to 1 page. Put pace targets for each section and exactly when you'll fuel. Read it twice the day before.
steps.proof: A 1 page race plan covering the 4 parts.
steps.pitfall: Planning to "see how you feel" and going out far too fast.

problems.prompt: Your race starts at 8 am and breakfast takes 3 hours to settle. When do you eat?
Name the 4 parts of the race plan.
problems.answer: Morning routine, warm-up, pacing and fuel.

problems.prompt: Your plan says gel at minutes 30, 60 and 90. How many gels do you carry for a 2 hour race?

steps.title: Arrive Early and Warm Up
steps.mastery: Get to the start with time to spare and a warm-up that matches the race.
steps.practice: Plan to arrive 60 minutes before the start and warm up for 10 to 20 minutes, ending 10 minutes before the gun.
steps.detail: Rushing raises stress before you've run a step. Arrive with time for parking, the bathroom line and gear check. Shorter races need a longer warm-up with a few strides. Long races like a marathon need only a few easy minutes.
steps.proof: A race morning timeline with arrival and warm-up times.
steps.pitfall: Arriving 10 minutes before the start and sprinting to the line.

problems.prompt: Your race starts at 9:00. When should you arrive?
Which needs a longer warm-up: a 5K or a marathon?
Your warm-up ends at 8:50 for a 9:00 start. Is that about right?

steps.title: Hold Back for the First Third
steps.mastery: Run the first third of the race below what adrenaline wants.
steps.practice: In your next race, keep the first third at goal pace or up to 5 seconds per mile slower, and log splits.
steps.detail: Adrenaline makes the start feel easy. That's a trap. Run the first third at or slightly under goal pace. It feels too slow, and it's what lets you finish strong. Many best times come from patient starts.
steps.proof: A race with the first third at or just under goal pace.
steps.pitfall: Banking time early and paying for it later.

problems.prompt: Your goal pace is 8:00 per mile in a 6 mile race. What should miles 1 and 2 be?
Mile 1 felt easy at 7:30 on an 8:00 goal. What usually happens?
Why does holding 8:00 pace in mile 1 feel wrong?

steps.title: Fuel on the Clock
steps.mastery: Take fuel on schedule during the race, even when you feel fine.
steps.practice: In your next race over 75 minutes, take every planned gel or drink at its set time and tick each one off on your plan.
steps.detail: By the time you feel low on energy, it's too late to catch up, since the gut can only absorb so much at once. Fuel by the clock instead of by feel. Use only products you tested in training, and sip water with gels so they go down easily.
steps.proof: Every planned fuel taken on time and ticked off.
steps.pitfall: Skipping the 60 minute gel because you feel great at mile 8.

problems.prompt: Your plan says a gel at 60 minutes and you feel great. Do you take it?
An aid station at mile 10 hands out a drink you've never tried. Do you take it?
problems.answer: Better not. Stick to what you practiced.

problems.prompt: You missed the 45 minute gel. Should you take 2 at once at 60 minutes?
problems.answer: No. Take 1 and get back on schedule.

steps.title: Get Through Rough Patches
steps.mastery: Ride out low moments without deciding the whole race is lost.
steps.practice: Write 3 coping tools for rough patches, like a short phrase to repeat, splitting the race into chunks, or a 3 point form check.
steps.detail: Almost every race has a bad stretch. It often passes within a few minutes. Shrink your focus to the next mile or the next aid station. Repeat a short phrase like "light and quick." Run through a form check: relax shoulders, quick steps, drive arms. Take fuel if it's due.
steps.proof: 3 coping tools written and used in training first.
steps.pitfall: Deciding at the first bad mile that the race is ruined.

problems.prompt: Mile 9 of 13 feels terrible. What do you focus on?
Name 3 points in a quick form check.
problems.answer: Relax shoulders, quick steps and drive arms.

problems.prompt: You feel awful at 70 minutes and your gel is due. What might help?
problems.answer: Take the gel, since low energy may be part of it.

steps.title: Review Within 3 Days
steps.mastery: Learn from each race while the details are fresh.
steps.practice: Within 3 days of the race, write what went well, what didn't, and 1 change for next time, using your splits.
steps.detail: Every race teaches something. Splits show where pacing slipped. Notes on fuel, sleep and nerves show what to repeat. Pick just 1 change so the next race actually improves.
steps.proof: A short race review with splits and 1 change written.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the lessons and repeating the same mistake next race.

problems.prompt: Your splits slowed by 40 seconds per mile after mile 8. What might the 1 change be?
Name the 3 parts of the review.
problems.answer: What went well, what didn't, and 1 change.

problems.prompt: Why write it within 3 days?

steps.title: Protect Sleep
steps.mastery: Treat sleep as the main recovery tool in your training week.
steps.practice: Log hours of sleep for 14 days next to how each session felt from 1 to 10.
steps.detail: Most adaptation happens while you sleep. Athletes in hard training often need 8 hours or more. A short night shows up the next day as heavy legs and a higher heart rate. The log usually makes the link obvious.
steps.proof: 14 days of sleep hours beside session ratings.
steps.pitfall: Cutting sleep to fit in an extra early session.

problems.prompt: Your sessions after 6 hours of sleep average 4 out of 10, and after 8 hours average 7. What's the lesson?
problems.answer: Sleep strongly affects how training goes.

problems.prompt: You can either sleep 1 more hour or add a 30 minute run. Which helps more during a hard block?
Do many athletes in hard training need about 6 hours of sleep, or 8 or more?

steps.title: Eat Enough Every Day
steps.mastery: Eat enough to match training so your body can repair.
steps.practice: Track food for 3 training days and check that you're eating carbs and 20 to 30 grams of protein at each meal.
steps.detail: Under-eating is a common reason for stalled progress and frequent injuries. Hard training days need more carbs. Protein at each meal helps repair. If weight drops steadily while training is steady, you may need more food.
steps.proof: 3 days of food logged with carbs and protein at each meal.
steps.pitfall: Dieting hard during heavy training weeks.

problems.prompt: You train 2 hours on Saturday. Should Saturday's carbs be higher or lower than a rest day?
Your weight dropped 5 pounds in 4 weeks of steady training and you feel flat. What might help?
Is a common protein target about 20 to 30 grams per meal, or 5?

steps.title: Cap Effort on Easy Days
steps.mastery: Hold easy days below a set effort so they help you recover.
steps.practice: Cap heart rate on your next 6 easy sessions at about 70 percent of max, slowing or walking whenever you go over.
steps.detail: Easy days are part of recovery. When they drift into moderate effort, you never fully recover and hard days lose quality. A heart rate cap removes the guesswork. Expect to walk some hills at first, and watch pace slowly improve at the same cap over weeks.
steps.proof: 6 easy sessions logged with time spent under the cap.
steps.pitfall: Letting every easy run creep up to a moderate pace because it feels better.

problems.prompt: Your max heart rate is 190. What's a 70 percent cap?
You hit 145 on a hill during an easy run with a 133 cap. What do you do?
problems.answer: Slow down or walk until you're back under.

problems.prompt: After 8 weeks, your pace at 133 drops from 11:00 to 10:20 per mile. What does it show?

steps.title: Check Morning Heart Rate
steps.mastery: Use morning resting heart rate as one signal of how recovered you are.
steps.practice: Take your pulse for 60 seconds before getting out of bed for 14 mornings and mark any day 5 or more beats above your average.
steps.detail: A morning heart rate well above your normal can mean you're tired, getting sick or under-slept. It's one signal among several. Combine it with sleep, soreness and mood. If 2 or more look bad, swap the hard session for an easy one.
steps.proof: 14 mornings logged with your average and any high days marked.
steps.pitfall: Doing a hard interval session on a morning your pulse is 10 beats high and you slept 5 hours.

problems.prompt: Your normal is 52. Today it's 60 and you slept poorly. What do you do with today's hard session?
problems.answer: Swap it for an easy day.

problems.prompt: Your pulse is 4 beats high but you feel great and slept 8 hours. Change the plan?
problems.answer: Probably not. It's only 1 small signal.

problems.prompt: Should you count your pulse for 60 seconds or 5 seconds?

steps.title: Take Real Rest Days
steps.mastery: Schedule full rest days so tissues can repair.
steps.practice: Plan 1 full rest day a week for 4 weeks, with only light walking allowed.
steps.detail: Bones, tendons and muscles rebuild between sessions. A weekly rest day gives them time. Many athletes place it after the long session or before a key workout. Light walking, stretching or an easy chore is fine.
steps.proof: 4 weeks with 1 full rest day each.
steps.pitfall: Training every single day for 3 months and calling rest lazy.

problems.prompt: Your long run is Sunday. Name a good rest day.
Is a 20 minute easy walk OK on a rest day?
You haven't taken a rest day in 6 weeks and your shins ache. What do you change?

steps.title: Move Lightly the Day After
steps.mastery: Use very light movement to ease stiffness after hard days.
steps.practice: Add 20 minutes of easy cycling, swimming or walking the day after 2 hard sessions this week.
steps.detail: Light movement increases blood flow and can ease stiffness without adding fatigue. Keep it truly easy, about 3 out of 10. If it turns into a workout, it stops being recovery.
steps.proof: 2 active recovery sessions at easy effort.
steps.pitfall: Turning an active recovery ride into a hard group ride.

problems.prompt: On a 1 to 10 scale, how hard should active recovery feel?
Name 2 good active recovery options.
Your 20 minute recovery spin turns into 45 minutes chasing friends. Is it still recovery?

steps.title: Map Your Year
steps.mastery: Lay out a training year with a build, a peak and a true off-season.
steps.practice: Draw a 12 month calendar and mark 1 or 2 goal races, the build blocks before each, and a 2 to 4 week off-season.
steps.detail: Athletes who improve for a decade plan across whole years. Pick 1 or 2 main goals. Build toward each, then rest. An off-season of 2 to 4 weeks lets the body and mind reset. Smaller races can sit inside build blocks as practice.
steps.proof: A 12 month calendar with goals, builds and an off-season marked.
steps.pitfall: Racing hard every month of the year with no break.

problems.prompt: Your main race is in October. When might the off-season go?
Is it common to have 1 or 2 main goal races a year, or 10?
A 10K falls in the middle of your marathon build. How could you use it?
problems.answer: As a practice race or hard workout.

steps.title: Take a Real Off-Season
steps.mastery: Rest properly after a season so the next one starts fresh.
steps.practice: Plan 2 to 4 weeks after your main race with no structured training, only easy play like hiking, swimming or games.
steps.detail: An off-season that's really off lets small aches heal and motivation return. You'll lose a little fitness, and that's fine. Stay active with fun, unplanned movement. Coming back hungry beats coming back burned out.
steps.proof: 2 to 4 weeks of unstructured activity after your main race.
steps.pitfall: Skipping the off-season and starting the next build tired and sore.

problems.prompt: Name 2 off-season activities.
problems.answer: Hiking and swimming for fun, for example.

problems.prompt: You lose a bit of fitness in 3 weeks off. Is that a problem?
Why take 3 weeks fully off after a 6 month season?
problems.answer: To heal aches and refresh motivation.

steps.title: Rebuild the Base Each Year
steps.mastery: Start each new season with a solid base block.
steps.practice: Plan the first 6 to 8 weeks after the off-season as mostly easy volume, with strides and strength work.
steps.detail: Every season starts with base. Easy volume rebuilds the engine. Add strides and strength to stay sharp. Skip hard intervals for now.
steps.proof: A 6 to 8 week base block planned.
steps.pitfall: Jumping into hard intervals in week 1 of the new season.

problems.prompt: Should the new season's base block be about 6 to 8 weeks, or 1?
In week 2 of the base block, should you run hard intervals?
problems.answer: Mostly no. Strides and strength are enough.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things to add to easy volume.

steps.title: Grow a Little Each Year
steps.mastery: Raise yearly training in small steps so progress keeps coming for years.
steps.practice: Add up last year's training hours from your log and plan this year at 5 to 10 percent more.
steps.detail: Long careers are built on small, steady increases. A big jump in one year often ends in injury or burnout by spring. If last year ended hurt, hold volume flat and change something else, like more strength work or better sleep.
steps.proof: Last year's total and this year's target written down.
steps.pitfall: Doubling yearly volume because you had a good race.

problems.prompt: Last year was 300 hours. What's a 10 percent increase?
Last year ended with a stress fracture. Should you add 10 percent?
problems.answer: Probably not. Hold steady and fix the cause first.

problems.prompt: Name 1 change besides more hours that can bring progress.
problems.answer: More strength work or better sleep.

steps.title: Adjust for Life Stages
steps.mastery: Reshape training as work, family and age change instead of quitting.
steps.practice: Write 2 specific ways your training could change in the next 5 years, like fewer but longer sessions or more recovery days.
steps.detail: A new job, a baby or turning 50 doesn't end endurance training. It changes the shape. Shorter sessions, fewer days, more recovery or new goals keep you going. Planning for it ahead makes the change feel like a choice.
steps.proof: 2 written changes for the next 5 years.
steps.pitfall: Trying to train like you did at 25 with half the free time.

problems.prompt: You have a new baby and 4 free hours a week. What might change?
problems.answer: Fewer, shorter sessions focused on what matters most.

problems.prompt: You're 52 and recover slower. Name 1 change.
problems.answer: More easy days between hard sessions.

problems.prompt: You can't race a marathon this year. Name a new goal that fits 3 hours a week.

steps.title: Keep It Fun
steps.mastery: Protect the enjoyment that keeps you training for decades.
steps.practice: List 3 things you enjoy about training, like group runs or new trails, and build 1 into each week for 8 weeks.
steps.detail: Athletes who last are usually the ones who still like it. Plans that are all numbers can grind the joy out. Group runs, new routes, trail days or a fun race keep it fresh.
steps.proof: 3 enjoyable things listed and 1 included each week for 8 weeks.
steps.pitfall: Making every session a test against a number.

problems.prompt: Name 2 ways to make training more fun.
You dread every session for 3 weeks. What might help?
problems.answer: Add something you enjoy, or take a short break.

problems.prompt: Should all 5 weekly sessions have a pace target?
problems.answer: No. Some can be just for fun.

steps.title: Review Each Season
steps.mastery: Look back after each season and carry the lessons into the next.
steps.practice: After your main race, write a 1 page season review: total hours, best result, injuries, and 2 changes for next year.
steps.detail: A season review shows patterns that weekly logs hide. Maybe injuries always come in the same month, or you raced best after a certain block. Two changes are plenty.
steps.proof: A 1 page season review with 2 changes.
steps.pitfall: Starting next season without looking back at this one.

problems.prompt: Your shins hurt every March for 3 years. What might the review suggest?
problems.answer: Look at what changes in February and build more slowly then.

problems.prompt: Name 4 things the season review covers.
problems.answer: Total hours, best result, injuries and changes for next year.

problems.prompt: Should the review pick about 2 changes, or 12?

steps.title: Pick 4 Big Lifts
steps.mastery: Choose a few heavy lifts that cover the legs, hips and upper body for an endurance athlete.
steps.practice: Pick 4 lifts, like a squat, a Romanian deadlift, a split squat and a row, and write them as your strength menu.
steps.detail: Endurance athletes don't need dozens of exercises. A squat pattern, a hinge, a single-leg lift and a pull cover most needs. Single-leg work matters because running and cycling are one leg at a time. Keep the list short so sessions stay short.
steps.proof: A 4 lift menu covering squat, hinge, single leg and pull.
steps.pitfall: Building a 12 exercise bodybuilding session that leaves legs wrecked for days.

problems.prompt: Your menu has squats, leg press and lunges. What's missing?
problems.answer: A hinge and an upper-body pull.

problems.prompt: Why include 1 single-leg lift like a split squat?
problems.answer: Running and cycling load 1 leg at a time.

problems.prompt: A 12 exercise session takes 90 minutes. What's a better target for 4 lifts?

steps.title: Lift Heavy, Keep Reps Low
steps.mastery: Use heavy sets with low reps, which improves economy without adding bulk.
steps.practice: Perform 3 sets of 4 to 6 reps on each of your 4 lifts, stopping 1 or 2 reps short of failure.
steps.detail: Heavy, low-rep lifting makes muscles and tendons stiffer and stronger, which can make each stride or pedal stroke cheaper. It doesn't make endurance athletes bulky, since the volume is low and you burn a lot of energy training. Rest 2 to 3 minutes between sets.
steps.proof: 3 sets of 4 to 6 reps on all 4 lifts, logged.
steps.pitfall: Doing sets of 20 with light weights and calling it strength work.

problems.prompt: You squat 3 sets of 20 with an empty bar. Is that heavy strength work?
problems.answer: No. Heavy work is about 4 to 6 reps near your limit.

problems.prompt: Will 2 sessions a week of 3 sets of 5 make a runner bulky?
problems.answer: No. The volume is low and running burns a lot.

problems.prompt: Should rest between heavy sets of 5 be about 2 to 3 minutes or 20 seconds?

steps.title: Lift Twice a Week
steps.mastery: Fit two short strength sessions into an endurance week.
steps.practice: Schedule 2 strength sessions a week for 6 weeks, each on a hard day or the day after one.
steps.detail: Two sessions a week is the usual dose. Put them on hard days, after the run or ride, or the day after. That keeps easy days truly easy. Avoid heavy legs the day before a key session.
steps.proof: 6 weeks with 2 strength sessions each.
steps.pitfall: Lifting heavy the day before your long run.

problems.prompt: Your hard run is Tuesday and your long run is Saturday. When could you lift?
problems.answer: Tuesday after the run, plus Wednesday or Thursday. Avoid Friday.

problems.prompt: Is the usual dose 2 strength sessions a week, or 5?
Why avoid heavy squats the day before a 20 mile long run?

steps.title: Add Springy Jumps
steps.mastery: Add low-volume jumps that teach tendons to store and return energy.
steps.practice: Add 3 sets of 10 pogo hops and 3 sets of 5 bounds to 1 strength session a week for 4 weeks.
steps.detail: Running is a series of small bounces. Plyometrics train the Achilles and calves to act like springs. Start with pogo hops: small, quick jumps on the balls of the feet with stiff ankles. Bounds come next: long, springy strides. Keep total contacts low at first and stop when you start landing heavily.
steps.proof: 4 weeks of plyometrics once a week, with contacts logged.
steps.pitfall: Doing 100 jumps on day 1 and waking up with sore Achilles tendons.

problems.prompt: Your pogo hops get loud and heavy on rep 8 of 10. What do you do?
3 sets of 10 hops plus 3 sets of 5 bounds. How many foot contacts per leg, roughly, if bounds alternate?
problems.answer: About 30 hops and 7 or 8 bounds per leg.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 tissues these jumps mostly train.
problems.answer: The Achilles tendon and the calves.

steps.title: Lighten Up Before Races
steps.mastery: Keep some strength work near races while cutting the fatigue it causes.
steps.practice: Drop to 1 lighter session a week in the 2 weeks before a race, with 2 sets instead of 3 and no heavy legs in the last 10 days.
steps.detail: Stopping lifting completely for weeks loses some of the benefit. Instead, cut the volume and keep the weights moderate. Heavy leg work in the final 10 days can leave you flat on race day, so switch to upper body and light activation work.
steps.proof: 2 pre-race weeks with 1 lighter session each.
steps.pitfall: Squatting heavy 3 days before a race.

problems.prompt: Your race is Sunday the 20th. When is the last heavy leg session?
In the 7 days before a race, should you skip all strength work?
problems.answer: Not all. Keep light upper body or activation work.

problems.prompt: Your normal session is 3 sets of each lift. What's the pre-race version?

steps.title: Check It's Paying Off
steps.mastery: Track strength and endurance side by side to see if the lifting helps.
steps.practice: Log your 4 lifts and your easy pace at the same heart rate every 4 weeks for 12 weeks.
steps.detail: Strength work should show up in two places: heavier lifts and cheaper easy running or riding. Compare pace at the same heart rate, or power at the same heart rate on a bike. If lifts rise but endurance drops, check whether lifting is eating into recovery.
steps.proof: 3 check-ins over 12 weeks with lifts and easy pace logged.
steps.pitfall: Lifting for months without checking whether it helps your endurance.

problems.prompt: Lifts are up 20 percent and easy pace is 10 seconds per mile faster at the same heart rate. What does it show?
Lifts went up but easy runs feel heavy and slow for 3 weeks. What might be wrong?
problems.answer: Lifting may be cutting into recovery.

problems.prompt: A cyclist checks progress every 4 weeks. What do they compare instead of pace?
problems.answer: Power at the same heart rate.

steps.title: Pick the Taper Length
steps.mastery: Choose how long to taper based on the race distance.
steps.practice: Write the taper length for your next race: about 7 days for a 5K or 10K, 10 to 14 days for a half, 2 to 3 weeks for a marathon.
steps.detail: Longer races build more fatigue, so they need longer tapers. Short races need only a week or so. The goal is to arrive fresh but still sharp. Too long a taper can leave you flat.
steps.proof: A taper length written for your next race.
steps.pitfall: Tapering 3 weeks for a 5K and feeling sluggish on race day.

problems.prompt: Your race is a half marathon. How long might the taper be?
Your race is a 5K. Is a 3 week taper a good idea?
Your marathon is November 10. When might the taper start?

steps.title: Cut Volume, Keep Some Speed
steps.mastery: Drop total training while keeping a little intensity so you stay sharp.
steps.practice: Plan taper weeks that cut volume by about 30 to 50 percent but keep 1 short session at race pace each week.
steps.detail: Fitness is already built. The taper only lets fatigue clear. Cut total time or distance a lot, but keep some short efforts at race pace so your legs remember the speed. Stopping all intensity tends to leave you flat.
steps.proof: A taper plan with lower volume and 1 race-pace session per week.
steps.pitfall: Cutting all fast running and feeling heavy-legged on race day.

problems.prompt: Your normal week is 40 miles. What's a 40 percent cut?
Should a 7 day taper include any race-pace running?
Your race-pace session usually has 5 reps of 1 mile. What's a taper version?

steps.title: Expect to Feel Odd
steps.mastery: Recognize the strange feelings tapering can bring.
steps.practice: Write 3 taper feelings you might expect, like restlessness, heavy legs or worry about losing fitness.
steps.detail: Tapering often feels bad. Legs can feel heavy as they repair. You may feel restless with extra energy or worry you're losing fitness. These are normal. Trust the plan.
steps.proof: 3 expected taper feelings written.
steps.pitfall: Adding extra sessions in the taper because you feel guilty.

problems.prompt: Your legs feel heavy 5 days before the race. Is that normal?
problems.answer: Yes, it's common during a taper.

problems.prompt: You feel restless and want to add a long run. What do you do?
Will 10 days of lighter training make you lose fitness?
problems.answer: No. Fitness holds over that time.

steps.title: Sleep and Eat Well
steps.mastery: Use the taper to bank sleep and keep fuel steady.
steps.practice: Aim for 8 hours of sleep for the 7 nights before the race and keep meals normal, adding carbs for the last 2 to 3 days.
steps.detail: With less training, you have time to sleep more. Sleep 2 nights before matters most, since race-night sleep is often poor. Keep eating normally. For races over 90 minutes, add carbs in the last 2 to 3 days.
steps.proof: 7 nights of sleep logged and carbs increased for the last 2 to 3 days if racing over 90 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Cutting food a lot because you're training less.

problems.prompt: Your race is Sunday. Which night's sleep matters most?
Your race takes 3 hours. Should you add carbs in the last 2 to 3 days?
Your 5K takes 25 minutes. Do you need to carb load?

steps.title: Rehearse Race Morning
steps.mastery: Practice race morning so nothing surprises you.
steps.practice: Run 1 rehearsal 7 to 10 days before the race with the same wake time, breakfast, clothes and warm-up.
steps.detail: A rehearsal finds problems early: a breakfast that sits badly, socks that rub, a warm-up that's too long. Fix them before race day.
steps.proof: 1 race morning rehearsal done.
steps.pitfall: Trying new shoes on race day.

problems.prompt: Should the rehearsal be 7 to 10 days out, or the day before?
Name 3 things to rehearse.
Your socks rubbed in the rehearsal. What do you do?
problems.answer: Switch to a pair you know works.

steps.title: Keep the Last 2 Days Calm
steps.mastery: Use the final 2 days to stay loose and fresh without adding fatigue.
steps.practice: Plan the 2 days before the race: 1 easy 20 minute run with 4 short strides, then a rest day or a short walk.
steps.detail: Nothing you do in the last 48 hours builds fitness, but you can still add fatigue. A short easy run with a few 20 second strides keeps the legs awake. Spend the rest of the time resting, eating normally and laying out your gear the night before so race morning is simple.
steps.proof: A written plan for the last 2 days, with gear laid out the night before.
steps.pitfall: Running a hard tempo 2 days before the race to check fitness.

problems.prompt: Your race is Sunday. What might Friday and Saturday look like?
problems.answer: Friday rest, Saturday 20 minutes easy with 4 strides, or the other way round.

problems.prompt: How long is each stride: 20 seconds or 2 minutes?
Why lay out gear the night before a 7 am race?
problems.answer: So race morning is simple and nothing is forgotten.

steps.title: Find Your Threshold Pace
steps.mastery: Put a number on your threshold with a short test so every tempo session has a target.
steps.practice: After a warm-up, run or ride 20 minutes as hard as you can hold evenly, and take 95 percent of your average pace or power.
steps.detail: Threshold is the effort where you're breathing hard but in control. A 20 minute test is a common estimate: go as hard as you can sustain evenly for 20 minutes, then take about 95 percent of that average. Pace it so the last 5 minutes are your strongest.
steps.proof: A 20 minute test result and an estimated threshold pace or power.
steps.pitfall: Starting the test like a sprint and limping through the last 10 minutes.

problems.prompt: Your 20 minute test averaged 200 watts. What's your rough threshold?
Your test pace was 8:00 per mile. Is threshold a bit faster or a bit slower?
problems.answer: A bit slower, around 8:20 per mile.

problems.prompt: In the 20 minute test, which 5 minutes should feel strongest?

steps.title: Feel Comfortably Hard
steps.mastery: Learn what threshold effort feels like without a device.
steps.practice: Score 3 threshold efforts from 1 to 10 and write how many words you could say during each.
steps.detail: Threshold usually sits around 7 out of 10. You can say short phrases but can't hold a conversation. Breathing is deep and steady, not gasping. Learning the feel lets you train well on hills, wind or bad watch days.
steps.proof: 3 efforts with effort ratings and talk notes.
steps.pitfall: Drifting into an 9 out of 10 effort and calling it threshold.

problems.prompt: You can only gasp 1 word. Is that threshold?
On a 1 to 10 scale, where does threshold usually sit?
Your watch dies on a 3 mile tempo run. How do you hold threshold?
problems.answer: Use breathing and short phrases as your guide.

steps.title: Run Cruise Intervals
steps.mastery: Break threshold work into reps so you can do more of it at good quality.
steps.practice: Run 4 reps of 6 minutes at threshold with 90 seconds easy between them.
steps.detail: Cruise intervals split threshold work into chunks. Short recoveries keep the effort steady. You'll get 24 minutes at threshold, more than most people can hold in one go with good form.
steps.proof: 4 reps of 6 minutes at threshold with steady pace.
steps.pitfall: Running the reps faster than threshold so the last one falls apart.

problems.prompt: 4 reps of 6 minutes. How many minutes at threshold?
In 4 x 6 minutes, how long is the recovery between reps?
Rep 4 is 20 seconds per mile slower than rep 1. What does it suggest?

steps.title: Build to a Continuous Tempo
steps.mastery: Hold threshold effort for one longer block.
steps.practice: Over 6 weeks, build from 2 reps of 10 minutes to 1 continuous 20 to 25 minute tempo.
steps.detail: Once cruise intervals feel controlled, join them up. Shorter recoveries, then longer reps, then one block. Keep the pace steady and slightly conservative.
steps.proof: 1 continuous tempo of 20 to 25 minutes after 6 weeks.
steps.pitfall: Jumping straight to 30 minutes continuous in week 1.

problems.prompt: Week 1 is 2 x 10 minutes. What might week 4 be?
problems.answer: 2 x 12 minutes with a short break.

problems.prompt: What's the 6 week goal?
For a 20 minute tempo, should the pace be aggressive or slightly conservative?

steps.title: Fit It Into the Week
steps.mastery: Place threshold work so it doesn't crowd out easy days.
steps.practice: Plan 1 threshold session per week for 6 weeks, with 2 easy days on either side.
steps.detail: Threshold work is hard. One session a week, sometimes 2 for experienced athletes, is enough. Keep the rest easy.
steps.proof: 6 weeks with 1 threshold session each.
steps.pitfall: Doing threshold every day.

problems.prompt: Do most people need 1 threshold session a week, or 5?
Threshold is Wednesday. What are Tuesday and Thursday?
Why not do threshold work all 7 days?
problems.answer: It's too hard to recover from.

steps.title: Retest Every 6 Weeks
steps.mastery: Retest threshold to update your training paces.
steps.practice: Repeat the 20 minute test after 6 weeks and update your zones.
steps.detail: Fitness changes, so the numbers you train by should too. Repeat the same 20 minute test in the same conditions. If your number rose, raise your training paces or power targets to match, or your sessions slowly become too easy.
steps.proof: Retest done and zones updated.
steps.pitfall: Training with old paces for months.

problems.prompt: Should you retest every 6 weeks or every 6 months?
Your new test is 210 watts. What's the new threshold?
Your threshold rose 10 watts. Why update your zones?

steps.title: Total Your Week
steps.mastery: Add up weekly time or distance so you can manage it.
steps.practice: Add up the total minutes or miles from your last 4 weeks of training and write each week's number.
steps.detail: Volume is total work across a week. Most overuse injuries come from a jump in volume, more often than from bad form. Knowing your recent weeks is the first step to building safely.
steps.proof: 4 weekly totals written down.
steps.pitfall: Guessing your weekly volume.

problems.prompt: Week 1: 90 minutes. Week 2: 100. Week 3: 160. What stands out?
Name the most common cause of overuse injuries, given 4 weeks of logs.
Should your 4 weekly totals be in minutes or miles?
problems.answer: Either. Pick one and stay with it.

steps.title: Grow by About 10 Percent
steps.mastery: Raise weekly volume in small steps so bones and tendons keep up with the heart.
steps.practice: Plan 4 weeks where weekly volume grows by about 10 percent each week, written as minutes per week.
steps.detail: Your heart and lungs adapt faster than bones and tendons. That's why big jumps feel fine for a week, then something starts to ache. A rough guide is no more than about 10 percent more each week. Treat it as a guide and bend it when your body says so. If you're new or coming back, hold steady for a few weeks first.
steps.proof: A written 4 week plan with weekly totals rising by about 10 percent.
steps.pitfall: Doubling your weekly volume because your breathing felt easy.

problems.prompt: This week is 100 minutes. What's next week at 10 percent?
Your lungs feel great after a 50 percent jump, but your shins ache. Why?
problems.answer: Bones and tendons adapt more slowly than the heart.

problems.prompt: You're coming back after 6 weeks off. Should you add 10 percent right away?
problems.answer: Better to hold steady for a few weeks first.

steps.title: Add a Lighter Week
steps.mastery: Build in easier weeks so the body can absorb the work.
steps.practice: Make every 4th week about 30 percent lighter than the week before it, and keep 1 short quality session.
steps.detail: Three building weeks pile up fatigue. A lighter 4th week lets the body catch up and adapt. Keep the routine, just shorten sessions. Many people feel their best in the week after a lighter one.
steps.proof: A plan with every 4th week about 30 percent lighter.
steps.pitfall: Building for 12 weeks straight with no easy week.

problems.prompt: Week 3 is 130 minutes. What's a 30 percent lighter week 4?
In the week 4 lighter week, should you stop training entirely?
problems.answer: No. Shorten sessions but keep the routine.

problems.prompt: Why do many people feel strong in week 5?
problems.answer: Fatigue cleared in the lighter week.

steps.title: Watch the Warning Signs
steps.mastery: Catch the signs that volume is rising faster than you can handle.
steps.practice: Rate soreness, sleep and mood from 1 to 10 each morning for 4 weeks, next to your weekly volume.
steps.detail: Overuse injuries usually announce themselves quietly first. Sleep gets worse, a shin or Achilles nags, mood drops. When 2 or more slide for several days, hold volume or drop it 20 percent. Pain that changes how you move means stop and get it checked.
steps.proof: 4 weeks of morning ratings beside weekly volume.
steps.pitfall: Running through a limp because the plan says so.

problems.prompt: Sleep drops from 8 to 5 and your shin aches for 4 days. What do you do?
problems.answer: Hold or cut volume about 20 percent.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things to rate each morning.
You start limping on runs. What do you do?

steps.title: Spread the Load
steps.mastery: Split weekly volume across several days instead of a few big ones.
steps.practice: Spread your weekly total across at least 4 days, with no single day over 35 percent of the week.
steps.detail: The same weekly total is easier on the body in more, shorter sessions. Two huge days a week stack stress on the same tissues. Keep the long session as the biggest day, but cap it at about a third of the week.
steps.proof: A week with volume spread across 4 or more days.
steps.pitfall: Cramming 160 minutes into 2 weekend sessions.

problems.prompt: 160 minutes across 4 days. What's the average per day?
Your week is 200 minutes. What's 35 percent?
Why are 4 sessions of 40 minutes easier than 2 of 80?
problems.answer: Stress on the same tissues is spread out.

steps.title: Find Your Zones
steps.mastery: Split effort into a few bands so each session has a clear target.
steps.practice: Estimate your max heart rate as 220 minus your age and write ranges for 3 zones: easy 60 to 70, moderate 70 to 80, hard 80 to 90 percent.
steps.detail: Zones give each session a job. Three is enough for most people: easy, moderate and hard. 220 minus age is a rough guess. Many people are 10 beats or more off, so check it against feel and the talk test.
steps.proof: 3 zones written with heart rate ranges.
steps.pitfall: Treating 220 minus age as exact.

problems.prompt: You're 25. What's your rough max heart rate?
With a max of 195, what's the top of the easy zone at 70 percent?
Your hard sessions feel easy at 170. What might be wrong?
problems.answer: Your real max may be higher than the formula says.

steps.title: Use Feel as a Zone Guide
steps.mastery: Match each zone to how it feels so you can train without a watch.
steps.practice: Write how each of your 3 zones feels on a 1 to 10 scale and in talk test terms.
steps.detail: Feel works when devices don't. Easy: 3 to 4 out of 10, full sentences. Moderate: 5 to 6, short phrases. Hard: 7 to 9, a few words. Use both feel and heart rate together.
steps.proof: 3 zones with feel and talk test notes.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring feel because the watch says you're fine.

problems.prompt: Easy zone feels like what on a 1 to 10 scale?
In the hard zone, can you say a full 10 word sentence?
Your watch says easy but you can't talk. Which do you trust?

steps.title: Keep Easy Days Easy
steps.mastery: Hold easy sessions in the easy zone so hard days can be truly hard.
steps.practice: Review your last 5 easy sessions and count how many stayed in the easy zone the whole time.
steps.detail: The most common mistake is drifting into moderate effort every day. That leaves you too tired for hard days and too fast for real base work. Check your data.
steps.proof: 5 easy sessions reviewed with zone time noted.
steps.pitfall: Making every run moderately hard.

problems.prompt: 3 of 5 easy runs drifted into moderate. What do you change?
Why does drifting into moderate on 3 easy days hurt?
problems.answer: It leaves you tired for hard days.

problems.prompt: Name 1 tool to keep easy days easy.
problems.answer: A heart rate cap or the talk test.

steps.title: Make Hard Days Hard
steps.mastery: Push hard sessions into the hard zone so they do their job.
steps.practice: In your next session of 6 intervals, check that each rep reaches the hard zone.
steps.detail: Hard days should feel hard. If you're still in moderate, push more. Fresh legs from easy days make this possible.
steps.proof: 1 session with every rep in the hard zone.
steps.pitfall: Holding back on hard days because you're tired from moderate easy days.

problems.prompt: Your reps only reach moderate. What do you do?
problems.answer: Push harder, or rest more before the session.

problems.prompt: Why can you push hard on Thursday after 2 truly easy days?
Name 2 ways to check each of the 6 reps.

steps.title: Track Zone Time
steps.mastery: See how your week splits across zones.
steps.practice: Add up minutes in each zone for 1 week.
steps.detail: Most good endurance plans put about 80 percent of training time in the easy zone and 20 percent in moderate and hard. Add up a week from your watch or log and see how close you are.
steps.proof: Weekly minutes per zone.
steps.pitfall: Not knowing your split.

problems.prompt: 240 minutes total, 200 easy. What percent is easy?
What's a good easy share?
Your easy share is 50 percent. What do you change?
problems.answer: Add easy time or cut moderate time.

steps.title: Justify in Words
steps.mastery: Write the reason a calculus conclusion follows, in the form graders expect.
steps.practice: Write a 2 sentence justification for a relative max at x = 3 when f prime changes from + to -.
