steps.detail: Specific beats general. "My friend texted to check in" works better than "friends." Small things count, like a good coffee. After a week, many people notice good moments more during the day.
steps.proof: 7 nights of 3 specific good things.
steps.pitfall: Writing the same 3 vague words each night.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "family" as a specific good thing.
problems.answer: "My sister called and made me laugh."

problems.prompt: Is "a good coffee at 10 am" too small to count?
After 7 nights, what change do many people notice?
problems.answer: They notice good moments more during the day.

steps.title: Read Back Each Month
steps.mastery: Reread your journal to spot patterns you can act on.
steps.practice: On the last day of the month, read your entries and write 3 patterns you see.
steps.detail: Reading back shows themes that are hard to see day to day. Maybe you worry more on Sundays, or feel better after seeing 1 friend. Each pattern can lead to a change.
steps.proof: 3 patterns written after reading a month of entries.
steps.pitfall: Never reading back, so patterns stay hidden.

problems.prompt: Give 1 example of a pattern you might spot.
You notice you feel better on days you see Sam. What could you change?
How long should the read back take for 30 short entries?

steps.title: Get Morning Light
steps.mastery: Get outdoor light early to set your body clock.
steps.practice: Spend 10 minutes outside within 1 hour of waking, 7 days running.
steps.detail: Morning light is the strongest signal for your body clock. It helps you feel awake now and sleepy at night. Even on cloudy days, outdoor light is many times brighter than indoor light. Never look straight at the sun.
steps.proof: 7 mornings with 10 minutes outside.
steps.pitfall: Staying in a dim room until noon.

problems.prompt: You wake at 7. When should you get outside?
It's cloudy. Is 10 minutes outside still worth it?
problems.answer: Yes. Outdoor light is still much brighter than indoor light.

problems.prompt: How does light at 8 am help sleep at 11 pm?
problems.answer: It sets your body clock so you get sleepy at night.

steps.title: Find Green Space Nearby
steps.mastery: Know a few green spots close enough to visit often.
steps.practice: List 3 green spaces within 15 minutes of home and visit 1 this week.
steps.detail: Parks, community gardens, trails or a quiet street with trees all count. Closer beats prettier, because you'll actually go. Note how long each takes to reach so you can fit it into a lunch break.
steps.proof: 3 spaces listed with travel times, and 1 visited.
steps.pitfall: Counting only big trips to the mountains as nature.

problems.prompt: Park A is 5 minutes away, Park B is 40 minutes away and nicer. Which do you visit weekly?
problems.answer: Park A, because you'll actually go.

problems.prompt: Does a street lined with 20 trees count as green space?
Name 2 types of green space besides parks.

steps.title: Reach 2 Hours a Week
steps.mastery: Aim for a weekly total of time in green space.
steps.practice: Log every visit to a park or trail for 7 days and add up the minutes, aiming for 120.
steps.detail: Some large studies suggest about 2 hours a week in nature is linked with better well-being. It doesn't need to be all at once. Short visits add up. Six 20 minute park walks reach the target.
steps.proof: A 7 day log adding up to about 120 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Thinking it only counts if it's 2 hours in 1 go.

problems.prompt: 6 park walks of 20 minutes. How many minutes is that?
Can 120 minutes be split into short visits?
You've logged 75 minutes by Friday. How much more for the target?

steps.title: Notice What's There
steps.mastery: Pay attention to what you see, hear and smell outdoors.
steps.practice: On 1 outdoor walk, name 5 things you see, 4 you hear and 3 you smell.
steps.detail: Noticing turns a walk into a break from your own head. Birds, leaves, wind, distant voices, cut grass. Counting gives your attention a job. It's an easy way to be present without sitting still.
steps.proof: 1 walk with 5 sights, 4 sounds and 3 smells named.
steps.pitfall: Walking on autopilot and noticing nothing.

problems.prompt: Name 2 sounds you might hear in a park.
Why count 5 sights, 4 sounds and 3 smells?
problems.answer: It gives your attention a job and pulls you out of your head.

problems.prompt: You reach 3 sounds and get stuck. What helps?
problems.answer: Stand still for 30 seconds and listen.

steps.title: Bring Some Inside
steps.mastery: Add bits of nature at home for days you can't get out.
steps.practice: Add 2 natural touches at home, like 1 plant and a desk moved within 6 feet of a window.
steps.detail: Plants, daylight and a view of trees help on days you're stuck inside. Open the curtains first thing. Move your desk or reading chair closer to a window if you can.
steps.proof: 2 natural touches added at home.
steps.pitfall: Keeping the curtains closed all day.

problems.prompt: Name 2 ways to bring nature inside.
problems.answer: A plant and opening the curtains.

problems.prompt: Your desk faces a wall 15 feet from the window. What could you change?
problems.answer: Move it closer to the window.

problems.prompt: It's raining all of Saturday. How do the indoor touches help?
problems.answer: They give some daylight and green when you can't go out.

steps.title: Plan a Longer Trip
steps.mastery: Schedule a longer stretch outdoors each month.
steps.practice: Pick 1 date this month for a trip of at least 3 hours to a park, beach or trail.
steps.detail: A longer trip gives a deeper break than a lunch walk. Pick the date first, then the place. Check the weather the day before and pack water, snacks and a layer. Invite a friend if you like.
steps.proof: 1 outdoor trip of 3 hours or more done this month.
steps.pitfall: Planning a trip but never setting a date.

problems.prompt: What's the first thing to decide for a monthly trip?
Name 3 things to pack for a 3 hour trail walk.
It's the 25th and you haven't gone. What do you do?
problems.answer: Pick a date in the next 5 days and put it in the calendar.

steps.title: Pick 1 Practice
steps.mastery: Choose one small daily practice from this tree to keep.
steps.practice: Pick 1 practice, like a 5 minute sit or a 20 minute walk, to do every day.
steps.detail: Pick the practice that helped you most. Keep it small. A practice that survives busy weeks beats a big one that stops when life gets hard.
steps.proof: 1 practice named and written down.
steps.pitfall: Picking 5 practices and keeping none.

problems.prompt: You want to start sitting, walking and journaling. How many should you start with?
Is 5 minutes too small to count?
You've tried 5 practices. Which 1 should you pick?
problems.answer: The one that helped you most.

steps.title: Set a 2 Minute Floor
steps.mastery: Set a tiny version for bad days so the habit never fully stops.
steps.practice: Write a 2 minute version of your practice for hard days.
steps.detail: On bad days, do the floor. Two minutes still counts. It keeps the habit alive until normal days return.
steps.proof: A 2 minute version written down.
steps.pitfall: Skipping completely on bad days.

problems.prompt: Your practice is a 20 minute walk. What's a 2 minute version?
problems.answer: Step outside and walk to the corner and back.

problems.prompt: Does 2 minutes count?
Why have a 2 minute floor?

steps.title: Tie It to a Cue
steps.mastery: Link your practice to something you already do every day.
steps.practice: Pick 1 daily cue, like after coffee, and practice right after it for 14 days.
steps.detail: A cue makes it automatic. Pick something you do every day without fail. Do the practice right after.
steps.proof: 14 days of practice after your cue.
steps.pitfall: Relying on motivation.

problems.prompt: Give 2 examples of a cue.
problems.answer: After coffee and after brushing your teeth.

problems.prompt: Why use a cue like "after coffee"?
Will motivation alone carry you through 30 days?

steps.title: Track the Streak
steps.mastery: Keep a visible record so you can see the habit forming.
steps.practice: Mark each day you practice on a calendar for 30 days.
steps.detail: Seeing the streak helps you keep going. Mark it right after you practice. If you miss a day, don't miss the next one. Missing twice is when habits start to slip.
steps.proof: 30 days marked.
steps.pitfall: Quitting after 1 miss.

problems.prompt: What's the rule after a miss?
You practiced 25 of 30 days. Good or bad?
You practice at 7 am. When do you mark the calendar?

steps.title: Plan for Bad Months
steps.mastery: Plan how your practice survives hard stretches.
steps.practice: Write 3 things that might break your practice and a plan for each.
steps.detail: Travel, illness and busy weeks happen. Plan for them. Use the floor. Keep the cue even if the place changes.
steps.proof: 3 disruptions with plans.
steps.pitfall: Assuming nothing will get in the way.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things that might break your practice.
You're traveling for 5 days. What's the plan?
problems.answer: Use the 2 minute floor and keep your cue.

problems.prompt: Why plan for the 3 disruptions ahead of time?

steps.title: Review Every 3 Months
steps.mastery: Check whether your practice still fits your life.
steps.practice: Every 3 months, write what's working and 1 change to make.
steps.detail: Life changes and your practice may need to change with it. Keep what works and adjust the rest.
steps.proof: A dated review with 1 change noted.
steps.pitfall: Keeping a practice that no longer fits.

problems.prompt: Should you review every 3 months or every 3 years?
What 2 things do you write?
Your new job starts at 7 am. What might change?
problems.answer: The time or cue for your practice.

steps.title: Share It
steps.mastery: Teach your practice to someone to deepen your own.
steps.practice: Teach 1 friend your practice and do it together once.
steps.detail: Teaching helps you understand it better. Doing it together adds support and fun. You might gain a practice partner.
steps.proof: 1 friend taught and 1 session together.
steps.pitfall: Keeping it all to yourself.

problems.prompt: Why teach your practice to 1 friend?
problems.answer: It helps you understand it better.

problems.prompt: After 1 shared session, what might you gain?
Should you teach 1 friend or 10 to start?

steps.title: Name Real Rest
steps.mastery: Tell rest apart from activities that just keep the brain busy.
steps.practice: List 10 things you do to unwind and mark each one as rest or stimulation.
steps.detail: Real rest gives the brain a break from input. Scrolling, TV and games often feel restful but keep the brain busy. Rest looks like a walk with no headphones, sitting outside or lying down with eyes closed.
steps.proof: 10 activities sorted, with at least 3 true rest options.
steps.pitfall: Counting 2 hours of scrolling as rest.

problems.prompt: Is 1 hour of scrolling rest or stimulation?
Name 2 examples of real rest.
problems.answer: A walk with no headphones and sitting outside.

problems.prompt: You watched 3 episodes and feel more tired. Why?
problems.answer: It kept your brain busy instead of resting it.

steps.title: Take a No Input Walk
steps.mastery: Walk with no phone, music or podcast, and let the mind wander.
steps.practice: Walk for 20 minutes with no headphones and no phone checks.
steps.detail: Most walks now come with a podcast. Without one, the mind wanders, sorts things out and rests. It might feel boring at first. That boredom is part of the rest.
steps.proof: A 20 minute walk with no headphones or phone checks.
steps.pitfall: Bringing earbuds "just in case," then putting them in.

problems.prompt: On a 20 minute no input walk, what do you leave behind?
problems.answer: Headphones and music, or anything that plays audio.

problems.prompt: The first 5 minutes feel boring. Is that a problem?
problems.answer: No. Boredom is part of the rest.

problems.prompt: With no input for 20 minutes, what does the mind do?
problems.answer: It wanders and sorts things out.

steps.title: Do Nothing for 10 Minutes
steps.mastery: Sit with no task and no input, just letting time pass.
steps.practice: Sit somewhere comfortable for 10 minutes with no phone, book or task.
steps.detail: This feels strange at first. You might feel restless or guilty. That's normal. Look out a window, watch the sky, or close your eyes. It isn't meditation, there's no task at all. It's a real break.
steps.proof: 10 minutes of doing nothing, without picking up a phone.
steps.pitfall: Treating it as a waste of time and stopping after 2 minutes.

problems.prompt: Is doing nothing for 10 minutes the same as meditation?
problems.answer: No. There's no task at all.

problems.prompt: You feel guilty at minute 3. What do you do?
Name 1 thing you can do while doing nothing.
problems.answer: Look out a window or watch the sky.

steps.title: Schedule Micro Breaks
steps.mastery: Add short screen-free breaks into the work day.
steps.practice: Take a 5 minute screen-free break every 90 minutes during 1 work day.
steps.detail: Long stretches of focus drain energy. A short break every 90 minutes helps. Stand up, look out a window, stretch or get water. Avoid the phone, which just switches screens.
steps.proof: 1 work day with a 5 minute break every 90 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Using breaks to check the phone, which doesn't rest the brain.

problems.prompt: In an 8 hour work day, how often should you take a micro break?
Name 2 good micro break activities.
problems.answer: Stretching and looking out a window.

problems.prompt: Is 5 minutes on your phone a good micro break?

steps.title: Plan a Rest Block
steps.mastery: Put longer rest time on your calendar each week.
steps.practice: Book 1 two hour rest block this weekend with no plans, chores or screens.
steps.detail: A whole afternoon with no plans can feel strange. But it lets the mind and body recover. Nap, sit outside, walk slowly or cook something simple. Protect it like an appointment.
steps.proof: A 2 hour rest block kept this weekend.
steps.pitfall: Filling the rest block with chores because you're free.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things you can do in a rest block.
problems.answer: Nap and sit outside, for example.

problems.prompt: Can you fold laundry during the 2 hour rest block?
Why put the 2 hour rest block on the calendar?
problems.answer: So it doesn't get filled with other plans.

steps.title: Notice How You Feel After
steps.mastery: Check which kinds of rest leave you fresher.
steps.practice: Rate your energy from 1 to 10 before and after 5 different rest activities this week.
steps.detail: Some activities leave you fresher, some just pass time. Rating before and after shows which ones work for you. Many people find walks and naps beat scrolling and TV.
steps.proof: 5 activities rated, with your top 2 named.
steps.pitfall: Assuming what works for others works for you.

problems.prompt: You rate 4 before a walk and 7 after. What does it show?
Why rate energy both before and after each of the 5 activities?
problems.answer: To see which rest truly works for you.

problems.prompt: Scrolling: 5 before and 4 after. Is it rest for you?

steps.title: Pick a Time and Place
steps.mastery: Tie a daily sit to a fixed time and spot so you don't have to decide each day.
steps.practice: Choose 1 time, like right after brushing your teeth, and 1 spot to sit for 10 minutes daily.
steps.detail: Habits stick best when they follow something you already do. After brushing your teeth, after coffee, or before getting into bed are common anchors. Use the same chair or cushion. The fewer choices you make each day, the more likely you'll sit.
steps.proof: A time, a place and a cue written down.
steps.pitfall: Sitting "whenever there's time," which usually means never.

problems.prompt: Name 2 good cues for a daily sit.
problems.answer: After brushing your teeth and after morning coffee, for example.

problems.prompt: Why use the same chair for all 7 days?
problems.answer: It removes a decision, so starting is easier.

problems.prompt: You plan to sit "when there's a gap." What usually happens?
problems.answer: There's never a gap, so it gets skipped.

steps.title: Start at 10 Minutes
steps.mastery: Keep the session short enough to do every single day.
steps.practice: Set a timer for 10 minutes and sit daily for 7 days.
steps.detail: Ten minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday. It builds the habit and the skill. If 10 minutes feels too long, start with 5. The timer means you don't keep checking the clock.
steps.proof: 7 sits of 10 minutes in 7 days.
steps.pitfall: Starting with 45 minutes, then quitting after 3 days.

problems.prompt: Which is better: 10 minutes daily or 70 minutes on Sunday?
Why set a 10 minute timer instead of watching the clock?
problems.answer: So you don't keep checking the clock.

problems.prompt: 10 minutes feels too long. What do you do?

steps.title: Set Up Your Posture
steps.mastery: Sit in a way that's upright and relaxed enough to last 10 minutes.
steps.practice: Sit on a chair with feet flat, back upright but not stiff, hands resting, for 10 minutes.
steps.detail: You don't need to sit cross-legged. A chair works well. Feet flat, back away from the chair back if you can, shoulders loose. Eyes closed or looking softly at the floor. If you hurt, shift. Comfort beats perfect form.
steps.proof: 10 minutes sitting upright without strain.
steps.pitfall: Forcing a cross-legged pose that makes your knees hurt.

problems.prompt: Do you need to sit cross-legged for a 10 minute sit?
Your back aches at minute 6. What do you do?
Name 2 options for your eyes.
problems.answer: Closed, or looking softly at the floor.

steps.title: Drop the Blank Mind Goal
steps.mastery: Let go of the idea that a good sit means no thoughts.
steps.practice: After each of your next 5 sits, write 1 line on what happened, not whether it was good.
steps.detail: Many people quit because they think they're doing it wrong. Thoughts will come. The sit is about noticing and returning. A short note, like "lots of planning, came back often", helps you see this without judging.
steps.proof: 5 one-line notes that describe the sit without grading it.
steps.pitfall: Writing "bad session" because thoughts kept coming.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "bad session, too many thoughts" as a plain note.
problems.answer: "Lots of thoughts, came back many times."

problems.prompt: Is a session with 50 thoughts a failure?
Why write "lots of planning" instead of "bad session, 3 out of 10"?
problems.answer: Grading makes you feel like you're failing.

steps.title: Track the Streak
steps.mastery: Keep a simple record so you can see the habit forming.
steps.practice: Mark each day you sit on a calendar for 30 days.
steps.detail: A visible streak helps. Mark it right after you sit. If you miss a day, start again the next day. Missing 1 day doesn't break a habit, but missing 2 in a row starts to. Aim for "never miss twice".
steps.proof: A 30 day calendar with your sits marked.
steps.pitfall: Giving up after 1 missed day.

problems.prompt: You miss Monday. What do you do Tuesday?
problems.answer: Sit as usual. Don't miss twice.

problems.prompt: You sit at 7 am. When should you mark the 30 day calendar?
You sat 24 out of 30 days. How did it go?
problems.answer: Well. That's a strong habit forming.

steps.title: Fix Your Wake Time
steps.mastery: Wake up at the same time every day to anchor your sleep.
steps.practice: Set 1 wake time and keep it for 14 days, weekends included, within 30 minutes.
steps.detail: A steady wake time is the strongest lever for better sleep. It sets your body clock. Bedtime follows on its own when you're sleepy. Big lie-ins on weekends act like jet lag every Monday.
steps.proof: 14 days waking within 30 minutes of the same time.
steps.pitfall: Sleeping in 3 hours on Saturday, which makes Sunday night hard.

problems.prompt: For your body clock, which of the 2 matters more: fixed bedtime or fixed wake time?
You wake at 7 on weekdays and 10 on weekends. What's the effect?
problems.answer: It's like jet lag every Monday.

problems.prompt: You wake at 7 on weekdays. What's a good weekend wake time?

steps.title: Make the Room Dark
steps.mastery: Block light so your body knows it's night.
steps.practice: Find and block 3 light sources in your bedroom, like a streetlight, a charger LED and a hall light.
steps.detail: Light tells the brain it's daytime. Even small lights can affect sleep. Use blackout curtains or a sleep mask. Cover little LEDs with tape. Keep the phone face down or in another room.
steps.proof: A bedroom where you can't see your hand in front of your face.
steps.pitfall: Sleeping with the TV on.

problems.prompt: Name 2 ways to block outside light.
problems.answer: Blackout curtains and a sleep mask.

problems.prompt: Your charger has a bright blue LED. What do you do?
You hold your hand 12 inches from your face at night. Should you see it?
problems.answer: Dark enough that you can't see your hand in front of your face.

steps.title: Keep the Room Cool
steps.mastery: Keep the bedroom cool, which helps you fall asleep and stay asleep.
steps.practice: Set your bedroom to about 65 to 68 F for 7 nights and note how you sleep.
steps.detail: Body temperature drops as you fall asleep. A cool room helps. Many people sleep best around 65 to 68 F, or about 18 to 20 C. Use lighter bedding if you wake up hot. A warm shower before bed can also help, since you cool down after.
steps.proof: 7 nights at a cool temperature, with sleep notes.
steps.pitfall: Cranking the heat up, which can cause restless sleep.

problems.prompt: What's a good bedroom temperature for many people?
problems.answer: About 65 to 68 F, or 18 to 20 C.

problems.prompt: You keep waking up hot at 3 am. What can you change?
problems.answer: Use lighter bedding or lower the temperature.

problems.prompt: Why can a warm shower 1 hour before bed help?
problems.answer: You cool down after, which helps sleep.

steps.title: Track Your Sleep
steps.mastery: Keep a simple sleep log to find patterns.
steps.practice: Write down bedtime, wake time and how rested you feel from 1 to 10 for 14 days.
steps.detail: A sleep log shows what helps and what hurts. Note caffeine, late screens or exercise too. After 2 weeks, look for patterns. Maybe late coffee means bad nights. Data beats guesses.
steps.proof: A 14 day sleep log with at least 1 pattern spotted.
steps.pitfall: Changing 5 things at once, so you don't know what helped.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things to log each day.
problems.answer: Bedtime, wake time and how rested you feel.

problems.prompt: Why log for 14 days?
problems.answer: It's long enough to spot patterns.

problems.prompt: Your log shows bad sleep after coffee at 4 pm. What do you change?
problems.answer: Stop coffee earlier in the day.

steps.title: Protect 7 to 9 Hours
steps.mastery: Give yourself enough time in bed to get the sleep you need.
steps.practice: Count back 8 hours from your wake time and set a bedtime alarm 30 minutes before that.
steps.detail: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Teens often need more. Count back from your wake time. A bedtime alarm reminds you to start winding down. If you're often tired in the day, you may need more.
steps.proof: A bedtime alarm set and kept for 7 nights.
steps.pitfall: Planning only 6 hours, then needing caffeine to get through the day.

problems.prompt: Do most adults need 5 to 6 hours of sleep, or 7 to 9?
You wake at 6:30. What's an 8 hour bedtime?
Why set an alarm 30 minutes before bedtime?

steps.title: Spot Short and Long Stress
steps.mastery: Tell useful short-term stress from long-term stress that wears you down.
steps.practice: List 5 stresses from this week and mark each one short-term or ongoing.
steps.detail: Short stress, like a deadline or a presentation, rises and then falls. It can help you focus. Ongoing stress, like money worries or a hard home situation, stays on. That's the one that wears you down and needs a plan.
steps.proof: 5 stresses sorted into short-term and ongoing.
steps.pitfall: Treating all stress as bad, when short bursts can help.

problems.prompt: A presentation on Friday. Short-term or ongoing?
Money worries every month. Short-term or ongoing?
Of 2 kinds, short-term and ongoing, which needs a plan most?

steps.title: Know Your Signs
steps.mastery: Notice the early signs that stress is building in you.
steps.practice: Write 6 signs you're stressed: 2 in the body, 2 in thoughts and 2 in behavior.
steps.detail: Stress shows up in different ways. In the body: tight shoulders, poor sleep. In thoughts: racing, worst-case thinking. In behavior: snapping at people, skipping meals. Knowing your signs helps you act early.
steps.proof: 6 personal signs, 2 in each group.
steps.pitfall: Only noticing stress when you're already overwhelmed.

problems.prompt: Name 1 body sign of stress.
problems.answer: Tight shoulders or poor sleep, for example.

problems.prompt: Name 1 behavior sign of stress.
problems.answer: Snapping at people or skipping meals.

problems.prompt: Why write 6 signs?
problems.answer: So you can spot stress building early.

steps.title: Complete the Cycle
steps.mastery: Help the body finish a stress response instead of carrying it.
steps.practice: After a stressful day, do 20 minutes of something physical, like a brisk walk or dancing.
steps.detail: The body gets ready for action when stressed. Moving helps it finish that cycle. A walk, a run, dancing in the kitchen or even a good cry can help. Thinking alone often doesn't clear it.
steps.proof: 20 minutes of movement after 2 stressful days.
steps.pitfall: Sitting still and replaying the day, which keeps the stress going.

problems.prompt: Name 2 ways to complete the stress cycle.
problems.answer: A brisk walk and dancing, for example.

problems.prompt: Why does a 20 minute walk help after a stressful day?
problems.answer: It helps the body finish the stress response.

problems.prompt: You replay a hard meeting for 2 hours on the couch. What might help more?

steps.title: Find What You Can Change
steps.mastery: Split a stress into what you can change and what you can't.
steps.practice: Take 1 ongoing stress and list 3 things you can change and 3 you can't.
steps.detail: Some stress has parts you can act on. Others you just have to accept. A long commute: you can change what you listen to, but not the traffic. Acting on what you can, and letting go of what you can't, eases the load.
steps.proof: 1 stress split into 3 changeable and 3 fixed parts, with 1 action picked.
steps.pitfall: Spending all your energy on the parts you can't change.

problems.prompt: Long commute. Name 1 thing you can change.
problems.answer: What you listen to, or when you leave.

problems.prompt: Why split a stress into 2 lists?
problems.answer: So you act on what you can and stop fighting what you can't.

problems.prompt: After making the lists, what's next?
problems.answer: Pick 1 action from the changeable list.

steps.title: Plan Recovery Time
steps.mastery: Build regular breaks so stress doesn't keep stacking up.
steps.practice: Schedule 3 recovery blocks of 30 minutes this week, doing something calming and screen-free.
steps.detail: Stress builds when there's no recovery. Plan it in like a meeting. A walk, a bath, reading a paper book or time with a friend all count. Screens often keep the brain busy, so they don't count here.
steps.proof: 3 recovery blocks done this week.
steps.pitfall: Using scrolling as recovery, which keeps the mind busy.

problems.prompt: Name 2 recovery activities.
problems.answer: A walk and reading a paper book, for example.

problems.prompt: Does 30 minutes of scrolling count as a recovery block?
problems.answer: Usually not. It keeps the brain busy.

problems.prompt: Why put 3 recovery blocks in the calendar like meetings?

steps.title: See a Thought as a Thought
steps.mastery: Notice that a thought is an event in the mind and may or may not be true.
steps.practice: Write 5 thoughts from today and put "I'm having the thought that" in front of each one.
steps.detail: Thoughts feel like facts, but they're things your mind produces. Adding the phrase creates a little space. You aren't arguing with the thought, just seeing it for what it is. That space makes it easier to choose what to do.
steps.proof: 5 thoughts rewritten, each starting with the new phrase.
steps.pitfall: Arguing with every thought, which keeps you tangled up in it.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "I'm going to fail" with the phrase.
problems.answer: "I'm having the thought that I'm going to fail."

problems.prompt: Does adding "I'm having the thought that" claim the thought is false?
problems.answer: No. It only shows it's a thought.

problems.prompt: After rewriting 5 thoughts, 1 still feels true. Is that OK?
problems.answer: Yes. The goal is space, and some thoughts may be true.

steps.title: Learn the Common Traps
steps.mastery: Name the common thinking traps so you can spot them.
steps.practice: Write an example from your life for 5 traps: catastrophizing, mind reading, all-or-nothing, "should" statements and labeling.
steps.detail: Minds fall into the same few traps. Catastrophizing jumps to the worst case. Mind reading guesses what others think. All-or-nothing sees only extremes. "Should" statements pile on pressure. Labeling turns one mistake into who you are.
steps.proof: 5 traps, each with a real example.
steps.pitfall: Believing a thought because it feels true.

problems.prompt: "If I mess up this test, my life is over." Which trap?
"She didn't text back, so she thinks I'm annoying." Which trap?
"I missed 1 workout, so the whole week is ruined." Which trap?

steps.title: Check the Facts
steps.mastery: Test a worrying thought against what you actually know.
steps.practice: Take 1 worrying thought and list 3 facts that support it and 3 that don't.
steps.detail: A thought can feel true without facts behind it. Listing both sides gives a fuller picture. Be fair to both. Often the facts against the worry are just as strong, which takes some of its power away.
steps.proof: 1 thought with 3 facts on each side.
steps.pitfall: Listing only facts that agree with the worry.

problems.prompt: Thought: "I always mess up presentations." Name 1 fact against it.
problems.answer: "The last 2 went fine," or a real example like it.

problems.prompt: You can only find 1 fact against the worry. What could help?
problems.answer: Ask a friend what they've seen.

problems.prompt: After listing 3 and 3, the worry feels smaller. Why?

steps.title: Write a Fair Thought
steps.mastery: Replace an extreme thought with a balanced one you believe.
steps.practice: Rewrite 3 extreme thoughts as balanced ones that you'd rate at least 6 out of 10 believable.
steps.detail: The goal is a fair thought, and it doesn't have to be cheerful. "I'll never get this" might become "This is hard right now, and I've learned hard things before." If you don't believe it, it won't help, so rate it.
steps.proof: 3 balanced thoughts, each rated 6 or more for believability.
steps.pitfall: Writing a fake happy line you rate 2 out of 10.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "I'll never get this."
problems.answer: "This is hard right now, and I've learned hard things before."

problems.prompt: Your rewrite feels 3 out of 10 believable. What do you do?
problems.answer: Make it more modest until it feels true.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Everyone hates me" fairly.
problems.answer: "Some people seem upset with me, and others still reach out."

steps.title: Let Thoughts Float By
steps.mastery: Let thoughts come and go without following each one.
steps.practice: Sit for 10 minutes and picture each thought on a leaf floating down a stream.
steps.detail: You don't need to act on every thought. Put each one on a leaf and watch it go. If you get pulled in, notice and come back to the stream. Pushing thoughts away tends to make them stick harder.
steps.proof: A 10 minute sit using the leaves picture.
steps.pitfall: Trying to block thoughts, which makes them louder.

problems.prompt: At minute 4 you realize you've been planning dinner for 2 minutes. What do you do?
problems.answer: Notice it, put the thought on a leaf and return.

problems.prompt: You try to push a worry away 5 times. What usually happens?
In the 10 minute sit, why picture leaves on a stream?
problems.answer: It shows thoughts come and go without you grabbing them.

steps.title: Keep a Thought Log
steps.mastery: Track thoughts and traps over time to spot your patterns.
steps.practice: Log 1 upsetting thought a day for 7 days: the thought, the trap and a fair version.
steps.detail: A log shows which traps you fall into most. Over time you'll catch them faster. Keep entries to 3 lines so the habit sticks. After a week, count which trap came up most.
steps.proof: A 7 day log with traps and fair versions.
steps.pitfall: Writing long entries that make you quit by day 3.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 parts of each entry.
problems.answer: The thought, the trap and a fair version.

problems.prompt: Mind reading shows up 4 times in 7 days. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: It's your most common trap, so watch for it.

problems.prompt: Your entries run to a full page and you skip day 4. What's the fix?

steps.title: Walk Daily
steps.mastery: Make a short daily walk a fixed part of the day.
steps.practice: Walk for 20 minutes every day for 14 days and mark each one on a calendar.
steps.detail: Walking lifts mood, helps sleep and clears the head, and it needs no gear. Tie it to a fixed time, like after lunch or before dinner. A rain jacket and good shoes turn bad weather into a small problem. Showing up every day matters more than distance.
steps.proof: 14 walks of 20 minutes marked on a calendar.
steps.pitfall: Skipping whenever it looks cloudy, so the habit never forms.

problems.prompt: You walked 12 of 14 days. Was that a good 2 weeks?
problems.answer: Yes. 12 days is a strong start.

problems.prompt: It's raining at 5 pm, your walk time. Name 2 things that help you go.
problems.answer: A rain jacket and good shoes.

problems.prompt: Is it better to walk 20 minutes daily or 2 hours on Sunday?

steps.title: Get Outside
steps.mastery: Take most walks outdoors for daylight and fresh air.
steps.practice: Take 5 of this week's 7 walks outside, at least 2 of them near trees or water.
steps.detail: Outdoor walks add daylight, air and changing views. Parks, trails and water tend to lift mood more than busy streets. A treadmill still helps fitness but misses the light. Even a quiet block with trees counts.
steps.proof: 5 outdoor walks this week, 2 near green space or water.
steps.pitfall: Walking only on a treadmill, which misses daylight.

problems.prompt: Name 2 places that count as green space for a walk.
problems.answer: A park and a trail, for example.

problems.prompt: A treadmill walk and a park walk, both 20 minutes. What does the park add?
You live on a busy street. Name 1 option within 10 minutes.
problems.answer: A quiet block with trees or a small park.

steps.title: Walk Slowly
steps.mastery: Walk at an easy pace that lets the mind settle instead of chasing a workout.
steps.practice: Take 1 walk of 30 minutes this week at a pace where you could chat easily the whole time.
steps.detail: Not every walk needs to count as exercise. An easy pace gives your mind room to wander and calm down. If you're too out of breath to talk, slow down. Look around instead of at your watch.
steps.proof: 1 walk of 30 minutes at a talking pace.
steps.pitfall: Turning every walk into a step count race.

problems.prompt: You can only say 3 words before needing a breath. Is this an easy walk?
problems.answer: No. Slow down until you could chat.

problems.prompt: On a 30 minute slow walk, what should you look at instead of your watch?
Name 1 benefit of a slow 30 minute walk.
problems.answer: It gives your mind room to settle.

steps.title: Walk to Think
steps.mastery: Use a walk to work through one problem.
steps.practice: Take 1 question on a 20 minute walk and write 3 ideas within 5 minutes of getting back.
steps.detail: Moving often loosens up stuck thinking. Bring just 1 question, like "How do I start the essay?" Don't force it. Let the mind wander back to it. Write ideas down soon after, before they fade.
steps.proof: 3 ideas written after a 20 minute walk.
steps.pitfall: Bringing 5 problems and walking around in a fog.

problems.prompt: You bring 4 questions on 1 walk. What happens?
Why write the 3 ideas within 5 minutes of getting back?
Turn "Fix my week" into a good walk question.
problems.answer: "What 1 thing would make Monday easier?" or something specific like it.

steps.title: Walk With Someone
steps.mastery: Turn walks into easy time with people.
steps.practice: Invite 1 friend or family member for a 30 minute walk this week.
steps.detail: Side by side feels less intense than face to face, so talk often flows more easily. It's a free way to see people. A standing weekly walk with someone also makes you more likely to go on days you'd skip.
steps.proof: 1 walk with someone this week.
steps.pitfall: Waiting for a perfect free day to invite anyone.

problems.prompt: Why can hard talks feel easier on a 30 minute walk?
problems.answer: Side by side feels less intense than face to face.

problems.prompt: How does a weekly walk with 1 friend help on lazy days?
problems.answer: You're less likely to skip when someone's waiting.

problems.prompt: Write a short invite for Saturday.
problems.answer: "Want to walk the park loop Saturday at 10?"

steps.title: Track the Effect
steps.mastery: Notice how walking changes your mood and sleep so you keep it up.
steps.practice: Rate your mood from 1 to 10 before and after 7 walks, and note your sleep each night.
steps.detail: Seeing the benefit helps the habit stick. Most people feel a bit better after a walk, often by 1 or 2 points. Note sleep too. If you sleep better on walking days, that's a strong reason to keep going.
steps.proof: 7 walks with before and after ratings, plus sleep notes.
steps.pitfall: Not noticing the benefit, so walks quietly drop off.

problems.prompt: Before: 5. After: 7. What changed?
You sleep better on 5 of 7 walking days. What does it suggest?
Why track for 7 walks instead of 1?
problems.answer: One walk can be a fluke. A week shows the pattern.

steps.title: Learn 5 Base Poses
steps.mastery: Hold five simple poses with safe form, covering forward bends, back bends, hips and rest.
steps.practice: Learn 5 poses: Mountain, Downward Dog, Child's Pose, Cat-Cow and Low Lunge, holding each for 5 breaths.
steps.detail: You don't need dozens of poses. These 5 cover the main ways the body moves. Use a beginner video or class to check your form. Bend your knees as much as you need. A mild stretch is the goal, and sharp pain means back off.
steps.proof: All 5 poses held for 5 breaths each without pain.
steps.pitfall: Forcing straight legs in Downward Dog on day 1, which strains the hamstrings and lower back.

problems.prompt: Your hamstrings pull hard in Downward Dog at breath 2. What do you change?
problems.answer: Bend your knees so the back stays long.

problems.prompt: Which of the 5 poses is the one to drop into for a rest?
You feel a sharp pain in your knee in Low Lunge. What do you do?
problems.answer: Come out of it, then pad the knee or make the lunge shorter. Sharp pain means stop.

steps.title: Move With the Breath
steps.mastery: Pair each movement with an in or out breath so the practice calms as well as stretches.
steps.practice: Flow through Cat-Cow 10 times, breathing in as the belly drops and out as the back rounds.
steps.detail: Matching breath to movement is what makes yoga feel different from stretching. It slows you down and gives your attention a place to rest. Opening moves usually go with the in breath and folding moves with the out breath. Keep the breath smooth and through the nose if you can.
steps.proof: 10 rounds of Cat-Cow with every move matched to a breath.
steps.pitfall: Holding your breath in a hard pose, which tenses the whole body.

problems.prompt: In Cat-Cow, does the in breath go with arching or rounding?
problems.answer: Arching, as the belly drops and the chest lifts.

problems.prompt: You fold forward from Mountain. In breath or out breath?
problems.answer: Out breath, since folding goes with the exhale.

problems.prompt: You notice you've held your breath for 3 seconds in a lunge. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: You're pushing too hard. Ease off until you can breathe smoothly.

steps.title: Build a 15 Minute Flow
steps.mastery: Put poses into a short sequence you can repeat without thinking.
steps.practice: Write a 15 minute sequence of 6 poses, from gentle to standing to lying down, and run it 3 times this week.
steps.detail: A short routine you'll repeat beats a long one you won't. Start on the floor to warm up, move to standing poses, then finish lying down. Save 2 or 3 minutes at the end to rest on your back. Write the order on a card so you don't stop to decide.
steps.proof: A written 6 pose flow done 3 times this week.
steps.pitfall: Picking poses on the fly each time, which makes starting feel like work.

problems.prompt: Your 6 pose flow starts with Warrior 2 and ends with Child's Pose. What would you change?
problems.answer: Start on the floor with Child's Pose, then standing poses like Warrior 2, and end lying down.

problems.prompt: Your flow is 15 minutes. How much of it should be rest at the end?
Why write the 6 poses on a card?
problems.answer: So you don't stop to decide what comes next.

steps.title: Use Props
steps.mastery: Use blocks, straps and cushions so poses fit your body instead of forcing it.
steps.practice: Use a block or a stack of 2 books in 1 pose and a strap or belt in another, 3 sessions running.
steps.detail: Props bring the pose to you. A block under your hand in a lunge keeps your back long. A strap around your foot lets you stretch a hamstring without rounding your back. A cushion under the hips makes sitting easier. Books and a belt work fine at home.
steps.proof: 2 poses done with props in 3 sessions.
steps.pitfall: Skipping props out of pride and rounding your back to reach the floor.

problems.prompt: You can't reach the floor in Low Lunge without rounding. What helps?
problems.answer: A block or 2 books under your hand.

problems.prompt: You don't own a yoga strap. Name 2 things that work instead.
A friend says props are for people who can't do yoga. Are they right?
problems.answer: No. Props help the pose fit your body and keep your form safe.

steps.title: Build Strength With Holds
steps.mastery: Use longer holds to build strength alongside flexibility.
steps.practice: Hold Plank for 30 seconds and Chair Pose for 30 seconds, 3 rounds each.
steps.detail: Yoga can be real strength work. Holding Plank, Chair and Warrior 2 works the core, legs and shoulders. Start at 20 to 30 seconds and add 5 seconds a week. Keep breathing the whole time, and stop when your form slips.
steps.proof: 3 rounds of 30 second holds in Plank and Chair Pose.
steps.pitfall: Letting the hips sag in Plank to last longer, which strains the lower back.

problems.prompt: Your hips sag at second 25 in Plank. What do you do?
problems.answer: Stop the hold. Good form matters more than time.

problems.prompt: You held Chair for 30 seconds this week. What's next week's target?
Name 2 poses that build leg strength.

steps.title: Keep It Going
steps.mastery: Practice often enough that flexibility and calm actually change.
steps.practice: Run your 15 minute flow 3 times a week for 4 weeks and note your forward fold reach each Sunday.
steps.detail: Changes come over weeks. Three short sessions a week work better than 1 long one. A simple marker helps you see progress, like where your fingers reach in a standing forward fold. Mid shin to ankle in 4 weeks is common.
steps.proof: 12 sessions in 4 weeks with 4 weekly notes.
steps.pitfall: Doing 1 long class and then nothing for 2 weeks.

problems.prompt: Which gives more change: 3 sessions of 15 minutes or 1 of 45?
Your fingers reach mid shin in week 1 and your ankles in week 4. What does it show?
You miss 2 sessions in week 3. What's the plan?
problems.answer: Pick up the next session as usual. Don't try to make them all up.

steps.title: Attention as Weighted Average
steps.mastery: Compute attention weights with softmax over similarity scores.
steps.practice: Compute attention weights for a query against 3 keys with scores 2, 0 and 0, then average 3 value vectors.
steps.detail: Each position scores every other, softmax turns scores into weights and the output is a weighted average of values.
steps.proof: Weights about 0.79, 0.11 and 0.11.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to apply softmax before averaging.

problems.prompt: Softmax of scores (1, 1)?
Values 10 and 20 with weights 0.25 and 0.75. Output?
Why divide scores by sqrt(d) with d = 64?
problems.answer: To keep scores from getting too large for softmax.

steps.title: Query, Key, Value
steps.mastery: Explain the 3 roles in attention.
steps.practice: For a 4 word sentence, write the shapes of Q, K and V with model size 8, and the shape of Q K^T.
steps.detail: Queries ask, keys answer whether they match and values carry the content. Q K^T gives a score for every pair of positions.
steps.proof: Q, K and V are 4 by 8, and Q K^T is 4 by 4.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up which matrix is transposed.

problems.prompt: Sequence length 10. Shape of the attention matrix?
Cost of attention grows how with length n = 1000?
What do the values hold, out of the 3 matrices Q, K, V?

steps.title: Multi-Head Attention
steps.mastery: Run several attention heads in parallel and combine them.
steps.practice: Split a model size of 512 into 8 heads and give the size of each head.
steps.detail: Each head can learn a different kind of relation, like syntax or position. Their outputs are joined and mixed by a final layer.
steps.proof: 8 heads of size 64.
steps.pitfall: Thinking each head sees only part of the sentence.

problems.prompt: Model size 768 with 12 heads. Head size?
Do the 8 heads share the same Q, K, V weights?
What layer mixes the 8 joined head outputs?

steps.title: Positional Information
steps.mastery: Add position information since attention ignores order.
steps.practice: Compute the sinusoidal position encoding for position 1 in the first 2 dimensions with model size 4.
steps.detail: Attention treats the input as a set. Adding a position signal tells the model which word came first.
steps.proof: sin(1) and cos(1), about 0.841 and 0.540.
steps.pitfall: Assuming attention knows word order by itself.

problems.prompt: Without position encodings, do "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same to 1 attention layer?
Name 2 kinds of position encoding.
Is the position encoding added or multiplied to the embedding of size 512?

steps.title: The Transformer Block
steps.mastery: Stack attention, a feed forward layer, residuals and normalization.
steps.practice: Draw a transformer block with 4 parts and label where the residual connections go.
steps.detail: Each block applies attention then a feed forward layer, each wrapped in a residual and layer norm. Stacking blocks builds depth.
steps.proof: A diagram with attention, feed forward, 2 residuals and 2 norms.
steps.pitfall: Leaving out the residual connections.

problems.prompt: Feed forward hidden size is often how many times the model size of 512?
Why add residual connections around each of the 2 sublayers?
problems.answer: To keep gradients flowing in deep stacks.

problems.prompt: GPT style models use which attention mask for 1 next token?
problems.answer: A causal mask that hides future positions.

steps.title: Chain Rule on a Graph
steps.mastery: Compute gradients by passing derivatives backward through operations.
steps.practice: Compute the gradient of L = (w x - y)^2 with respect to w for w = 2, x = 3 and y = 5 by drawing the computation graph.
steps.detail: Each node multiplies the incoming gradient by its local derivative. That is the chain rule, done backward from the loss.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to multiply by the local derivative at each node.

problems.prompt: d/dw of w x at x = 3?
d/du of u^2 at u = 1?
dL/dw for L = (w x - y)^2 with w = 1, x = 2, y = 4?

steps.title: Forward Then Backward
steps.mastery: Run a forward pass, store values, then backpropagate.
steps.practice: Run a forward and backward pass by hand for a 1 hidden unit network with ReLU on 1 example.
steps.detail: The forward pass saves every intermediate value. The backward pass reuses them to compute gradients efficiently.
steps.proof: All gradients for the 2 weights and 2 biases.
steps.pitfall: Recomputing forward values during the backward pass.

problems.prompt: ReLU derivative at input 3?
ReLU derivative at input -2?
Why store forward activations for 1 backward pass?

steps.title: Vanishing Gradients
steps.mastery: See how gradients shrink through many saturating layers.
steps.practice: Multiply 10 sigmoid derivatives of 0.25 together and compare with 10 ReLU derivatives of 1.
steps.detail: The sigmoid derivative is at most 0.25, so gradients shrink fast in deep networks. ReLU and residual connections keep them alive.
steps.proof: 0.25^10 is about 10^(-6), against 1 for ReLU.
steps.pitfall: Using sigmoid in every layer of a deep network.

problems.prompt: Max derivative of the sigmoid, reached at z = 0?
0.25^5 is about what?
Name 1 fix for vanishing gradients in a 50 layer network.

steps.title: Gradient Checking
steps.mastery: Compare backprop gradients with numerical estimates.
steps.practice: Check the gradient of L(w) = w^3 at w = 2 with (L(w + h) - L(w - h))/(2h) for h = 0.001.
steps.detail: A numerical estimate catches bugs in hand written backprop. The 2 should agree to many digits.
steps.proof: Numerical about 12.000001, against the exact 12.
steps.pitfall: Using a large h that makes the estimate inaccurate.

problems.prompt: Exact derivative of w^3 at w = 2?
Why use the centered difference with h = 0.001?
problems.answer: It is more accurate than a one sided difference.

problems.prompt: Backprop says 9 and the numerical check says 12. What does that mean?
problems.answer: The backprop code has a bug.

steps.title: Autograd in Practice
steps.mastery: Use a framework to compute gradients automatically.
steps.practice: Write 5 lines of PyTorch that compute the gradient of (w x - y)^2 at w = 2, x = 3, y = 5 and check it is 6.
steps.detail: Frameworks record operations and run backprop for you. Knowing what they compute helps you debug shapes and detached tensors.
steps.proof: w.grad equals 6.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to zero gradients between steps, so they add up.

problems.prompt: Which PyTorch call computes gradients for 1 loss?
Gradients doubled after 2 steps. Missing call?
Will a tensor created with requires_grad=False get a gradient after 1 backward?

steps.title: Fit the Residuals
steps.mastery: Build trees one after another, each fixing the errors left so far.
steps.practice: Run 2 boosting rounds by hand on 4 points: predict the mean, then fit a stump to the residuals with learning rate 0.5.
steps.detail: Each new tree fits what the current model still gets wrong. A small learning rate adds each fix gently.
steps.proof: Predictions move halfway toward each residual after round 2.
steps.pitfall: Using a learning rate of 1 and overfitting fast.

problems.prompt: Targets 2, 4, 6, 8. First prediction for all?
Residual for the point with target 8 after that?
A stump predicts 3 for it and the rate is 0.5. New prediction?

steps.title: Learning Rate and Trees
steps.mastery: Balance the learning rate against the number of trees.
steps.practice: Train gradient boosting with rates 0.3 and 0.03, using early stopping, and compare the best tree counts.
steps.detail: A smaller rate needs more trees but often generalizes better. Early stopping on a validation set finds the right count.
steps.proof: The 0.03 run needs roughly 10 times more trees.
steps.pitfall: Fixing 100 trees regardless of the rate.

problems.prompt: Rate 0.1 needs 300 trees. Roughly how many at 0.01?
Validation loss stops improving at tree 412. What does early stopping keep?
Going from 300 trees at rate 0.1 to 3000 at 0.01 usually costs what?

steps.title: Tune the Key Settings
steps.mastery: Tune tree depth, rows and columns sampled in boosting.
steps.practice: Tune max depth from 3 to 8 and subsample 0.6 to 1.0 for XGBoost with 5 fold CV.
steps.detail: Shallow trees with sampling usually work best. Depth controls interactions, and sampling rows and columns adds randomness that helps.
steps.proof: A chosen depth and subsample with their CV score.
steps.pitfall: Using depth 15 trees in boosting.

problems.prompt: Typical depth range for boosting trees, compared with depth 15?
Subsample 0.8 trains each tree on what share of 10,000 rows?
Why are shallow trees fine in boosting with 500 rounds?
problems.answer: Many trees add up the detail together.

steps.title: Boosting vs Forests
steps.mastery: Compare how boosting and random forests reduce error.
steps.practice: Train both on 1 tabular dataset and compare test score, training time and sensitivity to settings.
steps.detail: Forests average independent trees and are robust. Boosting fixes errors in sequence and usually scores higher but needs more tuning.
steps.proof: A table of score, time and tuning effort for both.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the default settings of boosting are always fine.

problems.prompt: Of the 2 ensembles, which reduces mostly variance, forest or boosting?
Which usually wins Kaggle tabular contests of the 2?
Which can train its 500 trees in parallel?

steps.title: Handle Categories in Boosting
steps.mastery: Feed categorical features to boosting libraries correctly.
steps.practice: Train LightGBM or CatBoost with 3 categorical columns as native categories and compare with one hot encoding.
steps.detail: Modern boosting libraries can split on categories directly. One hot encoding of high cardinality columns makes many weak features.
steps.proof: Native categories match or beat one hot with less memory.
steps.pitfall: One hot encoding a column with 10,000 values.

problems.prompt: One hot encoding a column with 50 values makes how many columns?
Which library is built around categorical features, CatBoost or XGBoost?
Why is target encoding risky without folds on 5000 rows?
problems.answer: It leaks the label into the feature.

steps.title: K-Means by Hand
steps.mastery: Group 1D or 2D points into k sets around movable centers.
steps.practice: Run 2 rounds of k-means with k = 2 on the points 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12 starting from centers 1 and 2.
steps.detail: Each round assigns every point to its nearest center and moves the center to the mean. It stops when nothing changes.
steps.proof: Centers end at 2 and 11.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to recompute the centers after assigning.

problems.prompt: Points 0, 2 and 10 with centers 1 and 9. Assignments?
New center for points 0 and 2?
Does k-means always find the best clusters from 1 start?
problems.answer: No, it can get stuck, so try several starts.

steps.title: Choose K
steps.mastery: Pick the number of clusters with the elbow and silhouette.
steps.practice: Run k-means for k = 2 to 8 and plot inertia, then mark the elbow and the best silhouette score.
steps.detail: Inertia always drops as k grows. The elbow is where the drop slows, and silhouette measures how well separated the clusters are.
steps.proof: A chosen k with the plot and silhouette scores.
steps.pitfall: Picking the k with the lowest inertia, which is always the largest k.

problems.prompt: Silhouette near 1 means what?
Silhouette near 0 means what for 2 clusters?
Inertia with k equal to the 100 points?

steps.title: Scale Before Clustering
steps.mastery: Standardize features so distance means something.
steps.practice: Cluster 200 customers on income in dollars and age in years, before and after standardizing, and compare.
steps.detail: Distances are dominated by the largest scale. Without scaling, income decides everything and age is ignored.
steps.proof: Clusters change after scaling, with age now mattering.
steps.pitfall: Clustering raw features with very different units.

problems.prompt: Income ranges over 100,000 and age over 60. Which dominates raw distance?
After standardizing 2 features, what is each standard deviation?
Does scaling matter for 2 features both in cm?
problems.answer: Less, if their spreads are similar.

steps.title: Other Clustering Methods
steps.mastery: Use DBSCAN or hierarchical clustering when k-means fails.
steps.practice: Cluster 2 interlocking moon shapes of 300 points with k-means and with DBSCAN and compare.
steps.detail: K-means assumes round clusters of similar size. DBSCAN finds dense regions of any shape and marks noise, and hierarchical clustering shows nested groups.
steps.proof: DBSCAN separates the 2 moons and k-means cuts across them.
steps.pitfall: Using k-means on clusters that are not round.

problems.prompt: Which method labels outliers as noise, of the 2?
DBSCAN needs which 2 settings?
A dendrogram of 50 points comes from which method?

steps.title: Check Clusters Make Sense
steps.mastery: Describe each cluster with its averages and decide if it is useful.
steps.practice: Summarize 4 customer clusters by the mean of 5 features and give each a short name.
steps.detail: Clusters only matter if they mean something. Profiling each with averages and naming it tests whether the grouping is useful.
steps.proof: 4 named clusters with their feature profiles.
steps.pitfall: Reporting cluster numbers without describing them.

problems.prompt: A cluster has high spend and low visits. Possible name?
2 of 4 clusters have nearly the same means. What does that suggest?
Can clusters from 1 random start of 4 runs differ?

steps.title: Convolution by Hand
steps.mastery: Slide a small filter over an image and compute each output.
steps.practice: Apply the 3 by 3 vertical edge filter [[1, 0, -1]] in every row to a 5 by 5 image with a dark left half and a bright right half.
steps.detail: Each output is the sum of the filter times the patch under it. Edge filters respond where brightness changes.
steps.proof: A 3 by 3 output that is large along the edge and 0 elsewhere.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the output shrinks without padding.

problems.prompt: Output size of a 3 by 3 filter on a 5 by 5 image, no padding?
Output size on a 32 by 32 image with padding 1 and stride 1?
Output size on 32 by 32 with a 3 by 3 filter and stride 2, no padding?

steps.title: Why Convolutions Share Weights
steps.mastery: Count parameters to see why convolution scales.
steps.practice: Compare parameters of a dense layer from a 32 by 32 by 3 image to 100 units with a conv layer of 32 filters of 3 by 3.
steps.detail: A filter reuses the same weights across the image, so patterns are found anywhere. That cuts parameters by orders of magnitude.
steps.proof: 307,300 for dense against 896 for conv.
steps.pitfall: Using dense layers directly on large images.

problems.prompt: Weights in 1 filter of 3 by 3 by 3, plus 1 bias?
Weights in 64 such filters?
Does a cat filter work in any corner of an image of 224 by 224?
problems.answer: Yes, the same weights slide everywhere.

steps.title: Pooling
steps.mastery: Shrink feature maps with max or average pooling.
steps.practice: Apply 2 by 2 max pooling with stride 2 to a 4 by 4 grid of numbers.
steps.detail: Pooling keeps the strongest response in each patch and halves the size. It adds some tolerance to small shifts.
steps.proof: A 2 by 2 output of the 4 patch maxima.
steps.pitfall: Applying pooling with stride 1 and barely shrinking the map.

problems.prompt: 2 by 2 max pool of [[1, 3], [2, 0]]?
Size after 2 by 2 pooling with stride 2 on 28 by 28?
Parameters learned by a 2 by 2 max pooling layer?

steps.title: A Small CNN
steps.mastery: Train a small convolutional network on images.
steps.practice: Train a CNN with 2 conv layers and 1 dense layer on 60,000 MNIST digits and report test accuracy.
steps.detail: Even a small CNN beats a dense network on images. Stacked filters learn edges, then shapes, then digits.
steps.proof: Test accuracy around 98 to 99%.
steps.pitfall: Training on unnormalized pixel values from 0 to 255.

problems.prompt: MNIST images are how many pixels on a side?
How many classes in MNIST?
Scale pixel values 0 to 255 into what range first?

steps.title: Data Augmentation
steps.mastery: Grow an image dataset with flips, crops and shifts.
steps.practice: Train a CNN on 2000 images with and without random flips and crops and compare test accuracy.
steps.detail: Augmentation shows the model new versions of the same image, which reduces overfitting when data is limited.
steps.proof: Higher test accuracy with augmentation.
steps.pitfall: Flipping digits like 6 and 9 where a flip changes the label.

problems.prompt: Should you flip images of the digit 6 left to right?
problems.answer: No, it changes what the digit looks like.

problems.prompt: Is augmentation applied to the test set of 500 images?
Name 3 common image augmentations.
problems.answer: Flips, random crops and small rotations.

steps.title: K-Fold Basics
steps.mastery: Rotate held out folds to get a steadier score.
steps.practice: Run 5 fold cross-validation on 500 rows and report the mean and spread of the 5 scores.
steps.detail: Each fold takes a turn as the test set. Averaging the 5 scores is less dependent on one lucky or unlucky split.
steps.proof: 5 scores with their mean and standard deviation.
steps.pitfall: Reporting only the best fold.

problems.prompt: Rows per fold for 500 rows and 5 folds?
How many models are trained in 5 fold CV?

steps.title: Stratified Folds
steps.mastery: Keep class proportions the same in every fold.
steps.practice: Make 5 stratified folds for 1000 rows with 5% positives and check each fold has about 10 positives.
steps.detail: With rare classes, random folds can end up with no positives. Stratifying keeps each fold representative.
steps.proof: Every fold has 10 positives out of 200 rows.
steps.pitfall: Using plain random folds on a 1% class.

problems.prompt: 1000 rows, 5% positive, 5 folds. Positives per fold?
Why might a random fold have 0 positives with 20 positives in 1000 rows?
problems.answer: Chance can put them all in other folds.

problems.prompt: Does stratifying change the total number of rows per fold of 200?

steps.title: No Leakage in Folds
steps.mastery: Fit preprocessing inside each fold only.
steps.practice: Rebuild a pipeline so scaling and feature selection are fit inside each of 5 folds.
steps.detail: Scaling or selecting features on all data before splitting lets test information leak in. Pipelines fit every step on the training part of each fold.
steps.proof: A pipeline whose CV score drops slightly but is now honest.
steps.pitfall: Selecting features on the full dataset before cross-validation.

problems.prompt: You scaled all 1000 rows before 5 fold CV. Problem?
Name 1 tool that keeps steps inside folds in scikit-learn.
Leak free CV gives 0.81 and leaky CV gave 0.86. Which do you report?

steps.title: Group and Time Splits
steps.mastery: Split by group or time when rows are not independent.
steps.practice: Split 2 years of daily sales with a time based split that trains on the first 18 months and tests on the last 6.
steps.detail: Random splits let the model see the future or the same patient twice. Group and time splits match how the model will be used.
steps.proof: A split with no test date earlier than any training date.
steps.pitfall: Shuffling time series data before splitting.

problems.prompt: Data from 50 patients with 20 rows each. Split by row or by patient?
Months in the test set for an 18 and 6 split of 24 months?
Why not shuffle daily stock data before splitting into 5 folds?
problems.answer: Future days would train the model for past ones.

steps.title: Tune With Nested CV
steps.mastery: Tune hyperparameters without biasing the final score.
steps.practice: Use an inner 3 fold loop to tune and an outer 5 fold loop to score a model on 600 rows.
steps.detail: Tuning on the same folds you score on inflates the result. Nested CV keeps the outer folds untouched by tuning.
steps.proof: An outer score that is lower than the tuned inner score.
steps.pitfall: Reporting the best inner score as final.

problems.prompt: Total model fits for 5 outer folds, 3 inner folds and 4 settings?
Inner best 0.88 and outer 0.84. Which is honest?
What does the outer loop of 5 folds measure?
problems.answer: How well the whole tuning process works on new data.

steps.title: Load Model Artifact
steps.mastery: Load a serialized model file from cloud storage into the serving process without errors.
steps.practice: Write Python code that downloads model.pkl from an S3 bucket named prod-models and loads it with joblib.load.
steps.detail: Use boto3 client with explicit region_name='us-east-1'. Call client.download_file('prod-models', 'model.pkl', '/tmp/model.pkl'). Then import joblib and run model = joblib.load('/tmp/model.pkl'). Verify the loaded object's class with isinstance.
steps.proof: The script prints "Model loaded" and the object type is sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to set the correct S3 region, which raises a NoCredentialsError.

steps.title: Validate Input Data
steps.mastery: Reject malformed request payloads before they reach the model inference code.
steps.practice: Write a FastAPI dependency that validates a JSON payload with fields f1-f5 as floats between 0.0 and 10.0 using pydantic's confloat.
steps.detail: Define a pydantic BaseModel with f1: confloat(ge=0.0, le=10.0) … f5: confloat(ge=0.0, le=10.0). In FastAPI, add a Depends on this model in the prediction endpoint. FastAPI will automatically return a validation error for out-of-range values.
steps.proof: Sending {"f1":5,"f2":-1,"f3":3,"f4":7,"f5":2} returns a 422 error; a valid payload returns status 200.
steps.pitfall: Using conint for float fields or omitting the range limits, which lets invalid values slip through.

steps.title: Log Prediction Requests
steps.mastery: Emit structured logs for every inference call that include input features and timestamps.
steps.practice: Add a logger that writes a JSON line with timestamp, request_id, and f1-f5 values to CloudWatch Logs for each POST /predict.
steps.detail: Create a logger with logging.getLogger('predict'). Set formatter to json.dumps. In the endpoint, generate a UUID for request_id, capture datetime.utcnow().isoformat(), and log the dict. Ensure the logger handler points to CloudWatch via the awslogs driver.
steps.proof: A sample log entry appears in CloudWatch: {"timestamp":"2026-10-19T12:34:56Z","request_id":"abc123","f1":4.2,…}.
steps.pitfall: Logging raw Python objects instead of serializable primitives, causing serialization errors.

steps.title: Monitor Data Drift
steps.mastery: Detect when live input distributions diverge from the training data distribution.
steps.practice: Configure a SageMaker Model Monitor baseline using the training dataset CSV and schedule a drift detection job every 30 minutes.
steps.detail: Upload the training CSV to s3://prod-models/baseline/. In SageMaker console, create a DataQualityMonitor, point to the baseline location, and set the schedule expression rate(30 minutes). Choose the same schema as the inference payload. Review the drift metrics in the Model Monitor UI.
steps.proof: The monitoring dashboard shows a drift metric > 0.7 for feature f3 after the simulated shift, triggering a warning.
steps.pitfall: Using the wrong S3 path for the baseline, which makes the monitor compare against an empty dataset.

steps.title: Set Up Alerting
steps.mastery: Automatically notify the on-call team when a monitoring metric exceeds a threshold.
steps.practice: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the custom metric ModelInputMean > 8.0 and attach an SNS topic model-alerts that forwards to Slack via AWS Chatbot.
steps.detail: Define a CloudWatch metric alarm with threshold 8.0, evaluation periods 1, and action SNS topic arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:model-alerts. In AWS Chatbot, configure a Slack workspace, channel #ml-ops, and link the SNS topic. Test by publishing a metric value of 9.0 with put-metric-data.
steps.proof: When the metric crosses 8.0, a message appears in the #ml-ops Slack channel: "⚠️ ModelInputMean exceeded threshold: 8.3".
steps.pitfall: Attempting to subscribe a Slack webhook directly to SNS, which is unsupported.

steps.title: Track Model Performance
steps.mastery: Collect real-time accuracy or error metrics for the live model.
steps.practice: Instrument the prediction endpoint to compute MAE against a hidden label field and publish it as the custom metric ModelMAE every 5 minutes.
steps.detail: Assume the request includes a hidden "label" key for offline evaluation. After prediction, calculate mae = abs(prediction - label). Accumulate values in a list; every 5 minutes, compute the mean and call cloudwatch.put_metric_data with Namespace='ML/Production', MetricName='ModelMAE', Value=mae. Reset the list after each publish.
steps.proof: CloudWatch shows a steady MAE line; after a drift event it rises from 0.42 to 1.15.
steps.pitfall: Sending the metric with the wrong namespace, causing the alarm to never fire.

steps.title: Establish Retraining Trigger
steps.mastery: Automatically start a retraining workflow when a drift or performance metric crosses a limit.
steps.practice: Define a CloudWatch alarm on the custom metric Feature3_PSI > 0.25 that publishes to an SNS topic retrain-trigger, which invokes the Lambda function trigger_retrain.
steps.detail: Create the alarm with Namespace='ML/Production', MetricName='Feature3_PSI', Threshold=0.25, ComparisonOperator='GreaterThanThreshold', EvaluationPeriods=1, AlarmActions=['arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:retrain-trigger']. Subscribe the Lambda ARN arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:trigger_retrain to the SNS topic. Verify by publishing a metric value of 0.30.
steps.proof: When Feature3_PSI reaches 0.27, the Lambda logs "Retraining started" and the Step Functions execution ID appears in CloudWatch.
steps.pitfall: Using a metric filter on logs instead of a proper CloudWatch alarm, which never fires.

steps.title: Automate Retraining Pipeline
steps.mastery: Run a fully automated pipeline that retrains, validates, and registers a new model version.
steps.practice: Write an AWS Step Functions state machine that (1) launches a SageMaker training job, (2) runs a validation script, and (3) updates the model endpoint if validation MAE < 0.5.
steps.detail: Define states: Train (SageMakerStartTrainingJob), Wait (Wait for job completion), Validate (Lambda invoke that reads validation metrics), Deploy (SageMakerUpdateEndpoint). Use Catch blocks to send failure notifications. Deploy the state machine via the console or AWS CLI.
steps.proof: After the Lambda trigger, the state machine completes with status SUCCESS and the endpoint now serves version v2.
steps.pitfall: Skipping the validation step, which can promote a degraded model to production.

steps.title: Deploy Updated Model
steps.mastery: Swap the serving container to the newly trained model without downtime.
steps.practice: Execute a blue-green deployment by creating a new endpoint variant named "v2" with weight 0.0, then gradually shift traffic to 100% over 5 minutes using the UpdateEndpointWeights API.
steps.detail: Call sagemaker.create_endpoint_config with ProductionVariants for "v1" (weight 1.0) and "v2" (weight 0.0). Deploy the config to the existing endpoint. Then run a loop that calls update_endpoint_weights, increasing v2 weight by 0.2 every minute until it reaches 1.0, simultaneously decreasing v1. Monitor the endpoint health metrics throughout.
steps.proof: CloudWatch shows 0% traffic on v2 initially and 100% after the ramp; no 5xx errors are recorded during the transition.
steps.pitfall: Changing the primary variant directly, which can cause a brief outage if the new model fails to load.

steps.title: PCA in Plain Terms
steps.mastery: Find the directions of greatest variation in data.
steps.practice: Run PCA on 10 correlated features and report how much variance the first 2 components explain.
steps.detail: PCA rotates the data to new axes ordered by variance. The first few often carry most of the information.
steps.proof: The first 2 components explain a stated share, like 78%.
steps.pitfall: Running PCA on unscaled features with different units.

problems.prompt: Eigenvalues 6, 3, 1. Share explained by the first?
Share explained by the first 2 of those 3?
Are principal components correlated with each other, of 10?

steps.title: Choose How Many Components
steps.mastery: Keep enough components to explain a target share of variance.
steps.practice: Plot cumulative explained variance for 20 components and find how many reach 95%.
steps.detail: A cumulative plot shows the trade off between size and detail. 90% to 95% is a common target.
steps.proof: The number of components that reach 95%.
steps.pitfall: Keeping all components and gaining nothing.

problems.prompt: Cumulative variance 70%, 85%, 93%, 97%. Components for 95%?
Keeping 3 of 20 components shrinks the data by what share?
Why might 2 components still be useful at 60% variance?

steps.title: Visualize With t-SNE or UMAP
steps.mastery: Plot high dimensional data in 2D to see groups.
steps.practice: Plot 1000 handwritten digit images with t-SNE or UMAP and color the points by digit.
steps.detail: These methods keep nearby points nearby, which shows clusters. Distances between far clusters do not mean much.
steps.proof: A 2D plot where most digits form separate groups.
steps.pitfall: Reading the gap between 2 clusters as a real distance.

problems.prompt: Pixels in a 28 by 28 image?
Can you use t-SNE output of 2 columns as features for a new model?
problems.answer: Not reliably, since it cannot map new points well.

problems.prompt: Running t-SNE twice gives different plots. Why?
problems.answer: It is random and has no fixed solution.

steps.title: Compression With PCA
steps.mastery: Reconstruct data from a few components and measure the loss.
steps.practice: Compress 64 by 64 face images to 50 components and compare original and reconstructed images.
steps.detail: Keeping fewer components saves space and removes noise, but loses detail. Reconstruction error shows what was lost.
steps.proof: Reconstructed faces with an error per image.
steps.pitfall: Keeping too few components and losing key detail.

problems.prompt: Original pixels per 64 by 64 image?
Numbers stored per image with 50 components?
Going from 50 to 100 components makes reconstruction error do what?

steps.title: PCA Before a Model
steps.mastery: Use PCA as a preprocessing step and check if it helps.
steps.practice: Train a model on 100 raw features and on 20 PCA components, and compare CV score and training time.
steps.detail: PCA can speed training and reduce overfitting. It can also discard a low variance feature that predicts the label well.
steps.proof: A comparison of score and time for both versions.
steps.pitfall: Assuming PCA always improves accuracy.

problems.prompt: PCA is supervised or unsupervised, given 100 features?
Can the feature with the lowest variance of 100 be the best predictor of the label?
Where must PCA be fit in 5 fold CV?
problems.answer: Inside each fold, on training rows only.

steps.title: Explain a Prediction
steps.mastery: Explain 1 prediction by showing which features pushed it.
steps.practice: Compute SHAP values for 1 loan prediction and list the top 3 features that raised or lowered the score.
steps.detail: Explanations show why a model decided. SHAP splits a prediction into contributions from each feature that add up to the output.
steps.proof: 3 features with the direction and size of each push.
steps.pitfall: Explaining a model by its global importance when asked about 1 case.

problems.prompt: SHAP values +0.2, -0.1, +0.05 from a base of 0.5. Prediction?
A feature has SHAP value 0 for 1 row. Meaning?
problems.answer: It did not move that prediction.

problems.prompt: Can SHAP explain a random forest of 300 trees?

steps.title: Check Groups for Bias
steps.mastery: Compare model error and approval rates across groups.
steps.practice: Compute approval rate and false negative rate for 2 groups of 500 applicants each and compare them.
steps.detail: A model can be accurate overall and still fail one group. Comparing rates across groups is the first fairness check.
steps.proof: A table of both rates for both groups with the gaps.
steps.pitfall: Checking only overall accuracy.

problems.prompt: Group A approved 300 of 500, group B 200 of 500. Rates?
Ratio of B to A approval, 40% over 60%?
False negative rate 10% vs 25%. Which group is hurt more?

steps.title: Proxy Features
steps.mastery: Find features that stand in for a protected attribute.
steps.practice: Check how well 3 features predict a protected attribute in a dataset of 2000 rows.
steps.detail: Dropping a protected column is not enough when zip code or name predicts it. Testing for proxies shows hidden paths to bias.
steps.proof: Each feature with how strongly it predicts the protected attribute.
steps.pitfall: Assuming removing the protected column removes the bias.

problems.prompt: Zip code predicts group membership with 85% accuracy. Is it a proxy?
Name 1 common proxy for income in 2 words.
Removing a proxy lowers accuracy by 1%. Keep it out?
problems.answer: Often yes, if it carries bias.

steps.title: Fairness Trade Offs
steps.mastery: See why different fairness rules can conflict.
steps.practice: Compute demographic parity and equal opportunity for 1 model on 2 groups with different base rates of 30% and 50%.
steps.detail: Equal approval rates and equal true positive rates can conflict when groups differ in base rates. Teams must choose which matters.
steps.proof: Both metrics computed, showing they cannot both be equal.
steps.pitfall: Claiming a model is fair after checking 1 metric.

problems.prompt: Demographic parity compares what across 2 groups?
Equal opportunity compares what across 2 groups?
Base rates differ, 30% vs 50%. Can a perfect classifier satisfy demographic parity?

steps.title: Model Cards
steps.mastery: Document what a model is for and where it fails.
steps.practice: Write a 1 page model card with 6 sections: use, data, metrics, groups tested, limits and contact.
steps.detail: A model card tells users what a model should and should not be used for. Writing it forces the team to check gaps.
steps.proof: A model card with all 6 sections filled.
steps.pitfall: Shipping a model with no record of its limits.

problems.prompt: Name 2 sections of a model card.
A model was tested only on adults aged 18 to 65. Where do you note that?
Who reads a model card, out of 3 groups?

steps.title: One Step Downhill
steps.mastery: Update a parameter by moving against the gradient.
steps.practice: Minimize f(w) = (w - 3)^2 from w = 0 with learning rate 0.1 for 3 steps.
steps.detail: The update is w = w - rate x gradient. Each step moves toward the minimum, by less as the slope flattens.
steps.pitfall: Adding the gradient instead of subtracting it.

problems.prompt: Gradient of (w - 3)^2 at w = 0?
1 step with rate 0.5 from w = 0?
What w minimizes (w - 3)^2?

steps.title: Pick the Learning Rate
steps.mastery: See how too small or too large a rate behaves.
steps.practice: Run 20 steps on (w - 3)^2 from w = 0 with rates 0.01, 0.1 and 1.1 and plot w.
steps.detail: Too small crawls, a good rate converges and too large overshoots and diverges. Plotting the loss curve shows which is happening.
