steps.proof: 0.01 is slow, 0.1 converges and 1.1 diverges.
steps.pitfall: Raising the rate whenever training seems slow without watching the loss.

problems.prompt: Rate 1.0 on (w - 3)^2 from w = 0. Where does it go?
Loss goes up each epoch. Likely cause?
problems.answer: The learning rate is too high.

problems.prompt: Loss drops by 0.001 per epoch from 5.0. Likely cause?
problems.answer: The learning rate is too low.

steps.title: Stochastic and Mini-Batch
steps.mastery: Estimate the gradient from a sample of the data.
steps.practice: Compare full batch, mini-batch of 32 and single example gradient descent on 10,000 rows by time per epoch and loss curve smoothness.
steps.detail: Mini-batches give a noisy but cheap gradient. The noise can even help escape poor spots, and batches use hardware well.
steps.proof: A comparison showing mini-batch is fastest to a good loss.
steps.pitfall: Using full batch gradient descent on millions of rows.

problems.prompt: Updates per epoch with 10,000 rows and batch 32?
If the whole dataset is 1 batch, how many weight updates happen per pass?
Why is the batch 32 loss curve bumpy?
problems.answer: Each batch gives a noisy gradient estimate.

steps.title: Momentum and Adam
steps.mastery: Speed up descent with momentum and adaptive rates.
steps.practice: Train the same model with plain SGD, SGD with momentum 0.9 and Adam, and compare loss after 10 epochs.
steps.detail: Momentum smooths updates by remembering past gradients. Adam also scales each parameter step by its history, which often works well with little tuning.
steps.proof: Loss after 10 epochs for all 3 optimizers.
steps.pitfall: Assuming Adam is always best without trying SGD.

problems.prompt: Momentum 0.9 keeps what share of the last update?
Default Adam learning rate in many libraries?
Name 1 reason momentum helps in a long narrow valley.
problems.answer: It builds speed along the valley and damps zig zags.

steps.title: Gradients of a Loss
steps.mastery: Compute the gradient of mean squared error for a linear model.
steps.practice: Compute the gradient of MSE for y = w x with data (1, 2) and (2, 4) at w = 1.
steps.detail: MSE = mean of (w x - y)^2, and its gradient is the mean of 2x(w x - y). Here the error pulls w up toward 2.
steps.proof: Gradient = mean(2 x 1 x (1 - 2), 2 x 2 x (2 - 4)) = mean(-2, -8) = -5.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the factor of x from the chain rule.

problems.prompt: MSE at w = 2 for that data?
One step from w = 1 with rate 0.1 and gradient -5?
Gradient of (w x - y)^2 with respect to w?

steps.title: Linear Regression
steps.mastery: Fit a weighted sum plus a bias to predict a number.
steps.practice: Fit y = w x + b to the points (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7) and predict y at x = 10.
steps.detail: Linear regression finds the line with the smallest squared error. Each weight is the change in output for 1 unit of that input.
steps.pitfall: Reading a weight as causal without thinking.

problems.prompt: y = 3x + 2. Predict at x = 4.
Weight 0.5 on hours studied. Effect of 4 more hours?
Two features with weights 2 and -1. Predict for (3, 4) with bias 1.

steps.title: Logistic Regression
steps.mastery: Turn a weighted sum into a probability with the sigmoid.
steps.practice: Compute sigmoid(z) for z = -2, 0 and 2, and classify each with a 0.5 threshold.
steps.detail: The sigmoid 1/(1 + e^(-z)) squashes any number into 0 to 1. Positive z means more likely class 1.
steps.proof: About 0.12, 0.5 and 0.88, giving 0, a tie and 1.
steps.pitfall: Treating logistic regression output as a raw score instead of a probability.

problems.prompt: sigmoid(0)?
z = 3. Is the probability above 0.9?
Weights (1, -2), bias 0, input (2, 1). Predicted class at threshold 0.5?

steps.title: Scale Your Features
steps.mastery: Standardize features so their weights compare fairly.
steps.practice: Standardize 2 features, income in dollars and age in years, to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 for 5 rows.
steps.detail: Features on very different scales slow gradient descent and make weights hard to compare. Standardizing fixes both.
steps.proof: Both columns rescaled with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
steps.pitfall: Fitting the scaler on the test set too.

problems.prompt: Mean 50, standard deviation 10. Standardize 70.
A test score of 35 sits how many standard deviations below a class mean of 50 with spread 10?
Why fit the scaler only on the training rows, out of 1000?
problems.answer: To keep test information out of training.

steps.title: Read the Weights
steps.mastery: Interpret linear model weights and their signs.
steps.practice: Fit a linear model with 4 standardized features and rank them by the size of their weights.
steps.detail: With standardized features, larger absolute weights mean stronger influence. The sign says the direction. Correlated features can split or flip weights.
steps.proof: 4 features ranked with signs explained.
steps.pitfall: Comparing weights across features with different units.

problems.prompt: Weights 0.8 and -0.3 on standardized features. Stronger effect?
A weight is negative. What does raising that feature do to the prediction?
2 nearly identical features get weights 5 and -4. Why?
problems.answer: They are correlated, so the weights are unstable.

steps.title: Start With a Baseline
steps.mastery: Use a linear model as the first benchmark on a new problem.
steps.practice: Train a mean predictor and a linear model on 1 dataset and report how much the linear model improves the error.
steps.detail: A simple baseline tells you whether a complex model is worth it. If a linear model is close to the best, prefer it.
steps.proof: Both errors reported with the improvement as a percentage.
steps.pitfall: Jumping to a neural network before trying a baseline.

problems.prompt: Mean predictor error 20 and linear error 12. Improvement?
A deep model scores 11.8 against linear 12. Worth it?
problems.answer: Probably not, given the extra cost.

problems.prompt: What does a mean predictor predict for every row of 500?

steps.title: Accuracy and Its Trap
steps.mastery: Compute accuracy and see where it misleads.
steps.practice: Compute the accuracy of a model that always predicts "not fraud" on 1000 transactions with 10 frauds.
steps.detail: Accuracy counts right answers. When one class is rare, always guessing the common class scores high and catches nothing.
steps.proof: 99% accuracy with 0 frauds caught.
steps.pitfall: Reporting accuracy alone on imbalanced data.

problems.prompt: 90 of 100 predictions right. Accuracy?
A rare disease affects 1 in 200. Accuracy of always saying healthy?
Why is that 99.5% model useless?
problems.answer: It never finds a single sick person.

steps.title: Precision and Recall
steps.mastery: Measure how many alarms were right and how many cases were caught.
steps.practice: Compute precision and recall when a model flags 50 emails, 40 are spam, and 80 spam emails exist.
steps.detail: Precision is correct flags over all flags. Recall is correct flags over all real positives. Raising one usually lowers the other.
steps.proof: Precision 40/50 = 0.8 and recall 40/80 = 0.5.
steps.pitfall: Swapping the denominators of precision and recall.

problems.prompt: TP 30, FP 10. Precision?
TP 30, FN 20. Recall?
A cancer screen should miss as few cases as possible. Favor precision or recall?

steps.title: F1 Score
steps.mastery: Combine precision and recall with their harmonic mean.
steps.practice: Compute F1 for precision 0.8 and recall 0.5, and for precision 0.9 and recall 0.1.
steps.detail: F1 = 2PR/(P + R) punishes a model that is good at only one. A very low recall drags F1 down even with high precision.
steps.proof: About 0.615 and 0.18.
steps.pitfall: Averaging precision and recall with a normal mean.

problems.prompt: F1 when precision and recall are both 0.7?
F1 for precision 1.0 and recall 0.5?
Why does F1 use the harmonic mean instead of (P + R)/2?
problems.answer: It stays low unless both are high.

steps.title: Confusion Matrix
steps.mastery: Lay out true and false positives and negatives in a 2 by 2 table.
steps.practice: Build a confusion matrix for 100 predictions with 35 TP, 5 FP, 10 FN and 50 TN, and compute 3 metrics from it.
steps.detail: The table shows every kind of mistake at once. Every metric is a ratio of its cells.
steps.proof: Accuracy 0.85, precision 0.875 and recall about 0.78.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up which axis is the prediction and which is the truth.

problems.prompt: Sum of all 4 cells for 100 predictions?
TN 50 and FP 5. Specificity?
Which cell holds sick people the model called healthy, of the 4?

steps.title: ROC and Thresholds
steps.mastery: Trade off catches and false alarms by moving a threshold.
steps.practice: Compute recall and false positive rate at thresholds 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 for 10 scored examples, then sketch the ROC curve.
steps.detail: Lowering the threshold catches more positives and raises false alarms. The ROC curve shows every threshold at once, and its area summarizes ranking quality.
steps.proof: 3 points on the ROC curve with the area estimated.
steps.pitfall: Judging a model at threshold 0.5 only.

problems.prompt: AUC of a model that guesses randomly?
AUC of a perfect ranker?
Raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 usually does what to recall?

steps.title: A Single Neuron
steps.mastery: Compute a weighted sum plus bias, then an activation.
steps.practice: Compute ReLU(w . x + b) for w = (0.5, -1), x = (4, 1) and b = 0.5.
steps.detail: A neuron is a linear model plus a nonlinearity. ReLU passes positive values and zeroes negative ones.
steps.proof: w . x + b = 1.5, and ReLU gives 1.5.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the bias.

problems.prompt: Compute ReLU(-2).
sigmoid of 0 for 1 neuron?
w = (1, 1), b = -3, x = (1, 1). ReLU output?

steps.title: Why Nonlinearity
steps.mastery: Show that stacking linear layers without activations stays linear.
steps.practice: Multiply 2 weight matrices [[1, 2], [0, 1]] and [[2, 0], [1, 1]] to show 2 linear layers equal 1.
steps.detail: Without activations, any number of layers collapses into a single matrix. Nonlinear activations let networks bend the decision boundary.
steps.proof: The product is 1 matrix, [[4, 2], [1, 1]].
steps.pitfall: Building deep networks with no activation functions.

problems.prompt: 3 linear layers with no activation equal how many linear layers?
Can 1 linear layer solve XOR on 4 points?
Name 2 common activations.

steps.title: Count Parameters
steps.mastery: Count the weights and biases in a network.
steps.practice: Count the parameters of a network with layers 784, 128, 64 and 10.
steps.detail: Each dense layer has inputs times outputs weights plus 1 bias per output. Counting them shows model size and memory use.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the bias terms.

problems.prompt: Parameters in a dense layer from 3 inputs to 2 outputs?
Parameters from 10 inputs to 1 output?
Memory for 1 million float32 parameters?

steps.title: Train a Small Network
steps.mastery: Train a 2 layer network and watch the loss fall.
steps.practice: Train a network with 1 hidden layer of 16 units on 2 moon shaped classes of 500 points for 200 epochs.
steps.detail: A small hidden layer can learn a curved boundary a linear model cannot. Plotting the loss and the boundary shows learning happen.
steps.proof: Loss falls and the boundary curves around both moons.
steps.pitfall: Training with a learning rate so high the loss explodes.

problems.prompt: Linear model accuracy on 2 moons is about 85%. Can a 16 unit network beat it?
Loss is NaN after epoch 3. First thing to check?
Output activation for 2 class probability, of 2 choices: sigmoid or ReLU?

steps.title: Softmax and Cross-Entropy
steps.mastery: Turn scores into class probabilities and measure the loss.
steps.practice: Compute softmax of scores (2, 1, 0) and the cross-entropy loss when the true class is the first.
steps.detail: Softmax exponentiates and normalizes so outputs sum to 1. Cross-entropy is -log of the probability given to the true class.
steps.proof: About (0.665, 0.245, 0.090), with loss about 0.41.
steps.pitfall: Using MSE for multi class classification.

problems.prompt: Softmax of (0, 0)?
A perfect prediction puts 100% on the true class. Its loss?
Cross-entropy if the true class gets probability 0.1?

steps.title: Identify Overfitting
steps.mastery: Recognize when a model's training performance is significantly better than its validation performance.
steps.practice: Train a linear regression on the Boston housing dataset using 80% of the data for training and 20% for validation, then write down the R² score for each split.
steps.detail: Load the dataset, split it with sklearn's train_test_split (test_size=0.2, random_state=1). Fit LinearRegression on the training set, predict on both sets, and compute r2_score for each. Record the two numbers side by side to spot the discrepancy.
steps.proof: You will see a training R² around 0.85 and a validation R² near 0.55, showing a clear gap.
steps.pitfall: Assuming a high training score alone means the model is good, without checking validation results.

problems.prompt: What is the validation R² score if the model's residual sum of squares is 300 and the total sum of squares is 1000?
A model has training R² = 0.85 and validation R² = 0.55. Does this indicate overfitting?
Why is a training R² of 0.90 insufficient to claim a good model if the validation R² is 0.60?
problems.answer: Because the large gap shows the model does not generalize and is overfitting to the training data.
problems.hint: Consider the difference between the two scores.

steps.title: Visualize the Gap
steps.mastery: Create a plot that clearly displays the difference between training and validation errors.
steps.practice: Plot training and validation mean squared error for a decision-tree regressor on the same Boston split, using depths 2, 5, and 10.
steps.detail: Import matplotlib, compute MSE for each depth on both splits, store the values in two lists, and plot them with distinct colors and a legend. Label the x-axis "Tree depth" and the y-axis "Mean Squared Error".
steps.proof: The graph will show training error dropping sharply while validation error plateaus or rises, especially at depth 10.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the axes unlabeled, making it hard to see which line belongs to which dataset.

problems.prompt: If a decision-tree regressor of depth 2 has a training mean squared error of 14, what value should be plotted on the y-axis for that point?
On the Boston housing split, a depth-5 tree yields training MSE 9 and validation MSE 11. What are the two y-values that should appear on the same plot?
A plot shows training MSE 4 at depth 10 and validation MSE 18 at depth 10. Explain why this pattern indicates overfitting.
problems.answer: The training error is much lower than the validation error, creating a large gap; the model has learned the training data too closely and fails to generalize to new data, which is the hallmark of overfitting.
problems.hint: Consider the gap between training and validation errors.

steps.title: Apply Regularization
steps.mastery: Use L2 regularization to reduce overfitting in a linear model.
steps.practice: Fit a Ridge regression on the Boston training set with alpha=1.0, then record the new training and validation R² scores.
steps.detail: Import Ridge from sklearn.linear_model, set alpha=1.0, fit on the training data, predict on both sets, and compute r2_score. Compare the gap to the one from the plain linear regression.
steps.proof: Both scores should move closer together, e.g., training R² ≈ 0.78 and validation R² ≈ 0.70.
steps.pitfall: Choosing an alpha that is too large, which under-fits and lowers both scores dramatically.

problems.prompt: If Ridge regression yields training RSS = 250 and total SS = 1000, what is the training R²?
A Ridge model gives training R² = 0.78 and validation R² = 0.70. Are the scores closer than the original gap of 0.85 vs 0.55?
When alpha is set to 100, training R² drops to 0.30 and validation R² to 0.28. What does this indicate about the model?
problems.hint: Consider the magnitude of the scores.

steps.title: Cross-Validate Properly
steps.mastery: Employ k-fold cross-validation to obtain a reliable estimate of model performance.
steps.practice: Run 5-fold cross-validation on a RandomForestRegressor (n_estimators=100) using the whole Boston dataset and note the mean validation R².
steps.detail: Use sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_score with cv=5, scoring='r2'. Print the array of scores, then compute its mean and standard deviation. Record these two numbers.
steps.proof: The reported mean R² will be around 0.70, with a small standard deviation, indicating stable performance.
steps.pitfall: Reporting only the score from a single random split, which can be misleading.

problems.prompt: In 5-fold cross-validation, how many different validation sets are used?
Five validation R² scores are 0.68, 0.71, 0.70, 0.69, 0.72. What is the mean validation R²?
If a single random train-test split yields validation R² = 0.85 but 5-fold cross-validation gives a mean of 0.70, what does this tell you?
problems.answer: The single split was overly optimistic; cross-validation provides a more reliable estimate of performance.
problems.hint: Think about variability across splits.

steps.title: Detect Overfitting Early
steps.mastery: Set up a training loop that stops when validation loss stops improving.
steps.practice: Train a small neural network on the Boston data for up to 200 epochs, using early stopping with patience=10 and monitor validation MSE.
steps.detail: Use TensorFlow or PyTorch, define a simple feed-forward net, compile with mean_squared_error, and add an EarlyStopping callback (monitor='val_loss', patience=10, restore_best_weights=True). Log the epoch at which training stops and the corresponding validation loss.
steps.proof: Training will halt before 200 epochs, and the final validation MSE will be close to the lowest observed value.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to reset the best-model weights after early stopping, so the saved model is over-trained.

steps.title: Report Overfitting Transparently
steps.mastery: Communicate the presence and mitigation of overfitting in a project report.
steps.practice: Write a short paragraph (100-150 words) for a mock project that includes the training and validation scores before and after regularization, the cross-validation mean, and the early-stopping epoch.
steps.detail: Structure the paragraph: state the original gap, describe the regularization step and its effect, mention cross-validation results, and conclude with the early-stopping outcome. Ensure each metric is presented with its exact numeric value.
steps.proof: The paragraph will list numbers such as training R² = 0.85, validation R² = 0.55, Ridge validation R² = 0.70, CV mean = 0.71 ± 0.03, stopped at epoch = 73, showing clear improvement.
steps.pitfall: Omitting any quantitative comparison, which makes the claim of reduced overfitting unverifiable.

steps.title: L2 Shrinks Weights
steps.mastery: Add a penalty on squared weights to keep them small.
steps.practice: Fit ridge regression on 20 noisy features with penalty values 0.01, 1 and 100 and compare the weights.
steps.detail: L2 regularization adds lambda times the sum of squared weights. Larger lambda pulls weights toward 0 and reduces variance.
steps.proof: Weights shrink as the penalty grows from 0.01 to 100.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to scale features before penalizing.

problems.prompt: L2 penalty term for weights (3, 4) with lambda 1?
Raising lambda from 1 to 100 does what to the weights?
Can ridge set a weight exactly to 0 with lambda = 10?

steps.title: L1 Picks Features
steps.mastery: Use an absolute value penalty to zero out weak features.
steps.practice: Fit lasso on 50 features where only 5 matter and count the nonzero weights.
steps.detail: L1 regularization adds lambda times the sum of absolute weights. Its corners push many weights to exactly 0, which selects features.
steps.proof: Around 5 to 8 nonzero weights.
steps.pitfall: Assuming lasso keeps the right features when they are highly correlated.

problems.prompt: L1 penalty for weights (3, -4) with lambda 1?
Which penalty, L1 or L2, tends to give exactly 0 weights?
2 correlated features matter. What might lasso do?

steps.title: Choose Lambda
steps.mastery: Pick the penalty strength with cross-validation.
steps.practice: Try 10 lambda values on a log scale from 0.001 to 1000 and pick the one with the best 5 fold CV score.
steps.detail: Too small a lambda overfits and too large underfits. A log grid covers the range, and CV picks the sweet spot.
steps.proof: A chosen lambda with its CV score.
steps.pitfall: Picking lambda by the test set.

problems.prompt: Log spaced values from 0.01 to 100 with 5 points?
Lambda 1000 gives CV error equal to the mean predictor. Why?
Lambda 0 equals which model?
problems.answer: Plain least squares with no penalty.

steps.title: Early Stopping and Dropout
steps.mastery: Regularize neural networks by stopping early or dropping units, so the weights stay simpler.
steps.practice: Train a network for 100 epochs, plot train and validation loss, and mark the epoch where validation loss is lowest.
steps.detail: Validation loss falls and then rises as the network starts to memorize. Stopping at the minimum and using dropout both limit overfitting.
steps.proof: A plot with the best epoch marked.
steps.pitfall: Training to the last epoch because training loss keeps falling.

problems.prompt: Validation loss is lowest at epoch 23 of 100. Which weights do you keep?
Dropout 0.5 at training time drops what share of units?
Is dropout used at test time on 1 prediction?

steps.title: Bias and Variance
steps.mastery: Explain the trade off regularization controls.
steps.practice: Fit 10 models on 10 bootstrap samples with lambda 0.01 and 100, then compare how much their predictions vary.
steps.detail: Low lambda gives low bias and high variance, high lambda the reverse. The best test error balances the 2.
steps.proof: Predictions vary more at lambda 0.01 than at 100.
steps.pitfall: Thinking less bias is always better.

problems.prompt: High variance shows up as what across 10 resampled models?
High bias shows up as what on training and test error, given 2 numbers like 25% and 26%?
Does more data usually lower bias or variance, given 10 times more rows?

steps.title: Order Matters
steps.mastery: Recognize problems where the sequence carries meaning.
steps.practice: Shuffle the words of 3 sentences and explain how meaning changes, then list 3 sequence prediction tasks.
steps.detail: Bag of words models ignore order. Sequence models read data in order, which matters for text, speech and time series.
steps.proof: 3 shuffled sentences explained and 3 tasks listed.
steps.pitfall: Treating time series rows as independent.

problems.prompt: "Dog bites man" vs "man bites dog". Same words, same meaning?
Name 1 sequence task in audio.
Predicting tomorrow sales from the last 30 days is what kind of task?

steps.title: Recurrent Networks
steps.mastery: Carry a hidden state from step to step.
steps.practice: Compute 3 steps of h = tanh(w h + u x) with w = 0.5, u = 1 and inputs 1, 0, 1 from h = 0.
steps.detail: The hidden state summarizes everything seen so far. The same weights are used at every step.
steps.pitfall: Using different weights at each time step.

problems.prompt: Compute tanh(0).
Does an RNN use the same weights at step 1 and step 50?
Why do plain RNNs forget inputs from 100 steps back?

steps.title: LSTMs and GRUs
steps.mastery: Use gates to keep information over long sequences.
steps.practice: Train a plain RNN and an LSTM on sequences of length 100 that need the first token to predict the last, and compare.
steps.detail: Gates decide what to keep, forget and output. They let gradients flow across long gaps that a plain RNN cannot bridge.
steps.proof: The LSTM solves the task and the plain RNN does not.
steps.pitfall: Expecting a plain RNN to remember 100 steps.

problems.prompt: How many gates does a GRU have?
Which LSTM gate removes old information, of the 3?
Which is usually faster to train, GRU or LSTM, with 1000 sequences?

steps.title: Tokens and Embeddings
steps.mastery: Turn words into vectors a network can use.
steps.practice: Tokenize 3 sentences into word ids from a 20 word vocabulary and look up a 4 number embedding for each.
steps.detail: Embeddings map each token to a learned vector. Similar words end up with similar vectors after training.
steps.proof: Each sentence as a list of ids and a list of 4 number vectors.
steps.pitfall: Feeding raw word ids as numbers into a model.

problems.prompt: Vocabulary 10,000 and embedding size 300. Parameters in the table?
Why not feed word id 482 directly as a number?
problems.answer: The number has no meaning, so the model would read false order.

problems.prompt: What happens to a word not in a 20 word vocabulary?
problems.answer: It maps to an unknown token.

steps.title: Forecast a Time Series
steps.mastery: Predict the next values of a series with lagged features.
steps.practice: Build lag features from 365 days of sales and predict the next 7 days, comparing with a naive last value forecast.
steps.detail: A naive forecast is a strong baseline for time series. Lag features turn forecasting into ordinary supervised learning.
steps.proof: A model error compared with the naive error over 7 days.
steps.pitfall: Using future values as features.

problems.prompt: Naive forecast for tomorrow if today is 120?
Lag 7 feature for day 100?
A model beats naive by 3% on 7 days. Worth it?
problems.answer: Maybe, depending on cost and stability.

steps.title: Split Iris Dataset
steps.mastery: Separate data into training, validation, and test sets with correct proportions.
steps.practice: Use pandas to split iris.csv into 90 training rows, 30 validation rows, and 30 test rows.
steps.detail: Load iris.csv with pandas, then use sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split twice: first split 80% train+val and 20% test, then split the train+val part 75% train and 25% validation to obtain 90/30/30 rows. Verify shapes with df.shape.
steps.proof: The three new DataFrames have 90, 30, and 30 rows respectively.
steps.pitfall: Using percentages that don't sum to 150 rows or mixing up validation and test splits.

problems.prompt: How many rows should the training DataFrame contain after splitting iris.csv as instructed?
Using pandas, split iris.csv into three DataFrames with 90 training rows, 30 validation rows, and 30 test rows. How many rows are in the validation DataFrame?
If you accidentally allocate 40 rows to the test set while keeping the training set at 90 rows, how many rows must the validation set contain to still use all 150 rows of the Iris dataset?
problems.hint: Total rows = 150; subtract training and test rows.

steps.title: Fit Simple Model
steps.mastery: Train a model on the training set without looking at validation or test data.
steps.practice: Fit a LogisticRegression on the training DataFrame using scikit-learn.
steps.detail: Import LogisticRegression, instantiate with default parameters, call model.fit(X_train, y_train). Keep X_val, y_val untouched for later.
steps.proof: model.predict on training data returns predictions without error.
steps.pitfall: Accidentally calling .fit on validation or test data.

steps.title: Evaluate on Validation
steps.mastery: Assess model performance on validation data to tune hyperparameters.
steps.practice: Compute accuracy of the trained model on the 30-row validation set.
steps.detail: Import accuracy_score, predict on X_val, compare to y_val, record the metric. Try changing C=0.5 and observe new accuracy.
steps.proof: accuracy_score(y_val, model.predict(X_val)) equals the reported number (e.g., 0.93).
steps.pitfall: Adjusting the model after looking at test-set results instead of validation.

steps.title: Select Hyperparameter
steps.mastery: Choose the hyperparameter that gives the best validation performance.
steps.practice: Run a loop over C values [0.1, 1, 10] and keep the model with highest validation accuracy.
steps.detail: For each C, instantiate LogisticRegression(C=...), fit on training data, compute validation accuracy, store best. After loop, refit model on training data with best C.
steps.proof: The loop prints the best C (e.g., 1) and its validation accuracy.
steps.pitfall: Choosing the hyperparameter based on test-set performance.

steps.title: Final Test Evaluation
steps.mastery: Report unbiased performance by evaluating the final model on the untouched test set.
steps.practice: Calculate accuracy on the 30-row test set using the model trained with the selected C.
steps.detail: Load X_test, y_test, predict, compute accuracy, and record it as the final result. Do not modify the model afterwards.
steps.proof: accuracy_score(y_test, final_model.predict(X_test)) matches the printed test accuracy (e.g., 0.90).
steps.pitfall: Re-training or tweaking the model after seeing this test accuracy.

steps.title: Labeled or Not
steps.mastery: Decide whether a problem is supervised or unsupervised.
steps.practice: Classify 6 tasks such as spam filtering, customer grouping and price prediction as supervised or unsupervised.
steps.detail: Supervised learning has the answer for each example. Unsupervised learning finds structure with no answers given.
steps.proof: Spam and price are supervised, grouping is unsupervised, with all 6 labeled.
steps.pitfall: Calling any task with data supervised.

problems.prompt: Grouping 500 songs with no genre labels. Type?
Predicting tomorrow temperature from 10 years of records. Type?
Finding 3 unusual transactions out of 1 million with no fraud labels. Type?

steps.title: Classification vs Regression
steps.mastery: Tell predicting a category from predicting a number.
steps.practice: Sort 5 supervised tasks into classification or regression, including predicting age and predicting 1 of 3 species.
steps.detail: Classification predicts a category and regression predicts a number. The choice sets the loss function and the metrics.
steps.proof: Age is regression and species is classification, with all 5 sorted.
steps.pitfall: Treating a numeric category code like 1, 2, 3 as a regression target.

problems.prompt: Predict house price in dollars. Type?
Predict 1 of 10 digits in an image. Type?
Predict star rating 1 to 5. Which 2 framings are possible?
problems.answer: Classification over 5 classes, or regression on the number.

steps.title: Semi-Supervised Data
steps.mastery: Use a few labels plus many unlabeled examples.
steps.practice: Plan how to use 100 labeled and 10,000 unlabeled images, naming 1 method.
steps.detail: Labels are expensive. Methods like pseudo labeling train on the labeled set, label the rest with the model and retrain on confident guesses.
steps.proof: A plan using pseudo labels on confident predictions.
steps.pitfall: Throwing away the unlabeled data.

problems.prompt: What share of the 10,100 images is labeled?
What does pseudo labeling add to the 100 labels?
problems.answer: Model guesses on unlabeled data, kept when confident.

problems.prompt: Why only keep guesses above 0.9 confidence?
problems.answer: Low confidence guesses add wrong labels.

steps.title: Reinforcement Learning
steps.mastery: Recognize learning from rewards rather than labels.
steps.practice: Describe the agent, actions, reward and state for teaching a program to play tic tac toe in 4 lines.
steps.detail: Reinforcement learning has no labeled answers. An agent acts, gets a reward and learns which actions pay off over time.
steps.proof: 4 lines naming agent, actions, reward and state.
steps.pitfall: Confusing a reward with a label for each move.

problems.prompt: In tic tac toe, what reward could a win give, if a loss gives -1?
Why is the reward for 1 move often delayed?
problems.answer: The win or loss comes at the end of the game.

problems.prompt: A robot gets +1 for each step forward. What might go wrong?
problems.answer: It may learn odd shortcuts that earn reward without the real goal.

steps.title: Pick the Approach
steps.mastery: Choose an approach from the data and goal.
steps.practice: For 3 real projects, write whether you would use supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning and why.
steps.detail: The data you have decides the approach. Labels point to supervised learning, raw data to unsupervised and a reward signal to reinforcement learning.
steps.proof: 3 projects with an approach and a reason each.
steps.pitfall: Choosing the most exciting approach rather than the one the data supports.

problems.prompt: You have 50,000 labeled X rays. Approach?
You have click logs with no labels and want customer types. Approach?
You can simulate a game 1 million times. Approach?

steps.title: Reuse a Pretrained Model
steps.mastery: Start from a model trained on a big dataset and adapt it.
steps.practice: Fine-tune a pretrained image model on 500 photos of 5 classes and compare with training from scratch.
steps.detail: Pretrained models already know general features like edges and shapes. Fine-tuning needs far less data than starting over.
steps.proof: Fine-tuning reaches much higher accuracy than scratch on 500 photos.
steps.pitfall: Training a large model from scratch on a few hundred examples.

problems.prompt: Photos per class for 500 photos and 5 classes?
Which layers learn general edges, early or late, of 50?
Why replace the final layer for 5 classes?
problems.answer: The original head predicts the old classes.

steps.title: Freeze or Unfreeze
steps.mastery: Choose which layers to train when fine-tuning.
steps.practice: Fine-tune with all layers frozen except the head, then unfreeze the last 2 blocks, and compare results.
steps.detail: Freezing protects general features and trains fast. Unfreezing more layers helps when your data differs from the original.
steps.proof: A comparison of both settings on validation accuracy.
steps.pitfall: Unfreezing everything with a high learning rate and wrecking the pretrained weights.

problems.prompt: With 200 images, freeze most layers or train all?
Learning rate for unfrozen pretrained layers: higher or lower than the head, at 10 times?
Your data is X rays and the model was trained on 1 million photos. Unfreeze more or less?

steps.title: Fine-Tune a Language Model
steps.mastery: Adapt a pretrained text model to a classification task.
steps.practice: Fine-tune a small pretrained text model on 2000 labeled reviews for positive or negative and report accuracy.
steps.detail: A pretrained text model already understands language. A few epochs on labeled examples teach it the task.
steps.proof: Accuracy on held out reviews after 3 epochs.
steps.pitfall: Training for 20 epochs and overfitting the small dataset.

problems.prompt: Typical epochs for fine-tuning on 2000 examples?
Why use a small learning rate like 2e-5?
problems.answer: To adjust the pretrained weights gently.

problems.prompt: Validation accuracy drops after epoch 3. What do you do?

steps.title: Parameter Efficient Tuning
steps.mastery: Train small adapters instead of all weights.
steps.practice: Compare full fine-tuning with LoRA of rank 8 by counting trainable parameters for a 4096 by 4096 weight matrix.
steps.detail: LoRA learns 2 thin matrices whose product updates the weight. It trains a tiny fraction of the parameters with similar results.
steps.proof: About 16.8 million for full against 65,536 for LoRA.
steps.pitfall: Assuming you must update every weight to adapt a big model.

problems.prompt: LoRA rank 8 on a 1000 by 1000 matrix. Trainable parameters?
Full parameters in that 1000 by 1000 matrix?
Name 1 benefit of training 1% of the parameters.
problems.answer: Less memory, so it fits on a smaller GPU.

steps.title: Prompting vs Fine-Tuning
steps.mastery: Decide whether a prompt or fine-tuning fits a task.
steps.practice: Try a prompt with 3 examples on a classification task, then fine-tune on 1000 examples, and compare accuracy and cost.
steps.detail: Prompting needs no training and works for many tasks. Fine-tuning wins when you have data and need consistent behavior.
steps.proof: A comparison of accuracy and cost for both.
steps.pitfall: Fine-tuning before trying a good prompt.

problems.prompt: Which needs labeled data, a 3 example prompt or fine-tuning?
A prompt reaches 92% and fine-tuning 94%. Which to ship?
problems.answer: It depends on cost and how much 2 points matter.

problems.prompt: What are the 3 examples in a few shot prompt called?

steps.title: One Decision Tree
steps.mastery: Split data with yes or no questions to predict a label.
steps.practice: Grow a depth 2 decision tree by hand on 8 rows of weather data to predict "play" or "stay in".
steps.detail: Each split asks the question that makes the children purest. Deep trees memorize, so depth is the main control.
steps.proof: A tree with 3 questions and 4 leaves that fits the 8 rows.
steps.pitfall: Growing a tree until every leaf holds 1 row.

problems.prompt: Max leaves of a binary tree of depth 3?
A leaf has 6 yes and 2 no. Prediction?
Why limit depth to about 5 on 1000 rows?

steps.title: Gini and Entropy
steps.mastery: Measure how mixed a node is to choose splits.
steps.practice: Compute the Gini impurity of a node with 8 yes and 2 no, and of a node with 5 and 5.
steps.detail: Gini = 1 - sum of squared class shares. A pure node scores 0 and a 50/50 node scores 0.5. Splits are chosen to lower impurity the most.
steps.pitfall: Choosing splits by accuracy alone.

problems.prompt: Gini of a pure node with 10 yes?
Gini of 3 equal classes?
Entropy of a 50/50 node in bits?

steps.title: Random Forests
steps.mastery: Average many trees grown on resampled data and random features.
steps.practice: Train a random forest with 200 trees on a dataset and compare its test score with a single tree.
steps.detail: Each tree sees a bootstrap sample and random subsets of features, so their errors differ. Averaging them cuts variance.
steps.proof: The forest beats the single tree on test score.
steps.pitfall: Using all features at every split, which makes trees too similar.

problems.prompt: What share of 1000 rows does a bootstrap sample leave out, roughly?
Typical features tried per split for 100 features in classification?
Does adding trees from 200 to 500 cause overfitting?
problems.answer: No, it mostly just costs time.

steps.title: Feature Importance
steps.mastery: Read which features a tree model relies on, with care.
steps.practice: Compute permutation importance for 5 features of a forest and compare it with the built in impurity importance.
steps.detail: Permutation importance measures how much the score drops when a feature is shuffled. Impurity importance can favor features with many values.
steps.proof: 5 features ranked by both methods with any disagreement noted.
steps.pitfall: Trusting impurity importance for a high cardinality ID column.

problems.prompt: Shuffling feature A drops accuracy from 0.9 to 0.7. Importance?
Shuffling feature B drops nothing. Importance?
Why can a random ID column look important by impurity in 1000 rows?
problems.answer: It has many split points and fits noise.

steps.title: When Trees Win
steps.mastery: Know when tree models beat linear models.
steps.practice: Compare a forest and a linear model on 2 datasets, 1 with a clear interaction between 2 features.
steps.detail: Trees handle interactions and odd shapes without manual features. Linear models win with few rows or truly linear patterns.
steps.proof: The forest wins on the interaction data, and results are close on the other.
steps.pitfall: Assuming trees always beat linear models.

problems.prompt: Price depends on size only when location is urban. Which model handles this naturally?
Only 50 rows and a linear trend. Which model is safer?
Do trees need feature scaling, out of 2 model types?

steps.title: Rules vs Examples
steps.mastery: Tell a hand written rule apart from a rule learned from data.
steps.practice: Write 3 hand coded rules for spotting spam, then list 3 example emails that would break them.
steps.detail: Hand written rules break on cases nobody imagined. Machine learning instead fits a function to many labeled examples, so it can pick up patterns you never wrote down.
steps.proof: 3 rules and 3 emails that slip past them.
steps.pitfall: Thinking machine learning means the computer understands the task.

problems.prompt: A rule says spam has the word "free". Name 1 spam email it misses.
You have 10,000 labeled emails. Rules or learning, and why?
problems.answer: Learning, since the data shows patterns rules would miss.

problems.prompt: A model scores 99% on emails it trained on and 70% on new ones. What went wrong?
problems.answer: It memorized the training emails instead of learning a general rule.

steps.title: Training and Test Data
steps.mastery: Split data so the model is judged on examples it never saw.
steps.practice: Split 1000 rows into 800 for training and 200 for testing with a fixed random seed, then report the size of each.
steps.detail: Scoring a model on its own training data rewards memorizing. A held out test set is a fair estimate of how it will do on new data.
steps.proof: 800 training rows and 200 test rows, with the seed recorded.
steps.pitfall: Tuning the model while looking at the test set.

problems.prompt: What share of 1000 rows is a 20% test set?
Why fix the random seed when splitting 1000 rows?
problems.answer: So the split can be repeated exactly.

problems.prompt: You tried 30 models and kept the best test score. Is that score still fair?
problems.answer: No, the test set was used to choose, so it is optimistic.

steps.title: Features and Labels
steps.mastery: Name the inputs and the answer in a learning problem.
steps.practice: List the features and the label for predicting house price from 5 columns of a housing table.
steps.detail: Features are what the model sees, and the label is what it predicts. Picking features that would not be known at prediction time leaks the answer.
steps.proof: 4 features such as size, rooms, age and location, with price as the label.
steps.pitfall: Including a column that is only known after the answer, like sale date for price.

problems.prompt: Predicting exam pass or fail from 3 columns. What is the label?
Is "final sale price" a fair feature for predicting the price?
problems.answer: No, it is the answer itself.

problems.prompt: A churn model uses "account closed date". What is wrong with that feature?
problems.answer: It is only known after the customer leaves, so it leaks the label.

steps.title: Underfit and Overfit
steps.mastery: Spot models that are too simple or too flexible.
steps.practice: Fit polynomials of degree 1, 3 and 15 to 20 noisy points from a curve and compare train and test error.
steps.detail: Degree 1 misses the curve, degree 15 chases the noise. The best model has low test error, not the lowest training error.
steps.proof: Degree 3 has the lowest test error, and degree 15 has the lowest train error.
steps.pitfall: Choosing the model with the lowest training error.

problems.prompt: Train error 2% and test error 30%. Underfit or overfit?
Train error 25% and test error 26%. Underfit or overfit?
Name 2 ways to reduce overfitting in a degree 15 model.
problems.answer: More data, or a simpler model or regularization.

steps.title: The Learning Loop
steps.mastery: Describe the steps from data to a deployed model.
steps.practice: Write the 6 steps from collecting data to monitoring a deployed model for a project of your choice.
steps.detail: Collect, clean, split, train, evaluate, deploy and watch. Most time goes into data, and models drift when the world changes.
steps.proof: 6 steps written with 1 risk for each.
steps.pitfall: Treating training as the only step.

problems.prompt: Which step usually takes the most time, of the 6?
A model trained in 2023 gets worse in 2025. Name the problem.
After deployment, what 2 things should you track every week?
problems.answer: The model score on fresh data and the input distribution.

steps.title: Stack a Major Triad
steps.mastery: Build a major chord from a root by stacking two thirds.
steps.practice: Build major triads on C, G and F, naming all 3 notes of each.
steps.detail: A major third then a minor third: 4 semitones then 3. C gives C E G, G gives G B D, F gives F A C. Every major triad has the same 4-then-3 shape, so the chord is the shape rather than the letters.
steps.proof: C E G, G B D and F A C.
steps.pitfall: Stacking 2 major thirds, which gives an augmented chord rather than a major one.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of a C major triad.
What are the 2 interval sizes in semitones, bottom to top?
Stacking 4 then 3 semitones from F gives which 3 notes?

steps.title: Make It Minor
steps.mastery: Convert a major triad to minor by lowering one note.
steps.practice: Turn C major into C minor and name which of the 3 notes moves, and by how much.
steps.detail: Flatten the middle note by a semitone: C E G becomes C Eb G, so the stack is 3 then 4 rather than 4 then 3. The root and the fifth do not move, which is why major and minor chords on the same root sound related rather than unrelated.
steps.proof: C Eb G, with only the third moved down 1 semitone.
steps.pitfall: Flattening the fifth as well, which gives a diminished chord.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of a C minor triad.
Which 1 of the 3 notes moves when major becomes minor, and how far?
What are the 2 interval sizes of a minor triad in semitones?

steps.title: Diminished and Augmented
steps.mastery: Build the two triads made of equal thirds.
steps.practice: Build a diminished and an augmented triad on C, naming the 3 notes of each.
steps.detail: Diminished is 3 then 3, C Eb Gb, and augmented is 4 then 4, C E G#. Both are symmetrical, which is why they sound unsettled: no note is obviously the root when every interval is the same size.
steps.proof: C Eb Gb and C E G#.
steps.pitfall: Calling C Eb Gb a minor chord, which has a perfect fifth rather than a diminished one.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of a C diminished triad.
Name the 3 notes of a C augmented triad.
What do the 2 interval sizes have in common in both chords?
problems.answer: They are equal, 3 and 3, or 4 and 4.

steps.title: Chords of a Key
steps.mastery: Name the triads that a major key produces on each degree.
steps.practice: Build triads on all 7 degrees of C major and label each major, minor or diminished.
steps.detail: Using only the key's own notes gives major on 1, 4 and 5; minor on 2, 3 and 6; diminished on 7. That pattern is the same in every major key, which is why chord numbers transfer between keys and letters do not.
steps.proof: Major on 1, 4, 5; minor on 2, 3, 6; diminished on 7.
steps.pitfall: Making every chord major, which forces 3 notes outside the key.

problems.prompt: Which 3 degrees of a major key carry major triads?
Which degree of the 7 carries the diminished triad?
In C major, what kind of triad sits on degree 2, and what are its notes?

steps.title: Add the Seventh
steps.mastery: Extend a triad to four notes and hear the difference.
steps.practice: Build a G dominant seventh, naming all 4 notes, and say which note wants to resolve.
steps.detail: Add a minor third above the fifth: G B D F. The F is a semitone above E, the third of C major, and that pull is what makes a dominant seventh want to land on C. Play G7 then C to hear it, then G7 alone and notice it does not feel finished.
steps.proof: G B D F, and the F resolves down to E.
steps.pitfall: Adding a major seventh to a dominant chord, which gives F# and removes the pull entirely.

problems.prompt: Name the 4 notes of a G dominant seventh.
Which of the 4 notes creates the pull towards C major?
problems.answer: The F, which falls a semitone to E.

problems.prompt: Which interval is added above the fifth of G B D to make a 4-note dominant seventh?

steps.title: Read a Chord Symbol
steps.mastery: Turn a written chord symbol into specific notes.
steps.practice: Name the notes of Am, D7 and Fmaj7-3 symbols.
steps.detail: The letter is the root, m means minor, 7 means a dominant seventh, maj7 means a major seventh. So A C E, D F# A C, and F A C E. The symbols are compact and unambiguous once you know that 7 alone means the flattened one.
steps.proof: A C E, D F# A C, and F A C E.
steps.pitfall: Reading D7 as a D major seventh, which gives C# instead of C.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of Am.
Name the 4 notes of D7.
Name the 4 notes of Fmaj7.

steps.title: Play Them in Time
steps.mastery: Change between chords cleanly at a steady tempo.
steps.practice: Play C, F, G, C at 60 BPM, 1 chord per 2 beats, with no gap at the changes.
steps.detail: The difficulty is the change, not the chord, so practice the join: play the last beat of one chord and the first of the next, 8 times, before running the sequence. A gap at the change is the thing a listener notices and the player does not.
steps.proof: 4 chords in 8 beats at 60 with no audible gap between them.
steps.pitfall: Practicing the 4 chords separately, which leaves every change unpracticed.

problems.prompt: At 60 BPM with 1 chord per 2 beats, how long do the 4 chords take?
What should be drilled 8 times before running the sequence?
Who notices the gap at 1 of the 4 chord changes first?

steps.title: Start From One Idea
steps.mastery: Write a motif short enough to develop.
steps.practice: Write a 2-bar motif of no more than 6 notes and play it 4 times.
steps.detail: Short ideas are workable and long ones are finished: 6 notes can be inverted, displaced and extended, while a 16-bar tune can only be repeated. Play it 4 times and check it survives repetition without becoming annoying, which is the test it has to pass.
steps.proof: A 2-bar motif of 6 notes or fewer that survives 4 repetitions.
steps.pitfall: Starting with a complete 16-bar melody, which leaves nothing to develop.

problems.prompt: Is the motif 2 bars of 6 notes, or 16 bars?
Why is a 16-bar tune a worse starting point than 6 notes?
problems.answer: It is already finished, so there is nothing left to develop.

problems.prompt: What test must the motif pass on the 4th repetition?

steps.title: Develop Before Adding
steps.mastery: Extend a piece by transforming what you have.
steps.practice: Write 8 bars using only your 6-note motif and 3 transformations of it.
steps.detail: The instinct when 8 bars are needed is to invent 4 new ideas, which produces a piece that goes nowhere because nothing returns. Transform instead: sequence it up a step, invert it, stretch it to double length. The listener hears development rather than a list.
steps.proof: 8 bars traceable to 1 motif and 3 named transformations.
steps.pitfall: Writing 4 new ideas in 8 bars, which sounds like a list rather than a piece.

problems.prompt: How many transformations fill the 8 bars, and of how many motifs?
Name 2 transformations available.
problems.answer: Sequencing it up a step, and inverting it.

problems.prompt: What does a piece of 4 unrelated ideas sound like?
problems.answer: A list rather than a piece.

steps.title: Plan the Shape First
steps.mastery: Decide a piece's sections before writing its notes.
steps.practice: Write a plan for 32 bars as 4 sections of 8, naming the loudest and the quietest.
steps.detail: Four boxes with a dynamic and a function each, state, develop, contrast, return, is enough of a plan. Naming the loudest and quietest sections in advance is what gives the piece a shape rather than a uniform intensity, which is the commonest fault in a first composition.
steps.proof: A 4-box plan with a named peak and trough.
steps.pitfall: Starting to write bar 1 with no plan, which produces 32 bars at 1 intensity.

problems.prompt: How many sections does the 32-bar plan hold, and of what length?
Which 2 sections are named in advance?
What is the commonest fault in a first 32-bar composition?
problems.answer: A uniform intensity with no shape.

steps.title: Write a Bass Line
steps.mastery: Support a melody with a line that moves independently.
steps.practice: Write a bass line under 8 bars of melody, moving in the opposite direction at least 4 times.
steps.detail: A bass line that follows the melody's contour adds thickness and nothing else. Moving against it creates 2 lines, which is what makes the texture sound composed. Mark the 4 places you moved against the melody so the choice is visible.
steps.proof: A bass line with 4 marked points of contrary motion.
steps.pitfall: Doubling the melody an octave down, which is 1 line played twice.

problems.prompt: How many times must the bass move against the melody in 8 bars?
What does doubling the melody 1 octave down produce?
Why mark the 4 points of contrary motion?
problems.answer: It makes the choice visible and checkable.

steps.title: Harmonize Your Own Tune
steps.mastery: Choose chords that support a melody you wrote.
steps.practice: Harmonize your 8-bar melody with no more than 5 chords, changing at most once per bar.
steps.detail: Fewer chords, changed less often, almost always sounds better than more: a chord per beat leaves no room for the melody to be the subject. Five chords across 8 bars is a reasonable ceiling for a first attempt, and the cadence is the 1 place worth spending an extra change.
steps.proof: 8 bars harmonized with 5 chords or fewer.
steps.pitfall: Changing chord on every beat, which buries the melody under harmony.

problems.prompt: What is the chord ceiling for the 8 bars, and how often may they change?
problems.answer: 5 chords, at most 1 change per bar.

problems.prompt: What happens to the melody when the chord changes on every 1 of 4 beats?
problems.answer: The melody stops being the subject.

problems.prompt: Where in the 8 bars is an extra chord change most worth spending?

steps.title: Write the Ending
steps.mastery: Finish a piece so it sounds finished rather than stopped.
steps.practice: Write 2 endings for the same 8 bars, 1 cadencing and 1 fading, and choose between them.
steps.detail: An ending is a decision, and the 2 obvious options sound very different: a perfect cadence closes, a fade leaves the piece open. Write both and play them to somebody. The one you keep should be the one that matches the plan, not the one that was easier to write.
steps.proof: 2 written endings and a stated reason for the choice.
steps.pitfall: Stopping when the material runs out, which sounds like an accident.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 endings this step asks for.
What should decide which of the 2 you keep?
problems.answer: The plan, not which was easier to write.

problems.prompt: What does stopping when the material runs out after 8 bars sound like?
problems.answer: An accident rather than an ending.

steps.title: Notate It Properly
steps.mastery: Write a score somebody else could read and play.
steps.practice: Notate your 32 bars with key, time signature, tempo, 3 dynamics and 2 articulations.
steps.detail: A score missing its tempo and dynamics is a set of pitches: the performer has to invent the parts you left out, and they will invent something else. Include the tempo as a number, not only a word, and put a dynamic at every section boundary.
steps.proof: A score carrying a numeric tempo, 3 dynamics and 2 articulation marks.
steps.pitfall: Notating only the pitches and rhythms and leaving the interpretation to be guessed.

problems.prompt: Name the 5 things this step requires on the score.
problems.answer: Key, time signature, tempo, 3 dynamics and 2 articulations.

problems.prompt: Why give the tempo as a number as well as a word like Allegro?
problems.answer: A word names a band of about 40 BPM; a number is exact.

problems.prompt: Where should a dynamic marking always appear across the 4 sections?

steps.title: Get It Played
steps.mastery: Hear your piece performed by somebody who is not you.
steps.practice: Give your score to 1 other player and note 3 places where what you heard differs from what you meant.
steps.detail: Another player reads what is on the page rather than what is in your head, which is the only honest test of a score. Where they play something unintended, the notation is usually at fault, a missing articulation, an ambiguous tempo, and that is fixable.
steps.proof: 3 differences noted, each traced to something on the page.
steps.pitfall: Telling the player what you meant before they read it, which destroys the test.

problems.prompt: How many differences does this step ask you to note, 3 or 10?
A player plays something you did not intend. Where is the fault usually?
problems.answer: In the notation, a missing or ambiguous mark.

problems.prompt: Why not explain your intentions to the 1 player before they read it?
problems.answer: It destroys the test of whether the score says what you meant.

steps.title: Revise From the Recording
steps.mastery: Rewrite a piece after hearing it, rather than after finishing it.
steps.practice: Listen to a recording of your 32 bars and make 3 specific changes to the score.
steps.detail: First drafts are too long, too uniform and too busy in the middle, in roughly that order. Cut before you add: removing 4 bars is more often the right change than writing 4 more. Mark the 3 changes on the score with the bar numbers and play it again.
steps.proof: 3 marked changes with bar numbers, and a second recording.
steps.pitfall: Treating the first version as finished because it is written down.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 usual faults of a first draft, in order.
problems.answer: Too long, too uniform, too busy in the middle.

problems.prompt: Which is more often right: cutting 4 bars or adding 4?
What must each of the 3 changes carry?

steps.title: Read the Dynamic Marks
steps.mastery: Order the common volume markings and say what each means.
steps.practice: Put these 6 in order from quietest to loudest: mf, pp, ff, p, f, mp.
steps.detail: The ladder is pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff, piano is quiet, forte is loud, and m is the middle of each. They are relative to the piece and the instrument rather than absolute, so mf on a flute and mf on a trombone are different sound levels.
steps.proof: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff in that order.
steps.pitfall: Reading p as loud because piano is an instrument, which inverts half the ladder.

problems.prompt: Put these 6 in order from quietest to loudest: mf, pp, ff, p, f, mp.
problems.answer: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff.

problems.prompt: Which of the 6 is louder, mp or mf?
Are the 6 markings absolute sound levels or relative?
problems.answer: Relative to the piece and the instrument.

steps.title: Play a Crescendo
steps.mastery: Grow the volume steadily across a stated number of bars.
steps.practice: Play 4 bars of a single repeated note growing from p to f, changing level once per bar.
steps.detail: Divide the range into 4 steps, p, mp, mf, f, one per bar, so the growth is even rather than arriving in the last beat. Recording it is the only reliable check: a crescendo almost always sounds bigger from behind the instrument than in front of it.
steps.proof: A recording where each of the 4 bars is audibly louder than the one before.
steps.pitfall: Staying at p for 3 bars and jumping to f in the last, which is a step rather than a crescendo.

problems.prompt: Name the 4 levels for a bar-by-bar crescendo from p to f.
You stay at p for 3 bars then jump to f. What have you played?
problems.answer: A step change, not a crescendo.

problems.prompt: Why record the 4 bars rather than judging while playing?
problems.answer: A crescendo sounds larger from behind the instrument than in front of it.

steps.title: Separate and Join Notes
steps.mastery: Play the same notes staccato and legato and hear the difference.
steps.practice: Play a 5-note phrase twice at 70 BPM, once fully detached and once fully joined.
steps.detail: Staccato shortens each note and leaves silence before the next; legato holds each until the next begins, with no gap and no overlap. The pitches and rhythm are identical, so the 2 versions isolate articulation as the only variable.
steps.proof: The 2 recordings differ only in the gaps between the 5 notes.
steps.pitfall: Playing staccato faster than legato, which changes the tempo as well as the articulation.

problems.prompt: What does staccato leave between 2 consecutive notes?
What is the gap between 2 legato notes?
Your staccato version of 5 notes is faster than the legato one. What went wrong?
problems.answer: The tempo changed as well as the articulation, so the comparison is spoiled.

steps.title: Accent One Note
steps.mastery: Make a single note stand out without disturbing the rest.
steps.practice: Play 4 equal crotchets at 70 BPM with an accent on beat 3 only.
steps.detail: An accent is a louder attack on 1 note, not a louder bar. Keep beats 1, 2 and 4 matched and lift only the third, then check by recording: an accent people can hear as an accent rather than as a lurch is a surprisingly small difference in level.
steps.proof: Beat 3 is audibly stronger and the other 3 beats are level with each other.
steps.pitfall: Also lengthening the accented note, which turns it into a rhythmic change rather than a dynamic one.

problems.prompt: Which of the 4 beats carries the accent in this exercise?
What must stay equal while beat 3 is accented?
You lengthen the accented note as well. What have you changed?
problems.answer: The rhythm, not only the dynamic.

steps.title: Shape a Phrase
steps.mastery: Give a phrase a high point and taper either side of it.
steps.practice: Play an 8-note phrase with its loudest note at note 5, growing to it and easing after.
steps.detail: Decide the high point before playing, then work backwards: notes 1 to 4 grow, note 5 peaks, 6 to 8 ease off. A phrase played at 1 level is the default and sounds like an exercise, which is what shaping is for.
steps.proof: A recording where note 5 is the loudest and the shape either side is even.
steps.pitfall: Putting the high point on the last note, which usually sounds like the phrase has stopped rather than arrived.

problems.prompt: In an 8-note phrase peaking at note 5, which notes grow?
What do notes 6 to 8 do?
What does an 8-note phrase played at 1 level sound like?

steps.title: Follow a Marked Score
steps.mastery: Play every dynamic and articulation a passage asks for.
steps.practice: Take 8 bars of marked music and list every dynamic and articulation mark in it before playing.
steps.detail: List them first, the p at bar 1, the crescendo over bars 3 to 4, the staccato in bar 6, so you know what the passage asks for rather than discovering it while playing. Then play it and mark the ones you missed. Most players miss about half at first reading.
steps.proof: A list of the marks in the 8 bars, with the ones you missed ticked off after playing.
steps.pitfall: Reading the notes at first sight and adding the dynamics on a later pass, which usually means never.

problems.prompt: Why list the marks in 8 bars before playing them?
problems.answer: So the passage is played as written rather than discovered mid-phrase.

problems.prompt: Roughly what share of the marks in 8 bars does a player miss at first reading?
You mark 2 misses after playing. What do those 2 become?
problems.answer: The targets of the next run-through.

steps.title: Match a Pitch
steps.mastery: Sing back a single played note accurately.
steps.practice: Sing back 5 played notes within your range and check each against the instrument.
steps.detail: Sing the note before checking, then play it again to compare. If you are consistently flat or sharp by the same amount, that is easier to fix than random error. Five notes is enough to see which it is.
steps.proof: 5 sung notes checked, with the direction of any consistent error noted.
steps.pitfall: Humming along while the note still sounds, which is matching rather than reproducing.

problems.prompt: You are flat on all 5 notes by about the same amount. Random or systematic error?
Why sing before playing the note a 2nd time?
problems.answer: Otherwise you are matching a sounding pitch rather than reproducing it.

problems.prompt: How many notes does this step ask for, and why not 1?
problems.answer: 5, so the pattern of error is visible.

steps.title: Two Intervals Apart
steps.mastery: Distinguish two well-separated intervals by ear.
steps.practice: Name 10 intervals drawn only from a minor second and a perfect fifth, and score yourself.
steps.detail: Start with 2 intervals that sound nothing alike, 1 semitone against 7. Getting 9 or 10 means the discrimination is reliable and a third interval can join. This is deliberately easy, because the habit of scoring and adding is what makes ear training work.
steps.proof: A score of 9 or 10 out of 10 before any interval is added.
steps.pitfall: Starting with a set of 6 intervals, where a score of 4 gives no information.

problems.prompt: How many semitones separate a minor second from a perfect fifth, 1 against what?
What score out of 10 allows a 3rd interval into the set?
Why not begin with 6 intervals?
problems.answer: A score of 4 out of 10 says nothing about which pairs are confused.

steps.title: Build the Interval Set
steps.mastery: Add intervals to your recognizable set one at a time.
steps.practice: Add a major third to your set of 2 and score 10 more, then decide whether to add a fourth.
steps.detail: One at a time, scoring each round. Note the confusions by pair rather than only the total: mistaking a major third for a perfect fourth is a specific thing to drill, and it disappears from view if you only record 7 out of 10.
steps.proof: A score out of 10 for the set of 3, with the confused pairs written down.
steps.pitfall: Adding 3 intervals at once after a good round, which usually collapses the score.

problems.prompt: Your set of 3 scores 7 of 10 with 3 thirds called fourths. What do you drill?
problems.answer: The third against the fourth specifically.

problems.prompt: Are intervals added to the set 1 at a time or 3?
Why record the confused pair rather than just 7 out of 10?
problems.answer: The pair names what to practice; the total does not.

steps.title: Hear Major From Minor
steps.mastery: Identify a chord's quality by ear.
steps.practice: Name 10 played triads as major or minor, keeping the root constant.
steps.detail: Keep the root the same so only the quality varies, that isolates what you are listening for. Aim for 9 of 10 before letting the root move, because a moving root adds pitch memory to a problem that was about quality.
steps.proof: 9 or more correct out of 10 with a fixed root.
steps.pitfall: Varying the root from the start, which makes 2 problems out of 1.

problems.prompt: Which 1 of the 3 notes differs between a major and a minor triad?
Why keep the root fixed for the first 10 trials?
problems.answer: It isolates quality from pitch memory.

problems.prompt: What score out of 10 lets the root start moving?

steps.title: Follow a Bass Line
steps.mastery: Sing the lowest line of a played progression.
steps.practice: Listen to a 4-chord progression 3 times and sing the 4 bass notes back.
steps.detail: The bass is the easiest line to isolate and the one that tells you most about the harmony. Three hearings, then sing; checking against the instrument afterwards usually shows the first and last notes right and the middle 2 approximate, which is normal and improves quickly.
steps.proof: 4 bass notes sung, with the number correct written down.
steps.pitfall: Trying to hear all 3 notes of every chord before the bass line is reliable.

problems.prompt: Which line of a 4-chord progression is easiest to isolate?
You get bass notes 1 and 4 right and 2 and 3 approximate. Normal or not?
problems.answer: Normal, the ends are easiest and the middle improves with practice.

problems.prompt: How many hearings before singing the 4 notes?

steps.title: Name a Progression
steps.mastery: Identify a common progression from a small set by ear.
steps.practice: Name 10 played progressions drawn from 1-4-5-1 and 1-5-6m-4, and score yourself.
steps.detail: Two progressions, both 4 chords, one cadencing and one looping. Listen for whether it closes: a 1-4-5-1 arrives and a 1-5-6m-4 does not. That single question answers most of the trials without identifying any individual chord.
steps.proof: A score out of 10, with the deciding cue written in 1 line.
steps.pitfall: Trying to name each chord in turn, which is slower and less reliable than hearing whether it closed.

problems.prompt: Which of the 2 progressions closes rather than loops?
What single question decides most of the 10 trials?
problems.answer: Whether the progression closed or not.

problems.prompt: Which is more reliable: naming 4 chords in turn, or hearing the shape?

steps.title: Transcribe a Short Phrase
steps.mastery: Write down a melody you have only heard.
steps.practice: Transcribe a 4-bar melody from a recording, 1 bar at a time, and check it by playing it back.
steps.detail: Work bar by bar and get the rhythm before the pitches, a correct rhythm with 2 wrong notes is closer than the reverse. Playing your transcription against the recording is the check, and any note that clashes is one to redo rather than to argue about.
steps.proof: 4 written bars that play back against the recording without clashing.
steps.pitfall: Transcribing pitches first and fitting the rhythm afterwards, which usually needs starting again.

problems.prompt: Which comes first in transcribing 4 bars: the rhythm or the pitches?
How do you check the 4 bars?
problems.answer: Play the transcription against the recording and listen for clashes.

problems.prompt: Is a correct rhythm with 2 wrong pitches closer than correct pitches with a wrong rhythm?

steps.title: Keep a Weekly Score
steps.mastery: Track ear training numerically so progress is visible.
steps.practice: Record your scores for 3 exercise types each week and compare 4 weeks of figures.
steps.detail: Ear training improves slowly and invisibly, which is why most people stop. Three numbers a week, intervals, chord quality, progressions, turns that into a line you can see. A score that has not moved in 4 weeks means the set is wrong, not that you cannot do it.
steps.proof: 4 weeks of 3 scores each, with any flat line identified.
steps.pitfall: Practicing without scoring, which leaves no way to tell progress from familiarity.

problems.prompt: How many numbers does this step record each week, 1 or 3?
A score has not moved across 4 weeks. What does that indicate?
problems.answer: The exercise set is wrong, rather than the ability being fixed.

problems.prompt: Practicing without a score across 4 weeks makes what impossible to tell?

steps.title: Find the Phrases
steps.mastery: Divide a piece into its natural units.
steps.practice: Mark the phrase endings in 16 bars and say how many bars each phrase runs.
steps.detail: Listen for where the line breathes: a cadence, a rest, a repeated rhythm starting again. Most phrases are 4 or 8 bars, and 16 bars usually divides into 4 of 4. Where a phrase is 5 bars, that irregularity is usually the most interesting thing on the page.
steps.proof: Phrase endings marked, with the bar count of each written in.
steps.pitfall: Marking phrases at bar lines rather than at cadences, which finds 16 phrases in 16 bars.

problems.prompt: 16 bars most often divides into how many phrases of what length?
Name 2 signals of a phrase ending.
problems.answer: A cadence, and a rest or breath in the line.

problems.prompt: A phrase runs 5 bars where the others run 4. Is that an error?
problems.answer: No, it is usually the most interesting moment in the passage.

steps.title: Label What Repeats
steps.mastery: Use letters to record a piece's sections and repeats.
steps.practice: Label a 32-bar piece with letters, giving the same letter to sections that repeat.
steps.detail: Call the first section A, and use A again only when the material returns. AABA is the commonest 32-bar shape, 8 bars each, and writing the letters takes 2 minutes and tells you most of what there is to know about the architecture.
steps.proof: A letter per 8-bar section, with repeats sharing a letter.
steps.pitfall: Giving a new letter to a section that returns with small changes, which hides the return.

problems.prompt: What is the commonest 32-bar form, in letters?
A section returns with a small variation. Same letter or new one?
problems.answer: The same letter, since the material has returned.

problems.prompt: How many bars does each section of AABA hold in a 32-bar piece?

steps.title: Binary and Ternary
steps.mastery: Tell a two-part form from a three-part one.
steps.practice: Label 2 short pieces as AB or ABA and say what makes each what it is.
steps.detail: Binary is a statement and a contrast; ternary adds a return, which changes how the piece feels far more than the extra section suggests. The return is what makes ternary sound resolved and binary sound like it stopped.
steps.proof: 1 piece labeled AB and 1 ABA, with the return identified.
steps.pitfall: Calling any 3-section piece ternary, when ABC is 3 sections and no return.

problems.prompt: Which of AB and ABA has a return?
Is a piece in 3 sections labeled ABC ternary?
problems.answer: No, ternary needs the return, not just 3 sections.

problems.prompt: What does the return do to how an ABA piece of 3 sections ends?
problems.answer: It makes it sound resolved rather than stopped.

steps.title: Verse and Chorus
steps.mastery: Identify the sections of a popular song form.
steps.practice: Map a 3-minute song into verse, chorus and bridge, with a bar count for each section.
steps.detail: The chorus repeats with the same words, the verse repeats with new ones, and the bridge appears once. Counting bars usually shows 8 or 16 per section and a chorus that arrives sooner than you remember, often inside the first 60 seconds.
steps.proof: A map of the song with a bar count against every section.
steps.pitfall: Labeling by intensity rather than by repetition, which calls any loud section a chorus.

problems.prompt: In a 3-minute song, what distinguishes a verse from a chorus?
problems.answer: The chorus repeats with the same words; the verse repeats with new ones.

problems.prompt: How many times does a bridge usually appear in a 3-minute song?
Why is loudness a poor test for a chorus in a 3-minute song?
problems.answer: Form is about repetition, not intensity.

steps.title: Follow a Sonata Exposition
steps.mastery: Identify the two theme areas and the key change between them.
steps.practice: Mark where the 2nd theme of a sonata exposition starts and name the key it arrives in.
steps.detail: The first theme is in the home key; the second arrives in the dominant, or in the relative major if the piece is minor. Finding the key change is easier than finding the theme: look for the new key signature's accidentals appearing consistently, then look 2 bars earlier.
steps.proof: The second theme marked, with its key named and justified by the accidentals.
steps.pitfall: Looking for the theme by its tune, when the key change is the reliable signal.

problems.prompt: In a major-key sonata, which key does the 2nd theme usually arrive in?
In a minor-key sonata, which key is the 2nd theme likely to arrive in?
Which is the more reliable signal of the 2nd theme, the tune or the key change?

steps.title: Track a Theme's Return
steps.mastery: Notice how returning material has been changed.
steps.practice: Compare a theme's first and last appearance and list 3 differences.
steps.detail: Returns are rarely literal: the key, the instrumentation, the accompaniment or the ending may differ. Listing 3 differences is what turns listening into analysis, and the change at the end is usually the most deliberate one, a return that has not changed has not gone anywhere.
steps.proof: 3 named differences between the 2 appearances.
steps.pitfall: Hearing a return as identical because the tune is the same, and missing the changed harmony under it.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things that commonly change when a theme returns.
problems.answer: The key, the instrumentation and the accompaniment.

problems.prompt: Which of the 3 changes is usually the most deliberate?
The tune is identical on both appearances. What should you check?
problems.answer: The harmony and accompaniment underneath it.

steps.title: Map a Whole Piece
steps.mastery: Produce a one-page diagram of a piece's architecture.
steps.practice: Diagram a 5-minute piece on 1 page, with sections, bar numbers and keys marked.
steps.detail: Boxes for sections, bar numbers under them, keys above, arrows for returns. On 1 page the proportions become visible, a development twice the length of the exposition, a coda that is a third of the piece, and those proportions are what a listener actually experiences.
steps.proof: 1 page showing every section with its bars and key.
steps.pitfall: Writing a list of sections rather than a diagram, which loses the proportions.

problems.prompt: What 3 things are marked on each box of the diagram?
problems.answer: The section, its bar numbers and its key.

problems.prompt: What does a diagram show that a list of 6 sections does not?
problems.answer: The proportions, how long each section is relative to the others.

problems.prompt: How are returns shown on the 1-page diagram?
problems.answer: With arrows back to the earlier section.

steps.title: Build a Form Yourself
steps.mastery: Write a short piece to a plan you chose in advance.
steps.practice: Plan 24 bars as ABA with 8 bars each, then write it and check the return is recognizable.
steps.detail: Write the plan before the notes: 8 bars of A, 8 of contrasting B, then A again with 1 deliberate change. Deciding the architecture first is what stops a piece wandering, and the deliberate change in the return is what stops it being a repeat.
steps.proof: 24 bars in ABA with the return carrying 1 intentional change.
steps.pitfall: Composing forwards until it feels finished, which usually produces 40 bars of A with no shape.

problems.prompt: How many bars does each section of a 24-bar ABA hold?
What does the returning A of 8 bars carry that the first A did not?
What usually happens to 24 bars composed forwards with no plan?
problems.answer: It wanders, lots of A and no shape.

steps.title: Hear Two Lines at Once
steps.mastery: Follow two independent melodies sounding together.
steps.practice: Play 4 bars of a 2-part piece, then play each line alone and sing 1 while playing the other.
steps.detail: Separating the lines is the skill: play the upper alone, then the lower, then sing the upper while playing the lower. Singing 1 part while playing another is where the independence becomes real rather than theoretical.
steps.proof: Both lines played alone, and the upper sung while the lower is played.
steps.pitfall: Hearing the 2 parts as a chord sequence, which loses the horizontal motion that is the point.

problems.prompt: What are the 3 passes over the 4 bars?
problems.answer: Upper line alone, lower line alone, then 1 sung while the other is played.

problems.prompt: What is lost by hearing 2 parts as a chord sequence?
problems.answer: The horizontal motion of each line.

problems.prompt: Which of the 3 passes makes the independence of 2 lines real?
problems.answer: Singing 1 part while playing the other.

steps.title: Move by Step
steps.mastery: Write a second line that moves mostly stepwise.
steps.practice: Write a lower line under an 8-note melody using steps of 1 or 2 semitones wherever possible.
steps.detail: Stepwise motion is what makes a line singable and audible as a line rather than as a series of notes chosen for their chords. Allow a leap when the harmony demands it, then step back in the opposite direction afterwards, which is how a leap stops sounding like a mistake.
