steps.detail: An ensemble removes the option of stopping, which is why this is the strongest version of the exercise. Agree the tempo and count 4 beats in. When you get lost, find the next bar line rather than the next note, coming back in on a bar line is recoverable and coming back mid-bar is not.
steps.proof: 8 bars played together with both parts ending in the same bar.
steps.pitfall: Trying to rejoin mid-bar after losing your place, which usually loses the other player too.

problems.prompt: You lose your place in bar 5 of 8. What do you look for?
problems.answer: The next bar line, not the next note.

problems.prompt: What is agreed before the 8 bars start?
problems.answer: The tempo, with 4 beats counted in.

problems.prompt: Why is duet reading of 8 bars stronger than reading alone?

steps.title: Group by Task Type
steps.mastery: Group tasks that need the same tools or mindset so you set up once.
steps.practice: Sort your next 15 tasks into 3 or 4 groups, like calls, emails, errands and deep work.
steps.detail: Every switch between task types costs a few minutes of warm-up. Calls need your phone and voice. Emails need your inbox open. Errands need the car. Grouping them pays that setup once and lets you move fast through the whole batch.
steps.proof: 15 tasks sorted into 3 or 4 named groups.
steps.pitfall: Doing tasks in the order they arrived, switching type every 10 minutes.

problems.prompt: Your list has 4 calls, 6 emails and 3 errands mixed together. How many groups?
Why do 4 calls in a row go faster than 4 calls spread through the day?
problems.answer: You set up once and stay in the same mode.

problems.prompt: Is "write report" a good fit for the email batch?
problems.answer: No. It's deep work and needs its own block.

steps.title: Check Email 3 Times a Day
steps.mastery: Limit email and chat to set windows instead of reacting all day.
steps.practice: Check email only at 9 am, 1 pm and 4 pm for 3 days, with notifications off in between.
steps.detail: Email is the classic batch. Checking it constantly breaks focus every few minutes. Three windows keep you responsive while protecting the rest of the day. Most messages can wait a few hours. Tell people how to reach you if it's urgent.
steps.proof: 3 days of email in 3 windows only.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the inbox open in a tab and checking every 5 minutes.

problems.prompt: An email arrives at 10:20. Your next window is 1 pm. When do you reply?
problems.answer: At 1 pm, unless it's a true emergency.

problems.prompt: Email waits until 1 pm. How do people reach you for something urgent at 10?
problems.answer: Give them another way, like a phone call.

problems.prompt: You check 40 times a day now. What's the target?

steps.title: Bundle Your Errands
steps.mastery: Collect errands through the week and run them in one trip.
steps.practice: Keep an errand list for 7 days and run every item in 1 trip on Saturday.
steps.detail: Each trip has fixed costs: getting ready, driving, parking. Doing 5 errands in 1 trip pays those once. Plan the route so you don't backtrack, and save cold food for last.
steps.proof: 1 trip covering every errand from the week.
steps.pitfall: Driving out 4 separate times for 4 small things.

problems.prompt: You need the bank, the pharmacy and groceries. Which goes last?
problems.answer: Groceries, so cold food goes straight home.

problems.prompt: Name 2 fixed costs of a single errand trip.
You made 5 trips last week. What's the target this week?

steps.title: Batch Chores
steps.mastery: Group household chores into one block instead of scattering them.
steps.practice: Finish all of this week's chores in 1 block of 90 minutes on a set day.
steps.detail: Chores spread across every evening never feel finished. One block lets you get into a groove, use the same supplies and be done. Put on music and work room by room.
steps.proof: 1 chore block of 90 minutes done this week.
steps.pitfall: Doing 10 minutes of chores every night and never feeling done.

problems.prompt: Why does 1 block of 90 minutes feel better than 9 bits of 10?
problems.answer: You finish and get into a groove.

problems.prompt: Name 1 way to make the 90 minutes go faster.
problems.answer: Put on music, or work room by room.

problems.prompt: You have 2 free mornings this week. How do you pick the chore day?
problems.answer: Pick the one with more energy and fewer plans.

steps.title: Test What Batching Saves
steps.mastery: Check which batches save time so you keep the useful ones.
steps.practice: Time 1 batch of 5 similar tasks and compare it to doing 5 one by one.
steps.detail: Batching usually saves time, but not always. Test it. If a batch takes 30 minutes and the scattered version took 50, keep it. If there's no gain, drop it.
steps.proof: 1 batch timed and compared to the scattered version.
steps.pitfall: Assuming every kind of batching helps.

problems.prompt: Batched emails took 30 minutes. Scattered took 50. How much did batching save?
A batch saved 0 minutes. What do you do?
Why time 1 batch instead of assuming all 4 of your batches help?

steps.title: Block Your Top Task
steps.mastery: Give your most important task a fixed slot on the calendar so it gets real hours.
steps.practice: Block 90 minutes on tomorrow's calendar for your most important task and name the block after it.
steps.detail: A task list doesn't know how many hours you have. A calendar does. Once the task has a slot, it competes fairly with meetings and plans. Name the block after the task, like "Draft history essay," so you know exactly what to start.
steps.proof: A named 90 minute block on tomorrow's calendar.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the big task on a list where it loses to every meeting.

problems.prompt: Your task list has 15 items and you have 2 free hours tomorrow. What goes in the calendar first?
problems.answer: A block for your single most important task.

problems.prompt: A friend asks to meet during your 90 minute block. Write a reply.
Rename a block called "Work" so it tells you what to do.
problems.answer: "Draft history essay intro," or something just as specific.

steps.title: Lay Out a Whole Day
steps.mastery: Plan a full day in blocks to see whether your tasks truly fit.
steps.practice: Block every hour of tomorrow from 9 to 5, including lunch, 2 breaks and an email slot.
steps.detail: Planning every hour shows the truth fast. Add the boring stuff too: lunch, travel, breaks, email. If the blocks add up to more than the day, cut tasks now. A plan that doesn't fit isn't a plan.
steps.proof: A fully blocked 8 hour day with breaks and lunch.
steps.pitfall: Leaving out lunch and breaks, then running late all afternoon.

problems.prompt: Your blocks add up to 10 hours and you have 8. What do you do?
problems.answer: Cut or move 2 hours of tasks before the day starts.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things besides tasks that need a block.
problems.answer: Lunch, breaks and an email slot.

problems.prompt: Why block 2 breaks in an 8 hour day?
problems.answer: Unplanned breaks get skipped, and you fade by 3 pm.

steps.title: Leave Buffer Between Blocks
steps.mastery: Space blocks so one delay doesn't knock over the whole day.
steps.practice: Add a 15 minute gap after every 2 blocks on tomorrow's plan.
steps.detail: Meetings run over and tasks take longer than planned. Gaps absorb that. Without them, one late meeting pushes every block back. If a gap isn't needed, use it for quick tasks or a walk.
steps.proof: A plan with a 15 minute gap after every 2 blocks.
steps.pitfall: Stacking blocks back to back with no room for delays.

problems.prompt: Your 10 am meeting runs 15 minutes over. With no gaps, what happens to your 4 pm block?
problems.answer: Everything shifts, and the 4 pm block may get cut.

problems.prompt: A gap isn't needed today. Name 2 good uses for it.
problems.answer: Quick tasks or a short walk.

problems.prompt: You have 6 blocks. How many 15 minute gaps does the rule give you?

steps.title: Move, Don't Drop
steps.mastery: Reschedule an interrupted block right away so the task doesn't vanish.
steps.practice: For the next 3 blocks that get interrupted, move the task to a new slot within 10 minutes.
steps.detail: Plans break. That's normal. The skill is repair. When a block gets taken, find the next free slot and move the task there right away. A task that's simply skipped tends to disappear for a week.
steps.proof: 3 interrupted blocks moved to new slots.
steps.pitfall: Shrugging off a lost block and never rescheduling it.

problems.prompt: A surprise meeting eats your 2 pm writing block. What do you do by 2:10?
problems.answer: Move the writing block to the next free slot.

problems.prompt: Why reschedule within 10 minutes?
problems.answer: Before the task fades from view.

problems.prompt: You lost 3 blocks this week and moved all 3. Did the plan fail?
problems.answer: No. Repairing it is the skill.

steps.title: Check Your Hit Rate
steps.mastery: Count how many blocks happen as planned and adjust how much you plan.
steps.practice: On Friday, count how many of this week's blocks happened as planned and write the percent.
steps.detail: The count tells you if your plans are realistic. If only 40 percent happen, you're planning too much or not protecting the time. Around 70 percent is a good target. Change 1 thing next week based on what broke most.
steps.proof: A weekly hit rate as a percent, with 1 change noted.
steps.pitfall: Never counting, so you keep making the same fantasy plan.

problems.prompt: 14 of 20 blocks happened. What's your hit rate?
Your hit rate is 35 percent. Name 1 likely cause.
problems.answer: You're planning too much, or meetings keep taking blocks.

problems.prompt: Most missed blocks were after 3 pm. What could you change?
problems.answer: Plan lighter tasks or fewer blocks late in the day.

steps.title: Pick 1 Inbox
steps.mastery: Choose a single trusted place where every new task and idea lands first.
steps.practice: Pick 1 capture tool, like a notes app or a pocket notebook, and delete or retire 2 others.
steps.detail: Capture fails when ideas are spread across sticky notes, texts to yourself and 3 apps. Choose one place that's always with you. A phone notes app or a small notebook both work. Fewer places means you'll actually check it.
steps.proof: 1 named capture tool, with the old spots retired.
steps.pitfall: Keeping 4 capture spots, so nothing is ever in one place.

problems.prompt: You jot tasks on sticky notes, in 2 apps and in texts to yourself. What's the first fix?
problems.answer: Pick 1 of them and stop using the others.

problems.prompt: Name 2 tools that work well as a single inbox.
problems.answer: A phone notes app and a pocket notebook.

problems.prompt: Your inbox is a desk notebook, but ideas hit you on the bus 3 times a week. What's wrong?

steps.title: Write It Down in 10 Seconds
steps.mastery: Capture anything the moment it shows up, before it slips away.
steps.practice: For 3 days, write every task, idea or promise into your inbox within 10 seconds of thinking it.
steps.detail: The brain is good at having ideas and bad at holding them. Speed matters more than neatness. A few words is enough, like "email Sam re rent." Sorting comes later, so don't decide anything while capturing.
steps.proof: 3 days of captures, with at least 20 items in the inbox.
steps.pitfall: Waiting to write it down "properly" later, by which point it's gone.

problems.prompt: You think "call Mom" at 8:14 pm. When should it hit the inbox?
Shorten "I need to remember to email Sam about the rent for March" to a capture.
While capturing 15 items, should you also decide which matter most?
problems.answer: No. Capture fast now and sort later.

steps.title: Empty Your Head
steps.mastery: Do a full sweep of everything on your mind into the inbox.
steps.practice: Spend 15 minutes writing every open loop you can think of, aiming for at least 30 items.
steps.detail: Most people carry dozens of small worries: a bill, a reply, a broken lamp, a gift to buy. A mind sweep gets them out. Go area by area: work, school, home, money, people, health. The relief afterward shows how much you were holding.
steps.proof: A list of 30 or more open loops from 15 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Stopping at 8 items because the big ones feel done.

problems.prompt: Name 3 areas to sweep through.
problems.answer: Work, home and money, for example.

problems.prompt: You've listed 9 things in 5 minutes and feel done. What helps?
problems.answer: Go area by area, like health and people, to find more.

problems.prompt: Why aim for 30 items?
problems.answer: Most people carry far more than they realize.

steps.title: Clear the Inbox Daily
steps.mastery: Process the inbox regularly so it stays trusted.
steps.practice: Spend 10 minutes each evening for 7 days moving every inbox item to a list, the calendar or the trash.
steps.detail: An inbox that's never emptied becomes a junk drawer, and you stop trusting it. Each day, go through it. Tasks go on the task list, dates go on the calendar, ideas go in notes, and junk gets deleted. Empty means every item has a home, even if the work isn't done yet.
steps.proof: An empty inbox at the end of 7 evenings.
steps.pitfall: Letting 200 items pile up until you avoid opening it.

problems.prompt: An inbox item says "dentist on the 14th at 3." Where does it go?
An item says "maybe learn Spanish someday." Where does it go?
problems.answer: In notes or a someday list.

problems.prompt: Your inbox has 0 items but 4 tasks aren't done. Is it empty?
problems.answer: Yes. Every item has a home, and that's what empty means.

steps.title: Trust It for 2 Weeks
steps.mastery: Rely on the system instead of your memory.
steps.practice: For 14 days, capture and process daily, and note any time something slipped through.
steps.detail: The point of capture is a calm head. That only works if the system catches everything. Any time you forget something, ask why it didn't get captured. Fix that gap, like keeping the notebook by the bed.
steps.proof: 14 days of capture with a short list of misses and fixes.
steps.pitfall: Capturing some things and trying to remember the rest.

problems.prompt: You forgot a promise made in a hallway. What's the fix?
problems.answer: Capture right after conversations, even with a quick phone note.

problems.prompt: After 14 days, 3 things slipped. Is the system broken?
problems.answer: No. Find each gap and fix it.

problems.prompt: What's the main sign capture is working?
problems.answer: You stop carrying lists in your head.

steps.title: Map Your Sharp Hours
steps.mastery: Find the hours of the day when your focus is naturally at its best.
steps.practice: Rate your focus from 1 to 10 every 2 hours from waking to bed for 5 days.
steps.detail: Most people have 2 to 4 sharp hours a day. For many it's mid-morning, for night owls it's later. Guessing isn't enough, so log it. After 5 days, look for the hours that score 7 or higher most often.
steps.proof: A 5 day log with your top 2 to 4 hours circled.
steps.pitfall: Assuming you're a morning person because you think you should be.

problems.prompt: Your 10 am ratings are 8, 7, 8, 9, 7. Your 3 pm ratings are 4, 5, 3, 4, 5. Which is a sharp hour?
Why log for 5 days instead of 1?
problems.answer: One day can be thrown off by bad sleep or a big event.

problems.prompt: Your best scores are at 9 pm. Is that a problem?
problems.answer: No. Plan your hardest work for those hours if you can.

steps.title: Put Hard Work in Sharp Hours
steps.mastery: Schedule your most demanding work into your best hours.
steps.practice: Move your hardest task into 1 of your sharp hours on 4 days this week.
steps.detail: Doing analytical work in your worst hours is a hidden tax. The same essay might take 1 hour at 10 am and 3 hours at 4 pm. Guard your sharp hours from meetings and email when you can.
steps.proof: 4 days where the hardest task landed in a sharp hour.
steps.pitfall: Spending your best morning hours on email.

problems.prompt: Your sharp hours are 9 to 11. Where does "Write lab report" go?
A meeting request comes in for 10 am, your peak. What could you offer instead?
The same task took 60 minutes at 10 am and 150 at 4 pm. What does that show?
problems.answer: Your sharp hours make hard work much faster.

steps.title: Fill Low Hours With Easy Work
steps.mastery: Use your low-energy hours for tasks that don't need deep focus.
steps.practice: List 6 low-focus tasks, like filing, errands or replying to messages, and put them in your 2 weakest hours.
steps.detail: Low hours aren't wasted. They're good for admin, tidying, routine replies and errands. Matching the task to the energy means less fighting with yourself.
steps.proof: 6 easy tasks placed in your 2 weakest hours.
steps.pitfall: Forcing hard thinking at 3 pm and getting nothing done.

problems.prompt: Name 3 tasks that suit a low-energy hour.
It's 3 pm and your focus is 3 out of 10. Write report or clear inbox?
Why fill your 2 weakest hours with easy tasks instead of resting?
problems.answer: They still need doing, and they don't need sharp focus.

steps.title: Take Real Breaks
steps.mastery: Break before you're drained so focus lasts through the day.
steps.practice: Work in 50 minute blocks with 10 minute breaks away from screens for 1 full day.
steps.detail: Focus fades after about an hour. A short break away from the screen, like a walk or a stretch, helps you come back fresh. Scrolling on your phone isn't a break for your brain.
steps.proof: 1 day of 50 and 10 blocks with screen-free breaks.
steps.pitfall: Pushing through 4 hours straight and crashing at 2 pm.

problems.prompt: You work 9:00 to 9:50. When's your break, and how long?
Is 10 minutes on social media a real break?
problems.answer: No. It keeps your brain busy.

problems.prompt: Name 2 good 10 minute breaks.

steps.title: Notice Sleep, Food and Movement
steps.mastery: Spot how sleep, meals and movement change your energy.
steps.practice: For 7 days, log hours of sleep, meal times and a walk yes or no next to your focus ratings.
steps.detail: Energy isn't fixed. A short night, a skipped lunch or a day stuck at a desk all drag focus down. Logging them beside your ratings shows which one hurts you most.
steps.proof: A 7 day log with sleep, meals and movement beside focus scores.
steps.pitfall: Blaming yourself for low focus without checking the basics.

problems.prompt: On days with 5 hours of sleep, your peak drops from 8 to 5. What's the lesson?
Your 2 pm slump is worse after a big lunch. What could you try?
problems.answer: A lighter lunch or a short walk after.

problems.prompt: You walked on 4 of 7 days and focus was higher on those days. What does it suggest?

steps.title: Plan the Week Around Energy
steps.mastery: Build your weekly schedule around your energy pattern.
steps.practice: Plan next week so each day has 1 deep work block in a sharp hour and easy tasks in low hours.
steps.detail: Once you know your pattern, plan with it. Put 1 big block each day in your best hours. Fill the rest with meetings, admin and errands. Protect the deep blocks as firmly as a class or a meeting.
steps.proof: A week planned with a daily deep block in sharp hours.
steps.pitfall: Booking meetings into every sharp hour and doing deep work at night.

problems.prompt: You have 5 deep tasks and 5 days. How would you spread them?
problems.answer: 1 per day in your sharp hours.

problems.prompt: Monday's sharp hours are taken by a class. What do you do with Monday's deep task?
problems.answer: Move it to the next best hour or another day.

problems.prompt: Why protect the 90 minute deep block like a class?
problems.answer: Otherwise it gets eaten by requests.

steps.title: Guess, Then Time It
steps.mastery: Estimate how long tasks take and check against reality.
steps.practice: Write a time estimate for 5 tasks, then time each one and write the actual minutes.
steps.detail: Everyone underestimates. The only fix is data. Guess first, then time it. After a few days you'll see your pattern, like always taking 1.5 times longer than you think.
steps.proof: 5 tasks with guessed and actual times.
steps.pitfall: Never checking, so estimates never improve.

problems.prompt: You guessed 20 minutes and it took 35. What's the ratio?
Why write a guess before starting the 5 minute timer?
problems.answer: To compare and learn your pattern.

problems.prompt: Most people's estimates are too low or too high?

steps.title: Find Your Multiplier
steps.mastery: Work out your personal estimation error so you can correct for it.
steps.practice: Time 15 tasks over 5 days and divide total actual minutes by total guessed minutes.
steps.detail: If you guessed 300 minutes and it took 450, your multiplier is 1.5. Use it on future guesses. It's simple and surprisingly accurate.
steps.proof: A multiplier from 15 tasks.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring the data because one task was quick.

problems.prompt: Guessed 300, actual 450. What's your multiplier?
Your multiplier is 1.5. You guess 40 minutes. What should you plan?
Why use 15 tasks instead of 2?
problems.answer: More tasks give a steadier number.

steps.title: Add Buffer
steps.mastery: Leave slack in plans for the unexpected.
steps.practice: Add 25 percent buffer to every block on tomorrow's plan.
steps.detail: Things go wrong: a slow computer, a call, a missing file. A buffer absorbs it. Without slack, one delay wrecks the whole day.
steps.proof: Tomorrow's plan with 25 percent buffer on each block.
steps.pitfall: Planning back to back with no room for delays.

problems.prompt: A task is estimated at 40 minutes. What's 25 percent buffer?
Why add a 25 percent buffer?
One 15 minute delay ruins your day. What was missing?

steps.title: Estimate Projects in Steps
steps.mastery: Estimate big projects by adding up their small steps.
steps.practice: Break 1 project into 6 steps, estimate each, add them up and apply your multiplier.
steps.detail: Big guesses are wild. Small guesses are closer. Estimate each step, add them, then multiply by your number. It's more accurate than guessing the whole.
steps.proof: 1 project estimated step by step.
steps.pitfall: Guessing "about a week" for a whole project.

problems.prompt: 6 steps of 30 minutes, multiplier 1.5. What's the total?
Why estimate 6 steps instead of the whole project?
You guessed "a week" for a project. What's a better method?
problems.answer: Break it into steps and add them up.

steps.title: Review Weekly
steps.mastery: Check your estimates each week and adjust.
steps.practice: On 3 Fridays in a row, compare planned and actual time for 5 tasks.
steps.detail: Your multiplier may change as you learn. A weekly check keeps it honest. If you're getting closer, great. If not, look at which kinds of tasks you misjudge most.
steps.proof: 3 weekly reviews with notes.
steps.pitfall: Setting a multiplier once and never checking again.

problems.prompt: You misjudge writing tasks most. What could you do?
problems.answer: Use a higher multiplier for writing.

problems.prompt: Should you review estimates every week or every 6 months?
Your multiplier dropped from 1.6 to 1.3. What does it show?

steps.title: Pick 3 Goals for 90 Days
steps.mastery: Choose a few goals for the next three months so effort isn't spread thin.
steps.practice: Write 3 goals for the next 90 days, each in a different part of your life.
steps.detail: Twelve goals means none get real attention. Three is enough to make progress on each. Spread them across areas, like school, health and money, so one doesn't crowd out the others.
steps.proof: 3 goals written, each in a different area.
steps.pitfall: Writing 12 goals in January and remembering none by March.

problems.prompt: You wrote 9 goals for 90 days. What's the problem?
problems.answer: Effort gets spread so thin that none move much.

problems.prompt: Name 3 areas to spread goals across.
problems.answer: School, health and money, for example.

problems.prompt: Your 3 goals are all about school. What's the risk?
problems.answer: Other areas, like health, get ignored.

steps.title: Add a Number and Date
steps.mastery: Make each goal clear enough that you'll know exactly when it's done.
steps.practice: Rewrite your 3 goals with a number and a date, like "Run 5K without stopping by June 1."
steps.detail: "Get fit" has no finish line. "Run 5K without stopping by June 1" does. A number tells you what done means. A date stops it drifting. If you can't tell whether it's done, it isn't clear enough.
steps.proof: 3 goals, each with a number and a date.
steps.pitfall: Keeping vague goals like "get better at math" that never finish.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Get better at math."
problems.answer: "Score 80 percent or higher on the May 20 math final."

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Save money."
Is "Read more books" clear?

steps.title: Write the First Step
steps.mastery: Give every goal a next action so it starts moving this week.
steps.practice: Write 1 next action for each of your 3 goals and put 1 of them on tomorrow's list.
steps.detail: A goal without a next action is a wish. The first step should be physical and small, like "Run 1 mile on Monday" or "Open a savings account." Put at least 1 on tomorrow's list.
steps.proof: 3 next actions written and 1 on tomorrow's list.
steps.pitfall: Writing goals and taking no step for 3 weeks.

problems.prompt: Goal: "Run 5K by June 1." Write a first step.
Goal: "Save 500 dollars by August 31." Write a first step.
problems.answer: "Set up a 20 dollar weekly transfer to savings."

problems.prompt: What's a goal without a next action?

steps.title: Track 1 Number per Goal
steps.mastery: Follow one number for each goal so progress is visible.
steps.practice: Pick 1 number for each goal, like miles run or dollars saved, and log it every Sunday for 4 weeks.
steps.detail: Numbers show progress that feelings miss. Pick the 1 number that best shows movement. Log it weekly. If it's flat for 2 weeks, the plan needs changing.
steps.proof: 3 numbers logged for 4 Sundays.
steps.pitfall: Guessing at progress and feeling either too good or too bad.

problems.prompt: Goal: save 500 dollars. Which number do you log?
Your number is flat for 2 weeks. What does it mean?
Week 1: 1 mile. Week 4: 2.5 miles. What does that show?

steps.title: Review in the Weekly Review
steps.mastery: Look at your goals every week so they stay in mind.
steps.practice: Add "Check 3 goals" to your weekly review checklist and do it for 4 weeks.
steps.detail: Goals without review are forgotten by February. Checking weekly keeps them close. Look at the number, the next action and whether this week has time blocked for it.
steps.proof: 4 weekly reviews with goals checked.
steps.pitfall: Writing goals once and never looking again.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things to look at for each goal in the review.
problems.answer: The number, the next action and time blocked this week.

problems.prompt: You checked goals 4 weeks in a row. What's the benefit?
problems.answer: They stay in mind and keep moving.

problems.prompt: A goal has no time blocked this week. What do you do?
problems.answer: Block time for it in the coming week.

steps.title: Decide at Day 45
steps.mastery: Decide halfway whether each goal still fits.
steps.practice: At day 45, mark each goal keep, adjust or drop, and write 1 reason for each choice.
steps.detail: Life changes, and goals can too. At the halfway point, check each one. Keep it if it's on track. Adjust the number or date if it's off. Drop it if it no longer matters. Dropping on purpose beats letting it fade.
steps.proof: 3 goals marked with reasons at day 45.
steps.pitfall: Sticking with a goal that no longer matters because you wrote it down.

problems.prompt: At day 45 you've saved 100 of 500 dollars. Keep, adjust or drop?
problems.answer: Adjust, like a new target of 350, or find more to save.

problems.prompt: At day 45, 1 goal no longer matters to you. Is dropping it a failure?
problems.answer: No. Dropping it on purpose is fine.

problems.prompt: What do you write next to each of the 3 choices?

steps.title: Start Tiny
steps.mastery: Begin a new habit at a size that can't fail.
steps.practice: Pick 1 habit and shrink it to under 2 minutes, like 1 push-up or 1 page of reading.
steps.detail: Tiny habits stick because they're easy on bad days. You can grow them later. Starting big, like 50 push-ups, works for a week and then stops.
steps.proof: 1 habit written in its tiny form.
steps.pitfall: Starting with 50 push-ups a day and quitting by day 6.

problems.prompt: Shrink "Read 30 minutes a day."
Shrink "Meditate 20 minutes."
Why does 1 push-up a day last longer than 50?
problems.answer: It still happens on bad days.

steps.title: Attach It to a Cue
steps.mastery: Link the habit to something you already do every day.
steps.practice: Write "After I [cue], I will [habit]" for your habit and stick it where the cue happens.
steps.detail: A cue triggers the habit without needing to remember. Pick something you already do daily, like pouring coffee or brushing teeth. Put a note where the cue happens.
steps.proof: 1 cue sentence written and posted.
steps.pitfall: Relying on memory, which fails on busy days.

problems.prompt: Write a cue sentence for reading 1 page.
problems.answer: "After I pour my coffee, I will read 1 page."

problems.prompt: Name 2 good daily cues.
Your cue is "After I pour coffee." Where should the note go?

steps.title: Keep the Same Time
steps.mastery: Do the habit at a steady time and place so it becomes automatic.
steps.practice: Run your habit at the same time and place for 14 days.
steps.detail: Consistency is what turns an action into a habit. Same time, same spot, same cue. After a few weeks, it starts to feel strange to skip it.
steps.proof: 14 days at the same time and place.
steps.pitfall: Doing it whenever there's a gap, at a different time each day.

problems.prompt: You did your habit at 7 am, 3 pm and 10 pm on 3 days. What's the problem?
Should you keep the same time for 3 days or at least 14?
After 3 weeks, skipping feels odd. What does that show?

steps.title: Track the Streak
steps.mastery: Mark each day you do the habit so progress is visible.
steps.practice: Mark a calendar each day you do your habit for 30 days.
steps.detail: Seeing a streak keeps you going. Mark it right after. If you miss a day, don't miss the next. Missing 1 day barely matters. Missing 2 in a row is how habits fade.
steps.proof: 30 days tracked on a calendar.
steps.pitfall: Quitting the whole habit after 1 missed day.

problems.prompt: You miss Tuesday. What's the rule for Wednesday?
problems.answer: Don't miss 2 in a row, so do it.

problems.prompt: You did 24 of 30 days. How did it go?
problems.answer: Well. That's a strong habit forming.

problems.prompt: You do the habit at 7:05 am. When should you mark the calendar?

steps.title: Grow It Slowly
steps.mastery: Increase the habit only once the small version is solid.
steps.practice: After 30 days, add a small step, like going from 1 push-up to 3.
steps.detail: Grow slowly so the habit stays easy. Add a little every few weeks. If you start skipping, shrink it back.
steps.proof: Habit grown by a small step after 30 days.
steps.pitfall: Jumping from 1 push-up to 50.

problems.prompt: You've done 1 push-up daily for 30 days. What's a good next step?
After growing it, you skip 4 days. What do you do?
Why go from 1 push-up to 3, instead of 1 to 50?

steps.title: Plan for Missed Days
steps.mastery: Decide ahead what you'll do after a miss.
steps.practice: Write a 1 line plan for missed days, like "do the 1 minute version the next morning."
steps.detail: Misses happen to everyone. A plan stops one miss from turning into a week. The usual plan is to do the tiny version the next day.
steps.proof: A 1 line missed day plan written.
steps.pitfall: Feeling guilty and quitting after a miss.

problems.prompt: Write a 1 line missed day plan.
problems.answer: "Do the 1 minute version the next morning."

problems.prompt: In a 30 day streak, do most people miss at least 1 day?
You missed 2 days while sick. What now?

steps.title: Pull Reference Off the Task List
steps.mastery: Keep only actions on the task list, and move everything else to notes.
steps.practice: Move 10 non-task items from your task list, like recipes, gift ideas or a Wi-Fi password, into a notes app.
steps.detail: A task list should only hold things to do. Ideas and info make it longer and harder to scan, so real tasks hide. Ask of each line: "Can I do this?" If not, it's reference and belongs in notes.
steps.proof: 10 reference items moved and a shorter task list.
steps.pitfall: Keeping a Wi-Fi password and "call dentist" on the same list.

problems.prompt: Is "Grandma's pie recipe" a task or a note?
Is "Buy 2 cups of flour for the pie" a task or a note?
Your list has 60 lines and 25 are reference. What happens when you move them?
problems.answer: The list drops to 35 real tasks and gets easier to act on.

steps.title: Choose 1 Notes Home
steps.mastery: Keep reference in one searchable place so you can always find it.
steps.practice: Pick 1 notes app or notebook and move notes from 3 other spots, like email drafts and paper, into it.
steps.detail: Notes scattered across 4 apps, email drafts and paper scraps can't be found when you need them. One home fixes that. Pick something you already open daily so it sticks. Searchable digital notes make finding things fast.
steps.proof: 1 notes home holding notes moved from 3 other places.
steps.pitfall: Keeping notes in 5 places and searching all of them every time.

problems.prompt: Your notes live in 2 apps, email drafts and a notebook. What's step 1?
problems.answer: Pick 1 home and start moving the rest into it.

problems.prompt: Why pick an app you already open 10 times a day?
problems.answer: You're more likely to keep using it.

problems.prompt: Name 1 advantage of digital notes over paper for reference.

steps.title: Use a Few Broad Folders
steps.mastery: Group notes into a handful of wide folders and let search do the rest.
steps.practice: Make 5 folders, like School, Home, Money, Health and Ideas, and file 20 notes into them.
steps.detail: Lots of tiny folders make every note a filing decision. Five to 8 broad ones are enough for most people. If you're unsure where a note goes, pick the closest and trust search to find it.
steps.proof: 5 folders with 20 notes filed.
steps.pitfall: Building 40 folders and spending more time filing than using notes.

problems.prompt: A note about car insurance. Which of the 5 folders?
A note could fit Home or Money. What do you do?
problems.answer: Pick the closer one and rely on search.

problems.prompt: You have 40 folders and can't find anything. What's the fix?
problems.answer: Merge them into 5 to 8 broad ones.

steps.title: Title Notes for Search
steps.mastery: Give notes titles you'd actually type when searching.
steps.practice: Rename 10 vague notes with clear titles, like "Wi-Fi password home" in place of "stuff."
steps.detail: Search works on words. A note called "misc" or "notes 3" is lost. Put the words you'd search for in the title: the thing, the place, the person. Add a year if it'll matter later.
steps.proof: 10 notes renamed with search-ready titles.
steps.pitfall: Titles like "misc" or "notes 3" that tell you nothing.

problems.prompt: Rename "stuff" for a note holding the home Wi-Fi password.
Rename "notes 3" for your 2026 tax deductions.
Why include a year in "Tax deductions 2026"?
problems.answer: So you can tell it apart from other years.

steps.title: Save Finds Right Away
steps.mastery: Capture useful info straight into notes before it's lost.
steps.practice: Save 5 useful finds this week, like a link or a fact, straight into your notes home with a clear title.
steps.detail: Good info disappears if you plan to save it later. Save it right away, title it and file it in a folder. It takes 30 seconds and saves a 20 minute search next month.
steps.proof: 5 items saved this week with clear titles.
steps.pitfall: Telling yourself you'll remember where you saw it.

problems.prompt: You find a great study tip on a website at 9 pm. What do you do?
problems.answer: Save the link to notes with a clear title right away.

problems.prompt: Saving takes 30 seconds. How much time can it save later?
You saved a link titled "link." What's wrong?
problems.answer: The title won't show up in search.

steps.title: Prune Once a Month
steps.mastery: Clear out old notes so search stays useful.
steps.practice: On the 1st of each month, delete or archive 10 notes you no longer need.
steps.detail: Old notes clog search results. Once a month, scan the oldest notes and delete or archive what's dead, like last year's class schedule. Ten is enough to keep things tidy.
steps.proof: 10 notes pruned on the 1st of the month.
steps.pitfall: Never deleting anything until search returns 50 results.

problems.prompt: Last year's class schedule. Keep, archive or delete?
Should the monthly prune clear about 10 notes or all 400?
You have 400 notes and storage is free. Why prune at all?

steps.title: Sort Urgent From Important
steps.mastery: Tell tasks that are loud from tasks that truly matter.
steps.practice: Sort 15 tasks into a 2 by 2 grid: urgent and important, important only, urgent only, neither.
steps.detail: Urgent tasks shout, like a ringing phone. Important tasks move your goals, like studying for a final in 3 weeks. Most days get eaten by urgent but unimportant stuff. The grid shows where your time should go.
steps.proof: 15 tasks placed in a 4 box grid.
steps.pitfall: Treating every urgent task as important.

problems.prompt: Studying for a final in 3 weeks. Which box?
A group chat pinging 10 times. Which box?
A bill due tomorrow. Which box?

steps.title: Protect the Important
steps.mastery: Make time for important tasks before urgent ones take over.
steps.practice: Block 1 hour on 3 days this week for a task from the important but not urgent box.
steps.detail: Important tasks rarely feel urgent until they're a crisis. Studying, exercise, planning and long projects all live here. Book time for them first, like a meeting with yourself.
steps.proof: 3 one hour blocks used on important tasks.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until an important task becomes an emergency.

problems.prompt: Name 2 tasks that are usually important but not urgent.
problems.answer: Studying for a far-off exam and exercise.

problems.prompt: Why book a 1 hour block for important tasks?
problems.answer: They never feel urgent until it's too late.

problems.prompt: You skipped 2 of 3 blocks for urgent emails. What could you change?
problems.answer: Turn off email during the block.

steps.title: Cut the Neither Box
steps.mastery: Drop tasks that are neither urgent nor important.
steps.practice: Delete or drop 5 tasks from the neither box.
steps.detail: Some tasks don't need doing at all. They clutter your list and your head. If it's not urgent and not important, cut it. You'll feel lighter.
steps.proof: 5 tasks deleted.
steps.pitfall: Keeping every task just in case, so the list never shrinks.

problems.prompt: A task says "reorganize old photos" and has sat for 6 months. Which box, and what do you do?
problems.answer: Neither. Drop it, or move it to someday.

problems.prompt: Why cut 5 tasks from the list at all?
problems.answer: They clutter your list and your head.

problems.prompt: You deleted 5 tasks and nothing bad happened in 2 weeks. What does that show?

steps.title: Delegate or Batch the Urgent
steps.mastery: Handle urgent but unimportant tasks quickly or hand them off.
steps.practice: Pick 3 urgent but unimportant tasks and either batch them into 1 slot or ask someone else to do them.
steps.detail: Many urgent tasks are other people's priorities. Batch quick replies into 1 slot instead of reacting all day. Hand off what someone else can do. Say no to some.
steps.proof: 3 urgent tasks batched or handed off.
steps.pitfall: Dropping deep work every time someone pings you.

problems.prompt: 6 quick requests come in by 11 am. What's a better plan than replying to each right away?
A coworker can do a task as well as you. What can you do?
Why are many of the 10 daily pings low priority for you?

steps.title: Pick Your 1 Thing
steps.mastery: Name the single most important task each day.
steps.practice: For 5 mornings, star 1 task that would make the day a win if it got done.
steps.detail: When everything feels important, nothing is. One starred task gives focus. Ask "If I only got 1 thing done today, what would it be?" Do that first if you can.
steps.proof: 5 days, each with 1 starred task and whether it got done.
steps.pitfall: Starring 4 tasks, which defeats the point.

problems.prompt: Write the question that finds your 1 thing.
problems.answer: "If I only got 1 thing done today, what would it be?"

problems.prompt: You starred 3 tasks. What's wrong?
problems.answer: It defeats the focus. Star only 1.

problems.prompt: Your starred task got done 4 of 5 days. How did it go?

steps.title: Name What You're Avoiding
steps.mastery: Find the feeling behind putting off a task.
steps.practice: For 3 tasks you're avoiding, write the feeling behind each: bored, anxious, confused or overwhelmed.
steps.detail: Procrastination is usually avoiding a feeling. Laziness is rarely the real cause. Bored, anxious, confused and overwhelmed each need a different fix. Naming the right one is half the work.
steps.proof: 3 tasks, each with a feeling named.
steps.pitfall: Calling it laziness, which points to no fix.

problems.prompt: You keep putting off a form because you don't know what 2 boxes mean. Which feeling?
You put off calling the doctor because you fear bad news. Which feeling?
You've put off 3 tasks for a week. Is that usually just laziness?
problems.answer: No. It's usually avoiding a feeling.

steps.title: Fix Confusion
steps.mastery: Clear up an unclear task so you know the first step.
steps.practice: For 1 confusing task, write 3 questions you need answered and ask 1 person today.
steps.detail: Unclear tasks get avoided because there's no obvious first move. List what you don't know. Ask a teacher, coworker or friend. Once you know the first step, starting is easy.
steps.proof: 3 questions written and at least 1 answered today.
steps.pitfall: Staring at a task you don't understand and hoping it clears up.

problems.prompt: You don't know what format the report needs. Write 1 question to ask.
problems.answer: "Do you want the report as slides or a doc?"

problems.prompt: Should you write 3 questions or 30?
Name 2 people you could ask about a confusing school task.

steps.title: Fix Fear
steps.mastery: Shrink a scary task down to its real size.
steps.practice: For 1 task you dread, write the worst case, how likely it is from 1 to 10, and what you'd do if it happened.
steps.detail: Fear makes tasks look huge. Writing the worst case shows it's usually unlikely and survivable. Then shrink the first step so it's small enough to take today.
steps.proof: 1 dreaded task with worst case, likelihood and plan written.
steps.pitfall: Avoiding the task until the deadline makes it worse.

problems.prompt: You rate the worst case 2 out of 10 likely. What does that tell you?
After writing the worst case, what's next?
problems.answer: Shrink the first step and take it.

problems.prompt: You dread asking for an extension. What's a tiny first step?

steps.title: Fix Boredom
steps.mastery: Make a dull task easier to get through.
steps.practice: For 1 boring task, add a timer, music or a small reward, and work for 25 minutes.
steps.detail: Boring tasks won't become fun, so add some help. A timer turns it into a race. Music lifts the mood. A small reward afterward gives a reason. Pick 1 or 2.
steps.proof: 1 boring task worked for 25 minutes with 1 helper.
steps.pitfall: Waiting for a dull task to start feeling interesting.

problems.prompt: Name 2 ways to make filing receipts less dull.
Is the boring task session 25 minutes or 3 hours?
Write a small reward for after 25 minutes of filing.
problems.answer: A 10 minute walk or a snack.

steps.title: Fix Overwhelm
steps.mastery: Break a huge task into steps small enough to start.
steps.practice: For 1 overwhelming task, write 5 small steps and finish the first one today.
steps.detail: Big tasks feel impossible because you see all of it at once. Small steps feel doable. Write them down so your head can let go, then focus only on step 1.
steps.proof: 1 big task split into 5 steps with step 1 done.
steps.pitfall: Thinking about the whole thing at once and freezing.

problems.prompt: Split "Move apartments" into 2 first steps.
Why write the 5 steps down?
problems.answer: So your head can let go and focus on step 1.

problems.prompt: You finished step 1 of 5. How should that feel?
problems.answer: Like progress. The task is 20 percent done.

steps.title: Spot Your Pattern
steps.mastery: Notice which feeling causes most of your procrastination.
steps.practice: For 14 days, log each time you put something off and the feeling behind it.
steps.detail: A pattern usually shows up. Maybe anxiety drives most of it, or confusion. Then you know which fix to reach for first.
steps.proof: A 14 day log with your top feeling named.
steps.pitfall: Treating each delay as a one-off.

problems.prompt: Anxiety shows up 8 of 12 times. What does that tell you?
What 2 things do you log each time?
Your top feeling is confusion. Which fix comes first?

steps.title: List Every Project
steps.mastery: Find everything you're doing that takes more than one step.
steps.practice: Write a list of every project you have going, aiming for at least 10.
steps.detail: A project is anything that needs more than 1 action, like planning a trip, fixing a bike or applying for a job. Most people have 10 to 30 and only think of 4. The rest hide as tasks that never get done.
steps.proof: A list of 10 or more projects.
steps.pitfall: Calling "Plan trip" a task and wondering why it never gets ticked off.

problems.prompt: Is "Plan birthday party" a task or a project?
Is "Text Sam the address" a task or a project?
You listed 4 projects in 5 minutes. What helps you find more?
problems.answer: Go area by area: school, home, money, health, people.

steps.title: Define Done
steps.mastery: Write what finished looks like for each project.
steps.practice: Write a 1 line done statement for 5 projects, like "Party held on May 3 with 10 friends."
steps.detail: Projects without an end drag on. A done line tells you when to stop and what to aim for. Make it something you could check off, with a date if it has one.
steps.proof: 5 projects with 1 line done statements.
steps.pitfall: Leaving projects open-ended so they never finish.

problems.prompt: Write a done line for "Fix bike."
problems.answer: "Bike rides with working brakes and gears by Saturday."

problems.prompt: Write a done line for "Job applications."
Why does a 1 line done statement help?
problems.answer: You know when to stop and what to aim for.

steps.title: Break Into Steps
steps.mastery: Split a project into steps small enough to finish in one sitting.
steps.practice: Break 1 project into 8 steps, each taking 1 hour or less.
steps.detail: Big projects stall because they're hard to start. Steps make them doable. Each one should be a single action, like "Book venue" or "Make guest list." Order them roughly so step 1 is obvious.
steps.proof: 1 project split into 8 ordered steps.
steps.pitfall: Leaving "Plan party" as one giant step.

problems.prompt: Name 3 steps for "Plan party."
problems.answer: Make guest list, book venue, send invites.

problems.prompt: Is "Organize everything" a good step?
problems.answer: No. It's too big and vague.

problems.prompt: Should each of the 8 steps take 1 hour or less, or a full week?

steps.title: Give Each Project a Next Action
steps.mastery: Make sure every active project has one clear thing to do next.
steps.practice: Write 1 next action beside each of your 10 projects.
steps.detail: A stalled project almost always has no next action. When every project has one, you can act on any of them in a spare 20 minutes. If you can't think of a next action, the project might need a done line first.
steps.proof: 10 projects, each with a next action.
steps.pitfall: Projects sitting for weeks because nobody knows the next step.

problems.prompt: Project "Bike repair" has no next action. Write one.
problems.answer: "Look up the brake pad size for my bike."

problems.prompt: You can't think of a next action for a project. What might be missing?
You have 20 free minutes. How does a next action list help?
problems.answer: You can pick one and act right away.

steps.title: Check Projects Weekly
steps.mastery: Look at every project in the weekly review to keep them moving.
steps.practice: Review your project list in 4 weekly reviews and update next actions.
steps.detail: Projects drift without a weekly look. In the review, check each one: is the next action still right, done, or stuck? Write a new next action wherever the old one is finished.
steps.proof: 4 weekly reviews with all projects checked.
steps.pitfall: Only looking at projects when something goes wrong.

problems.prompt: A next action from last week is done. What do you write?
A project hasn't moved in 3 weeks. What do you check first?
problems.answer: Whether the next action is clear and doable.

problems.prompt: Should you look at all 10 projects weekly or yearly?

steps.title: Close Finished and Dead Projects
steps.mastery: Close projects that are done or no longer wanted so the list stays honest.
steps.practice: Close 2 projects this week: 1 that's finished and 1 you've quietly given up on.
steps.detail: A list full of dead projects makes the live ones harder to see. Mark finished projects done and celebrate a little. Move dead ones to someday or delete them. Closing on purpose feels better than letting them rot.
steps.proof: 2 projects closed.
steps.pitfall: Keeping a dead project on the list for 6 months out of guilt.

problems.prompt: A project hasn't been touched in 6 months and you don't care anymore. What do you do?
problems.answer: Close it or move it to someday.

problems.prompt: Why close 2 finished projects instead of just ignoring them?
problems.answer: So the list shows only live work.

problems.prompt: You closed 2 projects. What should the list look like now?

steps.title: Write a Weekly Look Back
steps.mastery: Write a short reflection on how the week went.
steps.practice: Every Friday for 4 weeks, answer 3 questions in writing: what worked, what didn't, what to change.
steps.detail: Without reflection, you repeat the same week with more effort. Three questions keep it short. Write, don't just think, because writing forces clear answers. Ten minutes is enough.
steps.proof: 4 weekly reflections with 3 answers each.
steps.pitfall: Thinking it over in your head, where it stays vague.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 reflection questions.
problems.answer: What worked, what didn't and what to change.

problems.prompt: Why write the 3 answers instead of just thinking them?
Your reflection takes 45 minutes. What's the risk?
problems.answer: It feels like a chore, and you'll stop doing it.

steps.title: Find What Worked
steps.mastery: Pull out the choices that made good days good.
steps.practice: Look at your 3 best days this month and write 1 thing each had in common.
steps.detail: People study bad days and ignore good ones. Good days hold clues, like an early start, a short task list or a walk at lunch. Find what they share and do more of it.
steps.proof: 3 best days with 1 shared factor named.
steps.pitfall: Only studying what went wrong.

problems.prompt: Your 3 best days all started with a 7 am walk. What's the lesson?
Why study your 3 best days, not only the bad ones?
Name 1 common factor good days might share.
problems.answer: A short task list, for example.

steps.title: Spot Repeated Problems
steps.mastery: Notice problems that keep showing up across weeks.
steps.practice: Read 4 weeks of reflections and circle any problem that appears 2 or more times.
steps.detail: One bad day is noise. The same problem 3 weeks in a row is a pattern. Patterns are where small changes pay off most. Circle them and pick 1 to tackle.
steps.proof: 4 weeks read with repeated problems circled.
steps.pitfall: Treating every problem as a one-off.

problems.prompt: "Ran out of time Thursday" shows up 3 of 4 weeks. What is it?
A problem shows up in 1 of 4 weeks. Is it a pattern yet?
You found 4 patterns. How many should you tackle first?

steps.title: Make 1 Small Change
steps.mastery: Turn each reflection into one concrete change for next week.
steps.practice: Write 1 change for next week from your reflection and put it on your calendar.
steps.detail: Reflection without change is just a diary. Pick 1 small, specific change, like "Start Thursday's report on Wednesday." Put it on the calendar so it happens.
steps.proof: 1 change written and scheduled.
steps.pitfall: Writing 6 vague changes like "be better" that never happen.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Manage time better" as 1 change.
problems.answer: "Start Thursday's report on Wednesday at 3 pm."

problems.prompt: Why put the 1 change on the calendar?
Should you make 1 change per week or 6?

steps.title: Check Last Week's Change
steps.mastery: See whether last week's change worked before choosing a new one.
steps.practice: Start each reflection by rating last week's change from 1 to 5 for how well it worked.
steps.detail: Changes need checking. Some work, some don't. Rate it. Keep what scores 4 or 5, adjust what scores 3, drop what scores 1 or 2.
steps.proof: 4 weeks of changes rated.
steps.pitfall: Making new changes without checking old ones.

problems.prompt: Last week's change scored 5. What do you do?
It scored 2. What do you do?
problems.answer: Drop it and try something else.

problems.prompt: Why rate last week's change from 1 to 5 before choosing a new one?

steps.title: Look Back Each Quarter
steps.mastery: Reflect on a whole season to see bigger trends.
steps.practice: Every 3 months, spend 30 minutes reading your weekly reflections and write a 5 line summary.
steps.detail: Weekly reflections show small patterns. A quarterly look shows the big ones, like how your goals moved or which habits stuck. Five lines is enough.
steps.proof: A 5 line quarterly summary.
steps.pitfall: Never looking past the current week.

problems.prompt: Should the bigger look back happen every 3 months or every 3 years?
Should the quarterly summary be 5 lines or 5 pages?
Name 1 big trend you might spot.

steps.title: Book the Review
steps.mastery: Set a fixed weekly slot for reviewing your whole system.
steps.practice: Book 1 hour at the same time each week, like Friday at 3 pm, and call it Weekly Review.
steps.detail: Without a fixed slot, the review gets skipped when weeks get busy, which is when it matters most. Pick a time with low energy demands. Friday afternoon or Sunday evening are common.
steps.proof: A repeating 1 hour Weekly Review in your calendar.
steps.pitfall: Doing the review "when there's time," which is never.

problems.prompt: Name 2 common times for a weekly review.
Your week is packed. Should you skip the review?
problems.answer: No. Busy weeks need it most.

problems.prompt: Why hold the review at the same time all 52 weeks?
problems.answer: It becomes a habit instead of a decision.

steps.title: Empty Every Inbox
steps.mastery: Clear all capture spots so nothing is hiding.
steps.practice: In the review, empty 4 places: your capture inbox, email inbox, notes app and bag or desk papers.
steps.detail: Things pile up in more places than you think: loose papers, voice memos, screenshots, texts to yourself. Go through each and move items to lists, calendar or trash. The goal is zero untouched items.
steps.proof: 4 capture places at zero after the review.
steps.pitfall: Clearing the task inbox and ignoring the pile of papers in your bag.

problems.prompt: Name 3 places things hide besides your main inbox.
problems.answer: Bag papers, screenshots and texts to yourself.

problems.prompt: A receipt in your bag needs a refund claim. Where does it go?
problems.answer: A task on your list, like "Submit refund for 45 dollars."

problems.prompt: Your inbox had 23 items. When is it at zero?
problems.answer: When every item has been moved, done or deleted.

steps.title: Look at Every Project
steps.mastery: Check that each active project has a clear next action.
steps.practice: Read your project list and make sure all 5 or more projects have 1 next action written.
steps.detail: A stalled project is almost always one with no next action. Go down the list. If a project has none, write one now. If a project is no longer wanted, move it to someday or drop it.
steps.proof: Every active project with 1 next action.
steps.pitfall: Letting projects sit for weeks with nothing to do next.

problems.prompt: Project "Plan trip" has no next action. Write one.
A project hasn't moved in 4 weeks. What's the likely cause?
problems.answer: It has no clear next action.

problems.prompt: You no longer care about project 6. What do you do?
problems.answer: Move it to someday or drop it.

steps.title: Check the Calendar Both Ways
steps.mastery: Look back and ahead on the calendar to catch loose ends and prep needs.
steps.practice: Look at the past 7 days and the next 14 days, and write any task each event creates.
steps.detail: Past events leave follow-ups: thank-you notes, notes to file, promises made. Future events need prep: a gift, a form, a booking. Two weeks ahead gives time to act.
steps.proof: Follow-up and prep tasks written from 21 days of calendar.
steps.pitfall: Seeing a birthday on the calendar the morning of it.

problems.prompt: Last week you met a mentor. Name 1 follow-up task.
A trip is on day 12 of the next 14. Name 1 prep task.
problems.answer: Book a ride to the airport.

problems.prompt: Why look 14 days ahead instead of 2?

steps.title: Pick Next Week's Focus
steps.mastery: Choose the few outcomes that matter most for the coming week.
steps.practice: Write 3 outcomes you want by next Friday and block time for each.
steps.detail: The review isn't only cleanup. It's where you steer. Pick 3 outcomes instead of 20 tasks. Then put time on the calendar for each so they don't get buried.
steps.proof: 3 outcomes written, each with time blocked.
steps.pitfall: Ending the review with a list of 40 tasks and no focus.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "work on essay" as an outcome for Friday.
problems.answer: "Full draft of the essay done by Friday."

problems.prompt: Should you pick 3 outcomes for the week or 20?
Why block time on the calendar for all 3 outcomes?
problems.answer: So they don't get buried by other tasks.

steps.title: Keep a Checklist
steps.mastery: Use a fixed checklist so the review takes about an hour every time.
steps.practice: Write a 6 item review checklist and use it for 3 weeks in a row.
steps.detail: A checklist makes the review faster and stops you skipping steps. A common list: empty inboxes, review projects, check calendar back, check calendar ahead, review someday list, pick weekly focus.
steps.proof: A 6 item checklist used in 3 reviews.
steps.pitfall: Making up the review from scratch each week.

problems.prompt: Name 3 items for a review checklist.
problems.answer: Empty inboxes, review projects and check the calendar.

problems.prompt: Your review took 2.5 hours. What might help?
problems.answer: A checklist to keep it focused.

problems.prompt: After 3 weeks, 1 step always feels useless. What do you do?

steps.title: Count Your Yeses
steps.mastery: See how many commitments you've taken on before adding another.
steps.practice: List every commitment you agreed to in the last 30 days and mark which ones you wanted.
steps.detail: Most overload comes from small yeses that each seemed fine. Writing them all down shows the real load. Mark each one: wanted, fine, or regret. The regret column shows where a no would have helped.
steps.proof: A 30 day list of commitments, each marked wanted, fine or regret.
steps.pitfall: Judging each new request alone, without looking at the pile it lands on.

problems.prompt: You count 14 yeses in 30 days and regret 6. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: Almost half were yeses you didn't want.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 marks for each commitment.
Why look at 30 days instead of 1 request?
problems.answer: The load only shows when you see them all together.

steps.title: Ask What It Costs
steps.mastery: Weigh a request against what it pushes out.
steps.practice: For the next 3 requests, write what you'd have to drop or delay to say yes.
steps.detail: Every yes is a no to something else, often your own work or rest. Before agreeing, name the cost. "If I help with the fundraiser Saturday, my essay slips to Sunday night." Seeing the trade makes the choice honest.
steps.proof: 3 requests, each with its cost written down.
steps.pitfall: Saying yes as if your time were empty.

problems.prompt: A friend asks for 4 hours of help Saturday. Your essay is due Monday. What's the cost?
problems.answer: Less time for the essay, likely a late Sunday night.

problems.prompt: Why write the cost down for all 3 requests?
Finish the sentence: every 1 yes is a no to...
problems.answer: Something else, often your own work or rest.

steps.title: Use a Holding Line
steps.mastery: Buy time before answering so you don't agree on reflex.
steps.practice: Answer the next 5 requests with a holding line, like "Let me check and get back to you by tomorrow."
steps.detail: Reflex yeses happen in the moment. A holding line gives you a few hours to check your calendar and the cost. Always give a time for your real answer so people aren't left hanging.
steps.proof: 5 requests answered first with a holding line.
steps.pitfall: Saying "sure!" before you've looked at your week.

problems.prompt: Write a holding line for a request made at 3 pm.
problems.answer: "Let me check my week and get back to you by tonight."

problems.prompt: Why say "by 6 pm" in your holding line?
problems.answer: So the other person isn't left waiting.

problems.prompt: You used a holding line and then forgot to answer for 4 days. What went wrong?
problems.answer: You needed a reminder to reply by the time you promised.

steps.title: Decline in 1 or 2 Sentences
steps.mastery: Say no clearly and kindly without a long excuse.
steps.practice: Write 3 short no's you'd actually say and use 1 this week.
steps.detail: A clear no now is kinder than a yes you deliver late or badly. Keep it short. Thank them, decline, and offer something smaller only if you want to. Long excuses invite people to solve them for you.
steps.proof: 3 short no's written and 1 used.
steps.pitfall: Giving 4 reasons, which the other person then argues with.

problems.prompt: Write a 1 sentence no to "Can you lead the club fundraiser?"
problems.answer: "Thanks for thinking of me, but I can't take that on this term."

problems.prompt: You want to help a little. Write a no with a smaller offer.
problems.answer: "I can't run it, but I can help set up for 1 hour."

problems.prompt: Why avoid listing 4 reasons?

steps.title: Say It Early
steps.mastery: Decline at the start instead of agreeing and backing out later.
steps.practice: Spot 1 commitment you're dreading this month and tell the person within 48 hours that you can't do it.
steps.detail: Backing out early is far easier for everyone than backing out late. If you already know a yes was a mistake, say so now while there's time to find someone else. Apologize once, briefly, and don't over-explain.
steps.proof: 1 dreaded commitment ended within 48 hours.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until the day before, when nobody can cover for you.

problems.prompt: You agreed to help on the 20th but know it's too much. It's the 5th. When should you say so?
problems.answer: Now, by the 7th at the latest.

problems.prompt: Why is backing out 15 days ahead kinder than 1 day ahead?
problems.answer: They have time to find someone else.

problems.prompt: Write a 1 sentence message to back out of helping on the 20th.
problems.answer: "I'm sorry, I overcommitted and can't help on the 20th after all."

steps.title: Keep a No List
steps.mastery: Decide some answers ahead so you don't weigh them every time.
steps.practice: Write a no list of 5 things you'll decline by default, like weeknight events after 9 pm.
steps.detail: Some requests come up again and again. Deciding once saves you the stress each time. A no list might include late weeknights, extra committees or lending money. You can still make exceptions, but the default is no.
steps.proof: A 5 item no list written.
steps.pitfall: Agonizing over the same kind of request every week.

problems.prompt: Name 2 items that might go on a no list.
problems.answer: Weeknight events after 9 pm and joining another committee.

problems.prompt: A request matches your no list. What's your default answer?
Your no list says no events after 9 pm. Can you still make an exception?
problems.answer: Yes, but no is the default.

steps.title: Shrink the First Step
steps.mastery: Make the first move so small it feels almost silly to skip.
steps.practice: For 3 tasks you're avoiding, write a first step that takes under 2 minutes, like "open the file."
steps.detail: Most avoidance lives in the first 2 minutes. Shrink the opening move until it's easy: open the doc, write the title, put on running shoes. Once you've started, carrying on is far easier than starting was.
steps.proof: 3 tiny first steps written, and at least 1 done.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until you feel ready, which can take weeks.

problems.prompt: Shrink "Write essay" to a first step under 2 minutes.
problems.answer: "Open the doc and type the title."

problems.prompt: Shrink "Go for a run" to a first step.
Why does a 2 minute step work when "write essay" doesn't?
problems.answer: It's easy to start, and starting is the hard part.

steps.title: Use a 10 Minute Timer
steps.mastery: Promise yourself only ten minutes on a task you're dodging.
steps.practice: Set a timer for 10 minutes and work on 1 avoided task, with permission to stop when it rings.
steps.detail: Ten minutes feels doable even on a bad day. Often you'll keep going past the timer. If you stop, you still made real progress, and the task is no longer untouched.
steps.proof: 3 avoided tasks started with a 10 minute timer.
steps.pitfall: Planning a 3 hour session and never starting it.

problems.prompt: The timer rings at 10 minutes and you're on a roll. Do you have to stop?
problems.answer: No. Keep going if you want.

problems.prompt: You stop at 10 minutes. Was it worth it?
problems.answer: Yes. The task moved forward and is easier to restart.

problems.prompt: Why does a 3 hour plan often fail to start?
problems.answer: It feels too big to begin.

steps.title: Set Up the Night Before
steps.mastery: Get everything ready ahead of time so starting takes no effort.
steps.practice: For 3 nights, set out what tomorrow's first task needs, like the open file or a packed gym bag.
steps.detail: Setup is a hidden barrier. Hunting for the book or the charger eats your fresh start. Lay things out the night before. In the morning you sit down and begin.
steps.proof: 3 nights of setup done.
steps.pitfall: Spending the first 20 minutes looking for things.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things to set out the night before.
problems.answer: The book you need and a packed gym bag, for example.

problems.prompt: You spent 20 minutes at 8 am finding notes. What would have helped?
problems.answer: Setting them out the night before.

problems.prompt: Your first task is a run at 6 am. What do you set out?
problems.answer: Shoes, clothes and water by the door.

steps.title: Start at a Set Minute
steps.mastery: Tie starting to the clock instead of to a feeling.
steps.practice: Pick a start time for 1 task on 5 days and begin at that exact minute.
steps.detail: Waiting until you feel like it often means never. A set time removes the choice. When the clock hits 9:00, you start, even if it's just the 2 minute step.
steps.proof: 5 days of starting at the set time.
steps.pitfall: Telling yourself you'll start when you feel ready.

problems.prompt: Your start time is 9:00. It's 9:00 and you don't feel like it. What do you do?
Why does a set time like 9:00 help?
You waited for motivation 3 days in a row. What likely happened?

steps.title: Allow a Messy Start
steps.mastery: Begin without needing the work to be good yet.
steps.practice: Write a rough first draft of 1 task in 15 minutes with no editing.
steps.detail: Perfectionism blocks starting. Give yourself permission to be messy. A bad draft can be fixed later. A blank page can't. Turn off spellcheck if it distracts you.
steps.proof: 1 rough draft done in 15 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Rewriting the first sentence 10 times.

problems.prompt: You've rewritten 1 sentence 10 times in 20 minutes. What's going on?
Should you edit during the 15 minute draft?
Why is a bad draft better than 0 words?
problems.answer: You can improve a draft. A blank page gives you nothing.

steps.title: Count Your Starts
steps.mastery: Track starts so you can see the skill growing.
steps.practice: For 7 days, make a tally mark each time you start a task you'd been avoiding.
steps.detail: Starting is the skill this node trains, so count starts rather than finishes. Watching the tally grow shows that it's getting easier, even on days you don't finish much.
steps.proof: A 7 day tally of starts.
steps.pitfall: Counting only finished tasks and feeling like nothing changed.

problems.prompt: You started 9 avoided tasks in 7 days. Good week?
Why tally 9 starts instead of only 2 finishes?
problems.answer: Starting is the skill being trained.

problems.prompt: Week 1 had 4 starts and week 2 had 9. What does it show?

steps.title: Check Capture Holds Up
steps.mastery: Confirm that everything you need to remember lands in your inbox.
steps.practice: For 7 days, note every time you remember something that wasn't in your system.
steps.detail: A trusted system catches everything. Every miss shows a gap, like a promise in a hallway or an idea in the shower. Fix each gap with a capture tool in that spot.
steps.proof: 7 days of misses noted, each with a fix.
steps.pitfall: Accepting misses as normal.

problems.prompt: You remember a promise at 11 pm that wasn't captured. What's the fix?
Ideas come in the shower. Name 1 fix.
problems.answer: A waterproof notepad or capturing right after.

problems.prompt: Your log shows 0 misses for 7 days. What does that mean?

steps.title: Run Every Habit for a Month
steps.mastery: Keep capture, daily planning and the weekly review going for a full month.
steps.practice: Run capture daily, plan each evening and hold 4 weekly reviews in the next 30 days.
steps.detail: A system you trust is built by running it. Track all 3 habits for 30 days. Missing 1 day is fine. Missing a weekly review is the one that breaks trust fastest.
steps.proof: 30 days with capture, daily plans and 4 weekly reviews.
steps.pitfall: Skipping the weekly review, which lets everything drift.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 habits.
problems.answer: Capture, daily planning and the weekly review.

problems.prompt: Of the 3 habits, which breaks trust fastest when skipped?
You missed 2 evening plans in 30 days. Is the system broken?

steps.title: Test the Quiet Head
steps.mastery: Notice whether your mind feels clear when you work.
steps.practice: During 3 focused sessions, write a tally each time an unrelated task pops into your head.
steps.detail: The point of a trusted system is a quiet head. If tasks keep popping up, something isn't captured. Write each one down in the inbox and keep working.
steps.proof: 3 sessions with tallies.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring the pop-ups and losing focus.

problems.prompt: You get 8 pop-ups in 1 session. What does it suggest?
During a session you get 8 pop-ups. What do you do with each one?
problems.answer: Write it in the inbox and keep working.

problems.prompt: Your tallies drop from 8 to 2 over 3 weeks. What changed?

steps.title: Fix the Weak Link
steps.mastery: Find the part of the system that fails most and fix it.
steps.practice: Pick the 1 habit you skip most and change 1 thing about it this week.
steps.detail: Every system has a weak link. Find it and fix 1 thing: move the review time, simplify the inbox, set a reminder. Small fixes beat a new system.
steps.proof: 1 weak link named and 1 fix made.
steps.pitfall: Throwing out the whole system because 1 part fails.

problems.prompt: You skip the Friday review 3 weeks in a row. Name 1 fix.
problems.answer: Move it to a better time, like Sunday at 6 pm.

problems.prompt: 1 habit keeps failing. Is a brand new system the best fix?
Should you change 1 thing this week or 5?

steps.title: Handle a Busy Week
steps.mastery: Keep the system alive when life gets hectic.
steps.practice: Write a minimum version of each habit for busy weeks, like a 10 minute review.
steps.detail: Busy weeks are when systems break. A minimum version keeps it alive: 1 minute capture, 5 minute plan, 10 minute review. Then build back up.
steps.proof: Minimum versions written for 3 habits.
steps.pitfall: Dropping everything during busy weeks.

problems.prompt: What's a minimum weekly review?
Why have a 10 minute minimum review?
You used the minimums for 6 busy days. When do you return to the full version?

steps.title: Recover After a Break
steps.mastery: Restart the system after time away.
steps.practice: After any break of 3 or more days, run a full weekly review before starting normal work.
steps.detail: Breaks happen: travel, illness, holidays. A review on return catches everything that piled up. Then you're back on track.
steps.proof: A review done after a break.
steps.pitfall: Jumping back in without catching up.

problems.prompt: You're back from 5 days away. What do you do first?
Why run a full review after 5 days away?
Does a 1 day break need a full review, or 3 days or more?

steps.title: Trust It
steps.mastery: Give a single task your full attention, trusting the lists to hold everything else.
steps.practice: For 3 days, work on your top task for 90 minutes without checking anything else.
steps.detail: Trust means you can focus. If the system works, nothing is forgotten while you're busy. Notice the calm.
steps.proof: 3 days of 90 minute focus blocks.
steps.pitfall: Checking lists every 10 minutes.

problems.prompt: What's the sign you trust your system?
Should each focus block be 90 minutes or 9?
You check lists every 10 minutes. What does it suggest?
problems.answer: You don't trust the system yet.

steps.title: Find the Next Action
steps.mastery: Turn a vague topic into the very next physical step.
steps.practice: Rewrite 5 vague tasks on your list as next actions, like "Find the renewal email" for "Sort out insurance."
steps.detail: "Sort out insurance" is a topic. It has no first move, so it sits. A next action is something you could do right now: find, call, email, write, buy. Ask "what's the very first thing I'd do?" and write that.
steps.proof: 5 vague tasks rewritten as physical next actions.
steps.pitfall: Writing topics like "taxes" that give you nothing to start on.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Taxes" as a next action.
problems.answer: "Find last year's W-2 in the email."

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Birthday party" as a next action.
problems.answer: "Text 6 friends to ask if Saturday works."

problems.prompt: Is "Think about college" a next action?
problems.answer: No. Something like "List 5 colleges to look up" is.

steps.title: Start With a Verb
steps.mastery: Write every task so it begins with a clear verb.
steps.practice: Edit your task list so each of the first 15 items starts with a verb like call, email, buy or write.
steps.detail: A verb tells you what to do. "Dentist" could mean book, cancel or pay. "Call dentist to book a cleaning" is clear. Good task verbs are physical: call, email, buy, print, draft, ask, fill out.
steps.proof: 15 tasks, each starting with a verb.
steps.pitfall: Using fuzzy verbs like "handle" or "deal with" that hide the real action.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Dentist" with a clear verb.
Why is "Deal with email" weak?
problems.answer: "Deal with" hides what you'll actually do.

problems.prompt: Name 4 good physical task verbs.
problems.answer: Call, email, buy and print, for example.

steps.title: Add the Context
steps.mastery: Include enough detail that future you can act without thinking.
steps.practice: Add 1 key detail to 10 tasks, like a phone number, a link or a name.
steps.detail: A task should be doable without detective work. "Email Ms. Lee re: field trip form" beats "email teacher." Add the who, the what or the link. Future you is busy and will skip anything that needs figuring out.
steps.proof: 10 tasks with a name, number or link added.
steps.pitfall: Writing tasks so short that you can't remember what they meant.

problems.prompt: Improve "Email teacher."
problems.answer: "Email Ms. Lee about the field trip form."

problems.prompt: You wrote "Call about the thing" 3 days ago. What went wrong?
problems.answer: It left out the key detail, so it can't be acted on.

problems.prompt: Name 3 kinds of detail to add to a task.
problems.answer: A name, a phone number or a link.

steps.title: Split the Big Ones
steps.mastery: Break tasks that take more than an hour into smaller steps.
steps.practice: Find 3 tasks that would take over 60 minutes and split each into steps of 30 minutes or less.
steps.detail: Big tasks get avoided because they're hard to start. "Write essay" becomes "Write 3 bullet outline," "Draft intro," "Draft body paragraph 1." Each step should feel doable in 1 sitting.
steps.proof: 3 big tasks each split into steps under 30 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Leaving "Write essay" on the list for 2 weeks.

problems.prompt: Split "Clean garage" into 3 steps.
problems.answer: "Bag trash," "Sort tools into 1 box," "Sweep the floor."

problems.prompt: Should each split step take 30 minutes or less, or up to 3 hours?
Is "Study for finals" one task or a project?
problems.answer: A project. Split it into steps.

steps.title: Run the 2 Minute Rule
steps.mastery: Finish tiny tasks right away instead of listing them.
steps.practice: For 1 day, do any task under 2 minutes the moment it comes up, and count how many.
steps.detail: Writing down a 2 minute task and finding it later takes longer than just doing it. Reply to the quick text, file the form, take out the trash. Anything longer goes on the list.
steps.proof: A count of tiny tasks finished on the spot in 1 day.
steps.pitfall: Listing a 30 second reply, then forgetting it for a week.

problems.prompt: A text needs a yes or no. List it or do it?
A form takes 20 minutes. List it or do it now?
Why not list a 1 minute task?
problems.answer: Listing and finding it takes longer than doing it.

steps.title: Pick 3 for Today
steps.mastery: Choose a short list of what must get done today.
steps.practice: For 5 mornings, pick 3 tasks from your list as today's must-dos.
steps.detail: A list of 30 isn't a plan. It guarantees the day ends feeling behind. Pick 3 that matter most. If you finish them, great, take more. The rest of the list waits.
steps.proof: 5 days, each with 3 chosen tasks and how many got done.
steps.pitfall: Picking 12 must-dos and finishing 4.

problems.prompt: Your list has 28 items. How many go on today's must-do list?
You finished your 3 by 1 pm. What now?
Why does a 30 item list feel bad at 6 pm?
problems.answer: You can never finish it, so you always feel behind.

steps.title: Plan the Night Before
steps.mastery: Choose tomorrow's tasks before the day starts.
steps.practice: For 5 nights, spend 5 minutes before bed writing tomorrow's 3 tasks.
