steps.detail: Deciding at night means you start the morning knowing what to do. Your brain may even work on it overnight. Look at the calendar too, so you pick tasks that fit the time you have.
steps.proof: 5 nights of 3 tasks chosen in advance.
steps.pitfall: Starting the day by checking email and letting it decide for you.

problems.prompt: You have 3 hours of meetings tomorrow. How does that change your 3 tasks?
problems.answer: Pick smaller tasks that fit the free time.

problems.prompt: Should night planning take 5 minutes or 45?
What's the risk of opening email first at 8 am?
problems.answer: Other people's requests decide your day.

steps.title: Put the Hardest First
steps.mastery: Do the most important or hardest task early, while you're fresh.
steps.practice: For 5 days, start with your toughest of the 3 tasks before email or chat.
steps.detail: Energy and focus are usually best early. If you start with easy stuff, the hard task slides to 4 pm when you're tired. Do it first and the rest of the day feels lighter.
steps.proof: 5 days where the hardest task came first.
steps.pitfall: Clearing 20 small emails first and running out of energy.

problems.prompt: Your 3 tasks are: write report, reply to 2 emails, file receipts. Which comes first?
Why might the hard task fail at 4 pm?
problems.answer: You're tired and focus is lower.

problems.prompt: You're a night person and sharpest at 8 pm. Does "hardest first" still mean 8 am?
problems.answer: No. Do it in your sharpest hours.

steps.title: Match Tasks to Time
steps.mastery: Fit today's tasks to the hours you actually have free.
steps.practice: Write how many free hours you have today and estimate time for each of your 3 tasks.
steps.detail: People plan as if the day is empty. Check the calendar first. If you have 2 free hours, 3 tasks of 1 hour won't fit. Adjust before you start, not at 5 pm.
steps.proof: 3 tasks with time estimates that fit your free hours.
steps.pitfall: Planning 6 hours of tasks on a day with 2 free hours.

problems.prompt: You have 2 free hours and 3 tasks of 1 hour each. What do you do?
problems.answer: Drop 1 or shrink them so they fit.

problems.prompt: Before picking tomorrow's 3 tasks, what do you check?
Why adjust at 9 am instead of at 5 pm?
problems.answer: You can still choose what to drop.

steps.title: Close the Day
steps.mastery: End each day by checking what got done and setting up tomorrow.
steps.practice: Spend 5 minutes at the end of 5 days ticking off tasks and moving unfinished ones.
steps.detail: A short shutdown helps you stop thinking about work. Tick what's done. Move unfinished tasks to tomorrow or later. Then you can switch off knowing nothing is lost.
steps.proof: 5 end-of-day closes done.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the list a mess, so tomorrow starts with confusion.

problems.prompt: 2 of 3 tasks got done. What happens to the 3rd?
problems.answer: Move it to tomorrow or later.

problems.prompt: Should closing the day take 5 minutes or 1 hour?
Why does closing help you relax at 7 pm?

steps.title: List What You Use
steps.mastery: Take stock of every tool your system relies on.
steps.practice: List every app and notebook you use to plan, capture or track, with how many of the 7 days you open each.
steps.detail: Systems sprawl. A task app, 2 note apps, a planner, sticky notes, a calendar. Write them all down with how often you open each. Tools you rarely open are clutter, and they hide things.
steps.proof: A list of every tool with how often you use it.
steps.pitfall: Adding a new app without checking what you already have.

problems.prompt: You use 3 apps daily and 4 others once a month. Which are clutter?
problems.answer: The 4 you open once a month.

problems.prompt: Why note that 4 of your tools get opened once a month?
problems.answer: Rarely opened tools hide things and add clutter.

problems.prompt: Name 3 kinds of tools to include.
problems.answer: A task app, a notes app and a calendar, for example.

steps.title: Cut to the Core 3
steps.mastery: Shrink your setup to a calendar, a task list and a notes home.
steps.practice: Keep 1 calendar, 1 task list and 1 notes home, and retire every other planning tool this week.
steps.detail: Most people need only 3 tools: a calendar for times, a task list for actions and notes for reference. More tools mean more places to check and more places to forget. Move anything important out of the extras before you retire them.
steps.proof: 3 core tools kept and the rest retired.
steps.pitfall: Running 2 task apps at once, so neither is trusted.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 core tools.
problems.answer: A calendar, a task list and a notes home.

problems.prompt: You have 2 task apps. What do you do?
problems.answer: Pick 1 and move everything from the other into it.

problems.prompt: Before retiring 1 of your 2 note apps, what must you do?
problems.answer: Move anything important out of it.

steps.title: Stop Shopping for Apps
steps.mastery: Notice when tinkering with tools has become a way to avoid work.
steps.practice: Set a rule for 30 days: no new productivity apps and no system redesigns.
steps.detail: Rebuilding your system feels productive, but it's often a polished way to procrastinate. Switching apps has rarely been the real problem. Give your current setup 30 days before you change anything.
steps.proof: 30 days with no new apps or redesigns.
steps.pitfall: Spending a Sunday afternoon setting up a new app instead of doing the work.

problems.prompt: You spent 3 hours setting up a new planner. What might have happened?
problems.answer: It became a way to avoid the real work.

problems.prompt: Should you give your current setup 3 days or 30 before changing it?
You missed 3 deadlines. Is a new app likely to fix that?
problems.answer: Rarely. Habits matter more than tools.

steps.title: Learn 3 Shortcuts
steps.mastery: Get faster at the tools you keep.
steps.practice: Learn 3 shortcuts in your task app or calendar, like quick add or keyboard capture.
steps.detail: Speed makes a tool easier to use, and an easy tool gets used. Quick add, natural language dates like "Fri 3pm" and a keyboard shortcut for capture save seconds every time. Those seconds add up.
steps.proof: 3 shortcuts learned and used 10 times each.
steps.pitfall: Clicking through 4 menus to add a single task.

problems.prompt: Name 2 helpful shortcuts.
problems.answer: Quick add and natural language dates.

problems.prompt: Why does saving 10 seconds per task matter?
problems.answer: It makes the tool easy, so you keep using it.

problems.prompt: Type a quick-add task for a Friday 3 pm call with Sam.

steps.title: Match the Tool to the Habit
steps.mastery: Pick tools that support habits you already have.
steps.practice: Write which tool supports each of your 3 key habits: capture, daily plan and weekly review.
steps.detail: Tools should serve habits, not the other way around. If you capture on your phone, your inbox must be on your phone. If you plan on paper, a paper planner is fine. Check that each habit has a tool that fits how you work.
steps.proof: 3 habits, each matched to 1 tool.
steps.pitfall: Forcing a desktop-only tool when you capture on the go.

problems.prompt: You capture ideas on the bus. Should your inbox be desktop only?
problems.answer: No. It should be on your phone or in a pocket notebook.

problems.prompt: You love planning on paper. Is a paper planner OK?
Name the 3 key habits to match.
problems.answer: Capture, daily plan and weekly review.

steps.title: Review Tools Every 6 Months
steps.mastery: Check your setup twice a year and change only what's broken.
steps.practice: Book a 30 minute tools review every 6 months and change at most 1 thing.
steps.detail: A short review stops tools from drifting. Ask what's working, what's annoying and what's unused. Change only 1 thing per review so your system stays stable.
steps.proof: A 30 minute review in the calendar with 1 change noted.
steps.pitfall: Overhauling everything at once and losing track of tasks.

problems.prompt: Should you review your tools every 6 weeks or every 6 months?
You found 5 annoyances in the review. How many do you change?
Name 3 questions for the review.
problems.answer: What's working, what's annoying and what's unused.

steps.title: Ohm Law
steps.mastery: Use V = IR for a single resistor.
steps.practice: Find the current through a 6 ohm resistor on 12 V and the voltage across 220 ohms carrying 0.05 A.
steps.detail: Current equals voltage over resistance. Higher resistance means less current for the same voltage.
steps.proof: 2 A and 11 V.
steps.pitfall: Dividing the wrong way round.

problems.prompt: V = 9 V, R = 3 ohm. I?
I = 0.5 A, R = 20 ohm. V?

steps.title: Series and Parallel
steps.mastery: Combine resistors in series and in parallel.
steps.practice: Find the total resistance of 2 ohm and 6 ohm in series and in parallel.
steps.detail: Series resistances add. In parallel the total is smaller than the smallest branch.
steps.proof: 8 ohm and 1.5 ohm.
steps.pitfall: Adding parallel resistances directly.

problems.prompt: 3 resistors of 4 ohm in series?
Two 10 ohm resistors in parallel?
3 ohm and 6 ohm in parallel?

steps.title: Kirchhoff Rules
steps.mastery: Use Kirchhoff junction and loop rules to solve a network.
steps.practice: Solve a circuit with a 12 V battery, a 4 ohm resistor in series with 2 parallel 6 ohm resistors for every current.
steps.detail: Currents into a junction equal currents out, and voltages around any loop sum to zero.
steps.proof: Total 7 ohm, 12/7 A from the battery and 6/7 A in each branch.
steps.pitfall: Losing track of sign when going around a loop.

problems.prompt: 3 A in, 1 A out of 1 branch. Other branch?
Battery 9 V, drops of 4 V and 2 V. Third drop?
Voltage across 2 parallel branches on a 6 V source?

steps.title: Power and Energy
steps.mastery: Compute electrical power and cost.
steps.practice: Find the power of a 2 A kettle on 230 V and the cost of running it 0.1 h at 15 cents per kWh.
steps.detail: P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R. Multiply power in kW by hours to get kWh, then by the price per kWh to get the cost.
steps.proof: 460 W and about 0.7 cents.
steps.pitfall: Using watts when the price is per kilowatt hour.

problems.prompt: P for 12 V and 3 A?
P in a 10 ohm resistor with 2 A?
Energy in kWh for 2000 W for 3 h?

steps.title: Real Batteries
steps.mastery: Include internal resistance in a circuit.
steps.practice: Find the terminal voltage of a 9 V battery with 1 ohm internal resistance driving 8 ohms.
steps.detail: Some voltage is lost inside the battery. Terminal voltage = emf - Ir, and it drops as more current is drawn.
steps.proof: I = 1 A, terminal voltage 8 V.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring internal resistance when the load is small.

problems.prompt: emf 6 V, r = 0.5 ohm, I = 2 A. Terminal V?
Short circuit current for 9 V and r = 1 ohm?
Why is a bird on 1 power line safe?
problems.answer: No voltage difference across its body.

steps.title: Charge and Coulomb Law
steps.mastery: Compute the force between 2 charges.
steps.practice: Find the force between 2 charges of 2 microcoulombs each 0.3 m apart with k = 9 x 10^9.
steps.detail: F = k q1 q2/r^2, the same inverse square shape as gravity. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
steps.proof: 0.4 N, repulsive.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to convert microcoulombs to coulombs.

problems.prompt: Halve the distance. Force factor?
Charges of +3 and -3 microcoulombs. Attract or repel?
Charge of 1 electron in C?

steps.title: Electric Field
steps.mastery: Find E from a point charge with E = kq/r^2.
steps.practice: Find the field 0.5 m from a 5 microcoulomb charge and the force on a 2 nC charge placed there.
steps.detail: E = kq/r^2 is the force per unit charge. Multiply by a test charge to get the force on it.
steps.pitfall: Using the test charge to compute the field.

problems.prompt: E from 1 nC at 1 m with k = 9 x 10^9?
Force on 2 C in a field of 100 N/C?
Direction of E near a -4 microcoulomb charge?

steps.title: Field Lines
steps.mastery: Sketch field patterns for charges and plates.
steps.practice: Sketch field lines for a single + charge, a + and - pair and 2 parallel plates 1 cm apart.
steps.detail: Lines start on + and end on -. Closer lines mean a stronger field, and between plates the field is uniform.
steps.proof: 3 sketches with arrows.
steps.pitfall: Drawing field lines that cross.

problems.prompt: Can 2 field lines cross at 1 point?
Field between plates 0.01 m apart at 100 V?
Field inside a charged metal sphere of radius 1 m?

steps.title: Potential and Voltage
steps.mastery: Relate potential difference to energy per charge.
steps.practice: Find the energy gained by an electron crossing 100 V and its speed if it starts at rest, with m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg.
steps.detail: Voltage is energy per charge, so W = qV. Converting to kinetic energy gives the speed.
steps.proof: 1.6 x 10^-17 J and about 5.9 x 10^6 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Treating voltage as a force.

problems.prompt: Energy for 2 C across 12 V?
1 eV in joules?
Potential 0.5 m from 1 nC with k = 9 x 10^9?

steps.title: Capacitors
steps.mastery: Use Q = CV and the energy stored.
steps.practice: Find the charge and energy on a 100 microfarad capacitor at 12 V.
steps.detail: A capacitor stores charge in proportion to the voltage across it. The energy stored is 1/2 CV^2.
steps.proof: 1.2 mC and 7.2 mJ.
steps.pitfall: Using CV^2 without the half.

problems.prompt: Q on 10 microfarads at 5 V?
Energy in 2 F at 3 V?
Double V from 6 to 12 V. Energy factor?

steps.title: The EM Spectrum
steps.mastery: Order the spectrum by wavelength and frequency.
steps.practice: Order 7 regions from radio to gamma by wavelength and give 1 use of each.
steps.detail: All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy per photon.
steps.proof: Radio, microwave, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma with uses.
steps.pitfall: Thinking radio waves are sound.

problems.prompt: Which has higher frequency, UV or IR, out of the 7 regions?
Speed of 2.45 GHz microwaves in a vacuum?
Wavelength of a 100 MHz FM radio wave?

steps.title: Fields That Regenerate
steps.mastery: Describe EM waves as linked electric and magnetic fields.
steps.practice: Sketch an EM wave with E and B at right angles and explain in 2 sentences why it needs no medium.
steps.detail: A changing E field makes a B field and a changing B field makes an E field. The pair carries itself through empty space.
steps.proof: A sketch with E, B and the direction of travel all at 90 degrees.
steps.pitfall: Drawing E and B parallel.

problems.prompt: Angle between E and B in an EM wave?
Can light cross the 150 million km of vacuum to Earth?
Who predicted EM waves in the 1860s?

steps.title: Speed of Light From Constants
steps.mastery: Compute c from the electric and magnetic constants.
steps.practice: Compute c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0) with mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 and epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12.
steps.detail: Maxwell found that the wave speed comes straight from 2 measured constants. It matched the speed of light.
steps.proof: About 3.00 x 10^8 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Dropping the square root.

problems.prompt: mu0 epsilon0 value, roughly?
Light travel time from the Sun at 1.5 x 10^11 m?
Distance light goes in 1 ns?

steps.title: Energy and Intensity
steps.mastery: Use intensity and the inverse square law.
steps.practice: Find the intensity 2 m from a 100 W bulb radiating evenly, then at 4 m.
steps.detail: Power spreads over a sphere of area 4 pi r^2. Doubling distance cuts intensity to a quarter.
steps.proof: About 2.0 W/m^2 and 0.50 W/m^2.
steps.pitfall: Using a circle area instead of a sphere.

problems.prompt: Intensity factor going from 1 m to 3 m?
Sunlight at Earth is about 1360 W/m^2. At 2 AU?
Area of a sphere of radius 1 m?

steps.title: Polarization
steps.mastery: Use Malus law for polarizers.
steps.practice: Find the intensity through 2 polarizers at 60 degrees when 100 W/m^2 of unpolarized light enters.
steps.detail: The first polarizer halves unpolarized light. Each next one passes I cos^2 theta.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the first halving.

problems.prompt: Polarized 40 W/m^2 through a filter at 90 degrees?
At 45 degrees, 40 W/m^2 becomes?
Can sound waves in air at 340 m/s be polarized?

steps.title: Define Work
steps.mastery: State the definition of mechanical work as a scalar product of force and displacement.
steps.practice: Calculate the work done by a constant 10 N force pushing a crate 3 m horizontally.
steps.detail: Write the force vector and displacement vector. Verify they are collinear; if not, use the component of the force along the displacement. Multiply the magnitude of that component by the distance traveled. Record the result in joules.
steps.proof: Work = 10 N × 3 m = 30 J.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying force and distance without checking that the force is parallel to the displacement.

problems.prompt: What is the work done by a 5 N force moving an object 2 m in the direction of the force?
Calculate the work done by a constant 12 N force pushing a crate 4 m horizontally.
A 8 N force pushes a crate 3 m opposite to the direction of motion. What is the work done by the force?
problems.hint: Remember work = F·d·cosθ; opposite direction gives cosθ = -1.

steps.title: Introduce Kinetic Energy
steps.mastery: Relate a moving object's kinetic energy to its mass and speed.
steps.practice: Compute the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 4 m/s.
steps.detail: Use the formula KE = ½ mv². Plug in the mass and speed values, square the speed first, then multiply by the mass and ½. Write the answer with the unit joule.
steps.proof: KE = ½ × 2 kg × (4 m/s)² = 16 J.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to square the speed or omitting the ½ factor.

problems.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of a 1 kg object moving at 2 m/s?
Compute the kinetic energy of a 3 kg ball moving at 5 m/s.
A 0.5 kg projectile has a kinetic energy of 8 J. What is its speed?
problems.hint: Solve KE = ½ m v² for v.

steps.title: Work-Energy Theorem
steps.mastery: Apply the work-energy theorem to equate net work to the change in kinetic energy.
steps.practice: A 1 kg cart accelerates from 2 m/s to 5 m/s. Find the net work done on the cart.
steps.detail: Calculate initial KE with the initial speed, then final KE with the final speed. Subtract initial from final to get ΔKE, which equals net work. Keep units consistent.
steps.proof: ΔKE = ½·1·5² − ½·1·2² = 12.5 J − 2 J = 10.5 J, so net work = 10.5 J.
steps.pitfall: Using final speed for both terms or ignoring the initial kinetic energy.

problems.prompt: A 2 kg cart speeds up from 0 m/s to 3 m/s. What is the net work done on it?
A 1.5 kg sled accelerates from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. Find the net work done.
A 1 kg cart slows down from 4 m/s to 1 m/s. What is the net work done on the cart?
problems.hint: Work equals change in kinetic energy; final minus initial.

steps.title: Potential Energy of Gravity
steps.mastery: Express gravitational potential energy as the product of weight and height.
steps.practice: Find the gravitational potential energy of a 3 kg mass lifted 4 m above ground (g = 9.8 m/s²).
steps.detail: Multiply the mass by the acceleration due to gravity to get weight, then multiply by the vertical displacement. Record the result in joules, rounding if desired.
steps.pitfall: Using mass instead of weight (mg) or forgetting the height factor.

problems.prompt: What is the gravitational potential energy of a 2 kg mass lifted 3 m (g=9.8 m/s²)?
Find the gravitational potential energy of a 5 kg object raised 7 m above ground (use g=9.8 m/s²).
A 10 kg weight is suspended 0.5 m above the floor. What is its gravitational potential energy? (Use g=9.8 m/s²).
problems.hint: Weight = mg; then multiply by height.

steps.title: Conserve Mechanical Energy
steps.mastery: Use conservation of mechanical energy when non-conservative forces are absent.
steps.practice: A 0.5 kg pendulum bob is released from a height 0.6 m above its lowest point. Compute its speed at the bottom.
steps.detail: Set initial potential energy equal to final kinetic energy. Solve for speed by isolating v², then take the square root. Keep significant figures consistent.
steps.pitfall: Including friction or air resistance when the problem states a frictionless system.

problems.prompt: A 0.2 kg pendulum bob is released from 0.3 m height. What is its speed at the lowest point? (g=9.8 m/s²).
A 0.8 kg block slides down a frictionless 2 m high incline. Find its speed at the bottom.
A 0.5 kg pendulum bob reaches a speed of 4 m/s at the bottom of its swing. Assuming no friction, from what height was it released? (g=9.8 m/s²).
problems.hint: Set initial PE = final KE and solve for height.

steps.title: Solve Combined Work-Energy Ramp Problem
steps.mastery: Combine work from gravity and external forces to find final speed using the work-energy theorem.
steps.practice: A 1.5 kg skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a frictionless 2 m high ramp, then rides onto a level section where a constant 5 N push acts for 3 m. Find the speed at the end of the push.
steps.detail: Compute the work done by gravity as the loss of potential energy (mgh). Add the work done by the external push (force × distance). Set the sum equal to the change in kinetic energy, solve for the final speed, and keep units consistent.
steps.proof: Work_gravity = m·g·h = 1.5·9.8·2 = 29.4 J (gain). Work_push = 5 N·3 m = 15 J. Total work = 44.4 J = ΔKE = ½·1.5·v² → v = √(2·44.4/1.5) ≈ 7.68 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Treating the push as opposing motion or forgetting to add the gravitational work to the push work.

problems.prompt: Calculate the gravitational work on a 2.0 kg object that slides down a frictionless 3 m high ramp.
A 1.5 kg skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a frictionless 2 m high ramp and then receives a constant 5 N push along a horizontal 3 m section. What is the speed at the end of the push?
If the same skateboarder receives a constant 5 N force opposite to its motion along the 3 m horizontal section after the ramp, what is its speed at the end of the section?
problems.hint: Subtract the work done by the opposing push from the gravitational work before converting to kinetic energy.

steps.title: Isolate One Object
steps.mastery: Draw a single object alone with its forces.
steps.practice: Draw free-body diagrams for 4 cases: a 2 kg book on a table, a hanging lamp, a box being pushed and a falling ball.
steps.detail: Draw only the chosen object as a dot or box. Every force on it comes from something touching it or from gravity.
steps.proof: 4 diagrams with every force labeled by its source.
steps.pitfall: Adding forces the object exerts on other things.

problems.prompt: Forces on a 2 kg book resting on a table?
problems.answer: Weight down and normal force up.

problems.prompt: Forces on a 3 kg ball in free fall, no air?
Weight of a 2 kg book with g = 9.8 m/s^2?

steps.title: Name Every Force
steps.mastery: Label weight, normal, tension, friction and applied forces.
steps.practice: Label each force on a 5 kg crate pulled by a rope at 30 degrees across a rough floor.
steps.detail: Each force gets a name, a direction and a source. A force with no source is not real, like a "force of motion".
steps.proof: 5 forces: weight, normal, tension, friction and none extra.
steps.pitfall: Inventing a forward force that keeps a moving object going.

problems.prompt: Direction of kinetic friction on a crate moving right at 2 m/s?
Force from a rope on a hanging 4 kg mass?
Is there a forward force on a puck sliding at 3 m/s on ice?

steps.title: Components on a Slope
steps.mastery: Split weight into parts along and across an incline.
steps.practice: Split the weight of a 10 kg block on a 30 degree slope into parallel and perpendicular parts.
steps.detail: Tilt the axes to match the slope. Along the slope mg sin theta pulls down and across it mg cos theta presses in.
steps.proof: 49 N along and about 84.9 N into the slope.
steps.pitfall: Swapping sin and cos.

problems.prompt: Parallel part of 100 N on a 30 degree slope?
Perpendicular part of 100 N on a 60 degree slope?
Normal force on a 10 kg block on a 30 degree frictionless slope?

steps.title: Diagram to Equations
steps.mastery: Write Newton second law for each axis from the diagram.
steps.practice: Write sum F = ma along x and y for a 5 kg box pushed with 20 N against 8 N of friction, then solve for a.
steps.detail: Each axis gets its own equation. Forces along the motion go in one equation, balanced forces in the other.
steps.pitfall: Putting the ma term on the diagram as a force.

problems.prompt: Net force from 20 N right and 8 N left?
a for a net 12 N on 5 kg?
A 60 kg person in an elevator going up at 2 m/s^2 accel. Normal force with g = 9.8?

steps.title: Systems of Objects
steps.mastery: Draw linked diagrams for connected bodies.
steps.practice: Draw diagrams for 2 blocks of 3 kg and 2 kg joined by a string over a pulley, then find the acceleration.
steps.detail: Draw each block separately. The same tension acts on both, and both share the same acceleration size.
steps.proof: a = 2g/5 = 3.92 m/s^2 with the 2 kg block hanging.
steps.pitfall: Using 1 diagram for both and losing the tension.

problems.prompt: Masses 3 kg on a smooth table and 2 kg hanging. a with g = 9.8?
Tension in the string joining the 3 kg and 2 kg blocks?
Atwood machine with 5 kg and 3 kg. a with g = 9.8?

steps.title: Fluid Pressure at Depth
steps.mastery: Compute hydrostatic pressure using density, gravity, and depth.
steps.practice: Calculate the pressure at 5 m depth in freshwater (ρ = 1000 kg/m³).
steps.detail: Write down the formula P = ρ g h. Plug in the given density, the standard gravity 9.81 m/s², and the depth of 5 m. Multiply step-by-step, keeping units consistent (kg·m⁻¹·s⁻² = Pa). Verify the result is a positive pressure value.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to include the gravitational constant 9.81 m/s².

steps.title: Hydrostatic Pressure Difference
steps.mastery: Find pressure differences between two depths in the same fluid.
steps.practice: Find the pressure difference between 2 m and 8 m depth in oil (ρ = 850 kg/m³).
steps.detail: Compute the depth difference Δh = 8 m − 2 m = 6 m. Apply ΔP = ρ g Δh with ρ = 850 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². Multiply sequentially: 850 × 9.81 = 8338.5, then × 6 = 50031 Pa. Record the answer with appropriate units.
steps.pitfall: Using the deeper pressure alone instead of the difference Δh.

steps.title: Pascal's Principle Force Transfer
steps.mastery: Use equal pressure to relate forces on pistons of different areas.
steps.practice: Determine the force required on a 2 cm² piston to lift a 50 kg load on a 200 cm² piston.
steps.detail: Convert areas to the same units (cm² is fine because they cancel). Compute the ratio A₁/A₂ = 2/200 = 0.01. Multiply the load weight m g = 50 × 9.81 = 490.5 N by the ratio: 0.01 × 490.5 = 4.905 N. This is the minimum input force.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up which area belongs to the input versus the output piston.

steps.title: Buoyant Force on a Sphere
steps.mastery: Calculate buoyant force using displaced fluid volume.
steps.practice: Compute the buoyant force on a steel sphere of radius 0.1 m fully submerged in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³).
steps.detail: First find the sphere's volume: V = (4/3)πr³. With r = 0.1 m, r³ = 0.001 m³, so V ≈ 4.1888 × 10⁻³ m³. Then apply Archimedes' principle: F_b = ρ g V. Multiply 1000 kg/m³ × 9.81 m/s² = 9810 N/m³, then × 0.0041888 m³ ≈ 41.1 N. Record the force with units of newtons.
steps.pitfall: Using radius instead of volume or forgetting the 4/3 π factor.

steps.title: Continuity in Varying Pipe Diameters
steps.mastery: Apply the continuity equation to relate speeds in different cross-sections.
steps.practice: A pipe narrows from 0.2 m to 0.1 m diameter. If water speed in the wide section is 2 m/s, find the speed in the narrow section.
steps.detail: Compute areas: A₁ = π(0.2)²/4 = 0.0314 m², A₂ = π(0.1)²/4 = 0.00785 m². Ratio A₁/A₂ = 4. Multiply by v₁ = 2 m/s to get v₂ = 8 m/s. Verify that the product A₂v₂ equals A₁v₁.
steps.proof: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ → v₂ = (A₁/A₂) v₁ = (0.2²/0.1²) × 2 = 8 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Using diameters directly instead of areas (πd²/4).

steps.title: Bernoulli Exit Speed
steps.mastery: Use Bernoulli's equation to find fluid speed from a height difference.
steps.practice: Water at 3 m height in a tank exits a nozzle at ground level. Compute the exit speed ignoring losses.
steps.detail: Write Bernoulli between the surface (point 1) and the nozzle exit (point 2): P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂. With v₁≈0, h₁ = 3 m, h₂ = 0, and P₁ = P₂, solve for v₂: v₂ = √(2gh). Plug g = 9.81 m/s² and h = 3 m, calculate the square root to obtain ≈7.67 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Adding the atmospheric pressure term when it cancels out in the height-only case.

steps.title: Design a Simple Hydraulic Lift
steps.mastery: Combine Pascal's principle and force calculations to size a hydraulic system.
steps.practice: Sketch a lift with pistons of 5 cm² and 250 cm². If you press with 10 N on the small piston, calculate the maximum load it can lift.
steps.detail: Draw two cylinders sharing fluid. Label the small piston area A₁ = 5 cm² and the large piston area A₂ = 250 cm². Apply Pascal: F₂ = (A₂/A₁) F₁. Compute the ratio 250/5 = 50, then multiply by the input force 10 N to get F₂ = 500 N. Convert to mass by dividing by g if desired (≈51 kg). Ensure the sketch shows the fluid connection.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to keep the area ratio dimensionless or mixing N with kg.

steps.title: Identify Friction Types
steps.mastery: Distinguish static and kinetic friction and state their coefficient symbols and typical values.
steps.practice: Write down the static coefficient μs = 0.4 and kinetic coefficient μk = 0.3 for a rubber-on-concrete surface.
steps.detail: Look up a common material pair (e.g., rubber on concrete) in a textbook or reliable online table. Record the static coefficient as μs and the kinetic coefficient as μk, keeping the decimal format. Remember that static friction is usually larger than kinetic friction, so the numbers should reflect that relationship.
steps.proof: The symbols μs and μk appear correctly with the given numbers.
steps.pitfall: Confusing μs with μk or omitting the subscript, which leads to using the wrong coefficient in calculations.

problems.prompt: What is the static friction coefficient μs for rubber on concrete if it is 0.4?
A 2 kg block rests on a rubber-on-concrete surface. Which coefficient, μs or μk, is used to determine if it will start moving?
A student writes μs = 0.3 for rubber on concrete. Identify the mistake and give the correct static coefficient.
problems.answer: Mistake: used kinetic value; correct μs = 0.4.
problems.hint: Recall typical values for rubber on concrete.

steps.title: Calculate Static Friction Force
steps.mastery: Compute the maximum static friction force that prevents motion for a given normal force.
steps.practice: Find the maximum static friction force for a 7 kg crate on a horizontal floor with μs = 0.5.
steps.detail: First calculate the normal force: N = m · g (mass times gravity, g ≈ 9.81 m/s²). Then multiply N by the static coefficient μs. Write each intermediate value on paper to avoid arithmetic errors. Verify the final number is reasonable compared with the weight of the crate.
steps.proof: Maximum static friction = μs · m · g = 0.5 × 7 × 9.81 ≈ 34.3 N.
steps.pitfall: Using the kinetic coefficient instead of the static one, which underestimates the force needed to start motion.

problems.prompt: What is the normal force on a 7 kg crate on a horizontal floor (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
Find the maximum static friction force for an 8 kg crate on a horizontal floor with μs = 0.4.
A 5 kg block rests on a 20° incline with μs = 0.5. What is the maximum static friction force parallel to the surface?
problems.hint: Find normal force using mg cosθ first.

steps.title: Determine Kinetic Friction Force
steps.mastery: Calculate the kinetic friction force acting on an object moving at constant speed.
steps.practice: Compute the kinetic friction force on a 4 kg sled sliding on ice with μk = 0.08.
steps.detail: Use the same normal-force formula as for static friction. Multiply by μk, not μs. Record the calculation steps: N = 4 × 9.81 = 39.24 N, then Fk = 0.08 × 39.24 ≈ 3.1 N. Check that the kinetic force is smaller than the static maximum you computed earlier for a similar mass.
steps.proof: Kinetic friction = μk · m · g = 0.08 × 4 × 9.81 ≈ 3.1 N.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting that the normal force on a horizontal surface equals mg, leading to an incorrect denominator.

problems.prompt: What is the kinetic friction coefficient μk for ice if it is 0.08?
Compute the kinetic friction force on a 6 kg sled sliding on ice with μk = 0.05.
A 4 kg sled slides on a horizontal surface with μk = 0.08 while a horizontal push of 5 N is applied. What is the net force on the sled?
problems.hint: Subtract kinetic friction from the applied force.

steps.title: Analyze Circular Motion without Friction
steps.mastery: Identify the centripetal acceleration required for uniform circular motion and the net radial force needed.
steps.practice: Calculate the centripetal acceleration for a 2 kg mass moving at 3 m/s around a circle of radius 1.5 m.
steps.detail: Write the formula a_c = v² / r. Substitute v = 3 m/s and r = 1.5 m, then square the speed before dividing. Keep units consistent (meters and seconds). After finding a_c, you may later multiply by mass to get the required net radial force.
steps.pitfall: Using the wrong radius or speed in the v²/r formula, which flips the magnitude of the acceleration.

problems.prompt: What is the centripetal acceleration of an object moving at 2 m/s in a circle of radius 4 m?
Calculate the centripetal acceleration for a 2 kg mass moving at 3 m/s around a circle of radius 1.5 m.
A 0.5 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.8 m with angular speed 4 rad/s. Find the required centripetal force and state the acceleration.
problems.hint: Use a = ω²r.

steps.title: Combine Friction and Centripetal Force
steps.mastery: Determine whether static friction can supply the required centripetal force for a car turning on a flat road.
steps.practice: A 1500 kg car travels at 20 m/s around a curve of radius 50 m. With μs = 0.7, decide if the car can negotiate the turn without skidding.
steps.detail: First compute the needed centripetal force using m v² / r. Then find the maximum static friction using μs · m · g. Compare the two numbers: if the frictional limit is lower, the tires cannot provide enough grip. Write each number on a separate line to keep the comparison clear.
steps.proof: Required centripetal force = m v² / r = 1500 × 400 / 50 = 12 000 N. Maximum static friction = μs · m · g = 0.7 × 1500 × 9.81 ≈ 10 300 N. Since 12 000 N > 10 300 N, the car will skid.
steps.pitfall: Comparing the kinetic friction force instead of the static one, which would incorrectly suggest the car can turn safely.

problems.prompt: What maximum static friction force can a 1500 kg car generate on a flat road with μs = 0.7?
A 1500 kg car travels at 20 m/s around a curve of radius 50 m with μs = 0.7. Can it negotiate the turn without skidding?
problems.answer: The car will skid; required 12 000 N > maximum 10 300 N.

problems.prompt: If the road is banked at 10° and μs = 0.7, can the same 1500 kg car negotiate the 20 m/s turn on a radius of 50 m without skidding? (Assume g = 9.81 m/s².).
problems.answer: Yes; banking supplies ~2590 N, friction needs ~9410 N which is below the 10 300 N limit.
problems.hint: Resolve forces into radial components.

steps.title: Apply to Real-World Problems
steps.mastery: Set up and solve a friction-in-circular-motion problem from scratch, choosing appropriate coefficients and checking the result.
steps.practice: Design a banked turn for a roller coaster car of mass 800 kg traveling at 12 m/s on a curve of radius 30 m, assuming no reliance on friction (μ = 0). Calculate the required banking angle θ.
steps.detail: When friction is absent, the normal force provides the necessary radial component. Use tan θ = v²/(r g). Compute v² = 144, r g = 30 × 9.81 ≈ 294.3, then divide to get 0.49. Take the arctangent (use a calculator) and convert to degrees. Record the angle to the nearest whole degree.
steps.pitfall: Using the friction formula when μ = 0, or forgetting to convert the angle from radians to degrees when reporting the answer.

problems.prompt: For a car moving at 12 m/s on a curve of radius 30 m, what is the value of v² / (r g)?
Design a banked turn for a roller-coaster car of mass 800 kg traveling at 12 m/s on a curve of radius 30 m, assuming no friction (μ = 0). What banking angle θ (in degrees) is required?
problems.hint: Use tan θ = v² / (r g).

problems.prompt: If the same roller-coaster car (800 kg, 12 m/s, r = 30 m) were on a banked turn of 26° but the surface had a coefficient of friction μ = 0.2, what is the maximum speed the car could travel without slipping down the bank? (Give the speed in m/s, rounded to two significant figures.).
problems.hint: Use the banking-with-friction formula: v_max = √[r g (tanθ + μ) / (1 - μ tanθ)].

steps.title: Newton Law of Gravitation
steps.mastery: Compute gravity between 2 masses.
steps.practice: Compute the force between Earth, 6.0 x 10^24 kg, and a 70 kg person at radius 6.4 x 10^6 m with G = 6.67 x 10^-11.
steps.detail: F = G m1 m2 / r^2. The same law that holds you on the ground also holds the Moon in its orbit.
steps.proof: About 684 N, close to 70 x 9.8.
steps.pitfall: Measuring r from the surface instead of the center.

problems.prompt: Double the distance. Force changes by what factor?
Double 1 mass. Force changes by what factor?
Triple the distance from 1 R to 3 R. Factor?

steps.title: Field Strength g
steps.mastery: Find g at different heights and on other planets.
steps.practice: Compute g on the surface of Mars, mass 6.4 x 10^23 kg and radius 3.4 x 10^6 m.
steps.detail: g = GM/r^2. It depends on the planet mass and on how far you are from its center.
steps.proof: About 3.7 m/s^2.
steps.pitfall: Using Earth g everywhere.

problems.prompt: g at 2 Earth radii from the center, with 9.8 at the surface?
Weight of a 50 kg person where g = 3.7?
Does mass change from 50 kg on the Moon?

steps.title: Circular Orbits
steps.mastery: Set gravity equal to the centripetal force.
steps.practice: Find the orbital speed at 7.0 x 10^6 m from Earth center, using GM = 4.0 x 10^14.
steps.detail: For a circle, GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r, so v = sqrt(GM/r). The satellite mass cancels out completely.
steps.proof: About 7.6 km/s.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a heavier satellite needs to go faster.

problems.prompt: v = sqrt(GM/r) with GM = 4 x 10^14 and r = 1 x 10^7 m?
Does the orbital speed depend on a 500 kg vs 1000 kg satellite?
Higher orbit, r from 7 to 14 x 10^6 m. Faster or slower?

steps.title: Kepler Laws
steps.mastery: Use T^2 proportional to r^3.
steps.practice: Use Kepler third law to find the period of a planet at 4 AU from the Sun.
steps.detail: Planets farther out take longer to go around. Measured in years and AU, the rule for anything circling the Sun is simply T^2 = r^3.
steps.proof: T = 8 years.
steps.pitfall: Using T proportional to r.

problems.prompt: Period at 9 AU?
Mars at 1.52 AU. Period?
Where in an elliptical orbit around the Sun is a planet fastest?

steps.title: Escape and Energy
steps.mastery: Use gravitational potential energy to find escape speed.
steps.practice: Compute escape speed from Earth with GM = 4.0 x 10^14 and R = 6.4 x 10^6 m.
steps.detail: Gravitational PE is -GMm/r. To escape, kinetic energy must reach zero total energy, so v = sqrt(2GM/R).
steps.proof: About 11.2 km/s.
steps.pitfall: Using mgh for heights comparable to the radius.

problems.prompt: Escape speed is 11.2 km/s where orbital speed is 7.9 km/s. Ratio?
Sign of GPE far below infinity, at r = 2R?
Escape speed with 2GM/R = 1.0 x 10^8?

steps.title: First Law
steps.mastery: Use delta U = Q - W for a gas.
steps.practice: Find the change in internal energy when a gas absorbs 500 J and does 200 J of work.
steps.detail: Energy in as heat raises internal energy and work done by the gas lowers it. It is energy conservation for heat.
steps.proof: delta U = 300 J.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up the sign of work done by vs on the gas.

problems.prompt: Q = 100 J in, W = 100 J by gas. delta U?
Gas compressed with 50 J of work and no heat. delta U?
Q = -80 J, W = 0. delta U?

steps.title: Work on PV Diagrams
steps.mastery: Find work as the area under a pressure volume curve.
steps.practice: Find the work done by a gas expanding from 0.01 to 0.03 m^3 at 200,000 Pa.
steps.detail: At constant pressure W = P delta V. On a PV diagram the work is the area under the path.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting that a closed loop does net work equal to its area.

problems.prompt: W at 100,000 Pa from 1 to 3 L?
Work in a constant volume process at 2 x 10^5 Pa?
Area of a rectangle loop 100 kPa tall and 0.002 m^3 wide?

steps.title: Heat Engines
steps.mastery: Compute efficiency of an engine.
steps.practice: Find the efficiency of an engine taking 1000 J of heat and expelling 700 J.
steps.detail: Efficiency = W/Qh = 1 - Qc/Qh. Some heat must always be dumped, so no engine reaches 100%.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the heat expelled.

problems.prompt: Qh = 500 J, W = 150 J. Efficiency?
Efficiency 25% and Qh = 800 J. Work?
Heat dumped by the 25% engine taking in 800 J?

steps.title: Carnot Limit
steps.mastery: Find the maximum efficiency between 2 temperatures.
steps.practice: Compute the Carnot efficiency between 600 K and 300 K, and between 500 degrees C and 20 degrees C.
steps.detail: No engine beats 1 - Tc/Th with temperatures in kelvin. Bigger temperature gaps allow higher limits.
steps.proof: 50% and about 62%.
steps.pitfall: Using Celsius in the Carnot formula.

problems.prompt: Carnot limit for 400 K and 300 K?
Can a real engine between 600 and 300 K reach 55%?
Th = 1000 K, limit 70%. Tc?

steps.title: Entropy
steps.mastery: Estimate entropy changes and use the second law.
steps.practice: Compute the entropy change when 3340 J melts ice at 273 K and when 1000 J flows from 400 K to 300 K.
steps.detail: delta S = Q/T at constant temperature. Heat flowing hot to cold always raises total entropy.
steps.proof: 12.2 J/K, and +0.83 J/K total.
steps.pitfall: Thinking entropy can never decrease anywhere.

problems.prompt: delta S for 600 J at 300 K?
Total delta S for 1200 J from 600 K to 300 K?
Can a fridge at 5 degrees C lower its inside entropy?
problems.answer: Yes, by raising it more outside.

steps.title: Magnetic Fields
steps.mastery: Sketch fields around magnets and currents.
steps.practice: Sketch the field of a bar magnet and of a long straight wire carrying 5 A, with directions.
steps.detail: Field lines run from north to south outside a magnet. Around a wire they form circles given by the right hand grip rule.
steps.proof: 2 sketches with arrows.
steps.pitfall: Drawing straight lines out from a wire.

problems.prompt: Unit of magnetic field, named after 1 person?
Field around a wire: lines or circles, for 5 A?
Like poles of 2 magnets attract or repel?

steps.title: Force on a Wire
steps.mastery: Use F = BIL for a current in a field.
steps.practice: Find the force on a 0.2 m wire carrying 3 A at right angles to a 0.5 T field.
steps.detail: A current in a field feels a push across both. Fleming left hand rule gives the direction.
steps.pitfall: Using F = BIL when the wire is parallel to the field.

problems.prompt: Force when the wire runs parallel to a 1 T field?
Double the current from 3 to 6 A. Force factor?

steps.title: Charges in Fields
steps.mastery: Find the radius of a charge circling in a magnetic field.
steps.practice: Find the radius for a proton, 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, moving at 2 x 10^6 m/s in a 0.5 T field.
steps.detail: F = qvB acts as a centripetal force, so r = mv/(qB). Faster or heavier particles curve less.
steps.proof: About 0.042 m.
steps.pitfall: Expecting a magnetic force to speed a charge up.

problems.prompt: Does a magnetic field do work on a moving charge at 10^5 m/s?
Force on 1.6 x 10^-19 C at 10^6 m/s in 1 T?
Double B from 0.5 to 1 T. Radius factor?

steps.title: Induction
steps.mastery: Use Faraday law of induction.
steps.practice: Find the emf in a 100 turn coil when the flux drops from 0.02 to 0 Wb in 0.1 s.
steps.detail: A changing flux induces an emf equal to N times the rate of change. Lenz law says it opposes the change.
steps.pitfall: Expecting an emf from a steady field.

problems.prompt: Flux 0.5 T through 0.02 m^2. Phi?
Rod 0.5 m long moving at 4 m/s in 0.2 T. emf?
Magnet held still inside 1 coil. emf?

steps.title: Motors, Generators and Transformers
steps.mastery: Explain motors and generators and use the transformer ratio.
steps.practice: Find the secondary voltage of a transformer with 100 primary and 2000 secondary turns on 12 V AC.
steps.detail: Motors turn current into motion and generators turn motion into current. Transformers scale voltage by the turns ratio.
steps.pitfall: Using a transformer on DC.

problems.prompt: Ideal transformer, 10 W in. Power out?
Why do power lines use 400,000 V?
problems.answer: Lower current means less heat lost.

steps.title: Define Momentum
steps.mastery: State the definition of momentum as the product of mass and velocity and compute it for a given object.
steps.practice: Write the momentum of a 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s.
steps.detail: Take a piece of paper and write down the formula p = m·v. Identify the mass (3 kg) and the velocity (4 m/s) of the cart. Multiply the numbers, then write the result with the proper unit. Double-check that you have not swapped the numbers or omitted the unit.
steps.proof: p = 3 kg × 4 m/s = 12 kg·m/s.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to include the correct units (kg·m/s) or mixing up mass and velocity.

problems.prompt: What is the momentum of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s?
Calculate the momentum of a 5 kg cart traveling at 7 m/s.
A 4 kg sled moves west at 5 m/s. What is its momentum (include direction)?
problems.hint: Treat direction as part of the answer.

steps.title: Calculate Momentum Change
steps.mastery: Determine the change in momentum when an object's speed varies, using Δp = m·Δv.
steps.practice: Compute the change in momentum when a 2 kg ball slows from 6 m/s to 2 m/s.
steps.detail: Write the initial momentum p_i = m·v_i and the final momentum p_f = m·v_f. Subtract p_i from p_f to get Δp. Remember that a decrease in speed gives a negative Δp, indicating momentum loss. Verify the arithmetic and sign before finalising the answer.
steps.proof: Δp = 2 kg × (2 m/s, 6 m/s) = 2 kg × (-4 m/s) =, 8 kg·m/s.
steps.pitfall: Using final minus initial speed incorrectly, leading to a sign error.

problems.prompt: What is the change in momentum of a 1 kg ball that speeds up from 2 m/s to 5 m/s?
A 3 kg crate slows from 8 m/s to 3 m/s. Find Δp.
A 2 kg puck reverses direction, changing velocity from 4 m/s east to 2 m/s west. What is Δp?
problems.hint: Remember velocity sign.

steps.title: Impulse and Average Force
steps.mastery: Apply the impulse-momentum theorem (Impulse = Δp) to find average force over a time interval.
steps.practice: Find the average force on a 0.5 kg puck that speeds up from 0 m/s to 3 m/s in 0.2 s.
steps.detail: First calculate the change in momentum using the mass and the velocity change. Then divide that Δp by the time interval (0.2 s) to obtain the average force. Write each step clearly, keep track of units, and confirm that the force magnitude makes sense for a small puck.
steps.proof: Δp = 0.5 kg × 3 m/s = 1.5 kg·m/s;  F_avg = Δp / Δt = 1.5 kg·m/s ÷ 0.2 s = 7.5 N.
steps.pitfall: Dividing by the wrong time interval or forgetting to convert units, which gives an incorrect force.

problems.prompt: What impulse is delivered to a 1 kg ball that speeds up from 0 m/s to 2 m/s?
Find the average force on a 0.8 kg object that changes velocity from 1 m/s to 4 m/s in 0.5 s.
A 0.3 kg puck experiences a force that changes its momentum by -0.9 kg·m/s over 0.3 s. What is the average force?
problems.hint: Impulse = Δp.

steps.title: Elastic Collision Conservation
steps.mastery: Use conservation of momentum to solve for final speeds in a perfectly elastic collision.
steps.practice: A 1 kg cart moving at 4 m/s collides elastically with a 2 kg cart at rest. Find the 1 kg cart's speed after the collision.
steps.detail: Write the momentum conservation equation and the kinetic-energy conservation equation for an elastic collision. Solve the two equations simultaneously, or use the shortcut formula for v1'. Keep sign conventions consistent: a negative result means the cart reverses direction. Check the answer by confirming total kinetic energy is unchanged.
steps.pitfall: Applying the inelastic-collision formula instead of the elastic one, which yields the wrong speed.

problems.prompt: What is the speed of the 2 kg cart after it elastically collides with a 1 kg cart at rest, given the 2 kg cart was moving at 3 m/s?
A 1 kg cart moving at 5 m/s collides elastically with a 3 kg cart that is initially at rest. What is the final speed of the 1 kg cart?
Two carts collide elastically: m₁=2 kg moving at 4 m/s, m₂=3 kg moving at -1 m/s (opposite direction). What is the final velocity of the 2 kg cart?
problems.hint: Use the full elastic-collision formula: v₁' = (m₁-m₂)/(m₁+m₂)·v₁ + (2m₂)/(m₁+m₂)·v₂.

steps.title: Inelastic Collision Outcome
steps.mastery: Determine the common final velocity after a perfectly inelastic collision where objects stick together.
steps.practice: Calculate the speed after a 0.8 kg clay ball moving at 5 m/s sticks to a 0.2 kg block initially at rest.
steps.detail: Write the total initial momentum as the sum of each object's momentum. Since the block is at rest, its momentum term is zero but still write it for completeness. Divide the total momentum by the combined mass to get the final velocity. Verify that the result is between the initial speeds, as expected for an inelastic stick-together collision.
steps.pitfall: Adding the masses but forgetting to include the momentum of the stationary object (which is zero, but the term must be present).

problems.prompt: What is the final speed when a 0.5 kg ball moving at 4 m/s sticks to a 0.5 kg block initially at rest?
A 0.7 kg object moving at 6 m/s collides inelastically with a 0.3 kg object at rest and they stick together. What is their common speed after the collision?
A 0.9 kg cart moving at 5 m/s collides and sticks to a 0.1 kg cart moving opposite at 2 m/s. What is the final velocity (including direction) of the combined mass?
problems.hint: Include the momentum of the moving 0.1 kg cart (negative direction) before dividing by the total mass.

steps.title: Momentum Transfer in a Kick
steps.mastery: Apply conservation of momentum to a real-world interaction, solving for the recoil speed of the kicker.
steps.practice: A 0.2 kg soccer ball is kicked to 12 m/s. If the foot (1 kg) was initially at rest, calculate the foot's speed right after the kick assuming an isolated system.
steps.detail: Set the total initial momentum to zero because both foot and ball start at rest. After the kick, write the momentum of the ball (0.2 kg·12 m/s) and the unknown foot momentum (1 kg·v_foot). Solve for v_foot, remembering that the foot's velocity is opposite in direction to the ball's, hence the negative sign. Confirm the magnitude is reasonable for a human foot recoil.
steps.proof: Using m_ball·v_ball + m_foot·v_foot = 0, v_foot =, (0.2 kg·12 m/s) / 1 kg =, 2.4 m/s (foot moves opposite to ball).
steps.pitfall: Treating the foot as stationary after the kick or forgetting the opposite direction sign, which gives a positive speed for the foot.

problems.prompt: What is the momentum of a 0.2 kg soccer ball moving at 12 m/s?
A 0.2 kg soccer ball is kicked to 12 m/s. If the foot (1 kg) was initially at rest, what is the foot's speed right after the kick, assuming an isolated system?
A 0.5 kg ball is kicked to 8 m/s by a 2 kg foot that was initially at rest. Using conservation of momentum, calculate the foot's recoil speed and state its direction relative to the ball.
problems.hint: Set total momentum to zero and solve for the foot's velocity.

steps.title: Define Position and Displacement
steps.mastery: State the difference between position and displacement and compute displacement on a straight line.
steps.practice: Write the displacement for an object that moves from x = 2 m to x = 9 m on a straight line.
steps.detail: Mark the initial and final positions on a number line. Subtract the initial coordinate from the final coordinate, keeping the sign. Record the result as the vector displacement, not the summed path length.
steps.proof: Displacement = 9 m − 2 m = 7 m.
steps.pitfall: Confusing displacement with total distance traveled when the path changes direction.

problems.prompt: Write the displacement for an object that moves from x = 5 m to x = 8 m on a straight line.
Write the displacement for an object that moves from x =, 3 m to x = 4 m on a straight line.
An object moves from x = 2 m to x = 5 m, then back to x = 1 m on the same line. What is its net displacement?
problems.hint: Displacement = final position, initial position.

steps.title: Calculate Average Velocity
steps.mastery: Find average velocity by dividing total displacement by elapsed time.
steps.practice: Compute the average velocity of the object that moved 7 m in 2 s.
steps.detail: Take the displacement you just calculated and the time interval. Divide displacement by time, preserving the sign to indicate direction. Write the answer with units of meters per second.
steps.proof: Average velocity = 7 m / 2 s = 3.5 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Using total distance instead of displacement when the motion reverses.

problems.prompt: Compute the average velocity of an object that moves 4 m in 2 s.
Compute the average velocity of an object that has a displacement of 10 m over 5 s.
An object travels 6 m forward then 2 m backward in a total time of 4 s. What is its average velocity?
problems.hint: Use net displacement (forward minus backward) divided by total time.

steps.title: Determine Constant Acceleration
steps.mastery: Calculate constant acceleration as the change in velocity divided by the time interval.
steps.practice: Find the acceleration of a car that speeds up from 0 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 s.
steps.detail: Record the initial and final velocities. Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, then divide by the elapsed time. Keep the units as meters per second squared.
steps.pitfall: Treating acceleration as a speed rather than a rate of change of velocity.

problems.prompt: Find the acceleration of a car that speeds up from 0 m/s to 10 m/s in 2 s.
Find the acceleration of a vehicle that speeds up from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 5 s.
A car decelerates from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
problems.hint: Acceleration = (final velocity, initial velocity) / time.

steps.title: Apply SUVAT Equation
steps.mastery: Use the equation x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² to find position under constant acceleration.
steps.practice: Using x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², calculate the final position after 3 s for an object starting at x₀ = 5 m, v₀ = 2 m/s, a = 4 m/s².
steps.detail: Plug the given numbers into the formula step by step: multiply v₀ by t, compute a·t², halve it, then add all terms to x₀. Verify each arithmetic step before writing the final position.
steps.pitfall: Omitting the ½ factor on the acceleration term, which halves the contribution of the a t² part.

steps.title: Solve Multi-Stage Motion Problem
steps.mastery: Combine successive constant-acceleration segments to obtain total displacement.
steps.practice: An object moves with a = 2 m/s² for 5 s, then a =, 3 m/s² for 4 s. Starting from rest, find its total displacement.
steps.detail: Compute the distance covered in the first interval using s = ½at². Find the velocity at the end of that interval (v = at) and use it as the initial velocity for the second interval. Apply s = v₀t + ½at² for the second part, then add the two distances.
steps.proof: First stage: s₁ = ½·2·5² = 25 m. Second stage: v₁ = 2·5 = 10 m/s, s₂ = 10·4 + ½·(, 3)·4² = 40-24 = 16 m. Total displacement = 25 m + 16 m = 41 m.
steps.pitfall: Resetting the velocity to zero before the second stage instead of carrying over the final velocity from the first stage.

problems.prompt: An object starts from rest and accelerates at 1.5 m/s² for 3 s. What is its displacement?
An object moves with a constant acceleration of, 1 m/s² for 5 s, starting with an initial velocity of 8 m/s. What is its displacement?
An object starts from rest, accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s, then accelerates at, 4 m/s² for 2 s. Find its total displacement.
problems.hint: First find the velocity after the first stage and use it as the initial velocity for the second stage.

problems.prompt: A student calculates the total displacement for the motion in the previous problem by treating the second stage as starting from rest, obtaining 9 m + (0.5·(, 4)·2²) = 1 m. Explain why this method is incorrect.
problems.answer: The velocity at the end of the first stage is 6 m/s, not zero, so it must be carried into the second stage. Ignoring this velocity omits the distance traveled due to the existing motion, leading to an underestimate.
problems.hint: Remember the velocity at the end of the first stage is not zero.

steps.title: Identify Net Force on a Box
steps.mastery: Determine the resultant force acting on an object by vector addition of all applied forces.
steps.practice: Calculate the net force on a 5 kg box pushed with 12 N east and pulled with 8 N west.
steps.detail: Place the box on a frictionless surface. Write each force as a signed number along the east‑west axis (east positive, west negative). Add the numbers to get the net force. Verify the sign tells you the direction. This step builds the habit of treating forces as vectors before using Newton's laws.
steps.proof: 12 N − 8 N = 4 N east, which is the correct vector sum.
steps.pitfall: Adding magnitudes without keeping track of direction, especially when forces oppose each other.

problems.prompt: What is the net force on a 2 kg box pushed with 5 N east?
Calculate the net force on a 3 kg box acted on by 10 N north and 4 N south.
A 4 kg crate is pulled 7 N north and simultaneously pushed 9 N south. What is the magnitude and direction of the net force?
problems.hint: Treat opposite directions as opposite signs when adding the forces.

steps.title: Apply Newton's First Law
steps.mastery: Predict that an object with zero net force maintains its current state of motion.
steps.practice: State what happens to a 2 kg puck sliding at 3 m/s on a frictionless ice surface when no horizontal forces act on it.
steps.detail: Recall that the first law (inertia) says motion does not change without net force. Write the initial velocity vector, confirm that all horizontal forces sum to zero, and then state that the velocity remains unchanged for any amount of time. Use the result from step 1 to verify the net force is indeed zero.
steps.proof: The puck continues at 3 m/s in the same direction because the net force is zero.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the object will eventually stop even when friction is absent.

problems.prompt: A 1 kg puck slides at 2 m/s on a frictionless ice surface with no horizontal forces acting. What happens to its motion?
problems.answer: It continues at 2 m/s in the same direction.

problems.prompt: State what happens to a 2 kg puck sliding at 3 m/s on a frictionless ice surface when no horizontal forces act on it.
problems.answer: It continues at 3 m/s in the same direction.

problems.prompt: A 0.5 kg cart moves at 4 m/s on a frictionless track and then travels through a region with no forces for 5 s. What is its speed after this interval?
problems.hint: Use Newton's first law; speed is unchanged when net force is zero.

steps.title: Use Newton's Second Law for Acceleration
steps.mastery: Calculate an object's acceleration by dividing the net force by its mass (F = ma).
steps.practice: Find the acceleration of a 3 kg cart when a net horizontal force of 15 N acts on it.
steps.detail: Take the net force from step 1 (or any given value). Write the formula a = F/m, plug in the numbers, and solve for a. Double‑check that the force is in newtons and mass in kilograms so the result is in meters per second squared. Record the acceleration vector with the same direction as the net force.
steps.proof: a = F/m = 15 N / 3 kg = 5 m/s², which matches the calculation.
steps.pitfall: Confusing mass with weight or forgetting to keep units consistent.

problems.prompt: Find the acceleration of a 2 kg object acted on by a net force of 6 N east.
Find the acceleration of a 3 kg cart when a net horizontal force of 15 N acts on it.
problems.answer: 5 m/s² in the direction of the force.

problems.prompt: A 10 kg sled is pulled with 25 N north and 15 N south. What is its acceleration?
problems.hint: Subtract opposing forces before applying F=ma.

steps.title: Demonstrate Newton's Third Law Pairs
steps.mastery: Identify action‑reaction force pairs and state that they act on different bodies.
steps.practice: When a 10 N hand pushes a wall, write the force the wall exerts on the hand.
steps.detail: Label the hand as object A and the wall as object B. The force from A on B is 10 N forward; the reaction is a 10 N force from B on A backward. Emphasize that the two forces never cancel because they act on different bodies. Sketch a free‑body diagram for each object to visualize the pair.
steps.proof: The wall exerts a 10 N force on the hand opposite to the hand's push, satisfying the third law.
steps.pitfall: Applying the reaction force to the same object that experiences the action force.

problems.prompt: A hand pushes a wall with 5 N. What force does the wall exert on the hand?
A book rests on a table. The Earth exerts a 9.8 N downward force on the book. What force does the book exert on the Earth?
A person of 70 kg pushes a 100 kg crate with a horizontal force of 120 N. State the reaction force and the object on which it acts.
problems.answer: 120 N opposite direction acting on the person.
problems.hint: Action‑reaction forces act on different bodies.

steps.title: Solve a Two‑Body Interaction Problem
steps.mastery: Combine all three Newtonian laws to predict motion of interacting objects without assistance.
steps.practice: Two ice skaters, each 60 kg, push off each other with a 30 N force for 2 s. Calculate each skater's final speed.
steps.detail: Use the third law to note each skater experiences a 30 N force in opposite directions. Apply the second law via impulse: Δp = F·t, then Δv = Δp/m. Since initial speeds are zero, the final speed equals Δv. Verify that momentum is conserved (total momentum remains zero). Write the answer as 1 m/s east for skater 1 and 1 m/s west for skater 2.
steps.proof: Impulse = F·t = 30 N·2 s = 60 Ns; Δv = Impulse/m = 60 Ns / 60 kg = 1 m/s for each skater, moving in opposite directions.
steps.pitfall: Adding the forces together instead of treating them as separate action‑reaction pairs on each skater.

problems.prompt: Two 50 kg skaters push off each other with a 20 N force for 1 s. What is the final speed of each skater?
Two 60 kg ice skaters push off each other with a 30 N force for 2 s. Calculate each skater's final speed.
Two astronauts, masses 80 kg and 120 kg, push apart with a force that increases linearly from 0 to 40 N over 3 s. Assuming the average force is 20 N, find the final speeds of each astronaut.
problems.answer: 0.75 m/s for the 80 kg astronaut and 0.5 m/s for the 120 kg astronaut, opposite directions.
problems.hint: Use the average force to compute impulse, then divide by each mass.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.mastery: Use the law of reflection and plane mirrors.
steps.practice: Draw rays for a light hitting a mirror at 35 degrees to the normal, and locate the image of an object 2 m in front.
steps.detail: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. A plane mirror image sits as far behind as the object is in front.
steps.proof: Reflected at 35 degrees and the image 2 m behind.
steps.pitfall: Measuring angles from the mirror surface instead of the normal.

problems.prompt: Incidence 40 degrees. Reflection?
Object 3 m in front of a mirror. Distance to its image?
Mirror height needed to see your full 1.8 m height?

steps.title: Refraction and Snell Law
steps.mastery: Use n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2.
steps.practice: Find the angle in glass, n = 1.5, for light entering from air at 30 degrees.
steps.detail: Light slows in a denser medium and bends toward the normal. Snell law gives the new angle.
steps.proof: sin theta = 0.333, about 19.5 degrees.
steps.pitfall: Bending the ray away from the normal entering glass.

problems.prompt: Speed of light in glass with n = 1.5?
Light from water, n = 1.33, into air. Toward or away from the normal?
Critical angle for glass with n = 1.5 into air?

steps.title: Lenses
steps.mastery: Use the thin lens equation.
steps.practice: Find the image distance and magnification for an object 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm.
steps.detail: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di. A positive di means a real image on the far side, and m = -di/do gives its size.
steps.proof: di = 15 cm and m = -0.5.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up the sign of the focal length for a diverging lens.

problems.prompt: Object at 20 cm, f = 10 cm. di?
Object at 5 cm, f = 10 cm. di?
Power of a lens with f = 0.5 m?

steps.title: Dispersion and Color
steps.mastery: Explain how a prism splits white light.
steps.practice: Explain in 3 sentences why a prism makes a spectrum and why red bends less than violet.
steps.detail: The refractive index depends on wavelength. Violet at about 400 nm slows and bends more than red at about 700 nm.
steps.proof: 3 sentences on dispersion.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the prism adds color to white light.

problems.prompt: Wavelength of red light, roughly, in nm from 1 to 1000?
Which bends more in glass, 400 nm or 700 nm light?
A rainbow forms from dispersion in what, out of 3 options: dust, rain, wind?

steps.title: Interference and Diffraction
steps.mastery: Use the double slit to measure wavelength.
steps.practice: Find the wavelength when slits 0.1 mm apart give fringes 5 mm apart on a screen 1 m away.
steps.detail: Light through 2 slits forms bright and dark fringes. Fringe spacing = lambda L/d.
steps.proof: lambda = 500 nm.
steps.pitfall: Using the slit width instead of the slit spacing.

problems.prompt: lambda = 600 nm, d = 0.2 mm, L = 2 m. Fringe spacing?
Halve d from 0.2 to 0.1 mm. Fringes get wider or narrower?
Who did the double slit experiment around 1801?

steps.title: Photons
steps.mastery: Compute photon energy with E = hf.
steps.practice: Find the energy of a 500 nm photon with h = 6.63 x 10^-34 and c = 3 x 10^8.
steps.detail: Light comes in lumps of energy hf = hc/lambda. Shorter wavelengths mean more energy per photon.
steps.proof: About 4.0 x 10^-19 J, about 2.5 eV.
steps.pitfall: Using the wavelength in nm without converting to m.

problems.prompt: Energy of a photon at 10^15 Hz?
More energy per photon: 400 nm or 700 nm?
Photons per second from a 1 W beam of 4 x 10^-19 J photons?

steps.title: Photoelectric Effect
steps.mastery: Use KE max = hf - phi for emitted electrons.
steps.practice: Find the max KE of electrons from a metal with work function 2.0 eV under 3.5 eV photons.
steps.detail: Each photon frees at most 1 electron. Below a threshold frequency, no electrons come out however bright the light.
steps.pitfall: Thinking brighter red light can free electrons that blue light frees.

problems.prompt: Work function 4 eV, photon 3 eV. Electrons emitted?
Doubling the intensity at 3.5 eV changes what?
problems.answer: The number of electrons, not their max KE.

problems.prompt: Stopping voltage for a max KE of 1.5 eV?

steps.title: Energy Levels
steps.mastery: Find emitted wavelengths from level differences.
steps.practice: Find the photon energy and wavelength for a hydrogen jump from n = 3 to n = 2, with E = -13.6/n^2 eV.
steps.detail: Atoms emit photons equal to the gap between levels. That is why each element shows a unique line spectrum.
steps.proof: 1.89 eV and about 656 nm, red.
steps.pitfall: Using the energy of a single level instead of the difference.

problems.prompt: E of hydrogen level n = 1?
Energy to ionize hydrogen from n = 1?
Gap from n = 2 to n = 1?

steps.title: Matter Waves
steps.mastery: Use the de Broglie wavelength.
steps.practice: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron at 10^6 m/s and of a 0.15 kg ball at 40 m/s.
steps.detail: Every particle has lambda = h/p. For everyday objects it is far too small to notice.
steps.pitfall: Thinking only light has a wavelength.

problems.prompt: Momentum giving lambda = 6.63 x 10^-10 m?
Double the speed from 10^6 m/s. lambda factor?
Experiment showing electron waves in 1927, by Davisson and Germer?

steps.title: Uncertainty and Probability
steps.mastery: Use the uncertainty principle and probability amplitudes.
steps.practice: Estimate the minimum momentum uncertainty for an electron confined to 10^-10 m using delta x delta p >= h/(4 pi).
steps.detail: Position and momentum cannot both be sharp. Quantum outcomes are probabilities given by squared amplitudes.
steps.proof: About 5.3 x 10^-25 kg m/s.
steps.pitfall: Blaming the uncertainty on bad instruments.

problems.prompt: Amplitude 0.6 for 1 outcome. Probability?
Halve delta x from 2 to 1 nm. Minimum delta p factor?
h/(4 pi) to 2 figures?

steps.title: The 2 Postulates
steps.mastery: State the postulates of special relativity.
steps.practice: Write the 2 postulates of Einstein 1905 theory and explain why a 0.5c spaceship still measures light at c.
steps.detail: Physics is the same in every inertial frame, and light always moves at c. Everything else follows from these 2 ideas.
steps.proof: 2 postulates and 1 explanation.
steps.pitfall: Adding velocities to get light faster than c.

problems.prompt: Speed of light measured from a ship at 0.9c?
Year Einstein published special relativity, in the 1900s?
Is a frame accelerating at 2 m/s^2 inertial?

steps.title: Time Dilation
steps.mastery: Use the Lorentz factor gamma.
steps.practice: Compute gamma at 0.6c and 0.8c, and the time a 10 year trip at 0.8c takes on board.
steps.detail: gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2). Moving clocks run slow by this factor, as seen from the ground.
steps.proof: 1.25, 1.67 and 6 years.
steps.pitfall: Applying gamma to the wrong frame.

problems.prompt: gamma at 0.6c?
A muon lives 2.2 microseconds at rest. Lifetime at gamma = 10?
gamma at 0.99c, roughly?

steps.title: Length Contraction
steps.mastery: Find contracted lengths along the motion.
steps.practice: Find the length of a 100 m ship moving at 0.8c, as measured from the ground.
steps.detail: Lengths along the motion shrink by gamma. Distances across the motion do not change.
steps.pitfall: Contracting lengths perpendicular to motion.

problems.prompt: Ship 50 m at gamma = 2. Measured length?
Width of a 10 m wide ship at 0.8c?
Distance 4 light years shrinks to what at 0.6c?

steps.title: Mass and Energy
steps.mastery: Use E = mc^2 to trade mass for energy in relativity.
steps.practice: Find the energy in 1 g of mass and the mass lost when 3.2 x 10^-11 J is released in fusion.
steps.detail: Mass and energy are interchangeable. Tiny mass changes in nuclei release large energy.
steps.proof: 9 x 10^13 J and about 3.6 x 10^-28 kg.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to square c.

problems.prompt: E for 1 kg?
Rest energy of an electron, 9.1 x 10^-31 kg, in J?
Mass for 9 x 10^10 J?

steps.title: Simultaneity and Spacetime
steps.mastery: Show that simultaneity depends on the observer.
steps.practice: Explain with the train and 2 lightning flashes why events at the same time for 1 observer are not for another.
steps.detail: Light from both ends takes equal time only in the frame where the flashes are equal distances away. A moving observer sees 1 first.
steps.proof: A labeled sketch with a 3 sentence explanation.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the disagreement is just a signal delay.

problems.prompt: Spacetime interval for 5 s and 3 light seconds?
Can 2 observers in relative motion at 0.5c agree on the speed of light?
Can cause and effect swap order for events 1 s apart at the same place?

steps.title: Angular Quantities
steps.mastery: Convert between linear and angular motion.
steps.practice: Convert 3000 rpm to rad/s and find the speed of a point 0.2 m from the axis.
steps.detail: Angles are measured in radians. v = r omega links a point speed to the spin rate.
steps.proof: About 314 rad/s and 62.8 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Using degrees in v = r omega.

problems.prompt: Radians in 1 full turn?
omega for 60 rpm?
v at r = 0.5 m and omega = 4 rad/s?

steps.title: Torque
steps.mastery: Compute torque as force times lever arm.
steps.practice: Find the torque from 20 N on a 0.3 m wrench at 90 degrees and at 30 degrees to the handle.
steps.detail: Torque = r F sin theta. A longer handle or a more perpendicular push gives more turning effect.
steps.proof: 6 N m and 3 N m.
steps.pitfall: Using the full length when the force is at an angle.

problems.prompt: Torque of 10 N at 0.5 m, perpendicular?
Torque when the force points straight along a 0.4 m wrench?
Force needed for 12 N m on a 0.3 m wrench?

steps.title: Balance a Seesaw
steps.mastery: Use the balance of torques for equilibrium.
steps.practice: Find where a 30 kg child must sit to balance a 45 kg adult sitting 1.0 m from the pivot.
steps.detail: In balance the clockwise torques equal the counterclockwise torques. Heavier people sit closer to the pivot.
steps.proof: 1.5 m from the pivot.
steps.pitfall: Balancing forces instead of torques.

problems.prompt: 20 kg at 2 m balances what mass at 1 m?
A 100 N weight at 0.6 m needs what force at 1.2 m?
Sum of torques on a balanced 4 m beam?

steps.title: Moment of Inertia
steps.mastery: Use I to describe resistance to spinning.
steps.practice: Compute I for a 2 kg point mass at 0.5 m and compare a hoop and a solid disc of 2 kg and radius 0.5 m.
steps.detail: I = sum of mr^2. Mass far from the axis makes something harder to spin up, so a hoop has twice the I of a disc.
steps.pitfall: Using mass alone and ignoring how it is spread.

problems.prompt: I of a 3 kg point at 2 m?
Solid disc, 4 kg, radius 1 m. I = 1/2 MR^2?
Which rolls down a 30 degree ramp faster, a hoop or a solid disc?

steps.title: Angular Momentum
steps.mastery: Use conservation of L = I omega.
steps.practice: Find a skater spin rate when I drops from 4 to 1 kg m^2 starting at 2 rad/s.
steps.detail: With no outside torque, I omega stays fixed. Pulling arms in shrinks I, so the spin speeds up.
steps.proof: 8 rad/s.
steps.pitfall: Assuming kinetic energy is also conserved here.

problems.prompt: L for I = 3 kg m^2 and omega = 5 rad/s?
I doubles from 2 to 4 kg m^2. New omega from 6 rad/s?
KE before and after for the skater going from I = 4 to 1 kg m^2?

steps.title: Speed of Sound
steps.mastery: Use sound speed to find distances.
steps.practice: Find the distance to a cliff when an echo returns 2 s after a shout, with sound at 340 m/s.
steps.detail: Sound goes there and back, so halve the total distance. Speed depends on the medium and temperature.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to halve the echo path.

problems.prompt: Thunder 3 s after lightning. Distance?
Sound in water at 1500 m/s takes 0.2 s each way. Depth?
Is sound faster in steel or in 20 degrees C air?

steps.title: Pitch and Loudness
steps.mastery: Link pitch to frequency and loudness to intensity.
steps.practice: Compute the intensity ratio for a rise from 60 dB to 80 dB.
steps.detail: Pitch follows frequency. Loudness uses decibels, where each 10 dB is a factor of 10 in intensity.
steps.proof: A factor of 100.
steps.pitfall: Thinking 80 dB is only a third louder than 60 dB.

problems.prompt: Intensity factor for +10 dB?
Intensity factor for +30 dB?
Range of human hearing for a 20 year old, roughly, in Hz?

steps.title: Doppler Effect
steps.mastery: Predict the pitch shift from a moving source.
steps.practice: Find the heard frequency of a 500 Hz siren moving toward you at 20 m/s, with sound at 340 m/s.
steps.detail: A source moving toward you squashes the waves, raising the pitch. f heard = f v/(v - vs).
steps.proof: About 531 Hz.
steps.pitfall: Using a plus sign for an approaching source.

problems.prompt: Same siren moving away at 20 m/s. Heard f?
Does a stationary 500 Hz source sound shifted?
Pitch rises or falls as a car passes at 30 m/s?

steps.title: Pipes and Resonance
steps.mastery: Find resonant frequencies of open and closed pipes.
steps.practice: Work out the lowest 2 notes of a 0.85 m flute style tube open at both ends and the same tube capped at 1 end, with v = 340 m/s.
steps.detail: Air in a pipe vibrates at set notes. Open pipes use f = nv/2L, and closed pipes have only odd harmonics with f = nv/4L.
steps.proof: Open: 200 and 400 Hz. Closed: 100 and 300 Hz.
steps.pitfall: Including even harmonics for a closed pipe.

problems.prompt: Fundamental of a 0.5 m open pipe at 340 m/s?
Fundamental of a 0.5 m closed pipe?
Next harmonic of a closed pipe after 170 Hz?

steps.title: Beats and Resonance
steps.mastery: Use beats to tune and resonance to explain shattering glass.
steps.practice: Find the beat frequency of 440 and 444 Hz notes, and explain how a singer can break a glass at 900 Hz.
steps.detail: Two close notes beat at the difference frequency. Driving at a natural frequency builds large vibrations.
steps.proof: 4 beats per second, and resonance explained.
steps.pitfall: Thinking volume alone breaks the glass.

problems.prompt: Beats from 256 and 260 Hz?
A string at 438 Hz beats 2 times a second with 440 Hz. Fix?
problems.answer: Tighten it to raise the pitch.

problems.prompt: Why did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge fail in 1940?

steps.title: Temperature and Scales
steps.mastery: Convert between Celsius, kelvin and Fahrenheit.
steps.practice: Convert 25 degrees C to kelvin and Fahrenheit, and 98.6 F to Celsius.
steps.detail: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, so K = C + 273. Fahrenheit uses F = 9/5 C + 32 instead.
steps.proof: 298 K, 77 F and 37 degrees C.
steps.pitfall: Adding 273 for a temperature change.

problems.prompt: 0 degrees C in K?
100 degrees C in F?
A change of 10 degrees C is how many kelvin?

steps.title: Specific Heat
steps.mastery: Use Q = mc delta T for heating.
steps.practice: Find the heat to warm 2 kg of water from 20 to 80 degrees C with c = 4200 J/kg K.
steps.detail: Some materials need more energy per degree than others. Water has a high specific heat, which is why oceans change temperature slowly.
steps.pitfall: Using grams with a per kilogram value of c.

problems.prompt: Q for 1 kg of water warming 10 K?
Same Q into 1 kg of Cu with c = 385. Temperature rise?
Which heats faster under 1000 W, 1 kg of water or 1 kg of Al?

steps.title: Latent Heat
steps.mastery: Compute energy for changes of state.
steps.practice: Find the energy to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 degrees C with L = 334,000 J/kg, then warm it to 20 degrees C.
steps.detail: Q = mL for a change of state with no temperature change. Add mc delta T for each warming stage.
steps.pitfall: Adding a temperature change during melting.

problems.prompt: Energy to boil 1 kg of water at 100 degrees C, L = 2.26 x 10^6?
Energy to freeze 2 kg of water, L = 334,000?
Why does steam at 100 degrees C burn worse than water at 100?
problems.answer: It releases latent heat as it condenses.

steps.title: Heat Transfer
steps.mastery: Tell conduction, convection and radiation apart.
steps.practice: Name the main transfer in 4 cases: a metal spoon in soup, a room heater, sunlight and a boiling pot of 2 L.
