steps.practice: Find the probability of rolling an even number, a number above 4 and a 7 on 1 die.
steps.detail: When outcomes are equally likely, probability is favorable over total. It always lies between 0 and 1.
steps.pitfall: Giving a probability above 1 or below 0.

problems.prompt: Probability of heads on 1 fair coin?
Probability of a heart from a 52 card deck?
Probability of a 3 on a 6 sided die?

steps.title: Complement Rule
steps.mastery: Use P(not A) = 1 - P(A) to skip long counts.
steps.practice: Work out P(no 6) on a single die roll and P(at least 1 head) over 3 tosses of a coin.
steps.detail: Sometimes the opposite event is easier to count. At least one is the classic case for the complement.
steps.pitfall: Listing every case of at least one by hand.

problems.prompt: P(rain) = 0.3. P(no rain)?
P(at least 1 six in 2 rolls)?
P(at least 1 girl in 4 children) if each is 1/2?

steps.title: Addition Rule
steps.mastery: Add probabilities and subtract the overlap.
steps.practice: Find P(heart or king) for 1 card from a 52 card deck.
steps.detail: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Without subtracting, the king of hearts is counted twice.
steps.pitfall: Adding probabilities of events that overlap without subtracting.

problems.prompt: Can P(A or B) be 1.3 for 2 events?
Mutually exclusive A and B with P = 0.3 and 0.25. P(A or B)?

steps.title: Multiplication Rule
steps.mastery: Multiply probabilities of independent events.
steps.practice: Find the probability of 3 heads in 3 flips and of rolling a 6 then a 5.
steps.detail: When one event does not affect the other, the chances multiply. If it does, use the conditional chance for the second event.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying probabilities of events that depend on each other.

problems.prompt: P(2 heads in 2 flips)?
P(drawing 2 aces without replacement from 52 cards)?
A part fails 1% of the time. P(3 independent parts all work)?

steps.title: Simulate to Check
steps.mastery: Estimate a probability by running many trials.
steps.practice: Simulate 1000 rolls of 2 dice in a spreadsheet or Python and estimate P(sum = 7), then compare with 1/6.
steps.detail: Simulation checks your reasoning and handles problems that are hard to count. More trials give closer estimates.
steps.proof: An estimate near 0.167.
steps.pitfall: Trusting a simulation of only 20 trials.

problems.prompt: Exact P(sum = 7) with 2 dice?
You get 0.171 from 1000 trials. Close enough?
How does the error shrink when trials go from 100 to 10,000?

steps.title: Fit a Least Squares Line
steps.mastery: Find slope and intercept of the best fit line.
steps.detail: The slope is r times sy/sx and the line passes through (x bar, y bar). Least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals.
steps.pitfall: Swapping x and y and getting a different line.

problems.prompt: Mean of x for 1 to 5?
Mean of y for 2, 4, 5, 4, 5?
Predict y at x = 6 for y = 2.2 + 0.6x.

steps.title: Interpret Slope and Intercept
steps.mastery: Explain the slope and intercept in context with units.
steps.practice: Interpret the slope and intercept of price = 50,000 + 200 x size in square feet.
steps.detail: The slope is the predicted change per unit of x, here $200 per square foot. The intercept may not be meaningful if x = 0 is unrealistic.
steps.proof: $200 more per square foot, and a $50,000 intercept that is not a real house.
steps.pitfall: Interpreting an intercept outside the data range.

problems.prompt: Slope 3.5 points per hour of study. Predicted gain for 2 hours?
Is a house with 0 square feet in the data?
problems.answer: No, so the intercept is just a starting point.

problems.prompt: Slope -0.4 kg per week. Direction?

steps.title: Check Residuals
steps.mastery: Use a residual plot to judge a linear fit.
steps.practice: Plot residuals for the 5 point fit and describe any pattern.
steps.detail: Random scatter supports a line. A curve or a funnel in residuals means the model misses something.
steps.proof: A residual plot with a 1 sentence verdict.
steps.pitfall: Trusting r^2 without looking at residuals.

problems.prompt: Residual for (2, 4) with y = 2.2 + 0.6x?
Residuals form a U shape. What does that mean?
Residuals spread wider as x grows. Problem?

steps.title: Correlation and Outliers
steps.mastery: See how a single point can change a regression line.
steps.practice: Add 1 point at (20, 0) to the 5 point data and refit, comparing the slope and r.
steps.detail: A point far out in x has high leverage and can flip the slope. Always plot before trusting the numbers.
steps.proof: The slope turns negative with the new point.
steps.pitfall: Reporting a fit without plotting the data.

problems.prompt: A point at x = 20 when the rest sit at 1 to 5. High or low leverage?
Can 1 point change r from 0.7 to -0.2?
What should you do with an influential point among 50?
problems.answer: Check it, and report results with and without it.

steps.title: Prediction Limits
steps.mastery: Know when predictions from a line are unreliable.
steps.practice: Use a model fit on ages 10 to 18 to predict height at age 40, and explain the problem in 2 sentences.
steps.detail: Extrapolating beyond the data assumes the pattern continues, which often fails. Growth stops around 18.
steps.proof: 2 sentences on why the age 40 prediction is wrong.
steps.pitfall: Extrapolating a trend far beyond the data.

problems.prompt: Data covers x from 10 to 18. Is x = 15 interpolation or extrapolation?
Is x = 40 interpolation or extrapolation?
A trend of +5 cm per year from age 10 predicts what at 40?
problems.answer: An impossible height, which shows the risk.

steps.title: Population and Sample
steps.mastery: Tell the group you care about from the part you measure.
steps.practice: Name the population, sample, parameter and statistic for a poll of 500 voters about a 1 million voter city.
steps.detail: A parameter describes the whole population and a statistic describes the sample. We use statistics to estimate parameters.
steps.proof: Population: 1 million voters. Sample: 500. Parameter: city wide support. Statistic: sample support.
steps.pitfall: Calling a sample result a fact about the whole population.

problems.prompt: Average height of all 2000 students is a parameter or statistic?
Average height of 50 measured students?
Sample size for a poll of 1200 adults?

steps.title: Random Sampling
steps.mastery: Draw a simple random sample so every unit has an equal chance.
steps.practice: Pick a simple random sample of 10 students from a list of 300 with a random number generator.
steps.detail: Randomness removes the chooser bias. Every possible sample of 10 is equally likely.
steps.proof: 10 student numbers chosen at random with the method recorded.
steps.pitfall: Choosing the first 10 names on the list.

problems.prompt: Chance a given student is chosen in a sample of 10 from 300?
Is picking the 10 tallest students random?
Name a tool to pick 10 random numbers from 1 to 300.
problems.answer: A random number generator, like RANDBETWEEN in a spreadsheet.

steps.title: Stratified and Cluster
steps.mastery: Use strata or clusters when a simple random sample is hard or uneven.
steps.practice: Design a stratified sample of 60 students from 4 grades of different sizes, with each grade in proportion.
steps.detail: Stratified sampling guarantees each group is represented. Cluster sampling picks whole groups to save effort but can add variation.
steps.proof: A plan with the number from each grade.
steps.pitfall: Confusing strata, where you sample within every group, with clusters, where you sample whole groups.

problems.prompt: Grades of 300, 200, 100, 100 and a sample of 70. How many from the 300?
Sampling 5 whole classrooms out of 40 is which design?
Why stratify by grade for 1 survey?
problems.answer: To make sure each grade is fairly represented.

steps.title: Sampling Bias
steps.mastery: Spot designs that systematically miss part of the population.
steps.practice: Name the bias in 3 cases: an online poll, a survey at a gym about exercise and a phone poll of landlines only.
steps.detail: Voluntary response, undercoverage and convenience samples all produce biased results that more data cannot fix.
steps.proof: Voluntary response, convenience and undercoverage.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a bigger biased sample fixes the bias.

problems.prompt: A poll of 100,000 volunteers vs 1000 random people. Which is more trustworthy?
A survey asks only people at a library about reading. Bias?
Leading question "Don't you agree 3 hours of homework is too much?" Bias?

steps.title: Sample Size and Precision
steps.mastery: See how a larger random sample narrows uncertainty.
steps.practice: Compute the margin of error for a poll proportion of 0.5 with n = 100 and n = 400.
steps.detail: The margin shrinks with the square root of n. Quadrupling the sample halves the margin.
steps.proof: About 0.098 and 0.049.
steps.pitfall: Expecting doubling the sample to halve the margin.

problems.prompt: Margin of error formula for 95% and p = 0.5?
n needed for a 3% margin with p = 0.5?
Going from n = 400 to 1600 does what to the margin?

steps.title: State the Hypotheses
steps.mastery: Write a null and alternative hypothesis about a parameter.
steps.practice: Write H0 and Ha for testing whether a coin is fair after 60 heads in 100 flips.
steps.detail: The null says nothing is going on, like p = 0.5. The alternative says what you suspect, like p is not 0.5.
steps.proof: H0: p = 0.5 and Ha: p is not 0.5.
steps.pitfall: Writing hypotheses about the sample statistic instead of the parameter.

problems.prompt: Write H0 for a new drug with mean effect mu.
One sided alternative for "more than 50%"?
Is "p hat = 0.6" a valid hypothesis?
problems.answer: No, hypotheses are about the parameter p.

steps.title: Compute a p-Value
steps.mastery: Find how surprising the data would be if the null were true.
steps.practice: Compute the z statistic and 2 sided p-value for 60 heads in 100 flips of a fair coin.
steps.detail: z = (0.6 - 0.5)/0.05 = 2. The p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if the coin is fair.
steps.proof: z = 2, p-value about 0.046.
steps.pitfall: Calling the p-value the chance the null is true.

problems.prompt: Standard error of p hat for p = 0.5, n = 100?
1 sided p-value for z = 2?
z = 0.5. Is that surprising at the 0.05 level?

steps.title: Make a Decision
steps.mastery: Compare the p-value with alpha and state a conclusion in context.
steps.practice: Write a conclusion for p = 0.046 at alpha = 0.05 and at alpha = 0.01 in context.
steps.detail: Below alpha we reject the null. We never prove the null true, we only fail to reject it.
steps.proof: Reject at 0.05, fail to reject at 0.01, both said about the coin.
steps.pitfall: Saying "accept the null" or "prove the alternative".

problems.prompt: p = 0.03 and alpha = 0.05. Decision?
p = 0.20 and alpha = 0.05. Decision?
Does failing to reject prove the coin is fair over 100 flips?

steps.title: Tests for Means
steps.mastery: Run a 1 sample t test on a mean.
steps.practice: Test whether average sleep is 8 hours when 25 students average 7.4 with s = 1.5.
steps.detail: t = (7.4 - 8)/(1.5/5) = -2 with 24 df. The p-value is around 0.057 two sided, so not quite significant at 0.05.
steps.proof: t = -2, p about 0.057.
steps.pitfall: Using the population SD formula with a small sample.

problems.prompt: Standard error for s = 1.5, n = 25?
df for n = 25?
t = -2 with a 1 sided Ha: mu < 8. p-value roughly?

steps.title: Two Sample Tests
steps.mastery: Compare 2 groups with a test.
steps.practice: Test whether 2 teaching methods differ when 40 students each score means 78 and 74 with SDs 8 and 9.
steps.detail: The test statistic is the difference over its standard error, sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2). Random assignment makes a difference meaningful.
steps.proof: SE about 1.90, t about 2.1, p about 0.04.
steps.pitfall: Running 2 separate 1 sample tests instead of 1 comparison.

problems.prompt: SE for SDs 8 and 9 with 40 each?
Difference of means 78 and 74?
Paired data, the same 20 students before and after. Which test?
problems.answer: A paired t test on the differences.

steps.title: Clear the Interruptions
steps.mastery: Remove the things that will break a long block before it starts.
steps.practice: List the 5 things most likely to interrupt a 90-minute block and remove or defer each one now.
steps.detail: Do this before the block, not during: a phone face-down within reach is still a decision you make 40 times. Deal with the 5 by removing them from the room, silencing them, or telling somebody you are unavailable until a stated time. Anything you cannot remove gets a written note saying when you will handle it.
steps.proof: All 5 are removed, silenced or deferred in writing before the block begins.
steps.pitfall: Starting the block with the intention of ignoring 2 of them, which spends the block resisting instead of working.

problems.prompt: You cannot remove 1 of your 5 interruptions before a 90-minute block. What do you do with it?
problems.answer: Write down when you will handle it, so it stops competing during the block.

problems.prompt: Is a silenced phone left on the desk during a 90-minute block removed or deferred?
problems.answer: Neither, it is still 1 decision made repeatedly, so it leaves the room.

problems.prompt: Why deal with all 5 before the block rather than as they arrive?
problems.answer: Each one handled mid-block costs the state the block exists to build.

steps.title: One Difficult Thing
steps.mastery: Commit a whole block to a single hard piece of work.
steps.practice: Name the 1 difficult task a 90-minute block will hold, in 1 sentence, before starting.
steps.detail: A block with 3 tasks in it becomes a block of switching, and hard material needs the time that switching eats. Write the single task on the page where you can see it. If it turns out to be 4 tasks, that is a planning result worth having, and the block still runs on the first of them.
steps.proof: 1 written task, and the block's output is work on that task alone.
steps.pitfall: Sliding into email or an easier topic at the first hard point, which is the exact moment the block is earning.

problems.prompt: Your 90-minute block lists 3 tasks. What happens to the other 2?
problems.answer: They move out, the block runs on 1 task, and the others are scheduled separately.

problems.prompt: You hit a hard point 25 minutes in and want to switch to an easier topic. What is the instruction?
problems.answer: Stay, that point is where the block is doing its work.

problems.prompt: Why does hard material need a 90-minute block rather than 3 blocks of 30?
problems.answer: Getting back into difficult work costs time that short blocks spend repeatedly.

steps.title: Work in Timed Blocks
steps.mastery: Run a fixed block and stop when it ends rather than when you flag.
steps.practice: Run 2 blocks of 45 minutes with 1 break of 10, and record the finish time of each.
steps.detail: A fixed end makes the difficulty bearable and stops the block drifting into an hour of low-quality sitting. Set a timer out of sight. When it goes, stop mid-sentence if necessary, because stopping mid-thought makes the restart easier than stopping at a tidy boundary.
steps.proof: 2 recorded finish times, and the break taken between them was 10 minutes rather than 25.
steps.pitfall: Running 1 long block of 2 hours, where the last 40 minutes are sitting rather than working.

problems.prompt: You plan 2 blocks of 45 with a 10-minute break. What is the total elapsed time?
The timer goes mid-sentence. Finish the paragraph or stop?
problems.answer: Stop, an unfinished thought makes the next restart faster.

problems.prompt: Why is 1 block of 120 minutes usually worse than 2 of 45?
problems.answer: The tail of a long block is sitting rather than working, and it pushes out the break that would restore attention.

steps.title: Keep a Distraction Sheet
steps.mastery: Park an intruding thought in writing instead of acting on it.
steps.practice: Keep 1 sheet beside you for a 45-minute block and write down each intruding thought in under 5 words.
steps.detail: The thought arrives whether you want it or not; the choice is whether you leave the work. Five words is enough to release it, "check train times", and the sheet gets dealt with in the break. Count the entries: a block with 14 of them is telling you something about what needs sorting out before the next one.
steps.proof: A sheet of parked thoughts, none of which were acted on during the block.
steps.pitfall: Handling the small ones because they take 30 seconds, which is 30 seconds plus the way back.

problems.prompt: A thought arrives that would take 30 seconds to handle. Handle it or park it?
problems.answer: Park it, the cost is the 30 seconds plus getting back into the work.

problems.prompt: Your sheet holds 14 entries after 45 minutes. What does that number say?
problems.answer: That something outside the work needs sorting out before the next block.

problems.prompt: Why a 5-word limit on each entry?
problems.answer: Enough to let the thought go, short enough not to become the work.

steps.title: Mark Where You Stopped
steps.mastery: Leave a block with a note that makes the next one start fast.
steps.practice: End 1 block by writing 3 lines: where you stopped, what you were about to try, and the first action next time.
steps.detail: The expensive part of a block is the first 10 minutes, and this is what removes them. Write it while the work is still in your head, a note written the next morning is a guess. "Stuck on the sign in line 4; next try the substitution u = x - 1" is worth more than a page of summary.
steps.proof: 3 lines, ending with a named first action for the next block.
steps.pitfall: Writing "carry on where I left off", which is the note you will not be able to use.

problems.prompt: Which hand-off is usable: (a) "continue chapter 4", (b) "stuck on the sign in line 4; next try u = x - 1"?
problems.answer: (b). It names the exact next action.

problems.prompt: Why write the 3 lines at the end of the block rather than at the start of the next one?
problems.answer: The detail is still in your head; a day later it is reconstruction.

problems.prompt: What does a good hand-off save at the start of the next 45-minute block?
problems.answer: The first 10 minutes otherwise spent working out where you were.

steps.title: Protect the Same Hours
steps.mastery: Run deep blocks at a fixed time so they stop needing a decision.
steps.practice: Fix 2 deep blocks in the same 2 slots every week and defend them for 3 weeks.
steps.detail: A block scheduled by mood happens about half as often as one that is simply when you work. Pick 2 slots that are realistically yours, and treat everything else as negotiable around them. Record kept or missed for 3 weeks: below 4 out of 6, the slots are wrong rather than your discipline.
steps.proof: A 3-week record of the 2 weekly slots, marked kept or missed.
steps.pitfall: Choosing 2 slots you wish were free, which produces a record of misses and nothing else.

problems.prompt: Over 3 weeks you keep 3 of 6 fixed blocks. Is the problem the slots or the discipline?
problems.answer: The slots, below 4 of 6 usually means they were never realistically free.

problems.prompt: Why does a fixed weekly slot beat deciding each of the 7 days when to work?
problems.answer: It removes the decision, and a block left to mood happens roughly half as often.

problems.prompt: What are the 2 numbers this step asks you to record?
problems.answer: Blocks kept and blocks missed, over 3 weeks.

steps.title: Build Up the Length
steps.mastery: Extend block length gradually rather than attempting 3 hours cold.
steps.practice: Add 10 minutes a week to your longest block, starting from 45 and stopping at 90.
steps.detail: Long concentration is trained, not decided: an untrained 3-hour attempt produces 40 good minutes and the belief that you cannot do it. Add 10 minutes only after a full week of the current length held. If a week breaks down, repeat it rather than adding.
steps.proof: A weekly record showing 45, 55, 65 and so on, with each length held before the next was added.
steps.pitfall: Jumping from 45 to 120 in 1 week, which fails and teaches the wrong lesson.

problems.prompt: Starting at 45 minutes and adding 10 a week, how long until you reach 85?
A week at 65 minutes breaks down twice. Add 10 or repeat 65?
Why does an untrained 3-hour attempt teach the wrong lesson?
problems.answer: It produces about 40 useful minutes and the conclusion that long blocks are impossible.

steps.title: Judge the Block by Output
steps.mastery: Score a block on what it produced rather than how long it lasted.
steps.practice: Write 1 line of output for each of 3 blocks, problems solved, pages drafted, derivation finished, and compare.
steps.detail: Time at the desk is the input and is easy to mistake for the result. Recording output makes a 90-minute block that produced 2 solved problems visible next to a 45-minute one that produced 6. Where the long blocks produce less, the problem is usually the interruption sheet or the time of day.
steps.proof: 3 blocks with their outputs written down and compared.
steps.pitfall: Recording hours studied, which rewards sitting still.

problems.prompt: Block A ran 90 minutes and solved 2 problems; block B ran 45 and solved 6. Which was the better block?
problems.answer: B, the output is 3 times the rate.

problems.prompt: Why record output rather than the 90 minutes spent at the desk?
problems.answer: Hours reward sitting still; output shows whether the block worked.

problems.prompt: Your 90-minute blocks consistently produce less per minute than your 45s. Name 2 likely causes.
problems.answer: Interruptions during the long block, or running it at the wrong time of day.

steps.title: Read the Question Twice
steps.mastery: Establish what a question asks before writing anything.
steps.practice: Take 5 exam questions and underline the command word and the 2 constraints in each.
steps.detail: Command words are instructions: describe, explain, evaluate and calculate want different answers, and answering the wrong one scores near zero however good the content. Underline the command word, then the constraints, a date range, a named case, a unit, before any working starts.
steps.proof: 5 questions with the command word and constraints underlined.
steps.pitfall: Starting to write at the first familiar noun in the question, which is how a good answer to the wrong question happens.

problems.prompt: What is the difference between "describe" and "explain" in a 6-mark question?
problems.answer: Describe wants what happens; explain wants why it happens.

problems.prompt: A question says "evaluate, with reference to 2 examples". Name the 2 things that must appear.
problems.answer: A judgment, and 2 named examples supporting it.

problems.prompt: Why underline the 2 constraints before starting the working?
problems.answer: A correct answer outside the stated constraints scores little or nothing.

steps.title: Allocate Time by Marks
steps.mastery: Spend time on a question in proportion to what it is worth.
steps.practice: For a 90-minute paper worth 75 marks, work out the minutes per mark and the time for a 12-mark question.
steps.detail: Divide time by marks to get the rate, then multiply per question, and leave 10 per cent for reading and checking. Write the finish time beside each question on the paper before starting, so falling behind is visible at question 3 rather than at question 8.
steps.proof: A rate in minutes per mark and a written finish time beside each question.
steps.pitfall: Spending 25 minutes on a 4-mark question because it is interesting, which costs a whole later question.

problems.prompt: A 90-minute paper carries 75 marks. What is the rate in minutes per mark?
At 1.2 minutes per mark, how long does a 12-mark question get?
Why write finish times on the paper before starting question 1?
problems.answer: Falling behind becomes visible early, while there is still time to correct it.

steps.title: Answer What Is Asked
steps.mastery: Keep an answer inside the question rather than writing everything known.
steps.practice: Take 1 answer you wrote and cross out every sentence that the question did not ask for.
steps.detail: Extra content earns nothing and costs the time a later question needed. Read your answer against the command word and constraints: anything outside them goes. If half the answer disappears, that is time you can move to the questions you did not finish.
steps.proof: 1 marked-up answer where the crossings-out are all outside the question.
steps.pitfall: Writing everything you know on the topic in the hope that some of it earns credit.

problems.prompt: A 4-mark question gets 12 sentences from you. What is likely true?
problems.answer: Most of it is outside what was asked, and the time belonged to another question.

problems.prompt: Does extra correct content beyond a 4-mark question earn marks?
problems.answer: No, it earns nothing and costs time.

problems.prompt: You cross out half of 1 answer. What do you do with the time that represents?
problems.answer: Move it to the questions you did not finish.

steps.title: Show the Working
steps.mastery: Write the intermediate steps that method marks are given for.
steps.practice: Redo 3 problems writing every intermediate line, and count the marks a scheme would give for method alone.
steps.detail: A correct answer with no working scores the answer mark and loses the method ones; a wrong answer with full working keeps most of them. Write the formula, the substitution and the rearrangement as separate lines. This also makes a slip findable, which a page of mental arithmetic never is.
steps.proof: 3 problems with every line written, and a count of the method marks available.
steps.pitfall: Doing 2 steps in your head to save time, which loses both the marks and the chance to find the error.

problems.prompt: A wrong final answer with full working on a 5-mark question. Roughly what is kept?
problems.answer: Most of the method marks, often 3 or 4 of the 5.

problems.prompt: A right answer with no working on a 5-mark question. What is lost?
problems.answer: The method marks, keeping only the accuracy mark.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 lines worth writing separately in a calculation.
problems.answer: The formula, the substitution, and the rearrangement.

steps.title: Attempt Every Question
steps.mastery: Leave nothing blank, including what you cannot finish.
steps.practice: On a past paper, write at least 2 lines on every question including the 3 you cannot do.
steps.detail: A blank scores 0 with certainty; a stated formula and an attempt at substitution often scores 1 or 2. Go through at the end and put something on every blank, the definition, the relevant equation, or the first step. On a 75-mark paper this is routinely worth 5 marks.
steps.proof: No blank questions on the paper, and a count of marks the partial attempts earned.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the last question blank because time ran out, when 90 seconds of formula and substitution was available.

problems.prompt: 3 blanks on a paper, each worth 5 marks. What is the certain score for them?
What can 90 seconds on an unfinished question usually earn?
problems.answer: 1 or 2 method marks for the formula and a substitution.

problems.prompt: When in a 90-minute paper do you fill the blanks?
problems.answer: At the end, after every question you can do is done.

steps.title: Check in the Last Ten
steps.mastery: Use reserved time to check rather than to keep writing.
steps.practice: Reserve the last 10 minutes of a 90-minute paper and use them on units, signs and unanswered parts.
steps.detail: Check in a fixed order so nothing is missed: unanswered parts first, then final answers for units, then signs and magnitudes. Rereading prose for style is the least valuable use of the 10 minutes and the most tempting. Mark each question as checked so the pass is trackable.
steps.proof: A paper with every question marked checked, and the 3 kinds of error looked for.
steps.pitfall: Using the last 10 minutes to extend an answer that was already complete.

problems.prompt: In what order do you use the reserved 10 minutes?
problems.answer: Unanswered parts, then units on final answers, then signs and magnitudes.

problems.prompt: Is extending a complete 8-mark answer a good use of the last 10 minutes?
problems.answer: No, unanswered parts and unit checks are worth more.

problems.prompt: Why mark each question as checked during the 10-minute pass?
problems.answer: So the pass is trackable and no question is checked twice while another is missed.

steps.title: Plan the Long Answer
steps.mastery: Sketch the structure of an extended answer before writing it.
steps.practice: Plan a 16-mark essay answer in 4 bullet points and 1 line naming your conclusion, in 3 minutes.
steps.detail: Three minutes of planning buys a structure the marker can follow and stops the answer arriving at a conclusion it never argued for. Four bullets and a stated conclusion is enough; the plan is not marked, so it is written in note form and crossed out at the end if the paper asks.
steps.proof: 4 bullets and a named conclusion, written in 3 minutes before the answer.
steps.pitfall: Planning for 10 of the 20 minutes, which leaves an excellent plan and half an answer.

problems.prompt: A 16-mark answer has about 20 minutes. How long does the plan get?
What does the plan contain besides the 4 bullets?
problems.answer: One line naming the conclusion the answer will reach.

problems.prompt: Why does an unplanned 16-mark answer often reach an unargued conclusion?
problems.answer: The structure is being invented while writing, so the ending does not follow from the middle.

steps.title: Debrief the Paper
steps.mastery: Convert a completed paper into a list of specific fixes.
steps.practice: After marking a paper, write 3 fixes naming the question, the loss and the change.
steps.detail: "Do better on trigonometry" is not a fix. "Question 6: lost 3 marks for no units on final answers, add a unit check to the last 10 minutes" is. Three is enough to actually carry into the next paper, and they get checked against that paper's debrief.
steps.proof: 3 fixes, each naming a question, a loss and a change.
steps.pitfall: Writing a list of 12 fixes, none of which gets carried into the next paper.

problems.prompt: Turn "lost 3 marks on units" into a fix.
problems.answer: Add a unit check on every final answer to the reserved 10 minutes.

problems.prompt: Why cap the list at 3 fixes rather than 12?
problems.answer: 3 can be carried into the next paper; 12 cannot.

problems.prompt: What are the 3 parts of a usable fix?
problems.answer: The question, the loss, and the change to make.

steps.title: Explain to an Empty Room
steps.mastery: Deliver a topic aloud to nobody and hear where the explanation stops.
steps.practice: Explain 1 topic aloud for 3 minutes with the notes shut, and mark the 2 places you stalled.
steps.detail: Say it out loud rather than in your head, the head skips the joins and the mouth cannot. Stand up if it helps. When you stall, do not fix it yet: note where it happened and carry on to the end, because the second stall is often caused by the first.
steps.proof: You spoke for 3 minutes and can name the 2 points where the explanation broke down.
steps.pitfall: Explaining it silently, which skips exactly the joins that speaking exposes.

problems.prompt: Why does explaining aloud find gaps that explaining in your head does not, in under 20 words?
problems.answer: Speech has to supply the joins between ideas; silent thought skips them.

problems.prompt: You stall twice in a 3-minute explanation. Fix the first stall immediately or finish first?
problems.answer: Finish first, the second stall is often caused by the first.

problems.prompt: Which is the better record of the attempt: (a) "went badly", (b) 2 marked points where it stalled?
problems.answer: (b). Named stalls are 2 things to study; a feeling is none.

steps.title: Explain It to a Beginner
steps.mastery: Pitch an explanation at somebody who has none of the vocabulary.
steps.practice: Explain diffusion to a 10-year-old in 5 sentences, using no word they would have to look up.
steps.detail: Banning the vocabulary is the point: the terms are where understanding hides, because a sentence built from 3 technical words can be produced without meaning anything. Replace each term with what it does. If you cannot, that term is the thing to go and learn.
steps.proof: 5 sentences that a 10-year-old could follow, with no term left unexplained.
steps.pitfall: Keeping 1 technical word because there is no short substitute, which is the word you least understand.

problems.prompt: Explain "equilibrium" to a beginner in 1 sentence with no technical words.
problems.answer: Two things push against each other equally, so nothing moves overall.

problems.prompt: You cannot explain "entropy" without using "disorder" or "thermodynamic". What does that tell you?
problems.answer: That the term is being used as a label rather than understood, and it is the next thing to study.

problems.prompt: Which explanation is pitched right for a 10-year-old: (a) "osmosis is water moving down a potential gradient", (b) "water moves to where there is less water"?
problems.answer: (b). The first needs 2 terms explained before it means anything.

steps.title: Answer the Why Question
steps.mastery: Say why a result follows, not only what the result is.
steps.practice: State why dividing by a fraction multiplies by its reciprocal, in 3 sentences with 1 worked example.
steps.detail: The what is usually memorized and the why usually is not, so this is where an explanation breaks. Build from something you already accept, here, that dividing by 2 halves a quantity, and show the rule falling out of it. Finish with 1 example where the rule does the work.
steps.proof: Somebody who accepted your first sentence would have to accept the rule by the third.
steps.pitfall: Restating the rule in different words and calling it the reason.

problems.prompt: Why does 6 divided by 1/2 equal 12?
problems.answer: Because it asks how many halves fit in 6, and 12 halves do.

problems.prompt: Which is a why: (a) "invert and multiply", (b) "dividing asks how many of the divisor fit, and halves fit twice as often as wholes"?
problems.answer: (b). The first is the rule restated.

problems.prompt: State the 1 thing a why-explanation must start from.
problems.answer: Something the listener already accepts, so the result can be built rather than asserted.

steps.title: Take the Hard Question
steps.mastery: Field a question you did not prepare and locate the gap it exposes.
steps.practice: Give somebody your 5-sentence explanation and have them ask 3 questions you did not plan for.
steps.detail: A prepared explanation is a rehearsed path, and questions are what take you off it. Write each question down as it is asked rather than answering immediately, the ones you cannot answer are worth more than the ones you can, and they will be forgotten within a minute if unrecorded.
steps.proof: 3 written questions, marked answered or not.
steps.pitfall: Answering a question you half-know with confidence, which loses the gap it was pointing at.

problems.prompt: Of 3 unplanned questions you answer 2. Which is worth the most study time?
Why write a question down before answering it, in under 15 words?
problems.answer: An unrecorded gap is forgotten within a minute of the conversation moving on.

problems.prompt: Which is the better session: (a) 6 questions you all answered, (b) 3 questions with 1 you could not?
problems.answer: (b). It found something; the first only confirmed the rehearsed path.

steps.title: Explain With One Diagram
steps.mastery: Carry an explanation on a drawing you make as you speak.
steps.practice: Explain the carbon cycle while drawing it, using 6 arrows and no more than 8 words of label.
steps.detail: Drawing while speaking forces the structure out: what connects to what, and in which direction. Keep the labels down so the arrows do the work. If an arrow's direction is a guess, that is the part of the cycle you do not have, and a diagram makes it visible in a way a paragraph hides.
steps.proof: A drawing of 6 arrows whose directions you can each justify.
steps.pitfall: Drawing the diagram first and then narrating it, which lets a wrong arrow pass unnoticed.

problems.prompt: You cannot decide which way 1 of your 6 arrows points. What have you found?
problems.answer: The part of the cycle you do not actually hold, made visible by the drawing.

problems.prompt: Why draw the 6 arrows while speaking rather than drawing first and narrating after?
problems.answer: Speaking as you draw forces each arrow to be justified as it is made.

problems.prompt: State the 8-word limit this step puts on labels, and why it is there.
problems.answer: 8 words, so the arrows carry the structure instead of the text.

steps.title: Teach It Twice
steps.mastery: Re-explain a topic after fixing the gaps the first attempt exposed.
steps.practice: Fix the 2 stalls from your first attempt, then explain the same topic again inside 3 minutes.
steps.detail: The second telling is where the gain is: the first found the gaps, and an explanation that is never repeated leaves them found but unfixed. Time both attempts. A second run that is smoother but 90 seconds longer has usually added hedging rather than substance, so aim at the same length.
steps.proof: The second explanation covers the same ground in about the same time with no stall at the 2 marked points.
steps.pitfall: Rerunning the explanation without having looked up what stalled it, which rehearses the gap.

problems.prompt: Your 2nd attempt is smoother but takes 4 minutes 30 against 3 minutes. What likely changed?
problems.answer: Hedging and filler were added rather than substance.

problems.prompt: What has to happen between the 1st and 2nd attempt?
problems.answer: The 2 stalls get looked up and fixed, otherwise the gap is only rehearsed.

problems.prompt: Which shows more: (a) 1 explanation with 2 stalls, (b) 2 explanations where the 2nd has none?
problems.answer: (b). The gaps were found and then closed.

steps.title: Come With Your Own Work
steps.mastery: Arrive at a group session having already met the material alone.
steps.practice: Before 1 group session, work 6 problems alone and mark which 2 you could not finish.
steps.detail: A group is excellent for testing and explaining and useless for first exposure, because the fastest person in the room does the thinking while everybody else watches and feels productive. Arriving with 2 named sticking points means the session starts where your work stopped.
steps.proof: 6 attempted problems and 2 named sticking points, brought to the session.
steps.pitfall: Turning up to hear the topic explained, which is the one thing a group does badly.

problems.prompt: Which is a group session's best use: (a) hearing a topic explained first, (b) testing 6 problems you already attempted?
problems.answer: (b). First exposure is better done alone.

problems.prompt: You bring 2 named sticking points to a group of 4. What does that change?
problems.answer: The session starts on real difficulties instead of a general recap.

problems.prompt: Why does watching the fastest of 4 people solve a problem feel productive?
problems.answer: Following a solution resembles producing one, so recognition is mistaken for ability.

steps.title: Take Turns Explaining
steps.mastery: Rotate who explains so everybody produces rather than listens.
steps.practice: Split 4 topics between 4 people and give each person 5 minutes to explain theirs without notes.
steps.detail: Assign the topics before the session so nobody prepares all 4. The rule that makes it work is no notes: an explanation read aloud is a recital, and the stalls are the whole point. Whoever is not explaining writes down the questions the explanation left open.
steps.proof: All 4 explained for 5 minutes each, with a list of open questions per topic.
steps.pitfall: Letting the strongest person explain 3 of the 4 topics, which is a lecture with extra chairs.

problems.prompt: In a group of 4 with 4 topics, how many explanations does each person give?
Why is explaining for 5 minutes without notes the rule?
problems.answer: Reading aloud is recital; the stalls that expose gaps only happen without notes.

problems.prompt: What do the 3 listeners do during each 5-minute explanation?
problems.answer: Write down the questions it leaves open.

steps.title: Set Each Other Problems
steps.mastery: Write a problem for somebody else and mark their answer.
steps.practice: Write 3 problems each, swap with a partner, and mark the 3 you receive against your own solutions.
steps.detail: Setting a problem requires knowing what makes it hard, and marking one requires knowing what a complete answer contains, both are more demanding than solving. Write your own solution before swapping, because a problem you cannot solve is one you cannot mark.
steps.proof: 3 problems set with solutions, and 3 received problems marked.
steps.pitfall: Setting a problem without solving it first, which produces a question nobody can mark.

problems.prompt: Why write your own solution to all 3 problems before swapping them?
problems.answer: A problem you cannot solve is one you cannot mark.

problems.prompt: Which is harder: solving 3 problems or setting 3 and marking 3?
problems.answer: Setting and marking, they need what makes a problem hard and what a full answer contains.

problems.prompt: Your partner's answer is right by a method you did not expect. What do you do?
problems.answer: Mark it right and note the method, it is a second route worth having.

steps.title: Keep the Group to Four
steps.mastery: Hold a session at a size where everybody has to contribute.
steps.practice: Run 1 session with 4 people and 1 with 8, and count how many minutes each person spoke.
steps.detail: Above about 5 the session turns into an audience: 2 people talk, the rest attend. Counting spoken minutes makes it visible rather than arguable. Four is enough for a range of approaches and small enough that silence is conspicuous.
steps.proof: Two counts of spoken minutes per person, showing how the 8-person session distributed.
steps.pitfall: Inviting everybody who asks, which produces a room where 6 people are quietly wasting an evening.

problems.prompt: In an 8-person session, 2 people speak for 40 of the 60 minutes. What has the session become?
problems.answer: An audience, 6 people are attending rather than working.

problems.prompt: Why does 4 work better than 8 for a working session?
problems.answer: Everybody has to contribute, and silence is conspicuous.

problems.prompt: How do you settle an argument about whether a group of 7 is too big?
problems.answer: Count the spoken minutes per person and look at the distribution.

steps.title: Run to a Written Agenda
steps.mastery: Fix what a session will cover before it starts.
steps.practice: Write a 4-item agenda with minutes against each, and hold the session to within 10 minutes of it.
steps.detail: Without an agenda a session spends 50 minutes on the first person's question and ends. Four items with times, 15, 15, 20, 10, gives everybody a slot and makes overrun visible. Whoever is not explaining keeps time, which is easier than the explainer doing it.
steps.proof: The agenda with actual times beside the planned ones.
steps.pitfall: Writing 4 items with no times, which is a list rather than an agenda.

problems.prompt: An agenda plans 15, 15, 20 and 10 minutes. What is the session length?
Item 1 takes 35 of its 15 minutes. What is the effect on the other 3?
problems.answer: They lose 20 minutes between them, so at least 1 will not happen.

problems.prompt: Why does someone other than the explainer keep time against the 4 agenda items?
problems.answer: The person explaining cannot watch the clock and the argument at once.

steps.title: Test Each Other Cold
steps.mastery: Quiz the group from cards nobody has seen in advance.
steps.practice: Bring 10 cards the others have not seen and quiz 3 people, recording who missed what.
steps.detail: Cold questions from another person are the closest a group gets to exam conditions, and they catch the material everybody quietly agreed to skip. Record the misses by person and card: a card 3 people miss is a group weakness and belongs on the next agenda.
steps.proof: A grid of 10 cards against 3 people, with the misses marked.
steps.pitfall: Circulating the cards beforehand, which turns a cold test into a rehearsal.

problems.prompt: A card is missed by 3 of 3 people. What does that mean for the next session?
problems.answer: It is a group weakness and goes on the agenda.

problems.prompt: Why must the 10 cards be unseen by the others?
problems.answer: Circulated cards make it a rehearsal rather than a test.

problems.prompt: You record misses by person only, not by card. What is lost?
problems.answer: Which material the whole group is weak on, as opposed to who is weak.

steps.title: Split and Report Back
steps.mastery: Divide reading between members and deliver it back accurately.
steps.practice: Split 4 chapters between 4 people and have each report back in 8 minutes with 3 questions for the others.
steps.detail: This only works when the reporting is tested, otherwise the group ends up with 1 person's summary of material nobody else read. Each reporter brings 3 questions on their chapter, and the others have to answer them, which is what makes a lazy report obvious immediately.
steps.proof: 4 reports of 8 minutes, each followed by 3 questions the others answered.
steps.pitfall: Accepting 4 summaries with no questions, leaving everybody with 1 chapter and 3 rumors.

problems.prompt: Why does each of the 4 reporters bring 3 questions?
problems.answer: Answering them tests whether the report actually transferred the chapter.

problems.prompt: Without questions, what does the group end up holding after 4 reports?
4 chapters, 8 minutes each with 3 questions apiece. Roughly how long is the session?
problems.answer: About 50 minutes with the questions included.

steps.title: End With What Changed
steps.mastery: Close a session by recording what each person will do differently.
steps.practice: Finish 1 session with each of the 4 writing 1 line on what they will work on before the next one.
steps.detail: A session that ends on "that was useful" produces nothing by Thursday. One line each, specific enough to check, "redo the 3 ratio problems I missed", read aloud so the group has heard it. The next session opens by checking those 4 lines.
steps.proof: 4 written lines, and the next session opens by checking them.
steps.pitfall: Ending on general agreement that the topic is clearer, which cannot be checked.

problems.prompt: Which closing line is checkable: (a) "revise ratios more", (b) "redo the 3 ratio problems I missed tonight"?
problems.answer: (b). It names work that can be shown done.

problems.prompt: Why are the 4 lines read aloud rather than written privately?
problems.answer: The group has heard them, so the next session can check them.

problems.prompt: What is the first item of the next session's agenda?
problems.answer: Checking the 4 lines from last time.

steps.title: Mix Two Problem Types
steps.mastery: Alternate between 2 kinds of problem instead of blocking one kind.
steps.practice: Work 12 problems alternating quadratic factorizing and simultaneous equations, 1 of each in turn.
steps.detail: Blocked practice lets you reuse the last problem's method without deciding anything, which is why it feels easy and tests little. Alternating forces the choice of method to happen every time, which is the part you will need in an exam. Expect to get more wrong than in a blocked set.
steps.proof: The 12 worked problems alternate type, and you can name the method each one needed.
steps.pitfall: Sorting the sheet into 6 of one type and 6 of the other because it runs faster that way.

problems.prompt: Which is interleaved: (a) 6 factorizing then 6 simultaneous, (b) factorizing and simultaneous alternating 12 times?
problems.answer: (b). Only there does the method have to be chosen each time.

problems.prompt: You score 9 out of 12 blocked and 6 out of 12 interleaved. Which set taught you more?
problems.answer: The interleaved one, the lower score is the method choice being trained.

problems.prompt: State what a blocked set of 20 identical problems stops you practicing.
problems.answer: Deciding which method a problem needs, because the previous answer already settled it.

steps.title: Shuffle the Problem Set
steps.mastery: Remove the ordering cue a textbook exercise gives you for free.
steps.practice: Cut 15 exercise questions into strips, shuffle them, and work the first 8 in the order they come up.
steps.detail: A textbook exercise is grouped by the section that just taught the method, so question 7 is answered by whatever page 7 was about. Shuffling strips that cue out. Keep the answers separate so you cannot see which section a question came from while working it.
steps.proof: You worked 8 questions with no idea which section each came from, and marked them after.
steps.pitfall: Shuffling but leaving the section headings on the strips, which hands the cue back.

problems.prompt: Why is question 7 of a 20-question exercise easier than the same question in an exam?
problems.answer: It sits under the section that taught its method, so no choice of method is needed.

problems.prompt: You shuffle 15 strips but each keeps its section number. What has been lost?
problems.answer: Nothing, the section number is the cue, so it still tells you the method.

problems.prompt: Which is the better mixed set: 8 questions from 1 chapter shuffled, or 8 from 3 chapters shuffled?
problems.answer: The 3-chapter set. It mixes methods as well as order.

steps.title: Expect the Worse Score
steps.mastery: Read a lower session score as the cost of a method that lasts.
steps.practice: Record your score on 10 blocked problems and 10 interleaved ones, and write the gap between them.
steps.detail: Interleaved practice reliably scores worse on the day and better a week later, which is why almost everybody abandons it. Writing both scores down turns that into a number you expected rather than evidence you are getting worse. Compare again after a week on the same material.
steps.proof: You have 2 scores and a gap, and can say which one predicts next week's performance.
steps.pitfall: Going back to blocked practice after 2 sessions because the score dropped, which is the effect working.

problems.prompt: You score 8 out of 10 blocked and 5 out of 10 interleaved today. Which predicts next week better?
problems.answer: The interleaved 5, blocked scores measure the method being fresh, not retained.

problems.prompt: State the usual reason people give up on interleaving after 2 sessions.
problems.answer: The session score falls, which looks like getting worse and is the effect working.

problems.prompt: How would you test the claim after 7 days?
problems.answer: Work 10 fresh mixed problems from the same material and compare with the blocked group's score.

steps.title: Interleave Across Topics
steps.mastery: Mix problems from 3 topics so the topic itself has to be identified.
steps.practice: Build a 12-problem set drawing 4 each from trigonometry, logarithms and sequences, shuffled.
steps.detail: Mixing methods inside one topic is the easy version; mixing topics means the first decision is what kind of problem this even is. Keep a tally of which topic you misidentify, because that is a different error from getting the method wrong once you know the topic.
steps.proof: The set holds 4 problems from each topic in mixed order, with misidentifications tallied separately.
steps.pitfall: Grouping the 3 topics into blocks of 4 within the set, which rebuilds the cue.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 different errors a 3-topic mixed set separates.
problems.answer: Misidentifying the topic, and choosing the wrong method once the topic is known.

problems.prompt: You misidentify 3 of 12 problems' topics. What does that point at?
problems.answer: The cues that mark a problem as trigonometry rather than sequences, which is its own thing to study.

problems.prompt: Why is a set of 12 drawn from 3 topics harder than 12 from 1 topic shuffled?
problems.answer: The topic has to be identified first, which a single-topic set decides for you.

steps.title: Alternate Within a Session
steps.mastery: Rotate subjects inside 1 study block without losing the thread of either.
steps.practice: Run a 60-minute block as 3 rotations of 20 minutes across 2 subjects, ending on the harder one.
steps.detail: Switching has a cost, so the slices need to be long enough to get into the work, 20 minutes rather than 5. Write 1 line at each switch saying where you stopped, so the next rotation starts from the work instead of from re-reading. End on the subject you find harder, while the block still has your attention.
steps.proof: The block held 3 rotations, each with a hand-off line, and finished on the harder subject.
steps.pitfall: Slicing a 60-minute block into 6 switches of 10 minutes, where the switching costs more than the mixing gains.

problems.prompt: A 60-minute block covers 2 subjects. Is 3 rotations of 20 minutes or 6 of 10 the better split?
problems.answer: 3 of 20. At 10 minutes the switching costs more than the mixing gains.

problems.prompt: What goes in the 1-line hand-off written at each switch?
problems.answer: Where you stopped, so the next rotation resumes the work instead of rereading.

problems.prompt: Why end a 60-minute block on the harder subject rather than the easier one?
problems.answer: The harder work gets attention while some is left, rather than the last 20 minutes being spent on the easy subject.

steps.title: Mixed Paper Every Week
steps.mastery: Sit a mixed set weekly as the measure of what has actually held.
steps.practice: Build a 20-question mixed paper from the last 4 weeks and sit it in 45 minutes without notes.
steps.detail: This is the check on everything else: cards, blocked practice and rereading all flatter you, and a mixed paper across 4 weeks does not. Mark it hard, then tally the misses by topic, the topic with most misses is next week's opening work, whatever the schedule said.
steps.proof: A marked 20-question paper with the misses tallied by topic.
steps.pitfall: Building the paper from this week only, which makes it a test of what is freshest.

problems.prompt: Should the weekly mixed paper draw from this week or the last 4 weeks?
problems.answer: The last 4 weeks, so it tests what held rather than what is freshest.

problems.prompt: Your 20-question paper shows 5 misses in sequences and 1 elsewhere. What changes next week?
problems.answer: Next week opens on sequences, regardless of what the schedule had planned.

problems.prompt: Why is a mixed paper a better measure than a score of 18 out of 20 on today's cards?
problems.answer: Cards test single facts while fresh; the paper tests choosing methods across 4 weeks of material.

steps.title: Keep One Summary Page
steps.mastery: Retain a single page per subject worth reopening in a year.
steps.practice: Reduce 1 finished subject to 1 page holding its 8 main results, and file it where you will find it.
steps.detail: After an exam most material is discarded and the subject becomes something you once did. One page changes that: 8 results, the 2 or 3 organizing ideas, and nothing else. File the pages together by subject so the whole set is 1 folder rather than 6 notebooks.
steps.proof: 1 page per subject, holding its main results, filed in 1 place.
steps.pitfall: Keeping all 60 pages of notes, which is the same as keeping none because nobody reopens 60 pages.

problems.prompt: Which is more likely to be reopened in 12 months: 60 pages of notes or 1 page of 8 results?
problems.answer: The 1 page, 60 pages is functionally the same as keeping nothing.

problems.prompt: What belongs on the 1 page besides the 8 results?
problems.answer: The 2 or 3 organizing ideas, and nothing more.

problems.prompt: Why file all the subject pages together rather than 1 per notebook?
problems.answer: The whole set becomes 1 folder you can actually open.

steps.title: Review Once a Month
steps.mastery: Revisit a finished subject briefly at monthly intervals.
steps.practice: Put 4 monthly 20-minute reviews in the calendar for 1 finished subject, and keep the first one.
steps.detail: Twenty minutes a month is enough to keep a subject retrievable, which is a fraction of what relearning it costs. Work from the 1-page summary: cover it, produce what you can, then check. Put the dates in the calendar, because a review with no date does not happen once the deadline has gone.
steps.proof: 4 dated reviews in the calendar and the first one done.
steps.pitfall: Planning to review "now and then", which is how a subject quietly disappears over 6 months.

problems.prompt: How long is each of the 4 monthly reviews, and what does it work from?
problems.answer: 20 minutes, worked from the 1-page summary with the page covered.

problems.prompt: Why must the 4 reviews carry dates?
problems.answer: Without a deadline pushing them, undated reviews do not happen.

problems.prompt: Compare 20 minutes a month against relearning a subject from scratch.
problems.answer: The monthly review is a small fraction of the cost of relearning.

steps.title: Test It, Do Not Reread
steps.mastery: Make a maintenance review a retrieval attempt rather than a read.
steps.practice: Cover your 1-page summary and produce 6 of its 8 results from memory before looking.
steps.detail: The maintenance review has the same rule as everything else: produce first, check second. Rereading a page you wrote is comfortable, fast and nearly worthless. Aim at 6 of 8, below that the subject needs a longer session, above it the interval can stretch.
steps.proof: A count of how many of the 8 results you produced before uncovering the page.
steps.pitfall: Reading the page over twice and calling it a review.

problems.prompt: You produce 3 of 8 results from memory. Stretch the interval or run a longer session?
problems.answer: Run a longer session, 3 of 8 means the subject is fading.

problems.prompt: You produce 8 of 8. What can change?
problems.answer: The interval can stretch, to 2 months or more.

problems.prompt: Why is rereading your own 1-page summary nearly worthless as a review?
problems.answer: It tests recognition of your own handwriting rather than recall of the content.

steps.title: Use It on Something Real
steps.mastery: Apply a finished subject to a problem outside the course.
steps.practice: Find 1 use for a finished subject outside its course and spend 30 minutes on it.
steps.detail: Nothing maintains a subject like using it: statistics on a dataset you care about, a language on a menu, mechanics on a bicycle. Thirty minutes of real use is worth several reviews, because it forces the parts you skipped and shows which ones you never actually had.
steps.proof: 30 minutes of the subject applied outside the course, with 1 line on what it exposed.
steps.pitfall: Waiting for a use to come up naturally, which for most subjects is never.

problems.prompt: Name 1 real use of basic statistics outside a course, doable in 30 minutes.
problems.answer: Summarizing a dataset you care about, a mean, a spread and what they say.

problems.prompt: Why is 30 minutes of real use worth more than 3 reviews?
problems.answer: It forces the parts you skipped and exposes what you never actually had.

problems.prompt: What do you write down after the 30 minutes?
problems.answer: One line on what the use exposed as missing.

steps.title: Stretch the Intervals
steps.mastery: Lengthen maintenance gaps as a subject proves durable.
steps.practice: Move a subject from monthly to 3-monthly reviews after 3 consecutive reviews scoring 7 of 8 or better.
steps.detail: Maintenance should get cheaper. The rule is evidence-based rather than a feeling: 3 consecutive good scores earn a longer gap. A single weak review sends it back to monthly, which is cheap insurance against losing a subject you thought was safe.
steps.proof: A record of 3 review scores and the interval they earned.
steps.pitfall: Stretching to 6 months after 1 good review, which is usually where a subject is lost.

problems.prompt: How many consecutive reviews at 7 of 8 earn a longer interval?
A 3-monthly subject scores 4 of 8. What happens to the interval?
Why is stretching to 6 months after 1 good review risky?
problems.answer: One score is not evidence of durability, and that is usually where a subject is lost.

steps.title: Refresh Before You Need It
steps.mastery: Rebuild a dormant subject in advance of the thing that needs it.
steps.practice: Pick a subject you will need in 8 weeks and schedule 4 sessions of 45 minutes before then.
steps.detail: A subject needed for a course, a job or an interview is best rebuilt on a schedule rather than in a panic the week before. Four sessions: 1 to test what remains, 2 on the gaps, 1 to apply it. Starting from the 1-page summary makes the first session a measurement rather than a guess.
steps.proof: 4 dated sessions, the first of which measured what remained.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the refresh to the week it is needed, which is relearning under pressure.

problems.prompt: How are the 4 refresh sessions divided?
problems.answer: 1 to test what remains, 2 on the gaps, 1 to apply it.

problems.prompt: Why does session 1 work from the 1-page summary?
problems.answer: It measures what actually remains instead of guessing at it.

problems.prompt: You leave an 8-week refresh until the final week. What have you converted it into?
problems.answer: Relearning under pressure, which costs more and holds less.

steps.title: Notice What You Lost
steps.mastery: Identify which parts of a subject decayed and which held.
steps.practice: Compare a review score by section against your score 6 months ago and name the 2 weakest sections.
steps.detail: Decay is uneven: procedures you used stay, definitions you memorized go first, and anything you never derived goes fastest. Comparing by section rather than in total tells you which kind of material you lose, which changes how you learn the next subject.
steps.proof: A section-by-section comparison and the 2 weakest named.
steps.pitfall: Comparing totals, which hides that 1 section carried all the loss.

problems.prompt: Which usually decays fastest: a procedure you used 40 times or a definition you memorized once?
Your total score fell 3 marks but 1 of 6 sections lost all 3. What does the total hide?
problems.answer: That the loss is concentrated in 1 section rather than spread.

problems.prompt: A pattern of losing memorized definitions should change what about the next 8 topics?
problems.answer: More of it gets derived rather than memorized.

steps.title: Teach It Once a Year
steps.mastery: Explain a finished subject to somebody as a durable annual test.
steps.practice: Explain 1 finished subject for 15 minutes to somebody who does not know it, once a year.
steps.detail: Teaching is the hardest maintenance test and the cheapest to arrange: it needs the structure, the joins and the reasons, all of which decay silently. Fifteen minutes to a real person exposes more than an hour of private review, and their questions are the part you cannot anticipate.
steps.proof: A 15-minute explanation given, with the questions you could not answer written down.
steps.pitfall: Explaining it to somebody who already knows it, who will fill the gaps for you without either of you noticing.

problems.prompt: Why explain to somebody who does not know the subject rather than to 1 who does?
problems.answer: Someone who knows it fills the gaps for you without either of you noticing.

problems.prompt: What is worth writing down from the 15 minutes?
problems.answer: The questions you could not answer.

problems.prompt: Why does teaching test more than 1 hour of private review?
problems.answer: It needs structure, joins and reasons, which decay silently and cannot be faked aloud.

steps.title: Keep the Folder Alive
steps.mastery: Maintain the whole set of retained subjects as one small system.
steps.practice: Audit your folder of 1-page summaries, giving each subject a next-review date and dropping 1 you no longer want.
steps.detail: A retention system with 12 subjects in it and no dates is a drawer. Every page gets a next date and a current interval; anything you genuinely do not intend to keep gets dropped on purpose rather than by neglect. Twenty minutes, twice a year.
steps.proof: Every page in the folder carries a next-review date, and 1 has been deliberately dropped.
steps.pitfall: Keeping 12 subjects nominally alive and reviewing 2, which loses the other 10 without ever deciding to.

problems.prompt: Your folder holds 12 subjects and you review 2. What is happening to the other 10?
problems.answer: They are being lost by neglect rather than by a decision.

problems.prompt: What does every page in a 12-subject folder carry after the audit?
problems.answer: A next-review date and its current interval.

problems.prompt: Is the folder audited twice a year or every 2 weeks, and for how long?

steps.title: First-Letter Mnemonics
steps.mastery: Build a sentence whose initials recover an ordered list.
steps.practice: Make a mnemonic for the 7 colors of the spectrum in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
steps.detail: Take the initials, R O Y G B I V, and build a sentence whose words start with them in order. Make it concrete and slightly odd, because bland sentences do not stick. Test it by writing the 7 colors from the sentence alone an hour later.
steps.proof: The sentence returns all 7 colors in the right order an hour later.
steps.pitfall: Building a mnemonic with 2 words starting with the same letter, so the order goes ambiguous.

problems.prompt: Give the initials your mnemonic must cover for the spectrum's 7 colors in order.
problems.answer: R, O, Y, G, B, I, V.

problems.prompt: Your mnemonic for 5 items has 2 words beginning with S. What breaks?
problems.answer: The order between those 2 items, since the initials no longer distinguish them.

problems.prompt: Why does a slightly absurd 7-word sentence hold better than a plain one?
problems.answer: Odd images are recalled more reliably than bland ones.

steps.title: Numbers Into Images
steps.mastery: Convert an arbitrary number into a picture you can recall.
steps.practice: Turn the year 1453 into 1 concrete image and recall it correctly an hour later.
steps.detail: Split the number into pairs, 14 and 53, and give each pair a fixed image you reuse across all dates. Join the 2 images into 1 scene involving the event. The pairing has to stay fixed across every number you learn, or the images collide.
steps.proof: You can state 1453 from the image, and the image from the event.
steps.pitfall: Inventing fresh images per number, which is as much to remember as the digits were.

problems.prompt: Split 1815 into the 2 pairs this method uses.
Why must the image for the pair 53 stay the same across every date you learn?
problems.answer: Otherwise images collide and no number can be read back reliably.

problems.prompt: You built 6 fresh images for 6 dates. What is the problem?
problems.answer: 6 new images is as much to store as the 12 digits were.

steps.title: Walk a Memory Palace
steps.mastery: Place items along a familiar route and collect them in order.
steps.practice: Place 10 items along a route through your home, 1 per location, then recall all 10 in order.
steps.detail: Pick a route you know without thinking and fix the order of its 10 stops before placing anything. Put 1 item at each stop, interacting with it oddly rather than sitting beside it. Walk the route in your head twice immediately, then once again an hour later.
steps.proof: You can recite the 10 items in route order, and backwards.
steps.pitfall: Placing 2 items at 1 stop, which is where a palace usually loses something.

problems.prompt: How many items go at each of the 10 stops, and why?
problems.answer: 1. Two at a stop is where the route loses an item.

problems.prompt: Why should the route be fixed before any of the 10 items are placed?
problems.answer: The order of the stops is what supplies the order of the items.

problems.prompt: You can recall 10 items forwards but not backwards. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: The items are chained to each other rather than anchored to the 10 stops.

steps.title: Link a Chain of Facts
steps.mastery: Join a short sequence with images so each item pulls the next.
steps.practice: Chain the 5 stages of mitosis by linking each to the next with 1 vivid image.
steps.detail: A chain suits sequences of 5 to 8 where the order matters and the items are related. Link consecutive pairs, making each junction do something physical. The weakness is that a broken link loses the tail, so test by starting from the middle as well as the top.
steps.proof: You can give the 5 stages from stage 1 and from stage 3.
steps.pitfall: Building 1 long story where a forgotten junction takes the whole rest of the chain with it.

problems.prompt: Why test a 5-item chain by starting from item 3 as well as item 1?
problems.answer: To check the tail survives a broken junction rather than depending on the whole chain.

problems.prompt: Which suits a chain better: 6 ordered stages, or 40 unordered vocabulary words?
problems.answer: The 6 ordered stages, chains carry order and break down at length.

problems.prompt: State the failure mode of a 20-item chain.
problems.answer: One forgotten junction loses every item after it.

steps.title: Use It for the Arbitrary Only
steps.mastery: Choose memory techniques for material no reasoning can recover.
steps.practice: Sort 10 items into 2 lists, arbitrary and derivable, and build images for the arbitrary ones only.
steps.detail: Mnemonics are expensive to build, so they belong on names, symbols, dates and conventions. Anything derivable is cheaper to reconstruct than to encode, and a palace full of derivable facts is effort spent hiding the reasoning you should have learned.
steps.proof: Images exist for the arbitrary list only, and you can derive every item on the other one.
steps.pitfall: Building a mnemonic for a formula you could derive in 3 lines.

problems.prompt: Mnemonic or derivation for the symbol "K" for potassium?
problems.answer: Mnemonic, it comes from kalium and cannot be reasoned out.

problems.prompt: Mnemonic or derivation for the area of a trapezium, and does it take about 3 lines or 30?
problems.answer: Derivation, it follows from splitting the shape, in about 3 lines.

problems.prompt: Why is a memory palace holding 30 derivable formulas a poor use of it?
problems.answer: Each could be rebuilt from reasoning, so the encoding effort buys nothing.

steps.title: Test the Mnemonic Cold
steps.mastery: Check a mnemonic still returns its content after a day away.
steps.practice: Recall 3 mnemonics built yesterday and write out what each unpacks to, unprompted.
steps.detail: A mnemonic can feel solid the minute it is built and be gone by the next day, usually because it was abstract or too similar to another one. Test cold, with nothing in front of you. Where it fails, rebuild the image more concretely rather than repeating the old one.
steps.proof: 3 mnemonics recalled and unpacked correctly with nothing in view.
steps.pitfall: Testing the mnemonic while looking at the list it encodes, which proves nothing.

problems.prompt: A mnemonic built yesterday returns nothing today. Repeat it 10 times or rebuild the image?
problems.answer: Rebuild it more concretely, repetition of a weak image stays weak.

problems.prompt: Why test 3 mnemonics with the encoded list out of sight?
problems.answer: With the list visible the test measures recognition, not recall.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 usual reasons a fresh mnemonic fails within 24 hours.
problems.answer: It was too abstract, or too similar to another one you already use.

steps.title: Keep the Palace Stocked
steps.mastery: Maintain a set of routes and know what currently occupies each.
steps.practice: List your 3 routes and what each is holding, and clear 1 that is finished with.
steps.detail: Routes are reusable but not simultaneously, so leaving an exam's content in a route blocks it for the next subject. Keep an index card per route saying what is in it and when it was loaded. Clearing a route means walking it once deliberately empty before reloading.
steps.proof: 3 routes indexed with their contents, and 1 walked empty.
steps.pitfall: Loading a new list into a route that still holds an old one, which mixes the 2 sets.

problems.prompt: You load a 2nd list of 10 items into a route still holding the 1st. What happens?
problems.answer: The 2 sets interfere and neither reads back cleanly.

problems.prompt: What goes on the index card for each of the 3 routes?
problems.answer: What it holds and when it was loaded.

problems.prompt: How is 1 route cleared before its 10 stops are reused?
problems.answer: Walk its 10 stops once deliberately empty before loading anything new.

steps.title: Keep an Error Log
steps.mastery: Record every wrong answer in one place with what went wrong.
steps.practice: Start a 3-column log, problem, what I did, what was wrong, and enter 5 errors from your last set.
steps.detail: The third column is the one that matters and the one people leave out: not the right answer, but the specific move that failed. "Multiplied instead of divided in the ratio step" is an entry you can act on; "got it wrong" is not. Keep 1 log for the whole subject so patterns are visible.
steps.proof: 5 entries, each naming a specific wrong move rather than a wrong answer.
steps.pitfall: Writing the correct solution in column 3, which records the answer and loses the diagnosis.

problems.prompt: Which is a usable column-3 entry: (a) "the answer was 42", (b) "divided by the 3 : 2 ratio the wrong way round"?
problems.answer: (b). It names the move that failed.

problems.prompt: Why keep 1 log for a subject rather than 5 logs per topic?
problems.answer: Patterns across topics only show up when the errors sit together.

problems.prompt: You log 5 errors and 4 say "careless". What is wrong with the log?
problems.answer: "Careless" is not a diagnosis, each needs the specific step that went wrong.

steps.title: Sort Slip From Gap
steps.mastery: Tell an execution slip apart from something you did not know.
steps.practice: Label each of your 5 logged errors S for slip or G for gap, and count the 2 totals.
steps.detail: They need different fixes: a gap is studied, a slip is prevented by a check. Redo the problem immediately, if you now get it right without learning anything, it was a slip. Counting the 2 totals tells you whether to spend the week on content or on checking procedures.
steps.proof: 5 labeled errors and 2 totals you can state.
steps.pitfall: Calling a gap a slip because you understood the solution when you read it.

problems.prompt: You redo a missed problem immediately and get it right with no new learning. Slip or gap?
problems.answer: A slip, the knowledge was there and the execution failed.

problems.prompt: Of 10 errors, 7 are gaps. Does the week go on content or on checking?
problems.answer: On content, since most losses are things not known.

problems.prompt: Why is "I understood the solution when I read it" not evidence of a slip?
problems.answer: Following a solution is recognition; it does not show you could have produced it.

steps.title: Redo It From Blank
steps.mastery: Rework a missed problem from a blank page after the fix.
steps.practice: Redo 3 logged problems from blank paper 1 day later, with the log and solution shut.
steps.detail: Reading your own correction is not the same as being able to produce the solution, and the gap between those 2 is where repeat mistakes live. A day's delay is deliberate: it stops you reproducing the correction from short-term memory rather than from understanding.
steps.proof: 3 problems reworked correctly from blank paper, a day after the correction.
steps.pitfall: Redoing the problem 2 minutes after reading the solution, which tests the last 2 minutes only.

problems.prompt: Why wait a day before redoing a corrected problem rather than 2 minutes?
problems.answer: A 2-minute gap tests short-term memory of the correction, not the method.

problems.prompt: You redo 3 problems and miss 1 again. What happens to that entry?
problems.answer: It goes back in the log as a gap and is studied from the source, not redone again.

problems.prompt: Which shows the fix worked: (a) rereading your correction, (b) producing the solution from blank paper a day later?

steps.title: Count the Repeat Offenders
steps.mastery: Find the error you keep making across weeks of work.
steps.practice: Tally your log by error type and name the 1 type with the most entries over 3 weeks.
steps.detail: Individual errors feel like bad luck; a tally shows they are not. Group by the failing move, sign errors, ratio inversions, dropped units, and count. The top type is usually responsible for a surprising share of lost marks, and it is 1 thing to fix rather than twenty.
steps.proof: A tally by type, with the top type named and its count.
steps.pitfall: Grouping by topic rather than by failing move, which hides an error that crosses topics.

problems.prompt: Your 3-week tally shows 11 sign errors, 4 ratio inversions and 3 others. Where does the week go?
problems.answer: On sign handling, which is over half the losses.

problems.prompt: Why group 18 logged errors by failing move rather than by topic?
problems.answer: The same move fails across topics, and a topic grouping splits it into small piles.

problems.prompt: What does a log with 18 single-entry types suggest about the grouping?
problems.answer: The categories are too fine, the entries need grouping into fewer failing moves.

steps.title: Write the Prevention Rule
steps.mastery: Turn a repeated error into a check you run every time.
steps.practice: Write 2 one-line checks for your top error type, such as "circle every minus sign before expanding".
steps.detail: A rule has to be an action at a specific moment, not an intention. "Be careful with signs" changes nothing; "circle every minus sign before expanding" happens at a point in the work where it can be done. Two rules maximum, so they actually get used.
steps.proof: 2 checks, each naming an action and the moment it happens.
steps.pitfall: Writing 6 rules, which means none of them is running by Thursday.

problems.prompt: Which is a usable rule: (a) "be careful with units", (b) "write the unit beside every number before adding"?
problems.answer: (b). It names an action at a moment.

problems.prompt: Why cap the list at 2 rules?
problems.answer: More than 2 stops being run, so the rules become intentions again.

problems.prompt: Write a 1-line check for repeatedly inverting a 3 : 2 ratio.
problems.answer: Before multiplying, say aloud which quantity is getting bigger.

steps.title: Mark Like the Examiner
steps.mastery: Apply a mark scheme to your own work without giving yourself the benefit.
steps.practice: Mark 3 of your worked answers against a published mark scheme, awarding only what is written on the page.
