steps.detail: Marking your own work generously is the fastest way to a nasty surprise. Award marks only for what is on the paper: no credit for what you meant, knew, or would have written with more time. Where you lose a mark for presentation rather than content, that is worth logging too.
steps.proof: 3 scores from the mark scheme, with the lost marks itemized.
steps.pitfall: Awarding the method mark because you knew the method, when the page does not show it.

problems.prompt: You knew a method but did not write it, and the scheme gives 2 method marks. What do you award?
problems.answer: 0. The scheme pays for what is on the page.

problems.prompt: Why itemize the 4 lost marks rather than recording a total of 12 out of 16?
problems.answer: The items say what to fix; the total says only how it felt.

problems.prompt: A mark is lost for no units in the final line of a 6-mark answer. Content or presentation, and worth logging?
problems.answer: Presentation, and yes, it is a cheap, repeatable loss.

steps.title: Close the Log Weekly
steps.mastery: Clear an error log every week so it stays a worklist rather than a diary.
steps.practice: Go through last week's 12 entries and close each one: redone, studied, or rule written.
steps.detail: An open entry is work outstanding, and a log that only grows is a record of failure rather than a tool. Each Friday, every entry gets closed with a mark saying how, or is carried forward once. An entry carried twice is a sign the fix is bigger than the log and needs a study session of its own.
steps.proof: Last week's entries all closed or carried once, with the count of each.
steps.pitfall: Letting the log grow to 60 entries, at which point nobody opens it again.

problems.prompt: Of 12 entries, 9 are closed and 3 carried forward for the 2nd time. What do the 3 need?
problems.answer: A study session of their own, the fix is bigger than a log entry.

problems.prompt: Why close the log weekly rather than letting it reach 50 entries?
problems.answer: A log of 50 unclosed entries stops being opened, so the work never gets done.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 ways an entry can be closed.
problems.answer: Redone from blank, studied from the source, or turned into a prevention rule.

steps.title: Sit One Under Timed Conditions
steps.mastery: Reproduce the exam's conditions closely enough to feel them.
steps.practice: Sit 1 past paper in 90 minutes with no notes, no phone and no pauses, at a desk.
steps.detail: Familiarity is what takes the edge off, and it only comes from the real thing: timer running, materials away, no stopping for a cup of tea. Do it at the time of day the exam falls if you can. The first one will feel worse than the exam did in your imagination, which is the point.
steps.proof: 1 completed paper, sat unbroken in 90 minutes with nothing to hand.
steps.pitfall: Pausing the timer for 5 minutes to look 1 thing up, which removes the condition being practiced.

problems.prompt: You pause the timer for 5 minutes during a 90-minute mock. What has been lost?
problems.answer: The time pressure, which was the condition being practiced.

problems.prompt: Why sit a 90-minute mock at the same time of day as the real exam?
problems.answer: The state you will be in is part of what is being made familiar.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 things that must be away during a timed mock.

steps.title: Write the Blank Plan
steps.mastery: Have a written procedure for the moment nothing comes.
steps.practice: Write 3 steps to follow if you go blank, such as breathing, moving to question 4, and returning after 10 minutes.
steps.detail: Going blank is a state, and a decision made inside it is unreliable, so make the decision now, in writing, and follow it rather than thinking. Three steps at most: something physical, something procedural, and a time to come back. Rehearse it once in a mock so it is familiar.
steps.proof: 3 written steps, rehearsed once under timed conditions.
steps.pitfall: Planning to "stay calm and think it through", which is not a procedure and cannot be followed.

problems.prompt: Which is a usable blank plan: (a) stay calm and focus, (b) 4 slow breaths, move to question 4, return in 10 minutes?
problems.answer: (b). It is a sequence you can follow without deciding anything.

problems.prompt: Why decide the 3 steps in advance rather than in the moment?
problems.answer: Decisions made while blank are unreliable, so the procedure is made beforehand.

problems.prompt: What are the 3 kinds of step the plan holds?
problems.answer: Something physical, something procedural, and a time to return.

steps.title: Practice the First Five Minutes
steps.mastery: Rehearse the opening of a paper until it needs no decisions.
steps.practice: Rehearse the same 5-minute opening 3 times: write your name, scan all questions, mark times, start question 1.
steps.detail: The worst nerves are in the first few minutes, so make those minutes a routine rather than a set of choices. The same 4 actions in the same order, practiced 3 times, means the paper is under way before there is anything to panic about.
steps.proof: The same 4-action opening carried out 3 times in 5 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Opening by reading question 1 closely, which means the paper's shape is still unknown 10 minutes in.

problems.prompt: Name the 4 actions of the rehearsed opening, in order.
problems.answer: Name on the paper, scan every question, mark finish times, start question 1.

problems.prompt: Why scan all the questions before starting question 1?
problems.answer: So the paper's shape and the time plan are known before any writing.

problems.prompt: Why rehearse the opening 3 times rather than reading about it?
problems.answer: Under nerves a practiced routine runs where a remembered intention does not.

steps.title: Slow the Breathing Down
steps.mastery: Bring physical arousal down with a technique that works while seated.
steps.practice: Practice 6 cycles of 4 seconds in and 6 seconds out, seated, and take your pulse before and after.
steps.detail: A longer out-breath than in-breath reliably slows the heart, and 1 minute of it is enough to change the state. Practice it away from the exam so it is automatic. Taking the pulse before and after gives you evidence it works, which matters on the day you doubt it.
steps.proof: A pulse figure before and after 1 minute of the pattern.
steps.pitfall: Trying it for the first time in the exam hall, where an unfamiliar technique is 1 more thing to worry about.

problems.prompt: 6 cycles of 4 seconds in and 6 out takes how long?
In a 4-seconds-in, 6-seconds-out cycle, why is the out-breath the longer one?
problems.answer: A longer exhale slows the heart rate rather than raising it.

problems.prompt: Why take a pulse before and after the 1 minute?
problems.answer: It gives evidence the technique works, for the day you doubt it.

steps.title: Run the Worst Case
steps.mastery: State what would actually happen in the outcome you fear.
steps.practice: Write 3 sentences describing what follows if this exam goes badly, including the resit or retake route.
steps.detail: Unexamined, the fear has no shape and therefore no size. Written out, a resit in 4 months, a different offer, a year that looks different, it is usually survivable and always finite. This is not positive thinking: it is making the cost specific enough to stop being unbounded.
steps.proof: 3 written sentences naming what follows, including a route forward.
steps.pitfall: Refusing to think about it at all, which leaves the fear at whatever size it wants to be.

problems.prompt: Why write the worst case in 3 sentences rather than avoiding the thought?
problems.answer: Unexamined, the fear has no size; written down it is finite and usually survivable.

problems.prompt: What must the 3 sentences include besides the bad outcome?
problems.answer: The route forward from it, such as a resit or a different offer.

problems.prompt: Is writing the 3 worst-case sentences the same as telling yourself it will be fine?
problems.answer: No, it makes the cost specific rather than denying it.

steps.title: Keep the Routine Boring
steps.mastery: Fix the hours before an exam so nothing new happens in them.
steps.practice: Write the 6 things you will do in the 3 hours before the exam, in order, and change none of them on the day.
steps.detail: Novelty raises arousal, so the morning should be the one you have already had several times: same breakfast, same route, same arrival margin, same 1 page of notes. Deciding it in advance also removes 6 small decisions from a morning that has no capacity for them.
steps.proof: 6 written items in order, and the same list used in a mock morning.
steps.pitfall: Cramming a new topic in the last hour, which raises arousal and displaces what you had ready.

problems.prompt: Is reading 1 new topic in the last hour a good idea?
problems.answer: No, it raises arousal and displaces material you already had ready.

problems.prompt: Why write the 6 items in advance?
problems.answer: It removes 6 decisions from a morning with no capacity for them.

problems.prompt: Of the 6 fixed items, which may be read in the final hour before the exam?
problems.answer: The 1 page of summary you have already used, and nothing new.

steps.title: Handle the Hard Question
steps.mastery: Move on from a question that has stalled without losing the paper.
steps.practice: Set a 2-minute rule in a mock: if a question has not started in 2 minutes, mark it and move to the next.
steps.detail: A stalled question is expensive twice, the minutes and the state it puts you in. Mark it with a star, move on, and come back with the paper mostly done and the panic gone. Most people find 1 or 2 starred questions are straightforward on the second visit.
steps.proof: A mock paper with starred questions, all revisited before the end.
steps.pitfall: Staying on question 3 for 18 minutes because giving up on it feels like failing.

problems.prompt: A question has not started after 2 minutes. What do you do?
problems.answer: Star it, move to the next question, and return later.

problems.prompt: Why is 18 minutes on a stalled question expensive twice?
problems.answer: It costs the minutes and leaves you in a worse state for the rest of the paper.

problems.prompt: What often happens on the 2nd visit to a starred question?
problems.answer: It is straightforward, because the paper is mostly done and the panic has gone.

steps.title: Sleep the Night Before
steps.mastery: Protect the last night's sleep as part of the preparation.
steps.practice: Set a finish time 2 hours before bed for 3 nights running and record what time you actually slept.
steps.detail: An hour of revision at midnight costs more than it adds, because recall and time management both degrade with lost sleep. Stop 2 hours before bed and do something undemanding. Practice it for 3 nights rather than only the night before, since a single early night rarely works on command.
steps.proof: 3 recorded sleep times after a 2-hour wind-down.
steps.pitfall: Revising until 1am the night before, which trades 2 marks of content for a worse morning.

problems.prompt: Why practice the wind-down for 3 nights rather than only the night before?
problems.answer: A single early night rarely works on command, so the pattern needs establishing.

problems.prompt: What does 1 hour of revision at midnight cost?
problems.answer: More than it adds, recall and time management both degrade with lost sleep.

problems.prompt: Revision stops how long before bed, 2 hours or 20 minutes?

steps.title: Debrief Your Own Nerves
steps.mastery: Record what the state actually did to your performance, and adjust.
steps.practice: After a timed mock, write 3 lines on what nerves cost you: time, blanks, or rushed reading.
steps.detail: The point is to make it specific. If you lost 6 marks to misreading 2 questions, the fix is the underlining routine, not calmness in general. If you lost 10 minutes to a stall, the fix is the 2-minute rule. Nerves you can attribute to a mechanism are nerves you can work on.
steps.proof: 3 lines naming what the state cost and which routine addresses it.
steps.pitfall: Concluding only that you were nervous, which points at no change.

problems.prompt: You lost 6 marks to misreading 2 questions. Which routine is the fix?
problems.answer: The underlining of command words and constraints.

problems.prompt: You lost 10 minutes to a stall on question 3. Which routine is the fix?
problems.answer: The 2-minute rule for starring and moving on.

problems.prompt: Why is "I was nervous" not a usable debrief line?
problems.answer: It names no mechanism, so it points at no change.

steps.title: Notes in Your Own Words
steps.mastery: Restate a source's sentence in your own wording without losing what it claims.
steps.practice: Rewrite this in under 12 words: "Cellular respiration converts glucose and oxygen into ATP, carbon dioxide and water."
steps.detail: Read the sentence, look away from it, then write what it said. Looking away is the whole trick, with the sentence in view you will copy its structure and change 2 words. Check afterwards that nothing was dropped: the inputs, the outputs and the direction all have to survive.
steps.proof: Your version is shorter, shares few words with the original, and still names glucose and oxygen going in and ATP coming out.
steps.pitfall: Swapping synonyms while keeping the sentence shape, which is copying with extra steps.

problems.prompt: Restate in under 10 words: "Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level."
problems.answer: Prices across the economy keep climbing over time.

problems.prompt: Which is a note in your own words: (a) "Respiration converts glucose plus oxygen to ATP, CO2 and water", (b) "Cells burn sugar with oxygen to make energy, giving off CO2 and water"?
problems.answer: (b). The first only swapped a word or two of the original.

problems.prompt: A 40-word paragraph became a 38-word note. State what has gone wrong.
problems.answer: Nothing was compressed, so the note is a transcription rather than a note.

steps.title: Two-Column Note Page
steps.mastery: Split a page so cues sit apart from the material they recover.
steps.practice: Rule a page 1 third to 2 thirds, put 8 cue questions on the left and their answers on the right.
steps.detail: The narrow left column holds only questions or keywords; the wide right holds the substance. Nothing on the left may give the answer away, because the left column is what you will read with the right covered. Leave 4 lines at the foot of the page for a summary written after the session.
steps.proof: With the right column covered, the 8 cues alone tell you what the page held.
steps.pitfall: Writing statements rather than questions on the left, so covering the right proves nothing.

problems.prompt: Turn the note "The Treaty of Versailles imposed 132 billion marks in reparations" into a left-column cue.
problems.answer: How much did Versailles demand in reparations?

problems.prompt: Which cue is usable: (a) "Reparations: 132 billion marks", (b) "How large were the reparations?"
problems.answer: (b). The first states the answer, so covering the right column tests nothing.

problems.prompt: A page holds 8 cues and you recover 5 answers. What goes in the summary at the foot?
problems.answer: The 3 you could not recover, named so the next session starts there.

steps.title: Compress to a Line
steps.mastery: Reduce a page of notes to the one sentence that carries its point.
steps.practice: Take 1 page of notes and write a single sentence under 20 words that a reader could rebuild the page from.
steps.detail: Write the sentence after the page is finished, not during. Ask what the page would still be true without, and drop that first. If the sentence needs 2 clauses joined by and, the page probably covered 2 things and wants splitting in half.
steps.proof: Reading your sentence a week later brings the page's argument back.
steps.pitfall: Listing the page's topics instead of saying what it claims about them.

problems.prompt: Compress to under 15 words: notes covering supply, demand, and how price settles where the 2 curves meet.
problems.answer: Price settles at the quantity where what sellers offer matches what buyers will take.

problems.prompt: Which is a compression: (a) "Supply, demand, equilibrium, surplus, shortage", (b) "Price moves until the amount offered equals the amount wanted"?
problems.answer: (b). The first is a list of headings, not a claim.

problems.prompt: Your 1-sentence summary needs 2 clauses joined by "and". What does that suggest about the page?
problems.answer: It covered 2 separate points and should be split into 2 pages with 1 summary each.

steps.title: Mark the Gaps
steps.mastery: Flag on the page itself the places where your notes stopped making sense.
steps.practice: Go through 1 set of notes and put a "?" beside every line you could not explain to somebody in 30 seconds.
steps.detail: Do this the same day, while you still remember which lines you wrote confidently and which you copied. A question mark is a promise to come back, so each one needs either an answer or a deletion within the week, a page of unanswered marks is a page you have learned to skip.
steps.proof: Every line on the page is either explainable or carries a "?".
steps.pitfall: Marking nothing because the notes look familiar, which confuses recognizing your handwriting with understanding it.

problems.prompt: You can read a line of your notes but not explain it. What does the line get?
problems.answer: A question mark, answered or deleted within the week.

problems.prompt: Which page is in better shape: (a) 20 clean lines, none marked, (b) 20 lines with 4 marked "?"
problems.answer: (b). It knows where its 4 weak points are.

problems.prompt: A page carries 11 marks out of 14 lines. State what to do with the page.
problems.answer: Rewrite it from the source, the notes were copied rather than understood.

steps.title: Notes You Reuse
steps.mastery: Return to a page of notes and leave it better than you found it.
steps.practice: Reopen 1 page from last week, answer its 2 oldest "?" marks and add 1 link to another page.
steps.detail: A note you never reopen was a transcription with extra steps. Each visit should change the page: an answered mark, a tighter summary line, a cross-reference to the page that explains it. Date each change in the margin so you can see which pages get used and which you have been avoiding.
steps.proof: The page has fewer marks than last week and 1 new link on it.
steps.pitfall: Rewriting the page neatly instead of answering what it got stuck on.

problems.prompt: A page has been reopened 4 times with no change to it. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: It is being reread rather than used, so nothing on it is being fixed.

problems.prompt: Which counts as a reuse: (a) copying the page out neatly, (b) answering 2 of its "?" marks and linking it to the page that explains them?
problems.answer: (b). Neatness changes nothing the page got wrong.

problems.prompt: You have 12 pages and only 3 have margin dates. State what the other 9 are.
problems.answer: Pages written once and never used, which is the failure this step exists to catch.

steps.title: Identify Upcoming Assignments
steps.mastery: List all assignments and their due dates within the next month.
steps.practice: Write down the due date and required pages for Assignment 1, due in 12 days, covering pages 45‑60.
steps.detail: Open your course syllabus or online portal. Locate every assignment that falls within the next 30 days. For each, note the exact number of days until it is due and copy the page range or topic that must be covered. Record this information in a simple table so you can refer to it later when you start planning your study time.
steps.proof: The list shows Assignment 1: due in 12 days, pages 45‑60.
steps.pitfall: Missing the exact due‑day count or writing the wrong page range.

problems.prompt: What is the due‑day count for Assignment 1?
List the page range for Assignment 1.
If Assignment 1 is due in 12 days, on which calendar day (counting today as day 0) must it be submitted?
problems.hint: Add the due‑day count to today.

steps.title: Calculate Study Load
steps.mastery: Convert each assignment into total study minutes needed.
steps.practice: Estimate 30 minutes per 5 pages and compute minutes for Assignment 1 (pages 45‑60).
steps.detail: Decide on a realistic reading‑and‑note‑taking speed, such as 30 minutes for every 5 pages of textbook. Count the pages required for the assignment, divide by 5, then multiply by 30 to get the total minutes you will need. Write the result next to the assignment in your table so you have a clear time target.
steps.proof: 15 pages × 30 min/5 pages = 90 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Using the wrong pages‑to‑time ratio or forgetting to multiply.

problems.prompt: Calculate study minutes for Assignment 1 which has 15 pages, using 30 minutes per 5 pages.
Using 30 minutes per 5 pages, how many minutes are required for Assignment 1 (pages 45‑59)?
If you mistakenly used 25 minutes per 5 pages for the 15‑page Assignment 1, what incorrect total would you obtain?
problems.hint: Apply the wrong ratio to the 15 pages.

steps.title: Create Daily Slots
steps.mastery: Allocate specific study blocks each day to meet the total minutes before the due date.
steps.practice: Schedule three 30‑minute blocks on days 1, 3, and 5 leading up to Assignment 1.
steps.detail: Look at your personal calendar for the next 5 days. Choose three separate days that are free enough to host a focused 30‑minute session. Write the day numbers and the length of each block next to the assignment entry. Ensure the total of the blocks equals the minutes you calculated in the previous step.
steps.proof: Sum of blocks = 90 minutes, matching the needed time.
steps.pitfall: Over‑booking a day or leaving a day empty when minutes remain.

problems.prompt: How many minutes are in one 30‑minute study block?
If you schedule three 30‑minute blocks on days 1, 3, 5, what is the total study minutes scheduled?
If you add a fourth 30‑minute block on day 2, what total minutes would you have scheduled?

steps.title: Build a Mini‑Schedule
steps.mastery: Arrange the study blocks in chronological order with clear start times.
steps.practice: Write a schedule: Day 1 09:00‑09:30, Day 3 14:00‑14:30, Day 5 19:00‑19:30 for Assignment 1.
steps.detail: Take the days you selected and assign a concrete start time for each 30‑minute block. Use a 24‑hour or AM/PM format consistently. Record the three entries in a notebook or digital calendar so you can see the order and avoid double‑booking. Verify that the total time adds up to the required 90 minutes.
steps.proof: The three entries cover 90 minutes before the 12‑day deadline.
steps.pitfall: Confusing AM/PM or writing overlapping times.

problems.prompt: What is the start time of the Day 1 study block in the schedule?
How many total minutes are covered by the three schedule entries (each 30 minutes)?
If the Day 3 block is moved to 13:30‑14:00, does it overlap with the Day 5 block at 19:00‑19:30?

steps.title: Review and Adjust
steps.mastery: Check progress after each block and shift remaining blocks if needed.
steps.practice: After Day 1, note 30 minutes completed; move the Day 5 block to Day 4 to keep a buffer.
steps.detail: At the end of each study session, tick off the minutes you actually finished. If a block was missed or ran short, relocate the remaining time to an earlier day to maintain a safety margin before the deadline. Update your written schedule each time you make a change so the plan always reflects reality.
steps.proof: Total completed 30 min, remaining 60 min scheduled for Days 3 and 4.
steps.pitfall: Failing to update the schedule after a missed block.

problems.prompt: After completing the Day 1 block, how many minutes have been finished?
After moving the Day 5 block to Day 4, how many minutes remain scheduled for Days 3 and 4 combined?
If the Day 3 block is missed, how can you redistribute the remaining 60 minutes into two 30‑minute blocks on Days 4 and 5 to meet the deadline?
problems.answer: Schedule a 30‑minute block on Day 4 and another on Day 5.

steps.title: Cover the Solution
steps.mastery: Attempt a problem with the worked answer physically out of sight.
steps.practice: Fold the page so the solution is hidden and attempt 1 problem for 5 minutes before checking.
steps.detail: Reading a worked solution and following it feels like problem-solving and is closer to reading. Folding the page, or covering it with a card, makes the attempt unavoidable. Give it a fixed 5 minutes so the attempt has an end, then check in full rather than line by line.
steps.proof: A 5-minute attempt on paper, made before the solution was seen.
steps.pitfall: Glancing at the first line of the solution "to get started", which supplies the only decision that mattered.

problems.prompt: Which is problem practice: (a) reading 6 worked solutions, (b) attempting 3 problems with the solutions covered?
problems.answer: (b). Only the covered attempt makes you choose the method.

problems.prompt: You read the 1st line of a solution to get started. What has been given away?
problems.answer: The choice of method, which is usually the whole difficulty.

problems.prompt: Why fix the attempt at 5 minutes rather than working until it is solved?
problems.answer: It bounds the struggle so checking happens, and marks how far you got unaided.

steps.title: Write the Method First
steps.mastery: Name the method a problem needs before any working is done.
steps.practice: Write 1 line naming the method for 6 problems, without solving any of them.
steps.detail: Separating the choice from the execution trains the part exams actually test. For each problem write something like "factorize, then set each bracket to 0". Six of these takes 5 minutes and shows whether the difficulty is choosing or computing, which are 2 different things to practice.
steps.proof: 6 named methods, and you can say which of the 6 you were unsure about.
steps.pitfall: Starting the algebra while writing the plan, which merges the 2 skills again.

problems.prompt: Name the method for: solve x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0.
problems.answer: Factorize into (x - 2)(x - 3), then set each bracket to 0.

problems.prompt: Name the method for: find the angle in a right triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5.
You name all 6 methods correctly but get 3 wrong when solving. Which skill needs the work?
problems.answer: Execution, the method choice is already sound.

steps.title: Check Before Marking
steps.mastery: Test your own answer for sense before comparing it with the book.
steps.practice: Substitute your answer back into 3 problems and confirm each satisfies the original equation.
steps.detail: Substitution, units and rough size catch most errors without the answer key. For x = 4 in x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0, put 4 back and see 16 - 20 + 4 = 0. Doing this first means the key confirms your check rather than replacing it, and you keep the habit for an exam where there is no key.
steps.proof: 3 answers verified by substitution before the key was opened.
steps.pitfall: Going straight to the answers, which trains you to need them.

problems.prompt: Check x = 4 in x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0.
You calculate a speed of 3000 m/s for a cyclist. What does the sense check say?
problems.answer: It is far too large, about 3 orders of magnitude out, so the working has an error.

problems.prompt: Why substitute before opening the answer key, in under 20 words?
problems.answer: It builds the check you will need in an exam, where no key exists.

steps.title: Work to the Last Line
steps.mastery: Finish a problem completely rather than stopping when the route is clear.
steps.practice: Take 4 problems you would abandon once the method is obvious and carry each to a final numeric answer.
steps.detail: Stopping at "I know how to do this" hides the arithmetic slips, the sign errors and the simplification that is actually where marks go. Carry all 4 to a boxed final value with units, then mark them. Expect at least 1 of the 4 to be wrong despite the method being right.
steps.proof: 4 boxed final answers with units, marked right or wrong.
steps.pitfall: Counting a problem as done at the point you can see the route, which is where most marks are lost.

problems.prompt: You see the method for 4 problems and complete none. How many marks would that score in an exam?
problems.answer: Only the method marks, usually 1 or 2 of each question's total.

problems.prompt: Of 4 problems where the method was right, 1 comes out wrong. What does that number tell you?
problems.answer: That about a quarter of your losses are execution, not understanding.

problems.prompt: What are the 2 things a final answer must carry?

steps.title: Attempt Above Your Level
steps.mastery: Spend a bounded stretch on a problem you may not solve.
steps.practice: Spend 12 minutes on 1 problem a level above your usual, recording each thing you tried.
steps.detail: A problem you cannot do is where the learning is densest, and the record is what turns it from wasted time into work: 3 lines saying what you tried and why each stopped. After 12 minutes, read the solution and compare it against your list to see which of your attempts was closest.
steps.proof: A list of what you tried, and 1 line saying which attempt the solution resembled.
steps.pitfall: Giving a hard problem an hour, which costs the rest of the session for 1 question.

problems.prompt: Why bound a hard attempt at 12 minutes rather than working until it yields?
problems.answer: An unbounded attempt eats the session for 1 question, and the record is what carries the value.

problems.prompt: After 12 minutes you have 3 failed attempts written down. What do you do with them?
problems.answer: Compare them against the solution and see which was closest and why it stopped.

problems.prompt: Which is more use: 1 hard problem with 3 recorded attempts, or 8 routine problems solved?
problems.answer: The hard one, provided the attempts were recorded, that is where new method comes from.

steps.title: Time a Set of Ten
steps.mastery: Work a set under the clock at roughly exam pace.
steps.practice: Work 10 routine problems in 20 minutes, marking the clock time beside each as you finish it.
steps.detail: Pace is a separate skill from method, and the only way to find yours is to measure it. Writing the time beside each answer shows where you slowed: 1 problem eating 7 of the 20 minutes is the thing to study, and it is invisible if you only record the total.
steps.proof: 10 answers with times beside them, totaling about 20 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Stopping the clock to look something up, which makes the pace figure meaningless.

problems.prompt: 10 problems in 20 minutes gives what average per problem?
1 of your 10 problems took 7 minutes. What does the per-problem timing show that a total cannot?
problems.answer: Which single problem type is costing the pace.

problems.prompt: You pause the clock to look up a formula. What has the timing become?
problems.answer: Meaningless as a pace figure, because the exam will not pause.

steps.title: Build Your Own Problem
steps.mastery: Write a problem of a given type and solve it correctly.
steps.practice: Write 2 quadratic problems with integer roots, then solve them and check the roots are what you intended.
steps.detail: To set a problem you have to work backwards from the answer, which uses the method in reverse and exposes gaps that solving does not. Start from the roots, say 3 and -5, expand to get x^2 + 2x - 15, then solve your own expression and confirm the roots come back.
steps.proof: 2 problems whose solutions return the roots you started from.
steps.pitfall: Writing a problem with roots that are not integers by accident, then assuming your solving was wrong.

problems.prompt: Build a quadratic with roots 3 and -5.
Build a quadratic with roots 2 and 2, and say what is special about it.
Why does writing a problem expose gaps that solving 10 does not?
problems.answer: It runs the method backwards, which needs the structure rather than the procedure.

steps.title: Survey Before Reading
steps.mastery: Map a chapter's structure from its headings before reading a word of the body.
steps.practice: Take a 20-page chapter and write out its 6 headings, 2 figure captions and the summary box, in 4 minutes.
steps.detail: Read only what is in bold or large type, plus anything in a box. Write the headings down the left of a page as a list, leaving 3 blank lines under each. That list is the skeleton you will hang the reading on, and the blank lines are where the answers go.
steps.proof: You can say what the chapter covers, in order, without having read a paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Drifting into reading the first paragraph properly, which turns a 4-minute survey into 20 minutes.

problems.prompt: A chapter runs 18 pages with 5 headings and 3 figures. How many lines does your skeleton hold before you start reading?
problems.answer: 8, one per heading and one per figure caption.

problems.prompt: Which of these belongs in a survey: (a) the chapter summary, (b) the third paragraph of section 2, (c) the bold key terms?
problems.answer: (a) and (c). The paragraph is body text and waits until the reading pass.

problems.prompt: You surveyed a 30-page chapter in 12 minutes. State what went wrong and what the target was.
problems.answer: 12 minutes is a reading pass, not a survey; 30 pages of headings and boxes should take about 5 minutes.

steps.title: Turn Headings Into Questions
steps.mastery: Convert a heading into the question the section answers, so reading has a target.
steps.practice: Rewrite these 3 headings as questions: "Enzyme Inhibition", "The Marshall Plan", "Big-O Notation".
steps.detail: Put what, why or how in front of the heading and finish the sentence. "Enzyme Inhibition" becomes "How is an enzyme stopped from working, and by what?". A heading you cannot make a question of is one you do not yet know the shape of, which is itself worth noticing.
steps.proof: Each of your 3 questions can be answered in a sentence once the section is read.
steps.pitfall: Writing a question so broad, "What is this section about?", that any paragraph answers it.

problems.prompt: Turn the heading "Diminishing Returns" into a question worth reading for.
problems.answer: Why does each extra unit of input give less output, and where does the turn happen?

problems.prompt: Which is the better reading question for "The Krebs Cycle": (a) What is the Krebs cycle about? (b) What goes into the Krebs cycle and what comes out?
problems.answer: (b). It names what an answer must contain, so you can tell when you have found it.

problems.prompt: A section is headed "Results". Write 2 questions for it that a heading that vague cannot answer on its own.
problems.answer: Results of what measurement, and did they support the hypothesis?

steps.title: Read for the Answers
steps.mastery: Read a section hunting the answer to your own question rather than sentence by sentence.
steps.practice: Read 1 section with your question above it and stop at the sentence that answers it; mark that sentence with a bracket.
steps.detail: Keep the question visible at the top of the page. When you reach the answering sentence, bracket it and write the answer in your own words in the blank lines under the heading. If you finish the section without finding an answer, the question was wrong, rewrite it before moving on.
steps.proof: Every question on your skeleton has a bracketed sentence and a one-line answer under it.
steps.pitfall: Highlighting as you go instead of answering, which leaves a yellow page and no answers.

problems.prompt: You have read 4 pages of a section and found no answer to your question. What are the 2 possible causes?
problems.answer: The question was wrong for that section, or the answer is later in a part you have not reached.

problems.prompt: Which page is better evidence of reading to learn: (a) 30 highlighted lines, (b) 5 bracketed sentences with 5 answers written beside them?
problems.answer: (b). Highlighting records where you were; the written answers record what you got.

problems.prompt: A 6-heading chapter leaves you 6 answers of about 15 words each. How many words of notes is that, and what should they cover?
problems.answer: About 90 words, covering the answer to every question the chapter's headings raise.

steps.title: Recite Without Looking
steps.mastery: Say a section's answer aloud with the book shut, before reading the next one.
steps.practice: Close the book at the end of 1 section and say its answer aloud in under 30 seconds.
steps.detail: Do this at the section boundary rather than at the end of the chapter, while the material is still recoverable and the gap is still cheap to fix. Where the recitation stalls, open the book at that point only, read the 2 or 3 sentences you needed, and say it again from the top.
steps.proof: You can give the section's answer aloud twice running with the book shut.
steps.pitfall: Reciting with the page in view, which tests recognition rather than recall.

problems.prompt: A chapter has 6 sections. How many recitations does this step ask for, and when?
problems.answer: 6, one at the end of each section, before the next one is read.

problems.prompt: You stall halfway through reciting section 3. What is the next action: (a) reread section 3 whole, (b) open it at the stall, read 2 sentences, recite again?
problems.answer: (b). Reread only the gap, then test the whole thing again.

problems.prompt: Why is reciting at the end of each section better than one recitation at the end of a 6-section chapter?
problems.answer: The gaps are found while they are still cheap to fix, and each section is tested while it can still be recalled.

steps.title: Review the Whole Chapter
steps.mastery: Rebuild a chapter's argument from your own skeleton a day after reading it.
steps.practice: Cover your notes a day after reading and rebuild the chapter's 6 answers from the headings alone.
steps.detail: Work from the heading list with the answers covered. Write what you can, then uncover and mark what you missed with a dot. Two dots on the same answer over two reviews means the material never went in, and that answer is what tomorrow's session opens with rather than the next chapter.
steps.proof: You can produce the chapter's answers from its headings, and the dots show which 1 or 2 need another pass.
steps.pitfall: Rereading the notes instead of covering them, which feels like review and tests nothing.

problems.prompt: You rebuild 6 answers and miss 2. What does the next session open with?
problems.answer: The 2 missed answers, before any new chapter is started.

problems.prompt: Which is the review: (a) reading your notes twice, (b) covering them and writing the answers, then marking the misses?
problems.answer: (b). Only the covered attempt shows what you actually have.

problems.prompt: An answer collects a dot on 2 separate reviews. State what that means and what it changes.
problems.answer: It never went in, so it is retaught from the source rather than reviewed again.

steps.title: Shut the Book First
steps.mastery: Attempt an answer from memory before any source is opened.
steps.practice: Shut the book and write everything you can about 1 topic for 3 minutes, then open it and mark the misses.
steps.detail: The order matters more than the effort: attempt, then check. Opening the book first turns the exercise into reading, and the attempt is where the learning is, including the parts you get wrong, as long as you correct them straight after. Time it, so the blank page has a visible end.
steps.proof: You have a page written from memory and a marked list of what it missed.
steps.pitfall: Peeking when the page goes blank after 40 seconds, which is exactly the point the work starts.

problems.prompt: Which is retrieval practice: (a) covering the page and writing the 5 stages of mitosis, (b) highlighting the 5 stages again?
problems.answer: (a). Only the covered attempt makes you produce the answer.

problems.prompt: You go blank 40 seconds into a 3-minute attempt. What is the instruction?
problems.answer: Stay on the blank page for the remaining 2 minutes 20 before opening the book.

problems.prompt: State the order of the 2 halves of this step, and what happens if they are swapped.
problems.answer: Attempt then check; swapped, it becomes reading and tests nothing.

steps.title: Write the Question Card
steps.mastery: Turn material into questions that have one answer you can mark.
steps.practice: Write 10 question cards from 1 page of notes, each answerable in under 15 words.
steps.detail: One fact per card, and the question has to be specific enough that you can mark yourself right or wrong. "Describe the French Revolution" cannot be marked; "In what year did the Bastille fall?" can. Where a fact needs 3 cards to cover, write 3.
steps.proof: Each of the 10 cards can be marked right or wrong without argument.
steps.pitfall: Writing cards so broad that every attempt is partly right, which makes the deck unmarkable.

problems.prompt: Which card is markable: (a) "Explain photosynthesis", (b) "What 2 reactants does photosynthesis use?"
problems.answer: (b). Its answer is carbon dioxide and water, which is right or wrong.

problems.prompt: Split "Describe the causes of the First World War" into 2 markable cards.
problems.answer: Which alliance system bound Russia to Serbia? and What event of 1914 triggered the mobilizations?

problems.prompt: A page of notes yields 4 cards from 20 facts. State what has gone wrong.
problems.answer: The cards are too broad, 20 facts should give closer to 20 markable questions.

steps.title: Test Before You Reread
steps.mastery: Use a test as the first contact with material you met yesterday.
steps.practice: Open a session by testing 12 cards from yesterday before reading 1 line of anything new.
steps.detail: The first 5 minutes of a session are usually spent rereading yesterday's notes, which is the least useful thing available. Spend them on the cards instead. The misses tell you what to reread, so the rereading that follows is aimed at 3 cards rather than 6 pages.
steps.proof: Your session opens with a score out of 12 and a list of which ones to reread.
steps.pitfall: Reading the notes "just to warm up" first, which inflates the score and hides the gaps.

problems.prompt: You score 9 out of 12 on yesterday's cards. What do you reread?
Which opening is better: (a) reread 6 pages then test, (b) test 12 cards then reread what the misses point at?
problems.answer: (b). The test decides what the rereading is for.

problems.prompt: State why a score of 9 taken after rereading is worth less than a 9 taken before.
problems.answer: It measures what is on the page in front of you, not what you can produce without it.

steps.title: Say It Before You Check
steps.mastery: Commit to an answer aloud before the card is turned over.
steps.practice: Work 15 cards saying each answer aloud in full before flipping, with no half-answers allowed.
steps.detail: Saying it aloud stops the almost-answer, which is the thing that makes a deck feel easier than it is: the silent "yes, I know this" is not an answer and cannot be marked. If the spoken answer is partial, the card is a miss, however familiar it looked.
steps.proof: Every card in the run of 15 got a spoken answer and a hard right or wrong.
steps.pitfall: Counting "I knew that" as a hit once the back of the card is showing.

problems.prompt: You flip a card and think "of course, I knew it" without having said anything. Hit or miss?
problems.answer: A miss. Nothing was produced before the answer was visible.

problems.prompt: Why does saying each of 15 answers aloud raise your miss count on a deck you have used before?
problems.answer: Because it exposes the almost-answers that silent recognition was scoring as hits.

problems.prompt: Out of 15 cards you say 11 in full and half-answer 4. What is the score?
problems.answer: 11 out of 15, the 4 partials count as misses.

steps.title: Mark and Sort the Deck
steps.mastery: Split a tested deck by what it showed, so the next run is shorter.
steps.practice: Sort 20 tested cards into 3 piles, got it, shaky, missed, and count each pile.
steps.detail: Three piles rather than two, because the shaky ones are where the next session earns most and they disappear if you only track right and wrong. The missed pile goes back to the source now; the shaky pile is tomorrow's opening test; the got-it pile waits a week.
steps.proof: You can state the size of all 3 piles and when each is next seen.
steps.pitfall: Putting a card in got-it because you have seen it 5 times rather than because you answered it.

problems.prompt: A deck of 20 sorts into 12 got it, 5 shaky, 3 missed. Which pile opens tomorrow's session?
problems.answer: The 5 shaky, after the 3 missed have been reread from the source today.

problems.prompt: Why 3 piles rather than 2?
problems.answer: The shaky cards are where most is gained and a right-or-wrong split hides them among the hits.

problems.prompt: You answered a card correctly but slowly and with effort. Which pile?
problems.answer: Shaky. A hit that cost effort is not yet a hit you can rely on.

steps.title: Retrieval on Paper Weekly
steps.mastery: Produce a topic's whole content from a blank page once a week.
steps.practice: Fill 1 blank page from memory on a topic you tested 6 days ago, then mark it against your notes.
steps.detail: A card tests a fact; a blank page tests whether the facts are connected, which is the thing exams ask for and decks quietly skip. Write for 10 minutes without stopping, then mark in a different color: missing, wrong, and out of order all get their own marks.
steps.proof: The marked page shows what you have, and the gaps are in a different color from the content.
steps.pitfall: Rewriting your notes from memory in their original order, which tests the order rather than the material.

problems.prompt: What does a blank page test that a deck of 20 cards does not?
problems.answer: Whether the facts connect, order, structure and what follows from what.

problems.prompt: You produce 80% of a topic but in a jumbled order. How is that marked?
problems.answer: As content present but structure missed, which is its own mark and its own fix.

problems.prompt: Why mark the page in a 2nd color rather than correcting it in place?
problems.answer: So a later reader can see what was produced from memory and what was added afterwards.

steps.title: Count the Days You Have
steps.mastery: Work out the real hours available before planning anything.
steps.practice: Count the days to the exam, subtract the days already committed, and write the hours left at 2 usable hours a day.
steps.detail: Start from the calendar rather than the syllabus: 21 days at 2 usable hours is 42 hours, minus 6 days already committed leaves about 30. That number decides what the plan can contain. Written down, it also settles arguments with yourself about whether everything can be covered twice.
steps.proof: 1 figure for usable hours, built from days and daily capacity.
steps.pitfall: Planning from the topic list, which always produces a timetable needing more hours than exist.

problems.prompt: 21 days remain at 2 usable hours a day, with 6 days committed elsewhere. How many hours are left?
Your plan needs 45 hours and you have 30. What has to change?
problems.answer: The plan, 15 hours of it must be cut or compressed.

problems.prompt: Why start from the calendar rather than the 12-topic syllabus?
problems.answer: The syllabus always asks for more hours than exist, so the plan has to start from what is real.

steps.title: Weight Topics by Marks
steps.mastery: Give each topic time in proportion to what it is worth and how weak you are.
steps.practice: Score 8 topics 1 to 5 for marks carried and 1 to 5 for weakness, multiply, and rank them.
steps.detail: The product gives a rough priority that beats intuition, which over-weights whatever is most recently frightening. A topic worth 5 you are strong at scores 5; a topic worth 3 you cannot do scores 15. Allocate the 30 hours down the ranking until they run out.
steps.proof: 8 topics ranked by the product, with hours allocated down the list.
steps.pitfall: Giving equal time to 8 topics, which spends your best hours on what you already know.

problems.prompt: Topic A: marks 5, weakness 1. Topic B: marks 3, weakness 5. Which ranks higher?
Why multiply the 2 scores rather than adding them?
problems.answer: A topic has to be both heavy and weak to deserve the most time, which the product reflects.

problems.prompt: You allocate 30 hours equally across 8 topics. What is the cost?
problems.answer: The heaviest weak topics get under 4 hours each while strong ones get the same.

steps.title: Schedule Two Passes
steps.mastery: Plan for every topic to be met at least twice, separated by days.
steps.practice: Lay 8 topics across 3 weeks so each appears twice with at least 5 days between the 2 passes.
steps.detail: One pass is learning, and the second is where it becomes retrievable. Put the first passes in week 1 and 2 and the second passes in week 2 and 3, with the gap deliberate. A timetable where a topic appears once is a timetable that will be a surprise on the day.
steps.proof: A 3-week grid where all 8 topics appear twice with a gap of 5 days or more.
steps.pitfall: Filling 3 weeks with 1 long pass through everything, which finishes the week before and is gone by the exam.

problems.prompt: A topic is revised on day 3. What is the earliest its 2nd pass should fall?
problems.answer: Day 8, keeping at least a 5-day gap.

problems.prompt: Why does 1 pass through 8 topics over 3 weeks leave you exposed?
problems.answer: Nothing is revisited, so the earliest topics have faded by the exam.

problems.prompt: In a 3-week plan, which weeks hold the 2nd passes?
problems.answer: Weeks 2 and 3, after their first passes in weeks 1 and 2.

steps.title: Put Tasks Not Topics
steps.mastery: Write a timetable in checkable tasks rather than subject names.
steps.practice: Convert 4 timetable slots from topic names into specific tasks with a count in each.
steps.detail: "Tuesday: trigonometry" cannot be finished or failed; "Tuesday: 12 mixed trigonometry questions from paper 2, marked" can. The count matters because it makes the slot a fixed piece of work rather than an amount of sitting, and it tells you afterwards whether the slot was kept.
steps.proof: 4 slots each naming a task, a count and a source.
steps.pitfall: Writing topic names for 15 slots, which produces a timetable nobody can be behind on.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Tuesday: trigonometry" as a checkable task.
problems.answer: Tuesday: 12 mixed trigonometry questions from paper 2, marked.

problems.prompt: Why can a slot reading "revise chapter 5" not be failed?
problems.answer: Nothing in it is countable, so any amount of sitting satisfies it.

problems.prompt: What 3 things does each of the 4 slots name?
problems.answer: A task, a count and a source.

steps.title: Leave Slack in the Plan
steps.mastery: Build a timetable that survives losing 2 days.
steps.practice: Add 3 empty catch-up slots to a 3-week plan and leave them empty until something slips.
steps.detail: Every plan meets an illness, a family day or a topic that takes twice as long. A plan with no slack converts the first slip into a rewrite, and a rewritten plan is usually abandoned. Three empty slots across 3 weeks absorb that, and if nothing slips they become second passes on the weakest topic.
steps.proof: A 3-week plan with 3 slots deliberately empty.
steps.pitfall: Filling every slot because the topic list is long, which makes the plan brittle.

problems.prompt: You lose 2 days to illness with 3 catch-up slots planned. Does the timetable need rewriting?
problems.answer: No, the slack absorbs it and the plan stands.

problems.prompt: Nothing slips by week 3 and 3 slots are free. What goes in them?
problems.answer: Second passes on the weakest-ranked topics.

problems.prompt: Why does a plan with 0 slack usually get abandoned?
problems.answer: The first slip forces a rewrite, and the rewrite rarely survives.

steps.title: Review the Plan Weekly
steps.mastery: Adjust a timetable from what actually happened, once a week.
steps.practice: At the end of week 1, count slots planned and slots done, then re-rank the remaining topics.
steps.detail: A plan is a forecast and week 1 is the data. If 9 of 12 slots were kept, the capacity figure is about right; if 5 were, the plan needs cutting rather than more discipline. Re-rank the remaining topics too, because the weakness scores have changed since you started.
steps.proof: Week 1's planned and done counts, and a re-ranked topic list for week 2.
steps.pitfall: Keeping the original plan out of loyalty to it, which means revising to a forecast made before any data existed.

problems.prompt: You planned 12 slots in week 1 and kept 5. Cut the plan or try harder?
problems.answer: Cut it, the capacity estimate was wrong by more than half.

problems.prompt: Why re-rank the remaining topics after week 1?
problems.answer: The weakness scores have changed, so the priorities have too.

problems.prompt: You kept 11 of 12 slots. What does that say about the capacity figure?
problems.answer: It was about right, so the plan can stand.

steps.title: Timetable the Last Week
steps.mastery: Plan the final days as testing rather than as new learning.
steps.practice: Plan the last 5 days as 3 timed papers and 2 sessions on the errors they show.
steps.detail: The final week should contain almost no first contact: a new topic met 3 days out will not be retrievable and costs the consolidation of everything else. Alternate paper and repair, paper on day 1, errors on day 2, so each test has somewhere to be acted on.
steps.proof: A 5-day plan of 3 papers alternating with 2 error sessions.
steps.pitfall: Saving the hardest topic for the last 3 days because it needs the most work, which is when it can least be learned.

problems.prompt: In a 5-day final plan, how many days are papers and how many are repair?
Why should a topic not be met for the first time 3 days before the exam?
problems.answer: It will not be retrievable and it costs the consolidation of the rest.

problems.prompt: What does each of the 3 papers need scheduled after it?
problems.answer: A session on the errors it showed.

steps.title: Judge the Plan by Scores
steps.mastery: Measure a revision plan by test performance rather than by slots ticked.
steps.practice: Compare your paper scores at the start and end of 3 weeks, and say which topics moved.
steps.detail: A completed timetable is not the goal; a higher score is. Sit a paper in week 1 and another in week 3 under the same conditions, then compare by topic. A topic that got 6 hours and did not move needs a different method rather than more time, which is the most useful thing this comparison tells you.
steps.proof: Two comparable paper scores with a per-topic difference.
steps.pitfall: Judging the 3 weeks by how much of the timetable was completed.

problems.prompt: A topic got 6 hours across 3 weeks and its score did not move. More time or a different method?
problems.answer: A different method, 6 hours of the same approach has already been tested.

problems.prompt: Why sit the week-1 and week-3 papers under the same conditions?
problems.answer: Otherwise the difference measures the conditions rather than the revision.

problems.prompt: Which is the better measure of 3 weeks: 34 of 36 slots ticked, or 12 marks gained per paper?
problems.answer: The marks, the slots measure activity, not progress.

steps.title: Write the Finish Line
steps.mastery: Define what finishing looks like before starting a self-taught subject.
steps.practice: Write 1 sentence naming what you will be able to do at the end, with 2 things that will prove it.
steps.detail: With no course there is no syllabus and no exam, so the finish line has to be written or the project drifts. "Read a 200-line Python script and explain what it does" is a finish line; "learn Python" is not. The 2 proofs are what you will actually produce, and they double as the test.
steps.proof: 1 sentence and 2 named proofs you could show somebody.
steps.pitfall: Starting with "learn X", which has no end and therefore no progress.

problems.prompt: Which is a finish line: (a) learn Spanish, (b) hold a 10-minute conversation about your job in Spanish?
problems.answer: (b). It names something you can do and check.

problems.prompt: What do the 2 proofs also serve as?
problems.answer: The test of whether the subject is finished.

problems.prompt: Why does "learn Python" produce drift?
problems.answer: It has no end, so no session can be measured against it.

steps.title: Build the Syllabus
steps.mastery: Sequence a subject yourself, in dependency order.
steps.practice: Break your subject into 8 topics and draw 6 arrows showing which topic each one needs first.
steps.detail: Take the contents pages of 2 or 3 books and look for the order they agree on, that agreement is most of a syllabus. Then draw the dependencies, because the order you learn in matters more than the list. Where 2 books disagree on order, either is usually fine.
steps.proof: 8 topics with 6 dependency arrows, built from the agreement between 2 sources.
steps.pitfall: Inventing an order from scratch, when 3 contents pages already encode one.

problems.prompt: Where does the order for 8 topics come from most cheaply?
problems.answer: The agreement between the contents pages of 2 or 3 books.

problems.prompt: Two books disagree on whether topic 4 comes before topic 5. What do you do?
problems.answer: Pick either, where sources disagree, the order usually does not matter much.

problems.prompt: Why are the 6 arrows more important than the list of 8?
problems.answer: The learning order decides whether each topic is met with what it depends on.

steps.title: Set Your Own Deadline
steps.mastery: Impose a date that makes a self-taught project finite.
steps.practice: Set a date 10 weeks out, divide your 8 topics across it, and write the 2 checkpoint dates.
steps.detail: Nobody else will supply the deadline, and without one the project expands until it is abandoned. Ten weeks, 8 topics, with checkpoints at weeks 4 and 8 where you produce something. Tell somebody the date, because a deadline nobody knows about is a wish.
steps.proof: A finish date, 8 topics allocated, and 2 checkpoint dates somebody else knows.
steps.pitfall: Setting a date privately and moving it twice, which is the same as having none.

problems.prompt: 10 weeks and 8 topics. Roughly how long does each topic get?
Why tell somebody else the 10-week finish date?
problems.answer: A private deadline gets moved, and a moved deadline is no deadline.

problems.prompt: What happens at the week-4 and week-8 checkpoints?
problems.answer: You produce something that shows where the project actually is.

steps.title: Find the Problem Set
steps.mastery: Locate answered exercises for a subject nobody is setting you work in.
steps.practice: Find 2 sources of answered problems for your subject and work 5 of them today.
steps.detail: Self-teaching fails most often here: reading is easy to arrange and problems are not, so people read 6 books and cannot do anything. Look for textbooks with answers, problem collections, online judges or past papers. Without answers you cannot mark yourself, and unmarked practice entrenches errors.
steps.proof: 2 named sources with answers, and 5 problems worked and marked today.
steps.pitfall: Settling for a source with no answers because it is the one you found.

problems.prompt: Why is a source of 200 problems with no answers close to useless for self-teaching?
problems.answer: You cannot mark yourself, so errors get entrenched rather than caught.

problems.prompt: Name 2 kinds of source that supply answered problems.
problems.answer: Textbooks with answer sections, and past papers with mark schemes.

problems.prompt: You have read 6 books and worked 0 problems. What is the diagnosis?
problems.answer: Reading has replaced practice, which is the usual way self-teaching fails.

steps.title: Schedule It Like a Course
steps.mastery: Put self-taught work in fixed slots rather than in spare time.
steps.practice: Fix 3 weekly slots of 60 minutes for the subject and defend them for 2 weeks.
steps.detail: Spare time is the time that disappears first, so a subject living there is a subject that stops. Three fixed hours a week beats a nominal 10 that happen twice. Record kept or missed, because 2 weeks of that record tells you whether the slots are real.
steps.proof: A 2-week record of the 3 weekly slots, marked kept or missed.
steps.pitfall: Planning 10 hours a week of spare time, which produces 2 and a sense of failure.

problems.prompt: Which is better: 3 fixed hours a week or a nominal 10 in spare time?
problems.answer: The 3 fixed hours, spare time is what disappears first.

problems.prompt: You keep 3 of 6 slots over 2 weeks. What does the record suggest?
problems.answer: The slots are not realistically free and need moving.

problems.prompt: Why record slots kept and missed rather than the 10 hours studied?
problems.answer: It tests whether the schedule itself is real.

steps.title: Test Yourself on Schedule
steps.mastery: Create the tests a course would have set you.
steps.practice: Write a 10-question test for your first 2 topics, sit it cold a week later, and mark it.
steps.detail: Without tests, self-teaching runs on the feeling of understanding, which is exactly the thing that is unreliable. Write the test as you finish the topic, while you know what was hard, then leave it a week so sitting it is a real test. Mark it strictly against what you wrote.
steps.proof: A 10-question test, sat a week later, with a marked score.
steps.pitfall: Writing the test and sitting it the same afternoon, which measures the afternoon.

problems.prompt: When do you write the 10-question test, and when do you sit it?
problems.answer: Write it as the topic finishes; sit it about a week later.

problems.prompt: Why does sitting your own 10-question test the same afternoon measure very little?
problems.answer: The material is still in short-term memory, so it tests the afternoon.

problems.prompt: With 0 tests, what does self-teaching run on?
problems.answer: The feeling of understanding, which is the unreliable part.

steps.title: Get One Outside Reader
steps.mastery: Have somebody else check work nobody is marking.
steps.practice: Send 1 piece of your work to somebody who knows the subject and ask for 2 specific criticisms.
steps.detail: Self-teaching has no marker, and the errors you cannot see are exactly the ones you need found. Ask for 2 criticisms rather than an opinion, because "looks good" costs somebody nothing and tells you nothing. A forum, a colleague or a tutor for an hour all work.
steps.proof: 2 specific criticisms received, and 1 line on what each changes.
steps.pitfall: Asking whether the work is good, which invites encouragement rather than correction.

problems.prompt: Ask for an opinion or for 2 specific criticisms?
problems.answer: 2 specific criticisms, an opinion invites encouragement rather than correction.

problems.prompt: Why does a self-taught subject with 0 markers particularly need an outside reader?
problems.answer: There is no marker, so the errors you cannot see stay unfound.

problems.prompt: Name 2 places an outside reader can come from.
problems.answer: A subject forum, or a colleague or tutor for an hour.

steps.title: Keep a Work Log
steps.mastery: Record what each session produced so progress is visible without grades.
steps.practice: Log 6 sessions with 1 line each on what was produced, and read the 6 back.
steps.detail: A course supplies marks, deadlines and the sense of moving; a log is the substitute. One line per session naming the output, problems solved, pages read, a script that runs, and nothing about how it felt. Reading 6 back is what tells you whether the project is moving or circling.
steps.proof: 6 logged lines, each naming an output, read back in one go.
steps.pitfall: Logging hours and moods, which produces a diary rather than a record of progress.

problems.prompt: Which log line is usable: (a) "2 hours, felt slow", (b) "solved 8 of 10 exercises on gradients"?
What does reading 6 lines back in one go tell you?
problems.answer: Whether the project is moving or circling the same ground.

problems.prompt: In a self-taught subject, what do the 6 logged lines replace?
problems.answer: The marks and deadlines a course would have supplied.

steps.title: Finish and Prove It
steps.mastery: Deliver the proof you named at the start and judge yourself against it.
steps.practice: Produce the 2 proofs from your finish line and have 1 of them checked by somebody else.
steps.detail: Finishing is a decision, and without proofs the subject stays 80 per cent done forever. Produce both, compare them against the sentence you wrote at the start, and be strict: if a proof came out thinner than intended, name what is missing rather than adjusting the finish line to fit.
steps.proof: Both proofs produced, 1 externally checked, and a verdict against the original sentence.
steps.pitfall: Moving the finish line to match what you managed, which makes the whole exercise unfalsifiable.

problems.prompt: A proof comes out thinner than the finish line asked for. Adjust the line or name the gap?
problems.answer: Name the gap, adjusting the line makes the project unfalsifiable.

problems.prompt: Why have 1 of the 2 proofs checked externally?
problems.answer: Self-assessment at the finish is the least reliable point to rely on it.

problems.prompt: What keeps a self-taught subject at 80 per cent done forever?
problems.answer: Having no named proofs, so finishing is never a decision that can be made.

steps.title: Choose the Next Subject
steps.mastery: Use what one self-taught project revealed to pick and plan the next.
steps.practice: Write 3 lines on what went wrong in this project and 1 change you will make to the next plan.
steps.detail: The second self-taught subject should be cheaper than the first, and it only is if the failures are recorded: the slots that were not real, the reading that replaced problems, the finish line that was too vague. One change, not 6, carried into the next plan and checked at its first checkpoint.
steps.proof: 3 recorded failures and 1 specific change written into the next project's plan.
steps.pitfall: Starting the next subject the same way and finding out the same things again.

problems.prompt: Why 1 change carried forward rather than 6?
problems.answer: One gets applied and checked; 6 gets forgotten by week 2.

problems.prompt: Name 2 failures worth recording from a first self-taught project.
problems.answer: Slots that were never really free, and reading that replaced problem practice.

problems.prompt: When is the 1 carried change checked?
problems.answer: At the next project's first checkpoint, in about week 4.

steps.title: Start From the Question
steps.mastery: Choose material by the gap it fills rather than by what is available.
steps.practice: Write the 1 question you need answered, then name 2 sources likely to answer it and 1 that will not.
steps.detail: Searching before the question is stated is how 3 hours go on a reading list. State the gap in a sentence, "why does the sign flip when the inequality is multiplied by a negative", and the right kind of source becomes obvious: a worked-examples book, not a lecture series.
steps.proof: 1 written question, 2 candidate sources, and a reason the third was rejected.
steps.pitfall: Collecting 6 promising sources before knowing which question they are for.

problems.prompt: Your question is "why does the inequality sign flip on multiplying by -2". Which is the better source: a 40-minute lecture or a worked-examples page?
problems.answer: The worked-examples page, the question is narrow and specific.

problems.prompt: You have 6 sources and no written question. What is the next action?
problems.answer: Write the question, then discard the sources that do not answer it.

problems.prompt: Why does stating the gap in 1 sentence narrow the search?
problems.answer: The form of the answer implies the kind of source that carries it.

steps.title: Past Papers First
steps.mastery: Use past papers to see what is actually asked before reading around.
steps.practice: Take 3 past papers and tally how many marks each topic carried across them.
steps.detail: A syllabus lists topics; past papers show weights. Tallying 3 papers by topic usually shows 2 or 3 topics carrying a third of the marks and several worth 4 marks in 3 years. That tally decides where the reading goes, and it takes about 20 minutes to build.
steps.proof: A tally of marks per topic across 3 papers.
steps.pitfall: Working the papers for practice before reading them for pattern, which loses the survey.

problems.prompt: Across 3 papers, topic A carries 34 marks and topic B carries 6. Where does the reading go?
problems.answer: Mostly to topic A, which is nearly 6 times the weight.

problems.prompt: What does a syllabus not tell you that 3 past papers do?
problems.answer: How the marks are actually distributed across the topics.

problems.prompt: Why read the 3 papers for pattern before working them for practice?
problems.answer: Once they are worked they are no longer a clean survey of what gets asked.

steps.title: Judge a Textbook Fast
steps.mastery: Decide in 10 minutes whether a book answers your question.
steps.practice: Open 2 textbooks at the same topic and compare how each treats 1 worked example, in 10 minutes.
steps.detail: Check 3 things: does it work examples in full, does it state results you can check, and is the exercise set answered. A book that explains beautifully with no answered exercises is a bad study book however good the prose. Compare at the topic you are stuck on, not at chapter 1.
steps.proof: A 1-line verdict on each book, naming the deciding difference.
steps.pitfall: Judging by the introduction, which is the part written to be persuasive.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 things this step checks in a textbook.
problems.answer: Whether examples are worked in full, whether results are checkable, and whether exercises have answers.

problems.prompt: Book A explains beautifully with no answers; book B is terse with 200 answered exercises. Which to study from?
problems.answer: B, you cannot mark your work from A.

problems.prompt: Why compare the 2 books at the topic you are stuck on rather than at chapter 1?
problems.answer: Chapter 1 is written to persuade; the hard topic shows how the book actually teaches.

steps.title: Check Who Wrote It
steps.mastery: Establish a source's authority before trusting its content.
steps.practice: Take 2 online explanations of 1 topic and find who wrote each, then say which you would trust and why.
steps.detail: Look for an author, an institution, a date and something checkable, a reference, a derivation, a worked answer. A confident page with no author and no working is not a source, whatever the ranking said. Where you cannot establish authority, verify the claim against a second source before using it.
steps.proof: For each of the 2: an author or institution, a date, and your verdict.
steps.pitfall: Trusting a page because it is clearly written, which is uncorrelated with being right.

problems.prompt: A page has no author, no date and 3 confident claims. Usable or not?
problems.answer: Not on its own, verify each claim against a second source first.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things that make an explanation checkable rather than just confident.
problems.answer: A derivation you can follow and a worked answer you can verify.

problems.prompt: Why is clarity a poor proxy for correctness in 1 sentence?
problems.answer: A wrong explanation can be written just as clearly as a right one.

steps.title: Two Sources on a Hard Point
steps.mastery: Read 2 accounts of the same difficulty and use the difference.
steps.practice: Read 2 explanations of 1 topic you find hard and write the 1 sentence where they differ most.
steps.detail: When 1 explanation does not land, a second rarely repeats it, different books cut the idea in different places, and the join between the 2 cuts is often where your difficulty was. Where they conflict outright, that is worth resolving rather than averaging, and a third source settles it.
steps.proof: 1 sentence naming the biggest difference between the 2 accounts.
steps.pitfall: Rereading the same explanation 4 times on the theory that it will eventually land.

problems.prompt: Two sources conflict on a definition. Average them or find a 3rd?
problems.answer: Find a 3rd, a conflict is a fact to resolve, not to split.

problems.prompt: Why does a 2nd explanation help where rereading the 1st 4 times does not?
problems.answer: It cuts the idea in a different place, often exactly where the difficulty was.

problems.prompt: You read 2 accounts and they agree completely. What have you gained?
problems.answer: Confidence in the account, though not the alternative angle the step was after.

steps.title: Keep a Source List
steps.mastery: Record where each answer came from so it can be found again.
steps.practice: Start a list holding 6 sources with 1 line each on what it answered well.
steps.detail: Note what a source was good for rather than what it was about, "clear on why the discriminant decides the root count" is findable later; "algebra book" is not. Keep it to 1 file with the date you used each one, and cross out sources that disappointed you rather than deleting them.
steps.proof: 6 entries, each naming what that source answered.
steps.pitfall: Keeping 30 bookmarks with no note of what any of them was for.

problems.prompt: Which entry is useful in 6 months: (a) "stats textbook", (b) "clear on why n-1 appears in the sample variance"?
problems.answer: (b). It says what the source answered.

problems.prompt: Why cross out a disappointing source rather than delete it from a list of 6?
problems.answer: So you do not return to it a 2nd time having forgotten.

problems.prompt: What are the 2 fields every entry carries?
problems.answer: What it answered well, and the date you used it.

steps.title: Stop Collecting, Start Working
steps.mastery: Cap the search and begin with what you have.
steps.practice: Give a search 15 minutes, then stop and work the best source you found for 45 minutes.
steps.detail: Collecting feels like progress and is almost free of difficulty, which is why it expands. A 15-minute cap and a named next action ends it. If the source turns out wrong 20 minutes in, that is a result, go back and search again with a sharper question, not a longer list.
steps.proof: A 15-minute search, then 45 minutes of work in the source it chose.
steps.pitfall: Continuing to search because none of the 8 sources is perfect, which is how a week goes.

problems.prompt: You have spent 50 minutes finding sources and 0 working. What is the instruction?
problems.answer: Stop searching and work the best source you have for 45 minutes.

problems.prompt: The chosen source proves wrong 20 minutes in. Search longer next time or sharpen the question?
problems.answer: Sharpen the question, the list was not the problem.

problems.prompt: Why does collecting 8 sources expand to fill the time available?
problems.answer: It resembles progress and involves none of the difficulty of the actual work.

steps.title: Match Source to Stage
steps.mastery: Pick the kind of source that suits how far into a topic you are.
steps.practice: For 1 topic, name the source you would use at first contact, at practice stage, and 3 days before an exam.
steps.detail: First contact wants a clear linear explanation; practice wants a bank of answered problems; the last week wants past papers and your own 1-page summaries. Using the wrong one is why revision sometimes feels like starting again, a textbook chapter 3 days out is a source for a different stage.
steps.proof: 3 named sources, 1 per stage, with a reason each.
steps.pitfall: Opening a fresh textbook 3 days before an exam, which is first-contact material at the wrong time.

problems.prompt: Which source suits the 3 days before an exam: a new textbook chapter or 4 past papers?
problems.answer: The past papers, new material at that stage is first-contact work.

problems.prompt: What kind of source suits the practice stage, once 1 pass through the topic is done?
problems.answer: A bank of problems with answers you can mark yourself against.

problems.prompt: Why does opening a new textbook 3 days out make revision feel like starting again?
problems.answer: First-contact material re-teaches ground you have already covered instead of testing it.

steps.title: First Review Next Day
steps.mastery: Put the first review of new material inside 24 hours of meeting it.
steps.practice: Test 15 cards from today's material again tomorrow, before any of it is reread.
steps.detail: The steepest part of forgetting happens in the first day, so the first review is the one that pays most and the one most people skip. Put it in the calendar as you finish the material, not later, a review that has to be remembered is a review that does not happen.
steps.proof: Tomorrow's session opens with today's 15 cards and a score for them.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the first review 3 days because the material still feels fresh on day 1.

problems.prompt: You meet 20 new terms on Monday. When is the first review, and what does it consist of?
problems.answer: Tuesday, testing all 20 before any rereading.

problems.prompt: Which schedule loses more: (a) first review on day 1, (b) first review on day 4?
problems.answer: (b). Most forgetting happens inside the first day, so the day-4 review re-learns rather than reviews.

problems.prompt: Why schedule the day-1 review while finishing the material rather than the next morning?
problems.answer: A review that depends on remembering to do it is one that gets skipped.

steps.title: Double the Gap
steps.mastery: Grow the interval after each success so reviews cost less over time.
steps.practice: Set the next 4 review dates for a card first learned on day 1, doubling from a 2-day gap.
steps.detail: Start at 2 days and double while the card keeps coming back right: day 3, day 7, day 15, day 31. The gaps grow because a card recalled after a week is stronger than one recalled after a day, so it does not need asking again soon. Write the next date on the card rather than keeping the schedule in your head.
steps.proof: The card carries 4 dates, days 3, 7, 15 and 31, and each was set when the previous review passed.
steps.pitfall: Doubling the gap after a review you only half-passed, which loses the card entirely.

problems.prompt: A card is learned on day 1 and reviewed at a 2-day gap that doubles. Give the next 3 review days.
Your day-7 review of a card is a miss. What happens to the gap?
problems.answer: It resets to 2 days rather than doubling to 15.

problems.prompt: Why does a card recalled after 14 days need asking less often than one recalled after 1 day?
problems.answer: Recall after a long gap is evidence the memory is durable, so the next gap can be longer still.

steps.title: Reset on a Miss
steps.mastery: Send a failed card back to a short interval instead of nudging it.
steps.practice: Take 5 cards missed at a 15-day gap and reschedule each to 2 days rather than 10.
