steps.detail: A miss means the interval overtook the memory, and the fix is to go back near the start rather than to trim a few days off. It feels wasteful and is not: a card reset to 2 days and passed 3 times will outlast one that has been limping at 10-day gaps for a month.
steps.proof: All 5 missed cards sit at a 2-day gap, and none kept a gap longer than the one it failed at.
steps.pitfall: Dropping a missed card from 15 days to 10 so the deck stays small, which keeps failing it.

problems.prompt: A card fails at a 15-day gap. Reset it to 2 days or trim it to 10?
problems.answer: Reset it to 2 days, the interval already outran the memory.

problems.prompt: You reset 5 cards to 2 days. How many extra reviews does that add this week, and is it worth it?
problems.answer: About 10, and yes, 3 short passes make the card durable where a trimmed gap keeps failing.

problems.prompt: State the signal that a 15-day interval was set too long.
problems.answer: A miss at that interval, which is the deck telling you the gap overtook the memory.

steps.title: One Deck, Daily Slice
steps.mastery: Work a single dated deck so each day's review is only what is due.
steps.practice: Sort 60 cards by their next date and work only the 9 due today.
steps.detail: Dating every card turns a deck you cannot face into a daily slice you can. Sort once, then each session take the front of the pile until the dates run ahead of today and stop, even if you have time left, the cards behind are not due and working them early collapses the schedule.
steps.proof: Today's session held exactly the 9 due cards, and the rest of the 60 were untouched.
steps.pitfall: Carrying on into tomorrow's cards because the session felt short, which bunches the deck up again.

problems.prompt: Of 60 dated cards, 9 are due today and 14 tomorrow. How many do you work today?
You finish today's 9 cards with 10 minutes spare. What is the instruction?
problems.answer: Stop. Working ahead pulls tomorrow's cards forward and collapses the spacing.

problems.prompt: Why does dating each card make a 300-card deck workable?
problems.answer: Because a session only ever holds the few dozen that are due, not the whole deck.

steps.title: Spacing Across Subjects
steps.mastery: Fit several subjects' due cards into one daily block without dropping any.
steps.practice: Plan a 30-minute block covering 3 subjects with 8, 6 and 5 cards due.
steps.detail: Add the due cards up first, then divide the block, 19 cards in 30 minutes is about 90 seconds each, which is enough for a spoken answer and a mark. If the total will not fit, cut the subject with the shortest gaps rather than skipping a whole subject, because a skipped day resets every card in it.
steps.proof: All 19 due cards were worked inside the 30 minutes, across all 3 subjects.
steps.pitfall: Giving the first subject 25 of the 30 minutes and abandoning the third, which resets its whole schedule.

problems.prompt: 3 subjects have 8, 6 and 5 cards due in a 30-minute block. How long per card?
22 cards are due and you have 15 minutes. Which do you cut?
problems.answer: Some of the shortest-gap cards, which come round again soonest, not a whole subject.

problems.prompt: What happens to a subject's schedule when its day is skipped entirely?
problems.answer: Every card in it overruns its interval, so the next session is re-learning rather than review.

steps.title: Keep the Schedule Honest
steps.mastery: Audit a spacing schedule against what you actually did, weekly.
steps.practice: Count the cards that came due in the last 7 days and how many you actually worked.
steps.detail: Write both numbers down: due and done. A ratio under about 0.8 means the schedule is fiction and the deck is silently growing a backlog, which ends with a session nobody can face. The fix is fewer new cards this week, not a longer session next week.
steps.proof: You can state last week's due count, done count and the ratio between them.
steps.pitfall: Adding 20 new cards in a week where only half the due ones got worked.

problems.prompt: 70 cards came due last week and you worked 42. Give the ratio and what it means.
problems.answer: 0.6, a backlog is building and the schedule is not being kept.

problems.prompt: Your done-to-due ratio is 0.5. Do you lengthen the sessions or add fewer new cards?
problems.answer: Add fewer new cards. The intake is what created the backlog.

problems.prompt: Why record both the due count and the done count rather than only a score of 8 out of 10?
problems.answer: A high score on half the due cards hides a backlog that a score alone cannot show.

steps.title: One Page Per Topic
steps.mastery: Compress a topic onto a single page with nothing left off that matters.
steps.practice: Compress 12 pages of notes onto 1 side, keeping every result and dropping every example.
steps.detail: The constraint does the teaching: with 1 side you have to decide what the topic is actually made of. Keep definitions, results and the 1 or 2 worked patterns; drop prose, repeated examples and anything you could rebuild. If it will not fit, the topic is 2 topics.
steps.proof: 1 side that lets you answer questions on the topic without the original 12 pages.
steps.pitfall: Shrinking the handwriting to fit 12 pages onto 1, which compresses nothing.

problems.prompt: Which goes on the 1 page: (a) 3 worked examples of the same type, (b) the result they all illustrate?
problems.answer: (b). One pattern is kept; the repeats are dropped.

problems.prompt: Your 12 pages will not fit on 1 side. What is the likely cause?
problems.answer: The material is 2 topics and wants splitting into 2 pages.

problems.prompt: Why is writing smaller not a compression of 12 pages?
problems.answer: Nothing was decided about what matters, the same content is still there.

steps.title: Draw What Connects
steps.mastery: Show the relationships in a topic as a diagram rather than a list.
steps.practice: Draw 8 concepts from 1 topic as boxes and label every arrow between them with a verb.
steps.detail: Labeling the arrows is the part that does the work: "causes", "is a case of", "is measured by" are different relationships, and an unlabeled arrow hides which you meant. Eight boxes is enough for a topic and few enough to lay out. Arrows you cannot label are relationships you have not understood.
steps.proof: A diagram of 8 boxes where every arrow carries a verb.
steps.pitfall: Drawing 20 boxes joined by bare lines, which records the vocabulary and none of the structure.

problems.prompt: Label the arrow between "friction" and "heat" with a verb.
Why must each of the 8 diagram's arrows carry a verb?
problems.answer: Different relationships look identical as bare lines, so the structure is lost.

problems.prompt: You cannot label 2 of your 9 arrows. What have you found?
problems.answer: Two relationships you have not understood, which are the next thing to study.

steps.title: Hierarchy, Not a List
steps.mastery: Arrange a topic's content by what contains what.
steps.practice: Rearrange 15 flat bullet points into 3 groups with 2 levels of indentation.
steps.detail: A flat list of 15 says everything is equally important, which is never true. Find the 3 or 4 organizing ideas, then put the rest underneath where they belong. The grouping is a claim about the subject and can be wrong, which is exactly why it is worth making.
steps.proof: 15 points under 3 headings, and you can defend each placement.
steps.pitfall: Grouping by where things appeared in the book rather than by what they belong to.

problems.prompt: What does a flat list of 15 equal bullets claim about the material?
problems.answer: That all 15 matter equally, which is almost never true.

problems.prompt: Should 15 points be grouped by chapter order or by what contains what?
problems.answer: By what contains what, chapter order is the book's structure, not the subject's.

problems.prompt: Why is a grouping of 15 points worth making even when it might be wrong?
problems.answer: It is a claim about the subject, so being wrong is something you can find and fix.

steps.title: Summarize From Memory
steps.mastery: Produce the one-page summary without the notes open.
steps.practice: Rebuild your 1-page summary from blank paper, then compare it against the original and mark 3 differences.
steps.detail: Copying a summary teaches nothing; producing one is the whole exercise. Write it cold, then lay it beside the original. The differences fall into 2 kinds, things you forgot, and things you chose to leave off this time, and only the first kind is a gap.
steps.proof: A rebuilt page with the differences marked and sorted into forgotten and dropped.
steps.pitfall: Treating every difference as a memory failure, when some are better editing.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 kinds of difference between a remembered summary and the original.
problems.answer: Things forgotten, and things deliberately dropped as unnecessary.

problems.prompt: Your rebuilt page is 1 third shorter and still answers every question. What does that mean?
problems.answer: The original carried a third more than the topic needed.

problems.prompt: Why produce the summary cold rather than copying the 1-page original?
problems.answer: Copying tests handwriting; producing it tests the topic.

steps.title: Link Two Topics
steps.mastery: Connect 2 separate summaries at the point they actually meet.
steps.practice: Put 2 one-page summaries side by side and write 3 links between them, each naming the shared idea.
steps.detail: Topics are taught separately and examined together, so the joins are worth making explicitly. A link needs the shared idea named, "both are conservation arguments", rather than a line drawn between 2 pages. Write each link on both pages so either one leads to the other.
steps.proof: 3 named links, written on both summaries.
steps.pitfall: Linking 2 topics because they appeared in the same chapter, which is not a shared idea.

problems.prompt: Which is a real link: (a) both topics were in chapter 4, (b) both are conservation arguments?
problems.answer: (b). The first is a fact about the book.

problems.prompt: Why write each of the 3 links on both pages?
problems.answer: So either page leads to the other, whichever one you open.

problems.prompt: Name 1 shared idea between momentum and money supply worth writing as a link.
problems.answer: Both are quantities conserved in a closed system unless something enters or leaves.

steps.title: Compress the Compression
steps.mastery: Reduce a one-page summary to a card without losing what it recovers.
steps.practice: Reduce 1 page of summary to 10 lines on a card, and check the card still recovers the page.
steps.detail: The second compression is where the organizing ideas separate from the details: 10 lines can only hold structure, so anything that survives is load-bearing. Test by writing the page back from the card. What is missing from the rebuild goes back on the card, replacing something that was not needed.
steps.proof: A 10-line card that lets you rebuild the page, tested once.
steps.pitfall: Writing 10 lines of headings, which recovers the topics and none of the content.

problems.prompt: Which card is better: 10 headings, or 6 headings and 4 key results?
problems.answer: The second, headings alone recover the topics but not the content.

problems.prompt: You rebuild the page from the card and 2 results are missing. What changes on the card?
problems.answer: The 2 results go on, replacing lines that were not needed.

problems.prompt: Why does a 10-line limit reveal which ideas are load-bearing?
problems.answer: Only structure fits, so anything surviving the cut is doing real work.

steps.title: Summarize a Whole Course
steps.mastery: Fit a term's material onto one sheet that shows how the parts relate.
steps.practice: Put 8 topic cards onto 1 A3 sheet, with 6 arrows showing which topic a later one depends on.
steps.detail: This is the map you revise from, and its value is the arrows rather than the boxes: seeing that topic 7 needs topic 3 tells you the order to revise in and which failures will cascade. Build it from the cards you already have, and leave room to add arrows as you notice them.
steps.proof: 1 sheet with 8 topics and 6 dependency arrows you can each justify.
steps.pitfall: Laying the 8 topics out in the order they were taught, which hides the dependencies.

problems.prompt: Topic 7 depends on topic 3. What does that tell you about the revision order?
problems.answer: Topic 3 gets revised before 7, and failing 3 undermines both.

problems.prompt: Why are the 6 arrows more useful than the 8 boxes?
problems.answer: The boxes list the course; the arrows say what order it has to be learned in.

problems.prompt: What is wrong with laying 8 topics out in teaching order?
problems.answer: Teaching order is not dependency order, so the cascades stay hidden.

steps.title: Sort Given From Derived
steps.mastery: Separate what a subject asserts from what follows from it.
steps.practice: Split 10 facts from 1 topic into 2 columns: given by definition, and derivable from the others.
steps.detail: Definitions have to be memorized; consequences do not, because they can be rebuilt. Sorting them tells you how much of a topic is genuinely arbitrary, usually far less than it feels. For each derived fact write the 1 line of reasoning that recovers it from the givens.
steps.proof: The derived column has a 1-line derivation beside each entry, and the given column has none.
steps.pitfall: Filing something as given because you cannot derive it yet, which hides the reasoning you were about to learn.

problems.prompt: Is "a circle's area is pi r squared" given or derived, and from what?
problems.answer: Derived, it follows from the definition of pi and the limit of inscribed polygons.

problems.prompt: Of 10 facts you file 8 as given. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: Most are consequences you cannot yet derive, so the derivations are the work.

problems.prompt: Why does sorting 10 facts this way reduce what has to be memorized?
problems.answer: Anything derivable can be rebuilt from the few genuine definitions.

steps.title: Rebuild Without the Formula
steps.mastery: Recover a result from its reasoning when the formula is unavailable.
steps.practice: Derive the quadratic formula from completing the square on ax^2 + bx + c = 0, with the formula covered.
steps.detail: Work on paper with the source shut. Where you get stuck, note the line you stopped at, look up only that line, and carry on. The value is the record of where it broke, a derivation you can produce from scratch is one you will still have in a year, and the stuck lines are all you need to study.
steps.proof: A written derivation ending at x = (-b plus or minus root(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a.
steps.pitfall: Checking the next line each time it gets hard, which produces a copy rather than a derivation.

problems.prompt: In completing the square on x^2 + 6x + 5, what is added and subtracted?
You stall at 1 line of a 7-line derivation. What do you look up?
problems.answer: Only that line, then continue from it.

problems.prompt: Why is a 7-line derivation you can rebuild worth more than a formula you have memorized?
problems.answer: It survives being forgotten: the result can be recovered from the reasoning.

steps.title: Test With a New Case
steps.mastery: Apply a result to a case the examples never showed you.
steps.practice: Use the mole ratio method on a reaction you have never seen: 4 Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3, from 0.60 mol Fe.
steps.detail: Understanding is what survives a change of surface. Pick a case with different numbers, different names and the same structure, and do it without looking at the worked example. If you can only do the version you were shown, what you have is the example rather than the method.
steps.proof: You get 0.45 mol of O2, and can say which ratio you used and why.
steps.pitfall: Choosing a new case that is the worked example with the numbers changed, which tests nothing new.

problems.prompt: From 0.60 mol Fe in 4 Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3, how much O2 is needed?
How much Fe2O3 does 0.60 mol of Fe produce in that reaction?
You can do the worked example but not the same problem with new substances. State what you have.
problems.answer: The example memorized, not the method understood.

steps.title: Find What Breaks It
steps.mastery: State the conditions under which a rule stops holding.
steps.practice: Name 2 cases where "multiplying makes a number bigger" fails, with a worked value for each.
steps.detail: A rule you understand comes with its edges. Look for the case where a factor is 0, negative, fractional, or where a denominator vanishes. Write the value that breaks it rather than describing the case, because the number is the part you can check.
steps.proof: 2 worked counterexamples, such as 6 x 0.5 = 3 and 6 x -2 = -12.
steps.pitfall: Naming a case without working it, which leaves you unsure whether it really breaks the rule.

problems.prompt: Give a value showing that multiplying by 0.5 does not make a number bigger.
Where does "the square root of a square is the original number" fail? Give a value.
Why write the failing value, such as 6 x 0.5, rather than describing the kind of case?
problems.answer: The value can be checked; a description can be wrong without showing it.

steps.title: Two Ways to the Answer
steps.mastery: Reach one result by 2 independent routes and compare them.
steps.practice: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 6 and 10 and height 4 twice: by formula and by splitting it.
steps.detail: Two routes that agree are a check on the arithmetic and on the understanding at once, because a wrong idea rarely survives being approached from a second direction. Where they disagree, the disagreement localizes the error faster than rechecking either route alone.
steps.proof: Both routes give 32, and you can say which parts of the split correspond to the formula's terms.
steps.pitfall: Using the same method twice with different notation and calling it 2 routes.

problems.prompt: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 and 10 and height 4. What is its area?
Split that trapezium into a 6-by-4 rectangle and a triangle. What are the 2 areas?
Your 2 routes give 32 and 28. What does that tell you, and what next?
problems.answer: One route has an error; compare the corresponding terms to find which.

steps.title: Spot What Must Be Memorized
steps.mastery: Decide honestly which items no amount of reasoning will recover.
steps.practice: List 5 items from 1 subject that cannot be derived, such as the symbol Na for sodium.
steps.detail: Some things are arbitrary, names, symbols, dates, conventions, and reasoning about them is wasted effort. Getting this list short and correct means the memory techniques go where they earn, and everything not on the list is treated as reconstructible rather than learned by heart.
steps.proof: 5 genuinely arbitrary items, none of which anybody could derive.
steps.pitfall: Putting a derivable result on the list because memorizing feels faster today.

problems.prompt: Is the symbol "Na" for sodium given or derivable?
problems.answer: Given, it comes from the Latin natrium and cannot be reasoned out.

problems.prompt: Is the boiling point of water at 100 degrees Celsius arbitrary or derived?
problems.answer: Arbitrary in that the scale was defined by it, so the number is a convention.

problems.prompt: Why keep the must-memorise list short, in under 20 words?
problems.answer: Memory work is expensive, and anything derivable can be rebuilt instead of stored.

steps.title: Explain a Wrong Answer
steps.mastery: Say exactly why a plausible wrong method gives the wrong result.
steps.practice: Explain why (a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 is wrong, using a = 3 and b = 4 to show the gap.
steps.detail: Diagnosing an error is a harder test than getting it right, and it is the one that stops you repeating it. Work the wrong method and the right one on the same numbers, then name the missing piece, here the 2ab term, rather than only noting that the answers differ.
steps.proof: You show 49 against 25 and name 2ab = 24 as the missing term.
steps.pitfall: Stating the correct identity without showing where the wrong one loses its term.

problems.prompt: With a = 3 and b = 4, compare (a + b)^2 with a^2 + b^2.
problems.answer: 49 against 25, a difference of 24, which is 2ab.

problems.prompt: Name the term that (a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 drops.
Why is explaining why a^2 + b^2 is wrong more useful than restating the right identity?
problems.answer: It names the step that fails, which is what stops the mistake recurring.

steps.title: Know the Requirements
steps.mastery: Read audition requirements and list every item.
steps.practice: List the scales, excerpts and solo required for an All-State audition and set a date to have each ready.
steps.detail: Auditions are graded on specific items. Listing them with dates turns a big goal into a schedule.
steps.proof: A list of every requirement with a ready by date.
steps.pitfall: Preparing only the solo and forgetting the scales.

problems.prompt: Name 3 common parts of a violin audition.
The audition is in 10 weeks with 5 items. How many weeks per item if done in order?
Why set a ready date earlier than the audition by 2 weeks?
problems.answer: To leave time for mock auditions.

steps.title: Audition Scales
steps.mastery: Play required scales cleanly at the required tempo.
steps.practice: Play the 3 required scales at the required tempo 3 times each, recording the last run.
steps.detail: Scales are often the first thing judges hear. Clean, in tune scales at tempo set a strong impression.
steps.proof: 3 scales recorded clean at tempo.
steps.pitfall: Practicing scales slower than the required tempo only.

problems.prompt: An audition asks for 3 scales at 80 bpm. You play them at 70. Ready?
Your recording of 3 scales shows the top note flat each time. What do you drill?
problems.answer: The shift into the top note, slowly with a tuner.

problems.prompt: A scale is clean 2 of 3 times. What do you do?
problems.answer: Keep drilling until it is clean every time.

steps.title: Orchestral Excerpts
steps.mastery: Prepare excerpts with the style and tempo of the real piece.
steps.practice: Listen to 2 recordings of each excerpt, then practice each at tempo for 10 minutes a day.
steps.detail: Excerpts are judged on style as well as notes. Hearing professional recordings shows the right tempo and character.
steps.proof: Each excerpt learned with notes on tempo and style.
steps.pitfall: Learning excerpts without ever hearing the full piece.

problems.prompt: Why listen to 2 recordings of an excerpt instead of 1?
problems.answer: To hear more than 1 valid tempo and style.

problems.prompt: 4 excerpts at 10 minutes each is how much daily time?
An excerpt is marked Allegro but you play it slowly. What will the panel think?
problems.answer: You are not ready for the tempo.

steps.title: Mock Auditions
steps.mastery: Run full mock auditions and record them.
steps.practice: Record 3 full mock auditions in the 3 weeks before the audition and listen back honestly.
steps.detail: A mock audition is the best rehearsal for pressure. Listening back shows what judges will hear.
steps.proof: 3 recordings with notes on each.
steps.pitfall: Only practicing pieces separately and never in audition order.

problems.prompt: 3 mock auditions in 3 weeks is how many per week?
A recording shows rushed scales in 2 mocks. Fix?
problems.answer: Practice scales with a metronome at audition tempo.

problems.prompt: Should you stop and restart during a mock with 5 judges watching?
problems.answer: No, keep going as in the real audition.

steps.title: Handle Nerves
steps.mastery: Use a routine to stay calm on audition day.
steps.practice: Write a 15 minute warm up and breathing routine and use it before each of 3 mock auditions.
steps.detail: Nerves are normal. A fixed routine gives you something familiar to do, and slow breathing calms the body before you play.
steps.proof: A routine used 3 times with notes on how it felt.
steps.pitfall: Trying a new warm up on audition day.

problems.prompt: A 15 minute routine before 3 mocks adds up to how many minutes?
Your bow shakes at the start of 2 mocks. One fix?
problems.answer: Start with a long, slow open string to settle.

problems.prompt: Breathing in for 4 counts and out for 6 does what?

steps.title: Shape the Bow Hand
steps.mastery: Form a soft, curved hand with a bent thumb on the bow.
steps.practice: Hold a pencil with the bow hand shape for 1 minute, then move it to the bow and hold it for 1 minute.
steps.detail: The thumb sits bent between frog and grip, the fingers drape over the stick and the pinky rests curved on top. A pencil lets you build the shape without the weight of the bow.
steps.proof: 2 minutes of a curved hold with a bent thumb.
steps.pitfall: Locking the thumb straight, which makes the hand stiff.

problems.prompt: Hold a pencil in the bow hold for 60 seconds. What shape should the thumb make?
Where does the pinky go in a standard bow hold, with 4 fingers on the stick?
problems.answer: Curved on top of the stick.

problems.prompt: Your thumb straightens after 30 seconds. What do you change?
problems.answer: Bend it again and loosen the hand.

steps.title: Bow Hold Exercises
steps.mastery: Build finger strength and flexibility for the bow hold.
steps.practice: Make 10 finger crawls up and down the stick with the bow held upright.
steps.detail: Crawling the fingers up and down the stick trains the small muscles that keep the hold flexible. Holding the bow upright makes the pinky do real work.
steps.proof: 10 crawls without dropping the bow.
steps.pitfall: Rushing the crawls and losing the curved shape.

problems.prompt: Why do 10 finger crawls with the bow upright help the hold?
problems.answer: They build strength in the small finger muscles.

problems.prompt: Why hold the bow upright for crawls, not flat on 4 strings?
problems.answer: It makes the pinky and thumb carry the weight.

problems.prompt: Your pinky collapses flat after 5 crawls. What do you do?
problems.answer: Slow down and rebuild the curve before continuing.

steps.title: Bow Circles in the Air
steps.mastery: Move the bow without strings to feel balance and weight.
steps.practice: Draw 8 slow circles in the air with the bow, then 8 straight lines from frog to tip.
steps.detail: Air work shows how the bow balances in the hand without the string helping. The hold should stay soft even as the bow moves far from the body.
steps.proof: 16 air movements with the hold kept soft.
steps.pitfall: Squeezing the bow to stop it wobbling.

problems.prompt: Draw 8 circles in the air with the bow. Should the hold tighten or stay soft?
The bow tip wobbles during 8 lines. Grip harder?
problems.answer: No, keep the hold soft and slow down.

problems.prompt: Which finger balances the bow near the frog when you lift it 10 cm?

steps.title: Hold Through a Full Bow
steps.mastery: Keep the bow hold shape from frog to tip on the string.
steps.practice: Play 8 full bows on the D string at 60 bpm, 4 beats each, watching the hand shape.
steps.detail: At the frog the fingers bend more, and at the tip they straighten a little. The thumb stays bent the whole way.
steps.proof: 8 full bows with the shape kept.
steps.pitfall: Straightening the thumb near the tip.

problems.prompt: Over a 4 beat bow, does the thumb stay bent all the way to the tip?
At the frog, do the fingers bend more or less than at the tip during a 4 beat bow?
Your sound gets thin at the tip during 8 bows. One fix?
problems.answer: Add index finger weight near the tip.

steps.title: Check the Hold Daily
steps.mastery: Make a quick hold check part of every practice.
steps.practice: Start each practice with a 1 minute bow hold check for 7 days and note 1 thing to fix each day.
steps.detail: Bow holds drift without daily attention. A 1 minute check catches small problems before they become habits.
steps.proof: 7 days of notes with 1 fix each.
steps.pitfall: Skipping the check when you are in a hurry.

problems.prompt: A 1 minute hold check each day for 7 days adds up to how many minutes?
Day 3 of 7 shows a stiff pinky. What do you note?
problems.answer: One fix for the pinky to work on that day.

problems.prompt: You notice the same problem 3 days in a row. What do you do?
problems.answer: Ask your teacher for a specific exercise to fix it.

steps.title: Detache Strokes
steps.mastery: Play separate, smooth bows with no gaps between notes.
steps.practice: Play the G major scale in detache on the D and A strings, 4 notes per beat at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: Detache is one note per bow with no stop between. The bow changes smoothly, and the sound stays even. It is the most common stroke.
steps.proof: A smooth scale with no gaps between bows.
steps.pitfall: Stopping the bow between notes, which makes it choppy.

problems.prompt: In detache, how many notes go in 1 bow?
At 60 bpm with 4 notes per beat, notes per second?
You hear gaps between 4 notes. Which stroke did you play?

steps.title: Legato Slurs
steps.mastery: Play several notes in 1 bow with smooth connections.
steps.practice: Slur groups of 4 through a D major scale, 3 times, giving each note an equal share of the bow.
steps.detail: In a slur the bow keeps moving while the left hand changes notes. Plan the bow so each note gets an equal share.
steps.proof: A scale with 4 even notes in every bow.
steps.pitfall: Running out of bow on the 4th note.

problems.prompt: A slur of 4 notes uses how many bows?
You run out of bow on note 4. Fix?
Slur 2 notes across the D and A strings. What does the right arm do?
problems.answer: Moves to the A string level mid bow.

steps.title: Staccato
steps.mastery: Play short, separated notes with a clean start.
steps.practice: Play 8 staccato notes on the A string at 72 bpm, stopping the bow after each one.
steps.detail: Staccato bites the string with a little weight and then stops. The stop is as important as the start.
steps.proof: 8 clear staccato notes with silence between.
steps.pitfall: Letting the bow keep moving so notes run together.

problems.prompt: In staccato, does the bow stop between 2 notes?
Your staccato sounds scratchy on 3 of 8 notes. One fix?
problems.answer: Use less pressure at the start.

problems.prompt: Name 1 difference between staccato and detache.
problems.answer: Staccato stops between notes, and detache does not.

steps.title: Mixed Bowings
steps.mastery: Switch between slurs and separate bows inside one passage.
steps.practice: Play a G major scale with the pattern 2 slurred, 2 separate at 60 bpm, 2 times.
steps.detail: Real music mixes strokes. Practicing patterns teaches the bow to plan ahead so each note lands in the right part of the bow.
steps.proof: 2 runs of the pattern without losing bow position.
steps.pitfall: Drifting to the tip because the slurs use more bow.

problems.prompt: How many notes in 1 cycle of the 2 slurred, 2 separate pattern?
You drift toward the tip over 8 notes. Fix?
problems.answer: Use less bow on the slurs.

problems.prompt: Which uses more bow per note, a slur of 4 or a separate note, at the same tempo?

steps.title: Bowing From a Score
steps.mastery: Read slur and staccato marks and play them exactly.
steps.practice: Mark the bowings in 16 bars of an etude and play them at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: Composers and teachers write bowings for phrasing. Following them exactly is part of learning a piece, and planning helps avoid running out of bow.
steps.proof: 16 bars played with every marked bowing.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring slur marks and playing every note separate.

problems.prompt: A curved line covers 2 notes in bar 3. How do you bow them?
A curved line over 3 notes. What does it mean?
A dot over a note in a 4/4 bar. What does it mean?

steps.title: Open String Double Stops
steps.mastery: Play 2 open strings together with an even sound.
steps.practice: Play D and A open strings together for 8 whole bows at 60 bpm, 4 beats each.
steps.detail: Both strings must get equal weight. The arm sits at a level between the 2 strings, and the sound should blend into 1 chord.
steps.proof: 8 bows with both strings sounding evenly.
steps.pitfall: Favoring 1 string so the other fades.

problems.prompt: Playing D and A together, where does the right arm sit compared with the 2 single string levels?
Any 2 adjacent open strings make what interval, with 7 half steps?
D and A ring with no wobble for 8 bows. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: The fifth between them is in tune.

steps.title: One Finger, One Open
steps.mastery: Play a fingered note against an open string and tune it.
steps.practice: Play finger 1, 2 and 3 on the A string with the open D, holding each for 4 beats at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: The open string is a steady reference. Tune the fingered note until the 2 notes ring together.
steps.proof: 3 double stops tuned to ring.
steps.pitfall: Moving on before the double stop rings.

problems.prompt: Holding a double stop for 4 beats, what are you listening for?
problems.answer: The 2 notes ringing together without beats.

problems.prompt: Finger 1 on A against open D. What interval?
problems.answer: A major 6th, from D up to B.

problems.prompt: The pair beats fast for 4 beats. In tune?

steps.title: Thirds
steps.mastery: Play scales in thirds with both notes in tune.
steps.practice: Play a 1 octave G major scale in thirds at 50 bpm, 2 beats per pair.
steps.detail: Thirds use 2 fingers at once and test the hand frame. Tune the lower note first, then the upper one against it.
steps.proof: A scale in thirds with each pair ringing.
steps.pitfall: Tuning only the top note.

problems.prompt: In a scale in thirds, do 1 or 2 notes sound at once?
Tune which note first in each pair of 2?
G and B played together. Major or minor third?

steps.title: Octaves and Sixths
steps.mastery: Play octaves and sixths with a fixed hand frame.
steps.practice: Play 8 octaves on the G and D strings with fingers 1 and 4, checking each with a tuner.
steps.detail: Octaves need fingers 1 and 4 at a fixed spacing that gets smaller higher up. Sixths use finger pairs like 1 and 3 across strings.
steps.proof: 8 octaves within 10 cents each.
steps.pitfall: Keeping the same octave spacing in higher positions.

problems.prompt: Which 2 fingers play octaves?
Does the octave spacing get wider or narrower higher up the 4 string neck?
From G up to the next G, is an octave 7 or 8 letter names?

steps.title: Double Stops in Pieces
steps.mastery: Practice the double stops in a piece one at a time.
steps.practice: Find every double stop in 16 bars of a piece and tune each one 5 times with a drone.
steps.detail: Double stops in pieces come fast. Tuning each one slowly makes it automatic before you play it in tempo.
steps.proof: Every double stop tuned 5 times.
steps.pitfall: Playing double stop passages at full speed from the start.

problems.prompt: A passage has 4 double stops and you tune each 5 times. Total repetitions?
A double stop beats on every try in 5. What next?
problems.answer: Check each note alone, then together.

problems.prompt: Why use a drone when tuning the 4 double stops in a piece?
problems.answer: It gives a steady reference for both notes.

steps.title: Map First Position
steps.mastery: Know which finger plays which note on each string in first position.
steps.practice: Write the notes for fingers 0 to 4 on all 4 strings in first position in D major.
steps.detail: In D major first position, the A string gives A, B, C#, D, E. Writing it out links each finger to a note name before you rely on muscle memory.
steps.proof: A table of 20 notes for 4 strings and 5 fingers.
steps.pitfall: Playing by finger number without knowing the note names.

problems.prompt: Open A string, 1st finger in D major. Note?
On the D string in D major, which note does finger 2 play?
Which finger plays A on the E string, using the 4 note pattern E, F#, G, A?

steps.title: Use Finger Tapes
steps.mastery: Place tapes on the fingerboard to guide early intonation.
steps.practice: Place 3 finger tapes for D major with a tuner, then play D, E, F#, G on the D string 5 times each.
steps.detail: Tapes give a visual target while your ear and hand learn the distances. Check each note with a tuner while placing them.
steps.proof: 3 tapes placed and 4 notes played in tune.
steps.pitfall: Watching the tapes instead of listening.

problems.prompt: The basic D major pattern on 4 strings uses how many tapes?
Your F# is 15 cents flat while on the tape. Trust the tape or the tuner?
You play in tune without looking for 2 weeks. What can you do with the 3 tapes?

steps.title: Finger Patterns
steps.mastery: Learn where whole and half steps fall for each finger pattern.
steps.practice: Play the 2-3 pattern and the 1-2 pattern on the A string, 4 times each, naming the half step.
steps.detail: Fingers close together make a half step. In the 2-3 pattern, fingers 2 and 3 touch. Knowing the pattern before playing keeps notes in tune.
steps.proof: Both patterns played with the half step named.
steps.pitfall: Using the same finger spacing in every key.

problems.prompt: A half step is how many cents, out of the 1200 in an octave?
In the 2-3 pattern on the A string, which 2 of the 4 fingers touch?
On the A string, C natural uses low 2. Which 2 fingers touch in that 1-2 pattern?

steps.title: Play a First Melody
steps.mastery: Play a simple tune in first position with steady rhythm.
steps.practice: Play "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" in A major at 72 bpm, 3 times without stopping.
steps.detail: A familiar tune trains finger placement in context. Knowing how it should sound lets your ear catch out of tune notes.
steps.proof: 3 runs without stopping.
steps.pitfall: Stopping to fix every note instead of keeping the pulse.

problems.prompt: Twinkle in A major starts on which open string, of the 4?
How many beats does each quarter note get at 72 bpm in 4/4?
You stop 4 times in 1 run. What do you change?
problems.answer: Slow the tempo until you can play through.

steps.title: Practice With a Drone
steps.mastery: Play first position notes against a drone to train the ear.
steps.practice: Play a 1 octave D major scale against a D drone at 60 bpm, 2 beats per note.
steps.detail: A drone shows when a note clashes. Notes that ring with the drone are in tune, and beating means a note is off.
steps.proof: A scale where each note rings with the drone.
steps.pitfall: Playing too fast to hear the clash.

problems.prompt: A drone on D. Which scale fits best, D major or E major?
Your F# beats against the drone for 2 beats. In tune?
How many notes in a 1 octave D major scale?

steps.title: Set the Chin Rest
steps.mastery: Rest the violin on your collarbone with the jaw just steadying it.
steps.practice: Hold the violin with no hands for 10 seconds, using only your jaw and collarbone, 3 times.
steps.detail: The violin should sit on the collarbone, with the jaw adding light weight. If you have to clamp hard to keep it up, the chin rest or shoulder rest height is wrong.
steps.proof: 3 holds of 10 seconds each without clamping.
steps.pitfall: Squeezing the jaw hard, which tires the neck in 5 minutes.

problems.prompt: You can hold the violin with no hands for 2 seconds before it slips. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: The setup needs adjusting so the collarbone and jaw can hold it longer.

problems.prompt: You need to clamp hard to hold the violin for 5 seconds. What do you adjust?
problems.answer: The chin rest or shoulder rest height.

problems.prompt: Your neck aches after 15 minutes of practice. What is the likely cause?
problems.answer: Clamping the jaw instead of resting it.

steps.title: Fit the Shoulder Rest
steps.mastery: Adjust the shoulder rest so the violin sits level without lifting the shoulder.
steps.practice: Try 3 shoulder rest heights for 2 minutes each and note which keeps your shoulder down.
steps.detail: A shoulder rest fills the gap between collarbone and violin. Too low and you lift the shoulder, too high and you push the head forward. Small changes matter.
steps.proof: A chosen height noted after 3 trials.
steps.pitfall: Raising the left shoulder to meet the violin.

problems.prompt: A gap of about 5 cm sits between your collarbone and the violin back. What fills it?
Your left shoulder rises when you play for 2 minutes. Raise or lower the rest?
Your head tilts forward to reach the chin rest during a 5 minute scale. Fix?
problems.answer: Lower the rest or change the chin rest.

steps.title: Relax the Left Hand
steps.mastery: Hold the neck lightly so fingers can move freely.
steps.practice: Tap all 4 fingers on the A string 20 times while checking that the thumb stays loose.
steps.detail: The thumb and index base only guide the neck. Gripping slows the fingers and causes pain. You should be able to wiggle the thumb at any moment.
steps.proof: 20 taps with a thumb that can wiggle at any time.
steps.pitfall: Squeezing the neck between thumb and index finger.

problems.prompt: Tap 4 fingers on the A string 20 times. Which part of the hand should stay loose?
Can you wiggle your thumb while holding a note for 4 beats? What should be true?
problems.answer: Yes, the thumb should stay free.

problems.prompt: Your fingers feel slow after 10 minutes. Name 1 likely cause.

steps.title: Check in a Mirror
steps.mastery: Use a mirror to see posture problems you cannot feel.
steps.practice: Play open strings for 2 minutes in front of a mirror and list 3 things you notice about your posture.
steps.detail: A mirror shows a raised shoulder, a collapsed wrist or a tilted violin. Fixing what you see now prevents habits that are hard to undo later.
steps.proof: 3 posture notes from 2 minutes of mirror work.
steps.pitfall: Practicing posture only by feel.

problems.prompt: Name 3 posture problems a mirror can show in 2 minutes.
problems.answer: A raised shoulder, a collapsed wrist and a tilted violin.

problems.prompt: In the mirror the scroll points at the floor during a 1 minute test. Fix?
problems.answer: Raise the violin so the scroll is about level.

problems.prompt: Your left wrist bends back toward the neck for 3 notes in a row. What do you change?
problems.answer: Keep the wrist straight so the hand does not collapse.

steps.title: Hold for Longer Sessions
steps.mastery: Keep a relaxed hold through a whole practice session.
steps.practice: Practice for 20 minutes with a 1 minute break every 5 minutes, checking jaw, shoulder and thumb each time.
steps.detail: Tension creeps in as you tire. Short breaks with a quick check stop small tension from becoming pain and build a hold you can keep for an hour.
steps.proof: 4 checks during a 20 minute session.
steps.pitfall: Playing for an hour without a break and ignoring stiffness.

problems.prompt: How many checks in a 20 minute session with 1 every 5 minutes?
Name 3 places to check for tension.
Pain starts after 30 minutes. What do you do?
problems.answer: Stop, rest and check the setup with your teacher.

steps.title: Drone Practice
steps.mastery: Tune each note against a steady drone.
steps.practice: Play a 2 octave D major scale against a D drone at 50 bpm, 4 beats per note.
steps.detail: A drone makes intonation audible. In tune notes ring, and out of tune notes beat against it. Slow notes give time to adjust.
steps.proof: A scale where every note rings with the drone.
steps.pitfall: Moving on before a note rings.

problems.prompt: Holding each note 4 beats at 50 bpm against a drone gives how many seconds per note?
A note beats fast against the drone over 4 beats. Close or far from in tune?
The beats slow as you move your finger up 1 mm. What do you do?
problems.answer: Keep moving that way until they stop.

steps.title: Check With a Tuner
steps.mastery: Use a tuner to check notes your ear is unsure about.
steps.practice: Play 8 notes of a scale and check each with a tuner, writing the cents off for each.
steps.detail: A tuner gives an honest number. Writing it down shows patterns, like a 3rd finger that is always flat.
steps.proof: 8 notes with cents written down and a pattern noted.
steps.pitfall: Watching the tuner while playing instead of using your ear.

problems.prompt: A note reads -20 cents. Sharp or flat?
Finger 3 is flat on 5 of 8 notes. What does that show?
problems.answer: A habit of placing finger 3 too low.

problems.prompt: Is a note 5 cents off usually easy or hard to hear?

steps.title: Ring Tones
steps.mastery: Use sympathetic ringing of open strings to check pitch.
steps.practice: Play G, D, A and E with fingers 3 or 4 on lower strings and listen for the open string to ring, 4 notes, 3 times each.
steps.detail: When a fingered note matches an open string, the open string vibrates too. That ring is a built in tuner for some notes.
steps.proof: 4 notes played with the open string ringing.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring ring tones because a tuner is easier.

problems.prompt: Which finger on the D string plays the A that rings with the open A, of fingers 1 to 4?
You play G with finger 3 and a low open string hums along. Which string is that?
You play 4th finger A on D and nothing rings. What does that show?
problems.answer: The A is out of tune.

steps.title: Slow Scales
steps.mastery: Play scales slowly enough to hear every note.
steps.practice: Play a 2 octave G major scale at 40 bpm with 1 note per beat, stopping to fix any note that does not ring.
steps.detail: Slow practice is where intonation is built. At 40 bpm there is time to hear and correct each note before the next one.
steps.proof: A full scale at 40 bpm with every note fixed.
steps.pitfall: Playing scales fast and hoping intonation improves.

problems.prompt: How many notes in a 2 octave scale?
At 40 bpm, how long is each note?
Your 7th note keeps going flat at 40 bpm. What do you do?
problems.answer: Drill that shift or finger alone, then return to the scale.

steps.title: Record and Review
steps.mastery: Record a passage and mark every out of tune note.
steps.practice: Record 16 bars of a piece and circle every note that sounds out of tune on playback.
steps.detail: You hear intonation better as a listener than as a player. Circling notes gives a focused list to fix in the next session.
steps.proof: A marked score with every out of tune note circled.
steps.pitfall: Listening back without marking anything.

problems.prompt: You circle 6 out of 64 notes in 16 bars. What share is out of tune?
You circled 6 notes. What next?
problems.answer: Practice those 6 slowly with a drone.

problems.prompt: The same note is circled in 3 recordings. What does that mean?
problems.answer: It is a habit, so drill it daily.

steps.title: Straight Bow on G
steps.mastery: Draw the bow parallel to the bridge on the G string.
steps.practice: Play 8 full bows on the open G string at 60 bpm, 4 beats each, using a mirror to check the bow stays parallel.
steps.detail: A straight bow keeps the same contact point and a clean sound. The arm must open from the elbow, not swing from the shoulder.
steps.proof: 8 bows that stay parallel in the mirror.
steps.pitfall: Swinging the arm from the shoulder, which curves the bow.

problems.prompt: Name the 4 open strings from lowest to highest.
The bow drifts toward the fingerboard over 4 beats. Is it parallel?
Which joint does most of the opening on a 4 beat down bow?

steps.title: Clean String Crossings
steps.mastery: Change strings by moving the arm level, not the wrist alone.
steps.practice: Play G, D, A, E open strings, 4 beats each, then back down, 2 times at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: Each string has its own arm level. Moving the whole arm to the new level makes crossings clean, while flicking the wrist causes scratches.
steps.proof: 2 clean round trips across 4 strings.
steps.pitfall: Hitting 2 strings at once during a crossing.

problems.prompt: Crossing from the G string to the E string, how many of the 4 string levels does the arm use?
Which string needs the highest right arm level of the 4?
You hear 2 strings at once when crossing from D to A. Fix?
problems.answer: Move the arm to the A level before the new bow.

steps.title: Even Sound Across the Bow
steps.mastery: Keep the sound the same volume from frog to tip.
steps.practice: Play 6 whole bows on the A string at 60 bpm, 4 beats each, recording yourself and listening for volume changes.
steps.detail: The bow is heavier at the frog, so the arm lightens there and adds weight at the tip. A recording shows changes you miss while playing.
steps.proof: 6 bows with no clear loud or soft spots on the recording.
steps.pitfall: Letting the sound fade near the tip.

problems.prompt: On a 4 beat whole bow, which end is heavier in the hand, frog or tip?
Your recording fades near the tip on all 6 bows. What do you add?
problems.answer: Index finger weight near the tip.

problems.prompt: Why record instead of just listening while playing 4 beat bows?
problems.answer: You hear the sound more honestly from outside.

steps.title: Contact Point
steps.mastery: Keep the bow halfway between bridge and fingerboard for a clear sound.
steps.practice: Play 4 bows each at 3 contact points on the D string and describe each sound in 1 word.
steps.detail: Near the fingerboard the sound is soft and airy, and near the bridge it is bright and can crack. Halfway is the default.
steps.proof: 3 contact points tested with a word for each.
steps.pitfall: Letting the bow slide toward the fingerboard without noticing.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 contact points from fingerboard to bridge.
problems.answer: Near the fingerboard, halfway and near the bridge.

problems.prompt: Bow near the fingerboard for 4 beats. What sound?
Bow near the bridge cracks on 2 bows. Fix?
problems.answer: Use more bow speed or less weight, or move slightly away.

steps.title: Open String Rhythms
steps.mastery: Play steady rhythms on open strings to train both arm and pulse.
steps.practice: Play 4 quarter notes, 8 eighth notes and 16 sixteenth notes on the A string at 72 bpm.
steps.detail: Rhythms on open strings let you focus on the bow and the beat without the left hand. A metronome keeps the pulse honest.
steps.proof: All 3 rhythms played in time with the metronome.
steps.pitfall: Speeding up during the sixteenth notes.

problems.prompt: How many eighth notes fit in 1 beat of 4/4?
At 72 bpm, how many sixteenth notes per second roughly?
You rush the 16 sixteenth notes. Fix?
problems.answer: Slow to 60 bpm and count aloud.

steps.title: Watch the Conductor
steps.mastery: Follow the conductor beat pattern while playing.
steps.practice: Learn the 4/4 and 3/4 beat patterns and play 8 bars while watching a conductor video.
steps.detail: The downbeat goes down, and the last beat goes up. Glancing at the conductor keeps the section together.
steps.proof: 8 bars played in time with a conductor video.
steps.pitfall: Staring at the music and never looking up.

problems.prompt: In 4/4, which beat is the downbeat?
In 3/4, where does beat 3 go?
The conductor slows down in bar 6 of 8. What do you do?
problems.answer: Follow and slow down with them.

steps.title: Count Rests
steps.mastery: Count long rests and come in at the right bar.
steps.practice: Count a 24 bar rest in a part while listening to a recording, and enter on time 3 times.
steps.detail: Long rests are where entries go wrong. Counting bars on your fingers or with a pencil mark keeps your place.
steps.proof: 3 correct entries after a 24 bar rest.
steps.pitfall: Losing count and waiting for a neighbor to come in.

problems.prompt: A part shows a rest marked 24 over 1 bar. How many bars do you rest?
A multi bar rest shows 12. How many bars do you count?
You lose count during 24 bars. What helps you find your place?
problems.answer: Listen for a cue in another part.

steps.title: Match Bowings
steps.mastery: Copy the section bowings so all bows move together.
steps.practice: Copy the concertmaster bowings into 32 bars of your part and play them at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: A section looks and sounds unified when bows move together. Copying bowings in pencil and following them exactly is basic orchestra etiquette.
steps.proof: 32 bars with bowings copied and played.
steps.pitfall: Changing bowings without telling the section.

problems.prompt: In a 60 player orchestra, who usually sets the first violin bowings?
You copy bowings into 32 bars. Pen or pencil?
Why use pencil, not pen, on an orchestra part with 32 bars?
problems.answer: Bowings may change, and parts are shared.

steps.title: Listen Across the Section
steps.mastery: Blend your sound with the players around you.
steps.practice: Play 16 bars with a recording of the section and adjust your volume so you cannot hear yourself above it.
steps.detail: In a section, no one should stick out. Listening to the whole group and matching it is the key skill.
steps.proof: 16 bars blended with the recording.
steps.pitfall: Playing louder to be heard.

problems.prompt: Playing 16 bars with 8 other violins, should you hear yourself above them?
You hear yourself clearly above 8 others. What do you change?
Which section usually plays the melody in a 4 part string orchestra?

steps.title: Prepare a Part
steps.mastery: Learn an orchestra part before the first rehearsal.
steps.practice: Practice the 3 hardest passages of a part for 10 minutes each before the first rehearsal.
steps.detail: Arriving prepared lets rehearsal focus on ensemble, not notes. Pick the hardest passages first.
steps.proof: 3 passages practiced and marked.
steps.pitfall: Sight reading everything at the first rehearsal.

problems.prompt: With 1 week to prepare 3 hard passages, which do you practice first?
problems.answer: The hardest or most exposed one.

problems.prompt: 3 passages at 10 minutes each is how many minutes a day?
Your part has 8 hard passages and 1 day left. How do you pick?
problems.answer: Start with the hardest and most exposed.

steps.title: Treble Clef Notes
steps.mastery: Name every note on the treble staff quickly.
steps.practice: Name 30 random treble clef notes in under 90 seconds using a flashcard app.
steps.detail: The lines are E, G, B, D, F and the spaces are F, A, C, E. Fast naming frees your attention for rhythm and sound.
steps.proof: 30 notes named in under 90 seconds.
steps.pitfall: Counting up from the bottom line every time.

problems.prompt: What note is on the 2nd line of the treble staff?
What are the 4 spaces of the treble staff?
On the D string, which finger plays the G on the 2nd line?

steps.title: Count Rhythms
steps.mastery: Count rhythms aloud before playing them.
steps.practice: Clap and count 8 bars of mixed quarter, eighth and dotted rhythms at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: Counting aloud makes rhythm a plan rather than a guess. Clapping first separates the rhythm from the notes.
steps.proof: 8 bars clapped and counted with no mistakes.
steps.pitfall: Guessing rhythms by ear instead of counting.

problems.prompt: How many beats does a dotted half note get in 4/4?
How do you count 4 eighth notes in 1 bar of 2/4?
In 4/4, a dotted quarter plus an eighth fill how many beats?

steps.title: Key Signatures
steps.mastery: Read the key signature and remember the sharps and flats.
steps.practice: Name the key and the sharps for 5 key signatures from 0 to 4 sharps.
steps.detail: The key signature applies to every bar. Saying the sharps before playing prevents wrong notes, like playing F natural in D major.
steps.proof: C, G, D, A and E major with their sharps listed.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting a sharp after the first bar.

problems.prompt: D major has 2 sharps. Name them.
Which key has 3 sharps?
Name the 4 sharps of E major.

steps.title: Sight Read Daily
steps.mastery: Build the habit of playing unseen music with a steady pulse.
steps.practice: Sight read 8 bars of new music each day for 7 days, keeping a steady pulse even if notes are wrong.
steps.detail: Sight reading improves with volume. Keeping the beat matters more than every note, because in an ensemble the music will not wait.
steps.proof: 7 days of sight reading logged.
steps.pitfall: Stopping to fix mistakes while sight reading.

problems.prompt: Sight reading 8 bars a day for 7 days is how many bars?
You make 3 mistakes in 8 bars. Do you stop?
What do you check in the 30 seconds before sight reading?
problems.answer: Key, time signature, tempo and any tricky rhythms.

steps.title: Read the Markings
steps.mastery: Understand dynamics, tempo and articulation marks.
steps.practice: List the meaning of 10 markings like p, f, cresc. and Allegro from a piece you are learning.
steps.detail: Markings tell you how to play, not just what to play. Learning them early makes every new piece easier to read.
steps.proof: 10 markings listed with their meanings.
steps.pitfall: Playing every piece at one volume and tempo.

problems.prompt: What does p mean on a score with 4 dynamics?
What does Allegro mean?
What does a crescendo over 4 bars ask for?

steps.title: Two Octave G Major
steps.mastery: Cover the full range of G major with even tone and clean string changes.
steps.practice: Play a 2 octave G major scale at 60 bpm, 2 notes per beat, separate bows, 3 times.
steps.detail: G major starts on the open G and climbs through the D, A and E strings. Two octaves need a shift or fourth finger reaches.
steps.proof: 3 runs in tune and in time.
steps.pitfall: Rushing the top notes where the shift happens.

problems.prompt: Which open string does G major start on, of the 4?
G major has how many sharps out of its 7 notes?
How many notes up and down in a 2 octave scale?

steps.title: Three Octave Scales
steps.mastery: Extend scales to 3 octaves with planned shifts.
steps.practice: Play a 3 octave G major scale with shifts written in, at 50 bpm, 2 times.
steps.detail: Three octave scales need shifts to third position and higher. Writing the shifts and fingering keeps every run the same.
steps.proof: 2 runs with the same fingering both times.
steps.pitfall: Shifting in a different place each time.

problems.prompt: A 3 octave scale covers how many letter names from bottom to top?
Notes up and down in a 3 octave scale?
Why write the shift points on a 3 octave scale?
problems.answer: So every run uses the same fingering.

steps.title: Arpeggios
steps.mastery: Build broken chords from notes 1, 3 and 5 across 2 octaves.
steps.practice: Run the G major and G minor arpeggios over 2 octaves, slurring 3 notes per bow, 2 times each.
steps.detail: Arpeggios use notes 1, 3 and 5 of the scale. They train wide finger spacing and string crossings that pieces use often.
steps.proof: 2 clean runs of each arpeggio.
steps.pitfall: Letting the 3rd go sharp in minor arpeggios.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of a G major triad.
Which 1 note changes between G major and G minor triads?
How many notes up in a 2 octave arpeggio?

steps.title: Scales With Rhythms
steps.mastery: Vary scale rhythms to build evenness.
steps.practice: Play a 2 octave D major scale in 3 rhythms: long-short, short-long and even sixteenths at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: Changing rhythms exposes uneven fingers. When every rhythm is clean, the even version becomes much easier.
steps.proof: 3 rhythm versions played cleanly.
steps.pitfall: Only ever practicing scales in even notes.

problems.prompt: Name 3 rhythms to run a scale in.
Which version usually exposes a slow finger, of the 3?
At 60 bpm, how many sixteenth notes per beat?

steps.title: Daily Scale Routine
steps.mastery: Practice scales daily in a set order.
steps.practice: Plan a 7 day scale routine with 1 key per day, each with scale, arpeggio and 3rds.
steps.detail: A routine covers every key without thinking about it. Rotating keys over a week keeps intonation sharp in all of them.
steps.proof: A 7 day plan with a key for each day.
steps.pitfall: Practicing the same scale every day.

problems.prompt: How many keys in a 7 day routine with 1 per day?
Name 3 parts of each day in the routine.
About how long should a daily scale routine take for a 60 minute practice?

steps.title: Guide Finger Shifts
steps.mastery: Slide on the finger you are using to move between positions.
steps.practice: Shift from first to third position on the A string with finger 1, sliding slowly 10 times.
steps.detail: The finger stays on the string with light pressure as the hand moves. Hearing the slide helps you land in the right place.
steps.proof: 10 shifts landing on D in third position.
steps.pitfall: Lifting the finger and jumping, which makes landing a guess.

problems.prompt: Finger 1 in third position on the A string plays which note?
Shifting from first to third position moves finger 1 up how many letter names on 1 string?
You land sharp on 4 of 10 shifts. What do you change?
problems.answer: Slide more slowly and listen to the landing.

steps.title: Light Thumb
steps.mastery: Move the thumb with the hand so shifts stay smooth.
steps.practice: Shift between first and third position 10 times while keeping the thumb loose and moving with the hand.
steps.detail: A gripping thumb drags behind and makes shifts jerky. The thumb should travel with the hand like part of one unit.
steps.proof: 10 smooth shifts with the thumb moving with the hand.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the thumb behind in first position.

problems.prompt: When the hand shifts up 2 positions, does the thumb stay or travel?
Your shifts jerk on 5 of 10 tries. Likely cause?
Your thumb stays in first position while finger 1 reaches third. What problem does that cause?
problems.answer: A strained hand and jerky shifts.

steps.title: Shift on a Scale
steps.mastery: Use shifts inside a scale without losing rhythm.
steps.practice: Play a 1 octave A major scale on the A string with 2 shifts at 60 bpm, 3 times.
steps.detail: Shifting inside a scale must not slow the rhythm. Time the shift to happen just before the new note so it lands on the beat.
steps.proof: 3 runs with shifts landing on the beat.
steps.pitfall: Stopping the beat to make the shift.

problems.prompt: A 1 octave scale on 1 string with 2 shifts. How many positions does the hand use?
A shift makes the note late by 1 beat. Fix?
problems.answer: Start the shift earlier, during the previous note.

problems.prompt: Notes in a 1 octave A major scale?

steps.title: Higher Positions
steps.mastery: Reach fourth position and beyond with a steady hand frame.
steps.practice: Shift to fourth position on the A string, play E, F#, G#, A with fingers 1 to 4, 5 times, and check with a tuner.
steps.detail: Higher positions bring the hand over the body of the violin. The hand frame stays the same, but the notes get closer together.
steps.proof: 5 runs in fourth position within 10 cents.
steps.pitfall: Using the same finger spacing as first position.

problems.prompt: Compared with first position, are half steps in position 4 closer or wider?
Which note does finger 1 play in third position on the E string?
Your notes are sharp in fourth position by 15 cents. Why?
problems.answer: Fingers are spaced as in first position, too wide.

steps.title: Shifts in Pieces
steps.mastery: Plan and practice the shifts in a real piece.
steps.practice: Mark every shift in 16 bars of a piece and practice each one 5 times in isolation.
steps.detail: Shifts are where pieces fall apart. Isolating each shift turns the hardest moments into the most practiced ones.
steps.proof: Every shift marked and each drilled 5 times.
steps.pitfall: Practicing whole pieces and hoping the shifts improve.

problems.prompt: A piece has 6 shifts and you drill each 5 times. How many shifts in all?
A shift misses 3 of 5 times. What do you do?
problems.answer: Slow it down and add guide notes.

problems.prompt: After drilling 6 shifts alone, how do you check them in context?
problems.answer: Play the full passage at a slow tempo and listen.

steps.title: Choose the Right Piece
steps.mastery: Pick a solo slightly above your current level.
steps.practice: List 3 pieces at your level and 3 just above it with your teacher, and choose 1 to learn over 8 weeks.
steps.detail: A piece just above your level stretches you without being impossible. Too hard and progress stalls, too easy and you do not grow.
steps.proof: A chosen piece with an 8 week plan.
steps.pitfall: Picking a famous concerto far beyond your level.

problems.prompt: An 8 week plan for 1 piece gives how many days of practice at 6 days a week?
A piece needs 3 positions you have never played. Too hard or right?
Name 1 famous student concerto by Vivaldi.

steps.title: Learn in Sections
steps.mastery: Split a piece into sections and learn each one separately.
steps.practice: Divide a piece into sections of 8 to 16 bars and learn 1 section per day for 7 days.
steps.detail: Small sections make progress visible. Learning the hardest section first stops it from becoming the weak spot of the piece.
steps.proof: 7 sections learned in 7 days.
steps.pitfall: Always starting from the beginning and never reaching the end.

problems.prompt: A 96 bar piece in sections of 12 bars has how many sections?
Which section do you learn first of 7?
You always practice from bar 1. What happens to the last page?

steps.title: Slow Then Faster
steps.mastery: Raise the tempo of a hard passage in a piece gradually with a metronome.
steps.practice: Play a hard passage at 60 bpm, then raise by 4 bpm each day until you reach 96 bpm.
steps.detail: Small tempo steps keep accuracy as speed grows. If a step fails, go back to the last clean tempo for another day.
steps.proof: The passage at 96 bpm clean.
steps.pitfall: Jumping to full tempo and practicing mistakes.

problems.prompt: How many days from 60 to 96 at 4 bpm per day?
A step to 84 bpm fails. What tempo next day?
Why raise by 4 bpm instead of 20 bpm?
problems.answer: Small steps keep the passage accurate.

steps.title: Phrase and Shape
steps.mastery: Plan where each phrase of a piece goes and how it peaks.
steps.practice: Mark the high point of each phrase in 32 bars and plan dynamics to reach it.
steps.detail: Music moves toward points. Knowing where each phrase peaks makes your dynamics and bow choices sound intentional.
steps.proof: 32 bars with every phrase peak marked.
steps.pitfall: Playing every bar at the same intensity.

problems.prompt: A phrase of 8 bars usually peaks where, early or near bar 6?
A phrase of 8 bars peaks in bar 6. Where does the crescendo start?
After the peak in bar 6, what usually happens in bars 7 and 8?

steps.title: Perform for People
steps.mastery: Play your piece for others before the real performance.
steps.practice: Perform your piece for 3 people or a camera 3 times in the 2 weeks before a recital.
steps.detail: Performing changes how you play. Practice runs build calm and show which spots break under pressure.
steps.proof: 3 practice performances with notes on what slipped.
steps.pitfall: Playing it for the first time in public at the recital.

problems.prompt: You give 3 practice performances in 2 weeks. About how many days apart?
The same bar slips in 2 of 3 runs. What do you do?
problems.answer: Drill that bar slowly before the recital.

problems.prompt: Can a camera count as an audience for 1 run?

steps.title: Bow Weight
steps.mastery: Use arm weight, not pressing, to make a full sound.
steps.practice: Play 8 whole bows on the G string at 60 bpm, letting arm weight sink in, then 8 with pressing, and compare.
steps.detail: Weight from the relaxed arm gives a rich sound. Pressing with the hand tightens the sound and makes it crunch.
steps.proof: 16 bows compared, with notes on the 2 sounds.
steps.pitfall: Squeezing the bow to play louder.

problems.prompt: For a full sound on the G string over 4 beats, which works better: arm weight or squeezing the bow?
8 bows with arm weight and 8 with pressing. Which set usually sounds richer?
The sound crunches on 3 bows. What should you reduce?

steps.title: Bow Speed
steps.mastery: Change bow speed to shape volume and color.
steps.practice: Play 4 notes on the D string using whole bows in 4 beats, then in 2 beats, and compare the sound.
steps.detail: Faster bow speed adds air and volume. Matched with weight and contact point, speed is one of the 3 tools for tone.
steps.proof: 4 notes at 2 speeds with a note on each sound.
steps.pitfall: Using the same bow speed for every dynamic.

problems.prompt: Which bow speed in this drill is faster, 2 beats or 4?
Name the 3 tools for tone.
A fast bow near the fingerboard on 4 notes sounds how?

steps.title: Dynamics Ladder
steps.mastery: Play the same note at clearly different volumes.
steps.practice: Play an A on the D string at pp, p, mf, f and ff, 4 beats each, recording the 5 levels.
steps.detail: Clear dynamic levels need planned changes in speed, weight and contact point. A recording shows if the levels are really different.
steps.proof: 5 levels that sound clearly different on the recording.
steps.pitfall: Playing only mf with small changes.

problems.prompt: Order these 5 from soft to loud: f, pp, mf, ff, p.
Of mf and p, which is louder by 1 or more levels?
Your ff sounds like f on the recording. What do you add?
problems.answer: More weight and move the bow closer to the bridge.

steps.title: Crescendo and Diminuendo
steps.mastery: Grow and fade the sound smoothly within a bow.
steps.practice: Play 6 whole bows with a crescendo, then 6 with a diminuendo, each over 4 beats at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: A smooth crescendo needs gradual changes, not a jump at the end. Plan to reach the peak at the last beat.
steps.proof: 12 bows with smooth changes.
steps.pitfall: Getting loud too early and having nothing left.

problems.prompt: A crescendo over 4 beats should reach its peak on which beat?
You hit full volume by beat 2 of 4. Fix?
problems.answer: Spread the change across all 4 beats.

problems.prompt: A diminuendo over 4 beats ends how?
problems.answer: Soft, with the bow still moving.

steps.title: Tone in Repertoire
steps.mastery: Apply speed, weight and contact point to a real phrase.
steps.practice: Plan bow speed and contact point for 8 bars of a piece and record 2 versions.
steps.detail: Tone choices make a phrase sing. Writing a plan and comparing 2 recordings shows which choices work.
steps.proof: 2 recordings of 8 bars with notes on the better one.
steps.pitfall: Playing pieces with the same tone throughout.

problems.prompt: You record 2 versions of 8 bars. What do you compare?
problems.answer: Which choices of speed, weight and contact point sound clearer.

problems.prompt: A phrase peaks in bar 6 of 8. Where does the bow move toward the bridge?
Version 2 sounds clearer than version 1. What do you do next?
problems.answer: Write down its choices and use them.

steps.title: Use a Tuner App
steps.mastery: Get every string to its exact pitch before you play a note.
steps.practice: Tune all 4 strings with a tuner app to within 5 cents before every practice for 7 days.
steps.detail: Strings drift with temperature and playing. Tuning first means your ear learns correct pitches, not slightly wrong ones.
steps.proof: 7 days of tuning with every string within 5 cents.
steps.pitfall: Skipping tuning when in a hurry.

problems.prompt: Do most orchestras tune the A string to 440 or 415 Hz?
A tuner shows the D string at -12 cents. Raise or lower it?
A tuner reads +100 cents on the D string. How far off is it?

steps.title: Fine Tuners First
steps.mastery: Use fine tuners for small changes and pegs only for big ones.
steps.practice: Adjust each of the 4 strings by up to 10 cents using only fine tuners.
steps.detail: Fine tuners make small, safe changes. Pegs move pitch a lot and can slip, so save them for strings that are far out.
steps.proof: 4 strings adjusted with fine tuners only.
steps.pitfall: Turning a peg for a 5 cent change.

problems.prompt: Which do you use for a 5 cent change: peg or fine tuner?
The E string is 40 cents flat and the fine tuner is at its limit. What next?
problems.answer: Use the peg, then fine tune.

problems.prompt: You turn a fine tuner 1/4 turn clockwise on most violins. What happens to the pitch?

steps.title: Tune With Pegs
steps.mastery: Turn and push the pegs in so they hold.
steps.practice: Tune 1 string that is 50 cents flat using the peg, pushing it in as you turn.
steps.detail: Pegs hold by friction. Turning while pushing gently inward keeps the peg from slipping back. Tune up to the pitch, not down.
steps.proof: A string tuned from 50 cents flat that stays in tune for 5 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Turning without pushing, so the peg slips.

problems.prompt: Should you tune up to a pitch or down to it with a peg on a 4 string violin?
A peg slips after 2 minutes. What was missing?
You overshoot the E string by 200 cents with the peg. Why is that risky?
problems.answer: A whole step too high adds a lot of tension and can snap the thin E string.

steps.title: Tune by Fifths
steps.mastery: Tune strings against each other by listening for pure fifths.
steps.practice: Tune the D string to the A string by ear, playing both for 4 beats and listening for the beats to stop.
steps.detail: Adjacent strings are a fifth apart. When the fifth is in tune, the sound is calm. A fast wobble means one string is off.
steps.proof: D tuned to A by ear, then checked with a tuner within 5 cents.
steps.pitfall: Listening to one string at a time instead of the pair.

problems.prompt: Are adjacent strings like G and D 5 or 7 half steps apart?
You hear a fast wobble when playing D and A for 4 beats. In tune?
The wobble slows as you raise D. Keep going or stop?

steps.title: Tune in Under a Minute
steps.mastery: Tune all strings quickly so practice starts on time.
steps.practice: Time yourself tuning all 4 strings each day for 7 days and aim for under 60 seconds.
steps.detail: Fast tuning is a skill. With practice, a check of all 4 strings takes less than a minute, which removes the excuse to skip it.
steps.proof: 7 timed tunings, the last under 60 seconds.
steps.pitfall: Rushing and leaving a string 15 cents off.

problems.prompt: Target time to tune 4 strings?
Day 1 took 3 minutes and day 7 took 50 seconds. Goal met?
Which string do you usually tune first with a tuner, of the 4?

steps.title: Arm Vibrato Motion
steps.mastery: Rock the hand from the arm in a slow, even motion.
steps.practice: Rock your hand on the D string with finger 2 at 60 bpm, 2 motions per beat, for 1 minute.
steps.detail: Vibrato is a back and forth roll from the note toward the scroll. Starting slow with a metronome builds an even motion.
steps.proof: 1 minute of even motion with the metronome.
steps.pitfall: Rolling above the note, which makes it sound sharp.

problems.prompt: At 60 bpm with 2 motions per beat, how many motions per second?
Vibrato rolls the pitch toward the scroll or the bridge, of the 2?
problems.answer: Toward the scroll, below the note.

problems.prompt: Your vibrato sounds sharp on 3 notes. Why?

steps.title: Wrist Vibrato
steps.mastery: Make vibrato from a loose wrist for a faster motion.
steps.practice: Practice wrist vibrato with your hand against the violin body for 2 minutes, then on the A string with finger 2.
steps.detail: Wrist vibrato uses a smaller motion and can be faster. Resting the hand on the body first teaches the wrist to move freely.
steps.proof: 2 minutes on the body then on the string.
steps.pitfall: Locking the wrist and shaking the whole arm.

problems.prompt: Before trying wrist vibrato on the A string, where does the hand rest for 2 minutes?
Of the 2 kinds, arm or wrist, which is usually faster?
Your vibrato is tense after 30 seconds. Fix?
problems.answer: Stop, shake out the hand and restart slowly.

steps.title: Vibrato on Each Finger
steps.mastery: Make even vibrato on all 4 fingers.
steps.practice: Play vibrato on fingers 1 to 4 on the A string, 4 beats each at 60 bpm.
steps.detail: Fingers 1 and 4 are usually hardest. Practicing each finger alone builds an even vibrato so long notes sound the same whatever finger plays them.
steps.proof: 4 fingers with similar vibrato width and speed.
steps.pitfall: Only using vibrato on fingers 2 and 3.

problems.prompt: Which 2 of the 4 fingers usually find vibrato hardest?
Why do fingers 1 and 4 often have a weaker vibrato than 2 and 3?
problems.answer: They sit at the edges of the hand, so the rolling motion is harder.

problems.prompt: Your 4th finger vibrato is narrow over 4 beats. What do you do?
problems.answer: Practice it alone, slow, with a metronome.

steps.title: Vibrato Speed Control
steps.mastery: Change vibrato speed on purpose with a metronome.
steps.practice: Set a metronome to 60 bpm and switch between 2, 3 and 4 vibrato motions per click on a held D.
steps.detail: Expressive playing needs different speeds. Practicing set speeds gives you control, so you can choose a warm or intense sound.
steps.proof: 3 speeds played evenly.
steps.pitfall: Having only one vibrato speed for every piece.

problems.prompt: How many motions per second at 60 bpm with 4 per beat?
A slow vibrato at 2 per beat sounds how, compared with 4 per beat?
Name 3 vibrato speeds to practice at 60 bpm.

steps.title: Vibrato in Music
steps.mastery: Add vibrato to a slow piece where it serves the phrase.
steps.practice: Play 16 bars of a slow piece with vibrato on long notes only, then record and listen.
steps.detail: Vibrato should support the music. Using it on long notes and leaving short notes plain keeps the line clear.
steps.proof: 16 bars recorded with vibrato on long notes.
steps.pitfall: Adding vibrato to every note, which sounds nervous.

problems.prompt: Which notes get vibrato in this drill of 16 bars?
A recording sounds shaky on short notes. Fix?
Should vibrato continue through a 4 beat note?
problems.answer: Yes, keep it going to the end.

steps.title: Name the Reader
steps.mastery: Picture one specific reader before you write, so choices about tone and detail get easier.
steps.practice: Before your next piece, write 1 sentence describing the reader, like "a 16 year old who's never cooked."
steps.detail: "Everyone" is no audience. A specific reader answers questions for you: how much to explain, which words to use, how long to go. If your reader is a busy manager, short and direct wins. If it's a beginner, explain terms.
steps.proof: 1 sentence naming the reader, written before drafting.
steps.pitfall: Writing for "anyone," which ends up fitting no one.

problems.prompt: Your reader is "a manager with 2 minutes." Should the piece be long and detailed or short and direct?
Your reader is "a 12 year old new to science." Should you explain the word "molecule"?
Rewrite "people" as a specific reader for a recipe blog.
problems.answer: "A college student cooking dinner for the first time."

steps.title: State the Purpose
steps.mastery: Decide what the reader should know or do after reading.
steps.practice: Write 1 sentence starting "After reading this, the reader will..." for your next 3 pieces.
steps.detail: Purpose shapes everything. Should the reader agree, act, understand or feel something? Naming it keeps the piece on track. Anything that doesn't serve the purpose is a candidate for cutting.
steps.proof: 3 purpose sentences written before drafting.
steps.pitfall: Writing without knowing what the reader should take away.

problems.prompt: Finish this for a cover letter: "After reading this, the reader will..."
A paragraph in your essay is interesting but doesn't serve the purpose. What do you do?
Name 4 possible purposes.
problems.answer: To persuade, to inform, to get action or to entertain.

steps.title: Match Tone to the Reader
steps.mastery: Choose a tone that fits who's reading and why.
steps.practice: Write the same 3 sentence message twice: once to a friend and once to a teacher or boss.
